title: Agent
heading: Integrations
text: Settings Your own API is a settings/v1 section, in the dashboard, the CLI and for agents. Agent Chat Stored conversations on top of agent/v1: $agent.newChat() , $agent.chat(id).send(text) , $agent.chats . Agent binds those methods whenever a provider of agent.chat/v1 runs. Multisite A host whose agent section names a model runs it once for every instance and provides agent/v1 for them; $agent in each instance uses it. Each instance gets a share, set by per_instance (below). Each instance's Settings → LLM offers Off, the host's model or its own API; which model runs built in is the host's call. Today only instances that run as isolates (Pocker) reach the host's model. On a host: agent: model: qwen3-1.7b threads: 6 parallel: 1 # answers written at once; the rest wait their turn per_instance: concurrency: 2 # calls an instance may have waiting or running at once max_tokens: 512 # longest answer per call pinned_mb: 64 # memory an instance's warmed prompts may hold thread_cache_gb: 2.5 # disk for an instance's conversation state, in its own pb_cache

title: Agent
heading: Example
text: A PocketBase app that asks its model one question once the model is ready. // Command example is a PocketBase app with the agent extension that asks its model one question once it's ready. Name // a model in pocketone.yaml ( agent: {model: qwen3-0.6b} ) or choose one in Settings → LLM, run // go run . serve , and watch the log for "agent: answer". package main import ( "context" "log" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "pocketone.dev/ext/agent" agentv1 "pocketone.dev/ext/contracts/agent/v1" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{agent.New()}, nil, nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(e core.ServeEvent) error { go func() { a := agentv1.Contract.Must(app) for { st, _ := a.Status(context.Background(), extkit.Internal) if st.Ready st.Backend == "" { break } app.Logger().Info("agent: waiting", "status", st.Message) time.Sleep(5 time.Second) } res, err := a.Complete(context.Background(), extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{ Prompt: "In one sentence: what is PocketBase?", MaxTokens: 60}) app.Logger().Info("agent: answer", "text", res.Text, "backend", res.Backend, "error", err) }() return e.Next() }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Agent
heading: Prompt caching
text: The built-in model keeps the start of recent prompts: the internal state it computed while reading them (the attention keys and values). When a new prompt starts with exactly the same text, that state is copied in and only the rest is read. Reading the prompt is most of the wait on a CPU, so a repeated preamble or a chat's earlier turns cost almost nothing the second time. The answer is the same as reading the whole prompt again: the cached state is exactly what the model would recompute. agent: prompt_cache_mb: 256 # default; -1 turns it off Memory: each cached token takes about 230 KB for qwen3-0.6b and qwen3-1.7b , and 290 KB for qwen3-4b , so the default 256 MB holds about 1,100 tokens (870 for 4B). The least recently used entries make room for new ones. What it keeps: the start of each prompt, as much as fits. A prompt reuses the entry it shares the longest start with, if that's at least 32 tokens; its last token is always read again. On a multisite host: each instance's prompts only reuse that instance's entries, so timing can't tell an instance what another one sent. The budget is the host's, shared by all of them. Seeing it work: usage.cachedTokens in each answer is how many prompt tokens came from the cache. For your own API it's the provider's own figure, when it reports one (OpenAI's prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens ). Measured on an Apple M1 Max, a second prompt sharing a ~160-token preamble with the first: qwen3-0.6b read it in 56 ms instead of 473 ms, qwen3-1.7b in 0.13 s instead of 2.2 s. The cache matches only an identical start, so order a prompt from what never changes to what changes most: the preamble, then the conversation so far, then the new question with the excerpts picked for it after it. See Prompt caching in the docs.

title: Agent
heading: Warming and threads
text: Two more ways to skip reading the same text, both for the built-in model (your own API ignores them; providers cache prompts themselves): Warm a preamble: $agent.warm({ system: preamble }) reads it now, in the background, and keeps it in the prompt cache until forget() , so the first question after a start doesn't wait for it and other prompts can't push it out. It returns { id, warmed, forget() } at once; await $agent.warm.async(...) resolves once it's warm. The same text always gets the same id. On a multisite host each instance's warms are capped by per_instance.pinned_mb . Threads: thread: chatId on a call keeps the conversation's whole state afterwards, the model's own answer included, and the next call continues from it as far as its messages start the same way. Send the earlier turns exactly as before (excerpts and all) and each turn reads only the new question. States are kept in memory ( thread_memory_mb ) and on disk at half precision in pb_cache/agent/threads ( thread_cache_gb ), least recently used first: a thread survives a restart, and reading it back takes a fraction of a second where re-reading a long chat takes many. $agent.threads.list() and .forget(id) manage them. On a host each instance's threads are in its own pb_cache , within per_instance.thread_cache_gb . A thread is a cache, not storage: your app still sends the conversation. Agent Chat does all of this for you.

title: Agent
heading: The built-in engine
text: The model runs in ext/agent/engine : Go, no cgo, with assembly for the hot loops on arm64 (NEON) and x86 (AVX2), where it matches or beats llama.cpp-based servers on the CPU for short jobs. Other CPUs fall back to plain Go, which is many times slower. It reads GGUF files (Q4_K, Q6_K, Q8_0, F16) and runs the Qwen3 family. Other models work through your own API (Ollama, llama-server). examples/chat is a PocketPages app (no Go) that arms $agent with a preamble and context files read from disk and chats about PocketOne.

title: Agent
heading: License
text: MIT

title: Your own knowledge
text: A model knows a lot in general and nothing about your app. To answer questions about your docs, products or records, give it the relevant text with each question. Two parts do it: A preamble: who the assistant is and how it answers ("answer from the excerpts below; say you don't know rather than guess"). Context: the few passages that match the question, picked from your text each time. Picking matters: a small model on a CPU reads a few hundred words in a second or two, not your whole manual. Search first, then send only what matches.

title: Your own knowledge
heading: From files on disk
text:
Keep the preamble and your docs as Markdown files in pb_pages/_private/ (never served), and read them from page code: // pb_pages/_private/assistant.ts type Doc = { name: string; text: string } type Knowledge = { preamble: string; docs: Doc[] } const dir = (ctx: any): string = ${ctx.pagesDir}/_private const read = (path: string): string = toString($os.readFile(path)) function knowledge(ctx: any): Knowledge { const files = $os.readDir( ${dir(ctx)}/context ).filter((e) = e.name().endsWith(".md")) return { preamble: read( ${dir(ctx)}/preamble.md ), docs: files.map((e) = ({ name: e.name(), text: read( ${dir(ctx)}/context/${e.name()} ) })), } } // a simple search: the documents sharing the most words with the question function search(kb: Knowledge, question: string, n: number): Doc[] { const words = new Set(question.toLowerCase().split(/[^a-z0-9]+/).filter((w) = w.length 2)) return kb.docs .map((d) = ({ d, score: d.text.toLowerCase().split(/[^a-z0-9]+/).filter((w) = words.has(w)).length })) .filter((x) = x.score 0) .sort((a, b) = b.score - a.score) .slice(0, n) .map((x) = x.d) } export function answer(ctx: any, question: string): AgentAnswer { const kb = knowledge(ctx) const excerpts = search(kb, question, 2).map((d) = [${d.name}]
${d.text} ).join("

") // the preamble stays the same on every call, so the model reads it once (prompt caching); the excerpts change with // the question, so they travel with it return $agent.complete({ system: kb.preamble, prompt: ${question}

Excerpts to answer from:

${excerpts} , maxTokens: 300, temperature: 0.3, }) } A page calls it with ctx.resolve("assistant").answer(ctx, question) . Split long documents into sections at their headings so a match brings back one section, not a whole page.

title: Your own knowledge
heading: From records
text: The same works with your data: find the records that match (a filter, or a full-text search you keep in a field), format the useful fields as text, and pass them as the context. Only pass what the person asking is allowed to see.

title: Your own knowledge
heading: A complete example
text: examples/chat is a chat app about PocketOne built this way, as a PocketPages app with no Go: eleven docs pages as context, split into sections and ranked with BM25 (with a few synonyms, since people say "apps" where the docs say "instances"), answers streamed as they're written, and three follow-up questions suggested with a schema.

title: Remembering conversations
text: A model remembers nothing between calls. A chat feels continuous only because the app sends the conversation again with every question. So "memory" is something you build: you decide what to keep, where, and how much of it to send back each time.

title: Remembering conversations
heading: The short way: Agent Chat
text: The Agent Chat extension does everything below for you: it stores the chats, sends the recent turns with a summary of the older ones, keeps the start of each prompt stable for the cache, and gives each chat a thread so the built-in model reads only the new question. // when a user opens a new chat const id: string = $agent.newChat({ meta: { user: ctx.auth.id } }) // each question const chat: AgentChat = $agent.chat(id, { system: preamble, context: (q) = excerptsFor(q) }) if (chat.meta().user !== ctx.auth?.id) throw ctx.httpError(404, "no such chat") const answer: AgentAnswer = chat.send(question) // or chat.send(question, { onText }) to stream it chats := chatv1.Contract.Must(app) // when a user opens a new chat meta, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]string{"user": e.Auth.Id}) // e is the request ( core.RequestEvent) c, err := chats.New(ctx, extkit.Internal, chatv1.NewInput{Meta: meta}) // each question (check the chat's meta is the caller's first, as above) res, err := chats.Send(ctx, extkit.Internal, chatv1.SendInput{ID: c.ID, Text: question, System: preamble, Context: excerptsFor(question)}) // or chats.SendStream to stream it answer := res.Answer.Text $agent.chats.list({ meta: { user } }) lists a user's chats, chat.history() reads one back, and $agent.chats.forget({ meta: { user } }) deletes them all when the user goes. The rest of this page is how to build the same yourself, when you want your own collections or rules.

title: Remembering conversations
heading: Keep chats in your app
text: Store every chat as records, so it survives reloads and belongs to the person who had it. Two collections are enough: chats user (relation to users), title (text), summary (text) user = @request.auth.id messages chat (relation to chats), role (select: user, assistant), content (text) chat.user = @request.auth.id Each question then loads what it needs, asks, and saves both turns: // pb_pages/_private/chat.ts const preamble = (ctx: any): string = toString($os.readFile( ${ctx.pagesDir}/_private/preamble.md )) export function ask(ctx: any, chatId: string, question: string): string { const app = ctx.app const chat = app.findRecordById("chats", chatId) if (chat.getString("user") !== ctx.auth?.id) throw ctx.httpError(404, "no such chat") const recent = app .findRecordsByFilter("messages", "chat = {:chat}", "-created", 6, 0, { chat: chatId }) .reverse() .map((m: core.Record): AgentMessage = ({ role: m.getString("role") as "user" "assistant", content: m.getString("content") })) const summary = chat.getString("summary") const system = preamble(ctx) + (summary ? \n\nEarlier in this conversation: ${summary} : "") // thread: the built-in model keeps this chat's state, so next time it reads only the new question const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.complete({ system, messages: [...recent, { role: "user", content: question }], maxTokens: 350, thread: chatId }) const save = (role: string, content: string) = { const m = new Record(app.findCollectionByNameOrId("messages")) m.set("chat", chatId) m.set("role", role) m.set("content", content) app.save(m) } save("user", question) save("assistant", r.text) return r.text }

title: Remembering conversations
heading: Send the recent turns, summarize the rest
text:
Sending the whole chat every time works for a while, then gets slow (a built-in model reads every word, every call) and finally doesn't fit. The usual answer has two parts: A window: send only the last few turns as messages (six above). A summary of everything before it: when a chat grows past the window, ask the model to fold the turns that drop out into a few sentences, and keep that in the chat's summary : export function summarize(ctx: any, chat: core.Record, dropping: AgentMessage[]) { const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.complete({ system: "Update the summary of this conversation. Keep names, numbers, decisions and open questions. At most 80 words.", prompt: Summary so far: ${chat.getString("summary") "(none)"}

New turns:
 + dropping.map((m) = ${m.role}: ${m.content} ).join("
"), maxTokens: 150, temperature: 0.2, }) chat.set("summary", r.text.trim()) ctx.app.save(chat) } Run it when a chat passes the window, or every few turns, not on every question: it's an extra call. A cron can do it for idle chats, off the request path.

title: Remembering conversations
heading: Remember across chats
text: What someone said last week ("I'm on the Team plan", "we deploy with GitHub Actions") can carry into a new chat the same way you add your docs as context: keep short notes per user in a collection: a fact per record, written when the user states one, or pulled out at the end of a chat with a schema ( { type: "array", items: { type: "string" }, maxItems: 5 } ); with each new question, find the notes that match it (the same kind of search as in Your own knowledge) and add them under the preamble: "What you know about this user: ...". Let people see and delete their notes. Only use a user's notes in that user's chats.

title: Remembering conversations
heading: Keep the start the same
text: The model keeps the start of recent prompts, and with thread a chat's whole state, answers included, and skips re-reading them when the next prompt starts the same way. So send the preamble first, then the earlier turns exactly as you sent them last time, then the new question with its excerpts after it: each turn then reads only what's new. A window that slides by one turn per question changes the start every time. Prefer stretches: send every turn since the last summary, and when that passes your budget ( $agent.count(messages) ), fold the oldest into the summary and start a new stretch. Agent Chat works this way ( window , summarizeEvery ). See Prompt caching for how it works and how to check it. A cache isn't memory, though: you still send the turns every time. The window and the summary above decide how much that is.

title: Writing a preamble
text:
The preamble is the system text you send with every call: who the assistant is, what it may use, and how it answers. It's the biggest lever you have on the answers, and the one people most often get wrong by writing too much. const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.complete({ system: preamble, // the same text on every call messages: [...recentTurns, { role: "user", content: question + "

Documentation excerpts:

" + excerpts }], maxTokens: 350, }) r, err := agent.Complete(ctx, extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{ System: preamble, // the same text on every call Messages: append(recentTurns, agentv1.Message{Role: "user", Content: question + "

Documentation excerpts:

" + excerpts}), MaxTokens: 350, })

title: Writing a preamble
heading: What goes in it
text: Four short parts, in this order: Who it is and for whom. One or two sentences: "You are the help assistant for Acme Notes, a note-taking app. You answer questions from people using the app." What it may use. Say where answers come from: "Answer from the excerpts below." Without that line, a model happily fills gaps from what it thinks it knows. The rules. A short list, each a thing to do: "If the excerpts don't answer the question, say you don't know and suggest where to look." "Give settings and commands exactly as written, in backticks." "Never promise refunds; point people to support@acme.example." The shape of an answer. "Answer in a few sentences or a short list." If you need data rather than prose, use a schema instead of describing the format in words. The material it should use (the excerpts that match the question) goes with the question, not in the preamble: see Keep it the same. You are the help assistant for Acme Notes, a note-taking app. You answer questions from people using it. Answer from the documentation excerpts below. If the excerpts don't answer the question, say you don't know and suggest where in the docs to look. Give settings, menu names and commands exactly as the excerpts write them, in backticks . Never promise refunds or account changes; point people to support@acme.example. Answer in a few sentences or a short list.

title: Writing a preamble
heading: Keep it short
text: A built-in model reads the whole preamble on every call, and a small model follows a few clear rules much better than many. Aim for under 150 words. One rule per line , phrased as what to do, not what to avoid ("answer in English" works better than "don't answer in other languages"). Cut anything the model does anyway. "Be helpful and polite" changes nothing. Don't paste your docs into the preamble. Pick the passages that match each question and add them after it (Your own knowledge). One example beats a paragraph of description. If answers keep coming out in the wrong shape, add a single question and the answer you want, as a user and an assistant turn before the real conversation.

title: Writing a preamble
heading: Keep it the same
text: Write the preamble once, as a file ( pb_pages/_private/preamble.md , read with $os.readFile ), and send it unchanged on every call, first. Then the conversation, then the new question with its excerpts. That order matters for speed. The built-in model, like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, keeps the work it did on the start of a prompt and reuses it when the next prompt starts with exactly the same text, so a long, unchanging preamble is read once, not on every call. Anything that varies at the top (today's date, the user's name, the excerpts) breaks that: put it in the user's turn instead. See Prompt caching.

title: Writing a preamble
heading: Test it
text: Ask it the questions it should refuse or hand off, not only the easy ones: something the excerpts don't cover (it should say it doesn't know, not guess); something against a rule (a refund request); a follow-up that only makes sense with the turn before it. Change one line at a time and ask the same questions again. Turn temperature down (0.2 to 0.3) while you test, so differences come from your change, not chance.

title: Streaming answers
text: A model writes its answer a few words at a time. $agent.stream() hands you each piece as it's written, so a page can show the answer as it appears instead of after a wait: const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.stream({ prompt: question, maxTokens: 300 }, (text) = { // called with each piece, in order; return false to stop the answer there }) // r is the whole answer, as $agent.complete returns it s, err := agent.Stream(ctx, extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{Prompt: question, MaxTokens: 300}) if err != nil { return err } var r agentv1.CompleteResult err = s.Run(ctx, func(e any) error { c := e.(agentv1.Chunk) // a piece of text, in order; the last one is Done, with the whole answer if c.Done { r = c.Result } return nil // an error stops the answer there })

title: Streaming answers
heading: In a page
text:
A PocketPages API route forwards the pieces to the browser as server-sent events: // pb_pages/ask/+api.ts module.exports = { post(ctx) { const { question } = ctx.req.body() const stream = ctx.res.sse() try { const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.stream({ prompt: question, maxTokens: 300 }, (text) = stream.send("text", JSON.stringify(text))) stream.send("done", JSON.stringify({ usage: r.usage })) } catch (err: any) { stream.send("error", JSON.stringify(String(err.message err))) } stream.close() }, } // POST /ask, in your app's Go code (an app's own route; extensions use contracts instead) se.Router.POST("/ask", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { var in struct{ Question string } if err := e.BindBody(&in); err != nil { return e.BadRequestError("send {question}", err) } s, err := agentv1.Contract.Must(e.App).Stream(e.Request.Context(), extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{Prompt: in.Question, MaxTokens: 300}) if err != nil { return err } e.Response.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream") send := func(event string, v any) error { b, _ := json.Marshal(v) _, err := fmt.Fprintf(e.Response, "event: %s
data: %s

", event, b) e.Flush() return err } return s.Run(e.Request.Context(), func(ev any) error { if c := ev.(agentv1.Chunk); c.Done { return send("done", map[string]any{"usage": c.Result.Usage}) } else { return send("text", c.Text) } }) }) In the browser, read the response as it arrives: // in the browser const res = await fetch("/ask", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ question }) }) const reader = res.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader() let buf = "", answer = "" for (;;) { const { value, done } = await reader.read() if (done) break buf += value let i while ((i = buf.indexOf("

")) = 0) { const block = buf.slice(0, i) buf = buf.slice(i + 2) const event = (block.match(/^event: (. )$/m) [])[1] const data = (block.match(/^data: (. )$/m) [])[1] if (event === "text") answer += JSON.parse(data) // show it } } The browser's EventSource only makes GET requests, which is why this reads the stream with fetch .

title: Streaming answers
heading: Over HTTP
text: Outside your app's code, agent/v1's stream operation does the same over HTTP: POST /api/_c/agent/v1/stream with the same body as complete , as a superuser or with a token that has the agent scope. Each piece is an event: stream with {"text": "..."} , and the last one is {"done": true, "result": {...}} .

title: Structured answers
text: Most of what your code wants from a model is data, not prose: a label, a few fields pulled out of an email, a list of tags. Pass a JSON schema as schema , and the answer's parsed value is r.data : const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.complete({ system: "Extract the order from the email.", prompt: email, schema: { type: "object", properties: { name: { type: "string" }, city: { type: "string" }, items: { type: "array", maxItems: 10, items: { type: "object", properties: { what: { type: "string" }, count: { type: "integer" } }, required: ["what", "count"], }, }, }, required: ["name", "city", "items"], }, maxTokens: 200, }) // "Hi, this is Dana. Please send 3 blue mugs and 2 red plates to our Austin office." // r.data: { name: "Dana", city: "Austin", items: [{ what: "blue mugs", count: 3 }, { what: "red plates", count: 2 }] } r, err := agentv1.Contract.Must(app).Complete(ctx, extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{ System: "Extract the order from the email.", Prompt: email, Schema: json.RawMessage( { "type": "object", "properties": { "name": {"type": "string"}, "city": {"type": "string"}, "items": {"type": "array", "maxItems": 10, "items": {"type": "object", "properties": {"what": {"type": "string"}, "count": {"type": "integer"}}, "required": ["what", "count"]}} }, "required": ["name", "city", "items"] } ), MaxTokens: 200, }) var order struct { Name, City string Items []struct { What string Count int } } err = json.Unmarshal(r.Data, &order) // {Dana Austin [{blue mugs 3} {red plates 2}]}

title: Structured answers
heading: How the schema is enforced
text: With a built-in model the schema isn't a suggestion the model might ignore: as it writes, every token that would break the schema is ruled out, so the answer is always JSON of that shape. Even qwen3-0.6b fills in a schema correctly. The engine enforces type , enum , const , properties , required , additionalProperties , items , minItems , maxItems , anyOf and oneOf ; other keywords (formats, patterns, lengths) are allowed but not checked, so check those yourself. With your own API, the schema goes to the provider as response_format . Most enforce it; if one doesn't and the answer isn't JSON, $agent.complete throws bad_answer .

title: Structured answers
heading: Tips
text: An enum is the most reliable way to get one of a few labels. Keep maxTokens a little above what the JSON needs; an answer cut off by maxTokens isn't valid JSON. The schema is also added to the system prompt, so the model knows what each field is for: name fields plainly.

title: When the model is loading
text: The built-in model downloads the first time (hundreds of megabytes to a few gigabytes) and loads on every start (a few seconds). The app serves meanwhile. What a call does until the model is ready depends on how you make it: $agent.complete(opts) Throws not_ready at once, with the progress in the message. A page never hangs on it. await $agent.complete.async(opts) Waits for the model, up to opts.wait (a duration like "2m" ; default agent.timeout ), then answers. $agent.stream(opts, onText, { onWait }) With opts.wait , waits and calls onWait(status) about twice a second, so a page can show "downloading 42%". Without it, throws not_ready . $agent.warm(opts) Returns at once with warmed: false ; the warm runs once the model is ready. $agent.count(text) Answers at once with an estimate ( about four characters a token ) until the model can count exactly. // a page that streams the answer and shows progress while the model downloads const stream = ctx.res.sse() const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.stream({ system, messages, wait: "10m" }, (t) = stream.send("text", t), { onWait: (s) = stream.send("status", s.message), // "downloading qwen3-1.7b (42%)" }) stream.send("done", JSON.stringify({ text: r.text })) // Go has no onWait: poll Status while you wait, or pass Wait and let the call wait for the model r, err := agent.Complete(ctx, extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{System: system, Messages: messages, Wait: "10m"}) if st, _ := agent.Status(ctx, extkit.Internal); !st.Ready { log.Println(st.Message) // "downloading qwen3-1.7b (42%)" } Over HTTP, agent/v1 calls take the same wait field; without it a loading model answers 503 not_ready . A call that's waiting also waits for a warm of the same prompt start that's still running, rather than reading the same text beside it. Warms always let calls go first. $agent.status() says where it is at any time: { backend, model, ready, progress, message } .

title: On a multisite host
text: A multisite host runs one model for every app it serves, instead of each app loading its own. Name it in the host's pocketone.yaml : agent: model: qwen3-1.7b threads: 6 parallel: 1 # answers written at once; the rest wait their turn per_instance: concurrency: 2 # calls an app may have waiting or running at once max_tokens: 512 # longest answer per call pinned_mb: 64 # memory an app's warmed prompts may hold in the prompt cache thread_cache_gb: 2.5 # disk for an app's conversation state, in its own pb_cache Every app on the host then has $agent with no setup. An app that calls more often than its concurrency gets a busy error straight away, so one busy app can't queue up the model for everyone, and no answer runs longer than max_tokens . The host decides which model runs, because it knows the machine: its memory, its cores and how many apps share them. So an app's Settings → LLM offers three choices instead of a model list: Your host's model (the default): the model the host runs; API : the app's own OpenAI-compatible endpoint, for apps that need more than the shared model gives; Off. Each app's prompts, warms and threads are kept separately on the host's model (Prompt caching). Thread state is written to the app's own pb_cache , so it counts against the app's disk; the default (2.5 GB) is a quarter of a 10 GB app. An app's warms are released when it stops. Today apps that run as isolates (Pocker) reach the host's model; apps in containers will follow.

title: AI in your app
text: Your app can ask a language model. $agent.complete() sends a prompt and gives you the answer, from your pages' code; Go code calls the same thing through the agent/v1 contract: const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.complete({ prompt: "Summarize in one sentence: " + record.getString("body"), maxTokens: 60 }) // r.text is the summary r, err := agentv1.Contract.Must(app).Complete(ctx, extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{ Prompt: "Summarize in one sentence: " + record.GetString("body"), MaxTokens: 60}) // r.Text is the summary The examples show each thing in TypeScript, as PocketPages page code ( +api.ts , +page.ts ), and in Go: pick one above any example and the pages remember it. The Go examples call the contract package ( agentv1 , from pocketone.dev/ext/contracts/agent/v1 ) with a context.Context named ctx ; agent stands for agentv1.Contract.Must(app) . Use it for the small jobs that come up around your data: label a support ticket, pull an address out of an email, summarize a long post, write a title or an alt text, answer a question about your docs. It's built into pocketone . The model can be one PocketOne runs itself, on your server's CPU with nothing else to install, or any OpenAI-compatible API (OpenAI, OpenRouter, Groq, or Ollama on your own machine). Your code is the same either way.

title: AI in your app
heading: Try it in two minutes
text: Pick a model. In the dashboard, open Settings → LLM , choose Built-in and qwen3-1.7b , and save. The first time, PocketOne downloads it (1.8 GB) and shows the progress. Or add it to pocketone.yaml : agent: model: qwen3-1.7b Label support tickets as they come in. Make a tickets collection with two text fields, body and label , and a route that saves each new ticket with the label the model picks: // pb_pages/tickets/+api.ts: POST /tickets {"body": "..."} export function post(ctx: any) { const { body } = ctx.req.body() const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.complete({ system: "Label the support ticket.", prompt: body, schema: { type: "object", properties: { label: { enum: ["bug", "billing", "question"] } }, required: ["label"] }, maxTokens: 30, }) const ticket = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("tickets")) ticket.set("body", body) ticket.set("label", r.data.label) ctx.app.save(ticket) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: ticket.id, label: r.data.label }) } // POST /tickets {"body": "..."}, in your app's Go code se.Router.POST("/tickets", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { var in struct{ Body string } if err := e.BindBody(&in); err != nil { return e.BadRequestError("send {body}", err) } r, err := agentv1.Contract.Must(e.App).Complete(e.Request.Context(), extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{ System: "Label the support ticket.", Prompt: in.Body, Schema: json.RawMessage( {"type":"object","properties":{"label":{"enum":["bug","billing","question"]}},"required":["label"]} ), MaxTokens: 30, }) if err != nil { return err } var out struct{ Label string } if err := json.Unmarshal(r.Data, &out); err != nil { return err } col, err := e.App.FindCollectionByNameOrId("tickets") if err != nil { return err } ticket := core.NewRecord(col) ticket.Set("body", in.Body) ticket.Set("label", out.Label) if err := e.App.Save(ticket); err != nil { return err } return e.JSON(201, map[string]string{"id": ticket.Id, "label": out.Label}) }) Send it a ticket: curl -X POST localhost:8090/tickets -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"body": "I was charged twice this month"}' . Its label is billing . The schema makes the model answer with JSON in exactly that shape, and r.data is the parsed value: see Structured answers.

title: AI in your app
heading: What's next
text: Choosing a model: built in or your own API, which model, and how fast each is. Writing a preamble: the system prompt that sets how it answers. Remembering conversations: keep chats, summarize the old turns, recall past chats. Structured answers: JSON you can rely on, even from a small model. Streaming answers: show an answer as it's written. Your own knowledge: answer questions about your docs or data. On a multisite host: one model shared by every app on a server. Prompt caching: how the model skips re-reading what your prompts repeat, and how to order them for it. The API is agent/v1; the extension's reference is its README.

title: Prompt caching
text: Before a model writes a word, it reads your whole prompt: the preamble, the excerpts, the conversation so far. On a CPU, that reading is most of the wait. But most of a prompt is the same as last time: the same preamble on every call, the same earlier turns in a chat. The built-in model remembers the start of recent prompts. When your next prompt starts with exactly the same text, it skips re-reading that part and starts from where the prompts differ. There's nothing to turn on, and the answer is the same as if it had read everything again. How much it helps, on a laptop, for a second prompt that shares a ~160-token preamble with the first: qwen3-0.6b 0.47 s 0.06 s qwen3-1.7b 2.2 s 0.13 s

title: Prompt caching
heading: Order your prompt for it
text:
The cache only matches an identical start. Once one token differs, everything after it is read again. So put what never changes first and what changes most last: The preamble: the same text on every call (Writing a preamble). The conversation so far: the earlier turns exactly as you sent them last time. The new question, then the excerpts you picked for it (Your own knowledge). const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.complete({ system: preamble, // never changes: read once, then reused messages: [ ...earlierTurns, // same as last time: reused { role: "user", content: ${question}

Excerpts to answer from:

${excerpts} }, // new: read ], maxTokens: 350, }) r, err := agentv1.Contract.Must(app).Complete(ctx, extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{ System: preamble, // never changes: read once, then reused Messages: append(earlierTurns, // same as last time: reused agentv1.Message{Role: "user", Content: question + "

Excerpts to answer from:

" + excerpts}), // new: read MaxTokens: 350, }) The excerpts come after the question, in the same turn, because they change with every question. Anywhere earlier, they'd change the start of every prompt after them. Put the question first, too: next time this turn is part of the history and the excerpts are gone, so a prompt that started with the question still matches up to its end. With this order, each turn of a chat reads only what's new since the last one: the previous answer, the new question and its excerpts. What breaks the cache: Anything that changes at the top: today's date, the user's name, a random example, a counter. Put it in the user's turn instead. Rewriting history: trimming or reformatting earlier turns changes the start. A rolling summary (Remembering conversations) changes it each time it's rewritten, so rewrite it every few turns, not on every one.

title: Prompt caching
heading: Check that it's working
text: Every answer reports it in usage : const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.complete({ system: preamble, prompt: question }) // r.usage: { inputTokens: 431, outputTokens: 52, cachedTokens: 139 } r, err := agent.Complete(ctx, extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{System: preamble, Prompt: question}) // r.Usage: {InputTokens: 431, OutputTokens: 52, CachedTokens: 139} cachedTokens is how much of the prompt came from the cache. If it stays at 0 for prompts that should share a preamble, something at the top differs between them: compare two prompts side by side.

title: Prompt caching
heading: Settings
text: pocketone.yaml : agent: prompt_cache_mb: 256 # default; -1 turns it off Each remembered token takes about 230 KB for qwen3-0.6b and qwen3-1.7b (290 KB for qwen3-4b ), so the default holds about 1,100 tokens. That's enough for a preamble and a short chat. The least recently used prompts make room for new ones. On a small server, lower it to save memory; with more memory and long chats, raise it.

title: Prompt caching
heading: Warm the preamble
text: The cache fills as prompts come in, so the first question after a start reads the whole preamble, and a burst of other prompts can push it out. $agent.warm reads it ahead of time and keeps it: // pb_pages/_private/preamble.ts: read once per app, warmed the first time a page asks for it let text: string undefined export function preamble(ctx: any): string { if (text === undefined) { text = toString($os.readFile( ${ctx.pagesDir}/_private/preamble.md )) $agent.warm({ system: text }) // returns at once and warms in the background; never throws } return text } // when the app serves, in the background (Warm returns at once without Wait) app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(e core.ServeEvent) error { agentv1.Contract.Must(app).Warm(context.Background(), extkit.Internal, agentv1.WarmInput{System: preamble}) return e.Next() }) It returns { id, warmed, message, forget() } . warmed is false while it's still reading (or with your own API, which caches by itself; message says why). In async page code, await $agent.warm.async({ system: preamble }) resolves once it's in. The id comes from the text, so warming the same text again finds the same warm and costs nothing; after a model change it's warmed again on the new one. forget() lets it leave the cache like any other prompt. A warmed prompt is pinned: it stays in prompt_cache_mb until forgotten, so warm the one or two preambles you use, not every prompt. On a multisite host each app may pin up to per_instance.pinned_mb .

title: Prompt caching
heading: Threads: a conversation's own state
text: The cache keeps the start of prompts. A chat needs more: the model's answer from last turn is part of the next prompt, and reading it again costs as much as writing it did. thread keeps a conversation's whole state between calls, the answer included: const r: AgentAnswer = $agent.complete({ system: preamble, messages: turnsSoFar, thread: chatId }) r, err := agent.Complete(ctx, extkit.Internal, agentv1.CompleteInput{System: preamble, Messages: turnsSoFar, Thread: chatID}) The next call with the same thread continues from that state as far as its messages start the same way, so it reads only what's new. For that, send the earlier turns exactly as you sent them, question text and excerpts included, followed by the model's answer exactly as it came back. Trimming or rewriting the history costs one full read, then the thread carries on from there: trim rarely and in big steps, not one turn at a time ( $agent.count(messages) tells you when the conversation passes your budget). Thread states live in memory ( thread_memory_mb , default 512) and on disk, at half precision, in pb_cache/agent/threads ( thread_cache_gb , default 2): about 115 KB a token on disk for qwen3-0.6b and qwen3-1.7b . The least recently used go first. Reading one back from disk takes a fraction of a second; reading a 2,000-token chat again takes 15 to 60 seconds on a small CPU. $agent.threads.list() shows what's kept, $agent.threads.forget(id) drops one. Like the rest of pb_cache , they're never backed up and safe to delete. Agent Chat uses the chat's id as its thread and keeps the start stable for you.

title: Prompt caching
heading: On a multisite host
text: The host's model keeps each app's prompts apart: an app only reuses the start of its own prompts, never another app's, so answer timing can't reveal what another app sent. The memory budget is the host's, shared by all of them. Each app's warms are capped by per_instance.pinned_mb , and its threads are kept in its own pb_cache (counting against its disk) within per_instance.thread_cache_gb .

title: Prompt caching
heading: With your own API
text: Big providers cache prompts too, so the same ordering makes your own API faster and cheaper: OpenAI caches by itself for prompts over about a thousand tokens. Anthropic caches up to the points you mark in the request ( cache_control ). Google Gemini caches automatically, and can also hold a named cache with a lifetime for a large shared document. When the provider reports how much it reused (OpenAI does), it shows up as usage.cachedTokens too. A cache isn't memory. It makes text you send again faster to read, but you still send it every time: what goes into the prompt is still yours to decide (Remembering conversations).

title: API Tokens
text: Version 0.2.0 · Owners: @benallfree Walkthrough for app owners: API tokens. This page is the technical reference. Long-lived API tokens for your app: secrets that start with pbt_ , for CI, deploys, scripts and agents. Each token belongs to an account and acts as that account. It can be limited to scopes, given an expiry, and revoked on its own. Send one as Authorization: Bearer pbt_… . Ordinary PocketBase auth tokens keep working unchanged. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: API Tokens
heading: Install
text: Tokens is built into pocketone and always on. There's nothing to install or turn on. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: app := pocketbase.New() tokens.MustRegister(app, apitokens.Config{}) app.Start() To use $apiTokens in pb_hooks , bind it in jsvm's OnInit (the stock binary does): jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { tokens.BindJS(app, rt) }}) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/api-tokens .

title: API Tokens
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or environment variable for Tokens. In pocketone : any account (a superuser, or a record of any auth collection) can own tokens; a token never expires unless you give it an expiry. A Go build can narrow both (see Go config).

title: API Tokens
heading: Scopes
text: A token without scopes has its owner's full rights. A token with scopes works only on the requests its scopes cover, plus remote/v1's whoami ( /api/_c/remote/v1 ); anywhere else it gets 403 . Extensions, contracts and your own pb_hooks register the scopes. In pocketone they are: deploy Deploy Deploy code (hooks, migrations, pages, public files, packages), read files and logs superusers deploy:read Deploy Read deployed files and stream logs superusers , :read each contract the app provides That contract's operations under /api/_c/ / : remote and remote:read , restore and restore:read , settings and settings:read , bulkmail:read , cache , ... per contract Contract scopes are registered when the app serves, so Settings → API tokens on the running app lists every scope. The pocketone token command works offline and doesn't see them: token scopes lists only deploy and deploy:read , and token create --scope restore fails with unknown scope "restore" . Create a token with a contract scope from the dashboard or the REST API.

title: API Tokens
heading: Your own scopes
text: Declare a scope at the top level of a pb_hooks file. It then shows up in Settings → API tokens and on the OAuth server's consent page: // pb_hooks/scopes.pb.js $apiTokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes:read', // lower-case letters, digits, ":" and "_" description: 'Read notes', // shown in the token screen and on the consent page paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'], // URL prefixes where a token holding it works methods: ['GET'], // optional: only these methods (GET covers HEAD) }) $apiTokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes:write', description: 'Change notes', paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'] }) collections: ['users'] limits which accounts may hold the scope. Registering a name again merges its paths, methods and collections, so reloading hooks is safe. Two names whose headers would be the same ( notes:write and notes_write ) can't both be registered. Check a scope on your own route: routerAdd('POST', '/api/notes/archive', (e) = { / ... / }, $apis.requireAuth(), $apiTokens.requireScope('notes:write')) $apiTokens.requireScope refuses a signed-out request, and a token that doesn't hold the scope. Inside a handler, $apiTokens.hasScope(e, 'notes:write') tells you the same. Check a scope in a collection API rule. Every signed-in request carries X-Token-Scope- : 1 for each scope it holds, and rules read it as @request.headers.x_token_scope_ ( : becomes _ ): @request.auth.id = owner && @request.headers.x_token_scope_notes_write = "1" A PocketBase auth token or an unscoped API token holds every registered scope (except ones its collection can't hold). A scoped token holds only its own scopes. A signed-out request holds none. Headers a client sends with that prefix are always dropped, so they can't be forged. $apiTokens.ruleField('notes:write') returns the rule field for a name, and $apiTokens.scopes() lists every registered scope with its header and rule field.

title: API Tokens
heading: Scopes with values
text: A scope can let a token hold it for some values only, such as some record ids. The token's scope list then says name=value , once per value ( notes=abc123 , notes=def456 ). The bare name still means every value. Declare the values when you register the scope: $apiTokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes', description: 'Your notes', paths: ['/api/notes/'], values: { description: 'a note id' }, // shown in the token screen }) Paths and methods don't look at values: a token holding notes=abc123 authenticates on every path notes covers. Your route checks the value: routerAdd('GET', '/api/notes/{id}', (e) = { if (!$apiTokens.hasScope(e, 'notes', e.request.pathValue('id'))) throw new ForbiddenError('Not this note.') // ... }, $apis.requireAuth()) $apiTokens.hasScope(e, name, value) is true for the bare scope, for name=value , and for a PocketBase auth token or an unscoped token. Without a value it's true when the request holds the scope for any value. $apiTokens.scopeValues(e, name) returns { all: true } for every value, or { all: false, values: [...] } . The scope's header carries the values instead of 1 ( X-Token-Scope-Notes: abc123,def456 ), so a rule's = "1" still means every value. A value is 1–200 letters, digits and . _ : @ / + - . A scope registered without values refuses name=value . In Go, Values: &apitokens.ScopeValues{Description: "...", Check: func(owner, value) error} adds a check when a token is created (for example, that the owner owns that record).

title: API Tokens
heading: From the dashboard
text: Open Settings → API tokens (under Access ). Only superusers see this screen. Fill in a Name . Optionally set Expires in (days) , and tick any Scopes (none means full rights). A scope that takes values shows a box when ticked: leave it empty for every value, or list some, comma-separated. By default the token is yours. To make one for another account, fill in Owner collection (default _superusers ) and Owner (id or email) . Click Create token . Copy the token now: it's shown only once and never stored. The list shows each token's name, its first characters, owner, scopes, expiry and when it was last used (time and IP). Tokens issued by the OAuth server carry an oauth: label. Click Revoke and confirm to delete one; anything using it stops working at once. App users who aren't superusers manage their own tokens through the REST API.

title: API Tokens
heading: From the command line
text: The token command works on the local data dir, like superuser , so you can set up tokens before the first serve: pocketone token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci --scope deploy --ttl 720h # prints the secret pocketone token create --collection users --record user@example.com --name script pocketone token list # every token, or one owner's with an owner flag pocketone token revoke [ ...] pocketone token revoke --all --superuser admin@example.com pocketone token scopes Pick the owner with --superuser , or --collection --record . --scope can be repeated, and takes name=value for a scope with values; without --ttl the token never expires.

title: API Tokens
heading: Using a token
text: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_…" https://myapp.example.com/api/collections/notes/records An invalid, revoked or expired token leaves the request signed out, like an invalid PocketBase token. A scoped token used outside its scopes gets 403 ("This API token's scopes (…) don't allow this request."). A token can't be exchanged for a PocketBase auth token ( auth-refresh and impersonate refuse it), so revoking a token really ends its access. Expired tokens are deleted once a day. Deleting an account deletes its tokens.

title: API Tokens
heading: In the logs
text: A rejected token is logged at debug level: tokens: rejected API token . The daily cleanup logs tokens: deleted expired tokens with a count when it deletes any, and tokens: delete expired as a warning if it fails.

title: API Tokens
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: API Tokens
heading: Commands
text: What it adds to the pocketone binary (CLI reference): pocketone oauth clients add Registers a client (prints its id, and its secret once for a confidential client) pocketone oauth clients list Lists registered clients pocketone oauth clients rm Removes a client pocketone token create Creates an API token and prints its secret (shown once) pocketone token list Lists API tokens (all, or one owner's) [ pocketone token revoke [id...] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-token-revoke) Revokes API tokens by id, or all of one owner's (--all) pocketone token scopes Lists the scopes extensions registered

title: API Tokens
heading: api-tokens.verify/v1
text: verify pocketone remote api-tokens verify --token --ip POST /api/_c/api-tokens.verify/v1 api-tokens_verify_verify

title: API Tokens
heading: api-tokens/v1
text: Its HTTP API under /api/_c/api-tokens/v1/ , as the contract describes.

title: API Tokens
heading: oauth/v1
text: Its HTTP API under /api/_c/oauth/v1/ , as the contract describes.

title: API Tokens
heading: Works with
text: OAuth (in Tokens) Its access tokens are API tokens, issued with the client's id, the granted scopes and, when asked for, an audience. They show up under Settings → API tokens and can be revoked there. The OAuth server needs Tokens on the app. MCP An agent's OAuth sign-in to /mcp is an API token bound to /mcp that never expires; revoke it to disconnect the agent. Tool calls run as the token's owner. A full-access token's calls hold every registered scope; a token limited to scopes on the consent page has its calls checked like requests with those scopes ( WithScopes ). Deploy Registers deploy and deploy:read ; a deploy token is what CI uses. Remotes pocketone login takes a pasted API token when the remote has no OAuth server. In CI, put a token in P1_TOKEN (or P1_TOKEN_ ). remote/v1's whoami ( /api/_c/remote/v1 ) reports a token's id and scopes, whatever its scopes. Multisite It's a standard member, so every instance gets its own tokens, routes and screen; reconfigure it on the host's set with set.APITokens = apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{...}) . With Pocker, per instance, extensions: {api-tokens: {enabled: false}} turns it off and collections: [...] picks who may own tokens.

title: API Tokens
heading: Building on Tokens
text: Register a scope from Go. Extensions register their scopes on the app, usually on bootstrap, and guard their routes: tk := tokens.For(app) tk.MustRegisterScope(tokens.Scope{ Name: "notes:write", Description: "Change notes", Paths: []string{"/api/collections/notes/records"}, Methods: []string{"POST", "PATCH", "DELETE"}, // optional Collections: []string{"users"}, // optional: who may hold it }) se.Router.POST("/api/notes/archive", h).Bind(apis.RequireAuth(), tokens.RequireScope("notes:write")) Guards. A Go scope can add Match func( core.RequestEvent) bool : a token with the scope also works on any request it returns true for. It runs before the owner is loaded, so it may look only at the request. Shared scopes. Registering a name again merges its paths, methods, guards and collections, so several extensions can share one scope. Scope values. Values: &tokens.ScopeValues{Description, Check} lets a token hold a scope for some values only ( notes=abc123 ). Check(owner, value) runs when a token is created; an error refuses it. Routes check the value with tokens.HasScopeFor(e, "notes", id) , or list them with tokens.ValuesFor(e, "notes") ( all is true for every value). Through the contract: grant.HasScopeFor , grant.ScopeValues , and apitokensv1.SplitScope / JoinScope for the name=value form. Read the token on a request. tokens.FromRequest(e) returns the token a request used (nil for a PocketBase auth token), with its Owner , Scopes and Audience . tokens.HasScope(e, "x") is true for PocketBase auth tokens and unscoped API tokens. Without importing this package. Other extensions use the api-tokens/v1 contract instead: tokensv1.Contract.Of(app) registers scopes ( RegisterScope ), lists them and checks Reaches ; tokensv1.FromRequest(e) is the request's token (its Grant : owner, scopes, audience, client id); tokensv1.WithScopes limits in-process requests. Deploy and MCP work this way. The X-Token-Scope- headers work for rules and JS. Audience. A token created with CreateOptions.Audience (the OAuth server sets it from the RFC 8707 resource parameter) only works under that URL's path, plus remote/v1's whoami ( /api/_c/remote/v1 ); elsewhere it gets 403 . When the audience has a path (like https://host/mcp ), the token works there whatever its scopes: the scopes limit what that endpoint does on the token's behalf (MCP passes them on with WithScopes ), not the endpoint itself. Limit in-process requests. tokens.WithScopes(ctx, scopes) returns a context whose requests are checked like a token limited to scopes , whatever credential they carry: 403 where the scopes don't reach, and only those scopes in the X-Token-Scope- headers and HasScope . Requests made inside them with the same context inherit the limit, and a nested WithScopes only narrows it. No client value can set it. tokens.ScopesFromContext(ctx) reads it. Reaches(scopes, method, pattern) says whether scopes could cover a route pattern ( {name} segments match anything), and Scope.Infrastructure() whether a scope only reaches contract APIs ( /api/_c/ ). Go API. tokens.For(app) returns the service: Create(owner, CreateOptions{Name, Scopes, Expires, ClientId, Audience}) returns the secret and record; also Verify(secret) , List(owner) , Get(id) , Revoke(id) , RevokeAll(owner) , DeleteExpired() , RegisterScope , MustRegisterScope , Scopes() , Collections() and AllowedCollection(c) . tokens.BindJS(vm, app) adds $apiTokens ; the extkit extension ( tokens.New ) also binds it. JS. $apiTokens.registerScope({name, description, paths, methods, collections}) , $apiTokens.requireScope(name) , $apiTokens.hasScope(e, name) , $apiTokens.ruleField(name) and $apiTokens.scopes() .

title: API Tokens
heading: REST API (api-tokens/v1)
text: The api-tokens/v1 contract, at /api/_c/api-tokens/v1 . Any signed-in account; superusers see and manage everyone's. GET /api/_c/api-tokens/v1 Your tokens. Superusers see all, or one owner's with ?ownerCollection=&owner= . POST /api/_c/api-tokens/v1 {name, scopes, ttl \ expires} ( ttl in seconds, expires RFC 3339); superusers may add ownerCollection and owner . Returns the secret once. A scoped token can only create tokens within its own scopes. DELETE /api/_c/api-tokens/v1/{id} Revoke one. POST /api/_c/api-tokens/v1/revoke-all Revoke all of yours (superusers: {ownerCollection, owner} ). GET /api/_c/api-tokens/v1/scopes The registered scopes, who may own tokens, and whether you can. Owners can also list, view and delete their own tokens through the records API of _api_tokens_tokens .

title: API Tokens
heading: Checking a token from another server (api-tokens.verify/v1)
text: A server that a client hands one of this app's tokens to (a host in front of the app's accounts) asks the app what the token allows with the api-tokens.verify/v1 contract: POST /api/_c/api-tokens.verify/v1 with {"token": "pbt_...", "ip": " "} , as a superuser (scope api_tokens_verify ). The answer is {"valid": true, "grant": {...}} with the owner and the scopes (values included), or {"valid": false, "reason": "invalid" "expired"} . In Go, verifyv1.NewClient(appURL, superuserToken, nil) .

title: API Tokens
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app with API tokens: Settings → API tokens, the token API ( /api/_c/api-tokens/v1 ) and the token command. // Command example runs one PocketOne app with API tokens: Settings → API tokens in the dashboard, the token API (/api/_c/api-tokens/v1) // and the token command. // // go run ./example serve // go run ./example token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci // curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_..." http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "net/http" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/apis" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "pocketone.dev/ext/api-tokens" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" tk := apitokens.MustRegister(app, apitokens.Config{ Collections: []string{"_superusers", "users"}, // who may own tokens }) // an extension's scope: a token limited to "hello" only authenticates under /api/hello; a JWT or unscoped token // holds it too, and every request that holds it carries X-Token-Scope-Hello: 1 for rules and hooks tk.MustRegisterScope(apitokens.Scope{Name: "hello", Description: "Say hello", Paths: []string{"/api/hello"}, Methods: []string{"GET"}}) app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { se.Router.GET("/api/hello", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { return e.JSON(http.StatusOK, map[string]any{"hello": e.Auth.Email()}) }).Bind(apis.RequireAuth(), apitokens.RequireScope("hello")) return se.Next() }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: API Tokens
heading: Go config
text: tokens.MustRegister(app, apitokens.Config{ Collections: []string{"_superusers", "users"}, // who may own tokens (default: every auth collection) MaxTTL: 0, // cap on a token's lifetime (0: none) }) With MaxTTL set, a token asked for with no expiry or a later one gets the cap instead. If you narrow Collections , The OAuth server can only sign in accounts of those collections.

title: API Tokens
heading: Bringing tokens from another system
text: To keep tokens another system issued working (their owners already hold the secrets), register their prefix and store each one with Import , which keeps only its hash, as Create does: tk.RegisterPrefix("ph_pat_") // pbt_ is always registered rec, err := tk.Import(owner, "ph_pat_…", apitokens.CreateOptions{Name: "ci", Scopes: []string{"deploy"}}) Every registered prefix is checked the same way: a secret starts with one and has at least 32 characters after it. Import takes a pbt_ secret too (a token moving from another app). The one difference: tokens the app creates always start with pbt_ . A prefix is lower-case letters, digits and _ , ends with _ , and can't overlap one already registered. The old system's hash is usually of something else, so import a secret when it's next used (check it the old way, then Import it), not ahead of time.

title: API Tokens
heading: How it works
text: Tokens live in the _api_tokens_tokens collection: owner (collection id and record id), name, hash (SHA-256 of the secret; the secret itself is never stored), display prefix, scopes, expiry, last use (time and IP), OAuth client id and audience. The bearer check is a middleware that runs just before PocketBase's own auth middleware; a second one, right after it, sets the scope headers. Last use is written at most once a minute per token. example/main.go runs one app where superusers and users may own tokens, with a hello scope for GET /api/hello . Try it with go run ./example serve and go run ./example token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci (logins from devusers: admin@example.com / password, user@example.com / password).

title: API Tokens
heading: License
text: MIT

title: OAuth
text: Tokens includes an OAuth 2.1 authorization server whose access tokens are API tokens: the oauth/v1 contract. pocketone login signs in to it in the browser (or with a code on another device), and MCP clients such as Claude or ChatGPT connectors register themselves and connect. Superusers and app users sign in on your app's own pages, through PocketBase's own auth endpoints.

title: OAuth
heading: Install
text: It comes with Tokens, which is in every app's standard set. There's nothing to install or turn on. Its endpoints are under /api/_c/oauth/v1/ (see Endpoints); its metadata is at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server . In your own Go build, configure it through Tokens: set := standard.New() set.APITokens = apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{ Branding: tokens.Branding{Accent: "#4f46e5"}, }}) apitokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{Disabled: true}} leaves it out.

title: OAuth
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or environment variable for OAuth Server. In pocketone : superusers and every auth collection may sign in; access tokens last 30 days, refresh tokens 180 days (renewed on each refresh); tokens for MCP never expire, since MCP turns that on for /mcp ; client self-registration ( POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register ) is on, since MCP turns it on; Claude and Claude Code connect without registering (their client metadata documents from claude.ai and claude.com are trusted). A Go build can change these (see Go config).

title: OAuth
heading: Sign-in methods
text: The pages offer exactly the methods each auth collection has on, so you set them where you always do: the collection's options in the dashboard ( Collections → the collection → Options ). Password , One-time password (an emailed code) and OAuth2 providers each get their own form or button. Multi-factor authentication adds a second step. The collection's auth rule (for example verified = true ) applies. OAuth2 providers (Google, GitHub, …) are offered to app users only; PocketBase doesn't allow them for superusers. Register /api/_c/oauth/v1/provider/callback as a redirect URI with each provider. The pages show Settings → Application → Application name .

title: OAuth
heading: Behind a proxy
text: The server names itself (the issuer) after the scheme and host the browser used, with https when the request is TLS or X-Forwarded-Proto says so. If a proxy rewrites the host, set Config.Issuer in a Go build so the issuer and the provider callback URL stay stable.

title: OAuth
heading: Scopes
text: A client may ask for any scope registered with Tokens, including your own from $apiTokens.registerScope . offline_access is accepted (refresh tokens are always issued). The consent page lets the user decide: Full access (no scopes: the account's full rights) or Only these , with a box for each scope. The scopes the client asked for start ticked; the others the account may hold are there to tick, except ones that only reach contract APIs under /api/_c/ (like deploy ), which appear only when asked for. With no scopes asked, Full access starts selected. The token gets exactly what was ticked, and the token response's scope says which.

title: OAuth
heading: Your own sign-in pages
text: The built-in pages (sign-in, second step, one-time code, consent, device code, done, error) follow the system's light or dark mode and work on phones. They're the oauth set of Templates; to change them, eject it: pocketone template eject oauth # asks before overwriting files you changed; --force doesn't ask It copies the built-in Go templates to pb_templates/oauth/ : signin.tpl , mfa.tpl , otp.tpl , consent.tpl , device.tpl , done.tpl , error.tpl , and the shared head.tpl (with the CSS), foot.tpl and hidden.tpl . From then on the server renders your copy of each file, read on every request; delete a file to go back to the built-in one. To restyle every page, edit only head.tpl . See Custom page templates for the data they get.

title: OAuth
heading: Signing in
text: Whenever a client sends someone to your app ( pocketone login , Claude, an app of yours), they see: Sign in to : the form for app users ( users first; with several user collections, a tab for each). At the bottom, Sign in as a superuser switches to the superuser form, which looks clearly different: a Superuser badge, Superuser sign-in , its own colors and a warning. Sign in as a user instead goes back. One more step when the account has MFA, offering its other methods. After a password, when an emailed code is the only method left, it's sent right away. Check your email for an emailed code. The consent page: the client's name, the account, whether the client will act as a user (and which collection) or as a superuser, and the access: Full access or Only these scopes (see Scopes). Click Allow or Deny , or Not ? Use another account . With no user collection allowed, the superuser form is the only one. A browser stays signed in to these pages for 15 minutes. Failed attempts are limited to 10 per IP in 5 minutes. On another device (over SSH, say), the client shows a code like WDJB-MJHT . Open https:// /api/_c/oauth/v1/device/verify , enter it under Connect a device , sign in and allow. Codes last 10 minutes.

title: OAuth
heading: Log in from the command line
text: pocketone login prod With OAuth Server on the remote, Remotes opens your browser on the pages above, or shows a device code when there's no browser ( --device asks for one). The CLI's commands (deploy, remote control) need a superuser, so it asks for one ( account=_superusers , below): you land on the superuser form, even if this browser is signed in there as an app user. The client is the built-in pocketone-cli , named pocketone CLI on the consent page (the name follows the command, so another build shows its own).

title: OAuth
heading: See and revoke what's connected
text: Every sign-in creates an API token named " (OAuth)". They're listed under Settings → API tokens with an oauth: label; click Revoke to disconnect a client. Revoking the access token also ends its refresh token. A client can revoke its own tokens at POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/revoke , which pocketone logout does.

title: OAuth
heading: Register clients
text: Claude and the CLI need no registration, and MCP clients register themselves. For your own app: pocketone oauth clients add --name "My app" --redirect https://myapp.example.com/callback pocketone oauth clients add --name "Desktop" --redirect http://127.0.0.1/callback --public pocketone oauth clients list pocketone oauth clients rm add prints the client id, and the secret once for a confidential client. --public makes a client with no secret (PKCE only), for desktop and mobile apps. --redirect can be repeated. Redirect URIs must be https , http on a loopback address, or an app's custom scheme. Loopback URIs match any port (RFC 8252); others must match exactly.

title: OAuth
heading: In the logs
text: tokens: oauth: this collection may sign in but can't own API tokens; add it to apitokens.Config.Collections , once per collection, when Tokens is narrowed in a Go build. The page then says signing in with that account type "isn't set up on this server yet". tokens: oauth: auth methods (error) when a collection's sign-in methods can't be read. tokens: oauth: cleanup (warning) when the half-hourly removal of expired codes fails.

title: OAuth
heading: Works with
text: Tokens It's part of Tokens. Access tokens are API tokens owned by whoever signed in, with the client's id, the granted scopes and the audience. Every registered scope can be requested. Remotes remote/v1's whoami lists oauth/v1 (and the oauth feature, its metadata); pocketone login then signs in in the browser (loopback redirect with PKCE) or with a device code, and renews through the refresh token. MCP MCP points clients here from its protected resource metadata, turns on self-registration, and makes tokens bound to /mcp never expire. Tool calls run as whoever signed in. Deploy pocketone login gives the deploy commands a token for the account that signed in. Templates The pages are its oauth set: pocketone template eject oauth copies them to pb_templates/oauth/ to edit. Without Templates, the built-in pages. On a multisite host every instance that runs PocketOne has it, through the standard set.

title: OAuth
heading: Account type
text: An account parameter on /api/_c/oauth/v1/authorize or /api/_c/oauth/v1/device names the auth collection the client needs a token from ( _superusers , or a user collection). The sign-in page then shows only that form, with no links to the others. A browser signed in as another account type isn't taken to consent: it gets that form, with a line saying who's signed in and what the client needs. No other account type is issued a token. An account type that can't sign in here is an invalid_request error (sent back to the client, or the device request's 400). Without account , the user chooses, as before.

title: OAuth
heading: Audience (RFC 8707)
text: A resource parameter on /api/_c/oauth/v1/authorize , /api/_c/oauth/v1/device or /api/_c/oauth/v1/token (a URL on this server) binds the access token to it: the token then only works under that URL's path. So a token issued for /mcp can't deploy, and a deploy token can't drive MCP. Refreshed tokens keep it.

title: OAuth
heading: Building on the OAuth server
text: Go API. tokens.OAuth(app) returns the server. Issuer(e) is its public base URL; EnableDynamicRegistration() turns on POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register ; SetAccessTTL("/mcp", 0) sets the lifetime of tokens bound to a resource (0: never expire). FindClient , ListClients , AddClient and RemoveClient manage clients. Scopes. Register a scope with Tokens (Go or $apiTokens.registerScope ) and clients can ask for it; nothing else is needed. Render the pages yourself. Config.Render(e, page, data) renders any page (return handled=false to fall back), with PageData . It wins over ejected templates.

title: OAuth
heading: Example
text: The OAuth server is on wherever Tokens is (its example runs it). To brand it and let MCP connectors register themselves: set := standard.New() set.APITokens = apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{ DynamicRegistration: true, // MCP connectors register themselves (ext/mcp turns this on anyway) Branding: tokens.Branding{Accent: "#4f46e5", Footer: "Example OAuth server"}, }}) app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{})

title: OAuth
heading: Endpoints
text: GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server Metadata (RFC 8414). The issuer is Config.Issuer , else the request's own scheme and host. GET/POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/authorize Sign-in and consent pages. Authorization code with PKCE (S256 only; required). Optional account (see Account type) and resource . POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/token authorization_code , refresh_token and urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code . Refresh rotates without logouts: the old access token lives out its time, and the old refresh token works again for 2 minutes, so two processes refreshing at once both succeed. POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/device , GET/POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/device/verify Device flow (RFC 8628): codes like WDJB-MJHT , valid 10 minutes. POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/revoke Revocation (RFC 7009): an access token or a refresh token (revokes both). GET/POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/provider/callback Where OAuth2 providers send the browser back after sign-in. POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), when DynamicRegistration is on or an extension called EnableDynamicRegistration() (MCP does). Public clients by default. Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) belongs to the resource: MCP serves /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource .

title: OAuth
heading: Clients
text: pocketone-cli is built in: public, any http://127.0.0.1: /… or [::1] redirect, device codes. It's what pocketone login uses. Client ID metadata documents (CIMD): an https:// client id is fetched as a JSON document ( client_id must equal the URL; its client_name and redirect_uris are used; public clients only; cached 10 minutes). Only Config.CIMDHosts are trusted (default claude.ai , claude.com ); the metadata says client_id_metadata_document_supported . Registered clients live in _api_tokens_oauth_clients ; codes, device codes and refresh tokens in _api_tokens_oauth_codes .

title: OAuth
heading: How sign-in works
text: The pages never check passwords or codes themselves. Each step calls PocketBase's own auth endpoint in-process, through the app's router, so the collection's auth rule, MFA, rate limits, superuser IP limits and every onRecordAuth Request hook apply as for the REST API, and the record the endpoint returns is the one signed in: password: POST /api/collections/{c}/auth-with-password ; emailed code: POST …/request-otp , then POST …/auth-with-otp ; OAuth2: the browser goes to the provider with the state and PKCE from GET …/auth-methods , comes back to /api/_c/oauth/v1/provider/callback , and POST …/auth-with-oauth2 completes it (account linking and sign-up are PocketBase's); MFA: when an auth call answers 401 with an mfaId , the second page passes it along. Only collections with a sign-in method on are offered. Access tokens are owned by the signed-in record, so every collection that may sign in must also be allowed by Tokens (its default is every auth collection). The session is a 15-minute HttpOnly cookie on /api/_c/oauth/v1 ; forms carry a CSRF token; a provider round trip keeps its state in a signed 10-minute cookie.

title: OAuth
heading: Go config
text: apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{ Collections: nil, // who may sign in; default: _superusers + every auth collection AccessTTL: 30 24 time.Hour, // default; per resource with srv.SetAccessTTL("/mcp", 0) RefreshTTL: 180 24 time.Hour, // default, renewed on each refresh DynamicRegistration: false, // POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register (MCP turns it on) CIMDHosts: nil, // default claude.ai, claude.com; an empty non-nil slice turns CIMD off Issuer: "", // public base URL; default: the request's scheme and host Branding: tokens.Branding{LogoURL: "/logo.svg", Accent: "#4f46e5", Footer: "Acme Inc."}, }}) Branding also takes a Name (default: Settings → Application name). Accent is the button color (default #16161a ).

title: OAuth
heading: Custom page templates
text: The templates are Go html/template files, and their dot is PageData ( {{.AppName}} , {{.Action}} , {{.Hidden}} , {{.CSRF}} , {{.ClientName}} , {{.Scopes}} , {{.ScopeChoices}} , {{.Superuser}} , {{.Providers}} , {{.Error}} , …; see PageData in oauth_pages.go). Each page includes the others by name ( {{template "head" .}} ). Every POST form must include {{template "hidden" .}} and a step button. Steps: password , request_otp , otp , oauth2: , use: (switch forms; use: is the default user form), allow , deny , switch . Sign-in forms post collection ; the MFA and code pages also post mfa_id / otp_id . Consent posts access = full , or limited with a grant field per ticked scope (from data.scopeChoices : name , description , checked ). A consent form without access grants what the client asked for.
