text: MIT

title: Auto TLS
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Automatic HTTPS certificates through ACME, with CertMagic (Caddy's certificate engine). PocketBase already gets Let's Encrypt certificates for serve example.com . Auto TLS takes over that job and adds other certificate authorities, extra domains and wildcard certificates. Status: stable on a multisite host, beta on a single app. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Auto TLS
heading: Install
text: Auto TLS is built into pocketone and off by default . Turn it on with --autotls (or auto: true in pocketone.yaml ). It only does something when the app serves HTTPS, that is with serve or --https ; on plain HTTP it stays idle, and without it PocketBase's own certificates are used as before. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: import ( "pocketone.dev/ext/autotls" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" ) app := pocketbase.New() extkit.MustRegister(app, autotls.NewApp(autotls.Config{Auto: true, Email: "ops@example.com"})) app.Start()

title: Auto TLS
heading: Command-line flags
text: pocketone serve example.com --autotls --autotlsEmail ops@example.com pocketone serve example.com --autotls --autotlsDomains " .example.com" --autotlsDNS cloudflare # token in $CF_API_TOKEN --autotls false Turn it on. --autotlsEmail ACME account email, for expiry notices from the CA. --autotlsCA letsencrypt letsencrypt , letsencrypt-staging , zerossl , or an ACME directory URL. --autotlsDomains Extra domains, obtained at start (comma separated). Wildcards need --autotlsDNS . --autotlsDNS DNS provider for DNS-01 challenges. Only cloudflare is supported. --autotlsDNSTokenEnv CF_API_TOKEN Environment variable holding the DNS provider's API token.

title: Auto TLS
heading: pocketone.yaml
text: The autotls section sets the defaults for those flags. Flags win over the file. autotls: auto: true email: ops@example.com ca: letsencrypt domains: [" .example.com"] # wildcards need dns dns: provider: cloudflare api_token: $CF_API_TOKEN # read from the .env beside pocketone.yaml storage is only in the file: where certificates are kept (default pb_data/.autotls ). The DNS token can be given as api_token (write $VAR to read it from the .env beside the file) or through api_token_env , the name of an environment variable. api_token is only used when --autotlsDNS names the same provider as the file. The Cloudflare token needs permission to edit the zone's DNS. There are no dashboard settings.

title: Auto TLS
heading: autotls:
text: Automatic HTTPS certificates (ACME): auto, email, CA, domains, DNS-01, certificate storage. The --autotls flags win. auto bool Get certificates through ACME (CertMagic). Flag: --autotls. email string ACME account email, for expiry notices from the CA. Flag: --autotlsEmail. ca string letsencrypt (default), letsencrypt-staging, zerossl, or an ACME directory URL. Flag: --autotlsCA. storage string Where certificates are kept. Default pb_data/.autotls. domains list of string Extra domains to get at start; wildcards ( .example.com) need dns. Flag: --autotlsDomains. dns.provider string DNS provider for DNS-01 challenges (needed for wildcards): cloudflare. Flag: --autotlsDNS. dns.api_token string The provider's API token. Write $VAR to read it from the .env beside the file. dns.api_token_env string Or: the environment variable holding the token. Default CF_API_TOKEN. Flag: --autotlsDNSTokenEnv.

title: Auto TLS
heading: Use
text: Once on, there's nothing to click. Start the app as usual with serve (or --https ): Which hostnames get a certificate. The domains given to serve and their www. variants, issued on the first request for each, plus --autotlsDomains , obtained at start. Any other hostname is refused at the TLS handshake, so a random Host can't trigger issuance. How they're proved. TLS-ALPN-01 on the HTTPS port, or DNS-01 when a DNS provider is set (needed for wildcards). HTTP-01 isn't used on a single app, because port 80 is PocketBase's redirect server. Renewal is automatic. Where they're stored. pb_data/.autotls by default, separate from PocketBase's own .autocert_cache . Settings are checked at start, before anything touches the network. A wildcard domain without a DNS provider, a Cloudflare provider without a token, or an unknown provider stops the app with an error such as: tls.domains: wildcard " .example.com" needs a DNS provider (tls.dns); per-hostname certificates work without one With debug logging, the start shows autotls: CertMagic serves HTTPS certificates with the CA and extra domains. Use --autotlsCA letsencrypt-staging while testing, so failed attempts don't count against Let's Encrypt's rate limits.

title: Auto TLS
heading: Multisite hosts
text: On a multisite host (any runtime: pocker or docker), the stock pocketone binary runs autotls.New() , a host extension that gets certificates for every instance the host serves. It's configured by the same autotls section: autotls: auto: true email: ops@example.com storage: ./pb_root/.pocker-certs # default: .pocker-certs in the runtime's instance root domains: [" .example.com", "example.com"] dns: { provider: cloudflare, api_token_env: CF_API_TOKEN } # only needed for wildcards Without dns , every hostname the instance source maps gets its own certificate on its first TLS handshake, with any DNS host and no API token. Hostnames no instance serves never trigger issuance. Challenges include HTTP-01 on the host's port 80, as well as TLS-ALPN-01 and DNS-01. Certificate files ( server.tls.cert / key ) stay a core host feature. Setting both files and auto is an error. Certificates belong to the host, not to instances; the single-app extension ( NewApp ) is a separate type so it never runs per instance.

title: Auto TLS
heading: Building on Auto TLS
text: autotls.New() is a host extension ( multisite.Extension ) that provides the tls/v1 contract when auto is on. A host adds it to its host extensions (a pocker.Server built by hand takes it in Extensions too): h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Extensions: []multisite.Extension{autotls.New()}}) AutoTLS.Config can be set in Go before the server starts; the autotls section is read only when Auto is false there. autotls.SupportedDNSProviders lists the dns.provider values it understands.

title: Auto TLS
heading: Example
text: Auto TLS is built into pocketone : examples/pocketone/main.go registers it with the other default extensions.

title: Auto TLS
heading: How it works
text: Go module pocketone.dev/ext/autotls . On a single app, an OnServe hook swaps the TLS config of PocketBase's HTTPS server for CertMagic's. PocketBase's own host policy (the serve domains and www. ) decides which on-demand hostnames are allowed. The certificate manager stops when the app terminates. TLS 1.2 is the minimum; h2 and http/1.1 are offered, and acme-tls/1 stays on for TLS-ALPN challenges. A wildcard in domains covers one level ( .example.com covers a.example.com , not a.b.example.com ).

title: Backups
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Walkthrough for app owners: Point-in-time restore. This page is the technical reference. Restore an app to a moment from its own backups. Ask for "Tuesday 15:00" and the app restores the latest backup made at or before it, wherever its backups are kept (pb_data/backups or S3). Every app gets this; with PITR on, PITR answers instead and restores any second in its window. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Backups
heading: Install
text: Backups is built into pocketone and on by default ; there's nothing to install. In your own Go build: extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{backups.New()}, nil, nil) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/backups .

title: Backups
heading: Configure
text: There's nothing to configure: it reads the backups PocketBase already makes (Settings → Backups, including the automatic schedule and S3). An app turns it off with extensions: { backups: { enabled: false } } .

title: Backups
heading: Use
text: It's the default provider of the restore/v1 contract: # what can be restored (superuser token) curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" https://app.example.com/api/_c/restore/v1 # restore the latest backup at or before a moment curl -X POST -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"at":"2026-11-10T15:00:00Z"}' https://app.example.com/api/_c/restore/v1/restore The answer names the backup it restores. The app restarts to apply it, as a restore from Settings → Backups does. In the dashboard, Settings → Backups has a "Restore to a moment" section (restore/v1's own screen) that shows which backup a moment uses. Agents get the same through MCP ( restore_points , restore_restore_to ).

title: Backups
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Backups
heading: restore/v1
text: points pocketone remote restore points GET /api/_c/restore/v1 restore_points restore_to pocketone remote restore to --at POST /api/_c/restore/v1/restore restore_restore_to

title: Backups
heading: Integrations
text: PITR Also provides restore/v1, at any second rather than at backup times; when it's on for an app, Backups steps aside. S3 Fallback Backups kept on the host's storage are listed and restored the same way. Contracts restore/v1 is the contract; any extension or host can provide it instead.

title: Backups
heading: Example

title: Bulk Mail
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Walkthrough for app owners: Bulk mail. This page is the technical reference. Campaigns to your app's own users, from the dashboard. You pick who gets the mail with a collection, a view or SQL, write the message, and Bulk Mail sends it at a steady pace through your app's mail settings. It adds one-click unsubscribe, keeps a list of addresses that must never be mailed again, and handles bounces and spam complaints. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Install
text: Bulk Mail is built into pocketone and on for every app. Nothing is sent until a superuser starts a campaign. In your own Go build, register the extension before the app starts. Bind it into the JS runtime too if you want $bulkmail in pb_hooks : mail := bulkmail.New(bulkmail.Config{Rate: 5, Daily: 5000}) app := pocketbase.New() extkit.MustRegister(app, mail) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, mail) }}) app.Start() The module is pocketone.dev/ext/bulkmail .

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section or command-line flag. The limits are fixed in the binary; pocketone uses the defaults: Per second 5 The most messages this app sends per second. A campaign can only lower it. Per day 5,000 The most messages this app sends per UTC day, across all campaigns. In a custom build, set them with bulkmail.Config{Rate, Daily} . Daily: bulkmail.NoBulkMail forbids sending; the screens then say so.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Settings → Mail
text: Campaigns send through the app's own mail settings and from its sender, both set on Settings → Mail . Below that form there's a Bulk mail section: Postal address : shown in every campaign footer. Anti-spam laws require one. Unsubscribe mailbox : optional. Adds a mailto: alternative to the List-Unsubscribe header. Bounces and complaints (click to open): Amazon SES (SNS) endpoint : the URL to subscribe to the SNS topic your SES identity sends bounce and complaint notifications to. Allowed SNS topic ARNs : comma separated. Empty accepts any topic with a valid AWS signature. Generic webhook and Webhook secret : for other providers. The webhook is off until you set a secret. The section also shows this app's limits and how many messages it sent today. Click Save bulk mail settings . Unsubscribe links and the feedback URLs are built from Settings → Application → Application URL , so set it to the address people reach your app on. The settings are stored in the app's database (a _params row), so they go along with its backups. Secrets are never shown again after saving.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Use
text: The dashboard gets a Mail link in its menu, with two pages: Campaigns and Suppressions . Only superusers see them.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Write a campaign
text: Open Mail and click New campaign . It starts as a draft for verified users of users . Fill in Name , Subject and Body . Under Audience , choose who gets it: Filter : a Collection (or a view), an optional Filter in the same syntax as API rules, and the Email field that holds the address (an email or text field, or a view's computed column). SQL : a read-only SELECT that returns an email column. Every other column is available to the message. Click Count recipients to see how many match, how many are suppressed, and a few sample addresses. Optional: Vars (JSON) for values used in the message, a Schedule (UTC) , and Max per second to send slower than the app's limit. Click Save changes . Preview shows the message for one recipient; Send test mails it to the Test address . A view is the easy way to build a dynamic audience: it picks who gets mail and computes the columns the message uses. The example creates one called newsletter_audience .

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Placeholders
text: In the subject and body: {{record.field}} : a field or column of the recipient's row, for example {{record.name}} . {{email}} , {{campaign.name}} and {{unsubscribe_url}} . Campaign vars: {"promo": "X"} gives {{promo}} . A var can be computed once when sending starts: {"count": {"sql": "SELECT COUNT( ) AS value FROM users"}} . {{if record.field}}…{{else}}…{{end}} blocks, and {{if !record.field}} for the opposite. Values are HTML-escaped in the body. An unsubscribe footer with your postal address is always added.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Send
text: Click Send (or Schedule when a time is set) and confirm. The campaign page shows its status and progress (sent, queued, skipped, failed), and a Recipients table you can filter by status. While it runs you can Pause , Resume or Cancel it. Every address is queued once per campaign. Sending a finished campaign again mails only new matches. A message counts as sent only once the mail server accepts it, so a restart doesn't send twice or skip anyone. A permanent error (SMTP 5xx) fails that recipient. Other errors are retried, up to three attempts. A campaign pauses itself when more than 5% of its sends fail after the first 100, or when spam complaints pass 0.3% of its sends (at least 3). The reason shows next to its status.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Suppressions
text: Mail → Suppressions lists the addresses that never receive campaign mail, whatever the audience says. Unsubscribes, permanent bounces and complaints are added automatically. Click Add address to add one by hand, a row to edit or delete it, or Export CSV to download the list.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Unsubscribing
text: Every message has a signed unsubscribe link and the List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post: One-Click headers that Gmail and Yahoo require for bulk senders. Opening the link shows a confirm button, so link scanners can't unsubscribe anyone. The one-click request from a mail provider unsubscribes directly.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Try it locally
text: In dev mode with SMTP off, pocketone catches every mail, bulk mail included, in an inbox at http://127.0.0.1:8025: pocketone serve --dev

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Bulk Mail is a standard member, so every PocketOne app has it, standalone or an instance on a multisite host (reconfigure it with set.BulkMail = bulkmail.New(...) on the host's standard set). On Pocker each instance can override its limits (below). $bulkmail only reaches the instance's own data, so it's safe for untrusted tenants. Mailtrap In dev mode with SMTP off, campaign mail lands in the local inbox instead of being sent.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Per-instance settings (Pocker)
text: On Pocker, each instance's extensions.bulkmail settings apply over the Config given to bulkmail.New : instances: id: abc extensions: { bulkmail: { rate: 2, daily: 1000 } } id: free-plan-app extensions: { bulkmail: { daily: 0 } } # may not send bulk mail id: other extensions: { bulkmail: { enabled: false } } # no Bulk Mail at all

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Go API
text: bulkmail.For(app) returns the app's service: Start , StartLimit , Pause , Resume , Cancel , Preview , Test , CountAudience , Suppress , Unsuppress , IsSuppressed , Unsubscribe , UnsubscribeURL , Limits , and the hooks: OnSend fires before every campaign message (not test sends). Change the message, or return an error to fail that recipient. OnUnsubscribe fires when someone unsubscribes through a link or the one-click header. OnFeedback fires for each bounce or complaint a provider reports. Config.Mailer swaps the mail client, for example for a platform relay. Config.PublicURL sets the base of unsubscribe links instead of the Application URL.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: JS API
text: $bulkmail in pb_hooks : $bulkmail.start(id, [limit]) // limit: queue only the next N new recipients $bulkmail.pause(id); $bulkmail.resume(id); $bulkmail.cancel(id) $bulkmail.test(id, [to]); $bulkmail.preview(id, [email]) $bulkmail.count({collection, filter, email_field} {sql}) // {count, suppressed, sample} $bulkmail.suppress(email, [reason]); $bulkmail.unsuppress(email); $bulkmail.isSuppressed(email) $bulkmail.unsubscribe(email, [campaignId]); $bulkmail.unsubscribeURL(email, [campaignId]) $bulkmail.limits() // {rate, daily, sentToday} React to activity with record hooks on the collections below, for example onRecordAfterCreateSuccess((e) = { … }, "_bulkmail_suppressions") .

title: Bulk Mail
heading: API: contracts
text: Bulk Mail has no routes of its own. Its API is three contracts it provides, plus a section in settings/v1 ( ?extension=bulkmail : sender details, limits and the feedback endpoint URLs; secrets are never returned): bulkmail/v1 Count an audience; start, pause, resume, cancel, preview and test a campaign (superusers). mail.suppression/v1 The suppression list (check, suppress, unsuppress) and the unsubscribe link in every message (public, signed). Bulk Mail keeps it by default; when another extension provides it, Bulk Mail asks that one before queueing and before each send. mail.feedback/v1 Bounce and complaint reports from SES (SNS) or a webhook (public; X-Feedback-Secret ). Any extension can act on them. Campaigns and suppressions are created and edited through the regular records API. A campaign's from_name and from_address override the app's sender, but only through the records API, JS or Go (the dashboard doesn't show them), since the app's mail account can usually send only as identities it has verified.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app with bulk mail: the Mail page, campaigns to the app's own users and $bulkmail in JS hooks. Run it with go run ./example serve --dev from this folder; the dev mail trap at http://127.0.0.1:8025 catches every mail. // Command example runs one PocketOne app with bulk mail: a "Mail" page in the dashboard, campaigns to the app's // own users, and $bulkmail in JS hooks. // // Run it in dev mode: while SMTP is off, PocketOne's dev mail trap catches every mail (bulk mail included) and // shows it at http://127.0.0.1:8025, with nothing else to install: // // go run ./example serve --dev // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/bulkmail" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit/js" "pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" registerDemoView(app) // a "newsletter_audience" view to use as a campaign audience (demo.go) // the same extension value a multisite host gives every instance (set.BulkMail = mail on its standard set) mail := bulkmail.New(bulkmail.Config{ Rate: 5, // messages per second Daily: 5000, // messages per day; bulkmail.NoBulkMail forbids sending }) extkit.MustRegister(app, mail) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, mail) }, // $bulkmail in JS hooks }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Bulk Mail
heading: How it works
text: Go module pocketone.dev/ext/bulkmail , an extkit extension. example/main.go runs one app with Bulk Mail ( go run ./example serve --dev ). The audience is resolved when sending starts and queued into a ledger first (one row per campaign and address, unique). A background sender then mails one message at a time through the app's mail client, at the lower of the app's rate and the campaign's. SQL audiences and SQL vars run with SQLite's query_only on, inside a transaction that is always rolled back. Unsubscribe links are signed with HMAC and a per-app secret, generated on first use. SES feedback: SNS signatures are verified, and signing certificates are fetched only from sns. .amazonaws.com . Permanent bounces and complaints go on the suppression list.

title: Bulk Mail
heading: Data
text: _bulkmail_campaigns Content, audience, vars, status, counters, schedule. _bulkmail_sends The ledger: campaign, email, status ( queued , sent , skipped , failed ), reason, attempts. _bulkmail_suppressions Addresses that never receive campaign mail, with the reason. All are superuser-only system collections with fixed collection and field ids ( schema.go ). LegacyJSMigration() emits a PocketBase JS migration that creates the same collections, for apps that move onto this schema before they run this extension.

title: Bundle
text: Version 0.1.0 · Owners: @benallfree Ship an app's files inside the binary instead of folders on disk: its JS hooks ( pb_hooks ), migrations ( pb_migrations ) and public files ( pb_public ). Nothing is written to disk and nothing on disk can override them. PocketHost's mothership uses it for its own hooks. Formerly jsembed . Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Bundle
heading: Install
text: Bundle is not in the pocketone binary. Add it to your own Go build: embed the folders, pass the hooks and migrations to jsvm as extensions, and serve the public files. //go:embed hooks migrations public var files embed.FS hooks, _ := fs.Sub(files, "hooks") migrations, _ := fs.Sub(files, "migrations") public, _ := fs.Sub(files, "public") jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ Extensions: []any{bundle.Hooks(hooks), bundle.Migrations(migrations)}, }) bundle.Public(app, public, true) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/bundle .

title: Bundle
heading: Configure
text: Nothing to configure. List only what you bundle: without bundle.Hooks , hooks still come from HooksDir on disk, and the same for migrations.

title: Bundle
heading: Use
text: Hooks: .pb.js files come from the FS's root only. HooksDir is ignored, nothing is written to it, and hooks aren't watched. Migrations: files come from the FS's root only; MigrationsDir is ignored. require() : __hooks is the virtual root /pb_embedded/pb_hooks . Paths under it, and relative paths, load from the hooks FS. Everything else is "module not found": absolute disk paths, .. escapes, node_modules . JS that reads files itself ( $os.readFile(__hooks + ...) ) gets "no such file", since the root doesn't exist on disk. Public files: bundle.Public(app, fsys, indexFallback) serves the FS at GET /{path...} like pb_public , unless the app has its own route there. With indexFallback , unknown paths serve index.html (single-page apps).

title: Bundle
heading: Integrations
text: JSVM Hooks and Migrations are jsvm extensions ( HookFiles , Modules , MigrationFiles ).

title: Bundle
heading: Example
text: // Command example serves its JS hooks and public files from files embedded in the binary: no pb_hooks or pb_public // folder on disk. // // go run ./example serve // curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hello // curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/ package main import ( "embed" "io/fs" "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/bundle" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm" ) //go:embed hooks public var files embed.FS func main() { hooks, err := fs.Sub(files, "hooks") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } public, err := fs.Sub(files, "public") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{Extensions: []any{bundle.Hooks(hooks)}}) bundle.Public(app, public, true) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Bundle
heading: How it works
text: Hooks implements jsvm's HookFiles and Modules : the engine asks it for the hook files and for every module require() resolves, and it serves only paths under the virtual root, from the FS. Migrations implements MigrationFiles . Public binds the static route with apis.Static at the lowest priority, as PocketBase does for pb_public .

title: Bundle
heading: License
text: MIT

title: Cache
text: Version 0.1.0 · Owners: @benallfree Extensions and apps often compute the same thing many times: a rendered page, an answer from another API, a compiled module. Cache gives them named buckets to keep those results in, as bytes or as the Go values themselves, from one store in your app's process, with an optional folder on disk for more than fits in memory. Each bucket has its own budget, and you can change it without touching the code that uses it. On a multisite host the store is shared by every instance: one memory ceiling and one disk tier for all of them. Each instance still sees only its own buckets. On disk, identical bytes (the same compiled template, the same .wasm file) are one file however many instances or keys hold them. Cache provides cache/v1 and cache.clear/v1. Code that caches talks only to those contracts, so a cache shared between servers (Redis, Memcached) can replace this one later without any of it changing. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Cache
heading: Install
text: Cache is built into pocketone and on by default; there's nothing to install. Turn it off with cache: {enabled: false} in pocketone.yaml . In your own Go build it comes with the standard set, or on its own: extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{cache.New(cache.Config{})}, nil, nil)

title: Cache
heading: Configure
text: Nothing to configure: each bucket gets 32MiB of memory (and 256MiB of disk, when there's a disk tier), the store 128MiB for every bucket together. To change them, add a cache section to pocketone.yaml . The top keys are the store's; defaults fill in what a bucket's code leaves unset; buckets set a named bucket's limits over what its code asks for: cache: max_memory: 512MiB # the store: every bucket together disk: true # a disk tier in pb_cache/cache; leave out for memory only max_disk: 10GiB defaults: max_memory: 16MiB ttl: 10m buckets: pages.compiled: max_memory: 64MiB # one app's bucket max_disk: 1GiB The store, ceilings over every bucket together: max_memory Memory for every bucket together (default 128MiB) eviction Which values leave memory (or disk) first when the store reaches a ceiling: lru (default), mru , fifo , lifo disk Turns on the disk tier in pb_cache/cache , next to pb_data ; on a multisite host, in the host's own pb_cache (the store serves every instance) disk_path Puts the disk tier in a cache folder there instead, and turns it on. Relative paths are to the app's folder (the one holding pb_data ) when the app has the process to itself, and to the working directory when several apps share it (Pocker) max_disk Size of the disk tier (default 1GiB) Each bucket ( defaults and buckets. ), its own budget: max_items Most entries the bucket holds, in memory or on disk max_memory Most bytes of keys and values the bucket holds in memory (default 32MiB) max_disk Most bytes of disk files the bucket's keys point at, each counted in full even when shared (default 256MiB) eviction Which of its entries go first when the bucket is full ttl How long an entry lives unless its code says otherwise Sizes take KiB , MiB , GiB (or KB , MB , GB ); durations take s , m , h . The disk tier is pb_cache : never backed up or deployed, and emptied when the process starts. pocketone cache clear cache empties it by hand.

title: Cache
heading: cache:
text: The cache (cache/v1): one store for every app in the process (memory, disk tier), and caps per bucket. enabled bool Turns the cache off when false; extensions then run uncached. eviction string Which values leave memory (or disk) first when the store reaches its ceiling: lru, mru, fifo or lifo. max_memory int Memory for every bucket together, such as 512MiB. Default 128MiB. disk bool Turns on a disk tier in pb_cache/cache, next to pb_data (on a multisite host, the host's own pb_cache). disk_path string Puts the disk tier in a cache folder there instead of pb_cache, and turns it on. Relative: to the app's folder (the one holding pb_data) when the app has the process to itself, the working directory when several apps share it (Pocker). max_disk int Size of the disk tier for every bucket together, such as 10GiB. Default 1GiB. defaults.eviction string Which of the bucket's entries go first when it's full: lru, mru, fifo or lifo. defaults.max_items int Most entries the bucket holds. defaults.max_memory int Most bytes of keys and values the bucket holds in memory, such as 32MiB (the default). defaults.max_disk int Most bytes of disk files the bucket's keys point at, each counted in full, such as 256MiB (the default). defaults.ttl int How long an entry lives unless the code says otherwise, such as 10m. buckets map of object Caps per bucket name, over what its code asks for.

title: Cache
heading: Use
text: Nothing to click. A bucket that's full moves its values to the disk tier when there is one, and a read brings them back. The cache, disk tier included, starts empty with the process. On a multisite host, an instance that restarts or sleeps keeps its entries: the store belongs to the host. To empty an app's cache, as a superuser: pocketone remote cache clear (every bucket) or pocketone remote cache clear --bucket pages.compiled (one), through cache.clear/v1.

title: Cache
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Cache
heading: cache.clear/v1
text: clear pocketone remote cache clear --bucket POST /api/_c/cache.clear/v1 cache_clear_clear

title: Cache
heading: Integrations
text: Multisite Every instance that runs PocketOne has Cache (a standard member). With Pocker, every instance shares the host's one store (its memory, its disk tier), and sees only its own buckets: keys live under the instance's id. An instance that sleeps keeps its entries, so it wakes to a warm cache. An instance's extensions.cache may set enabled , defaults and buckets for itself; the store's keys are the host's only. Docker Each container runs its own pocketone , so it has its own store.

title: Cache
heading: Building on Cache
text: Open a bucket through cache/v1 at serve time, keep it, and get and set keys: b, err := cachev1.Open(app, "myext.answers", cachev1.Options{MaxItems: 1000, TTL: 10 time.Minute}) Declare cache/v1 in WorksWith : when nothing provides it, Open returns a bucket that keeps nothing, so your code runs uncached. Name buckets after your extension so they never collide. To cache Go values rather than bytes, make them cachev1.Item s and open the bucket with cachev1.OpenItems (Go values). Each key keeps its own value in memory, never shared with another key. A value that is also a cachev1.Marshaler is marshaled only when it goes to disk, and comes back decoded as long as its CacheVersion matches the reader's; one that isn't stays in memory only. Cache provides cache/v1 and cache.clear/v1 as defaults: another extension that provides them (a Redis cache, say) replaces it without any providers: line. On a multisite host, the host empties the whole store (every instance's buckets) with the extension's Clear .

title: Cache
heading: Example
text: A PocketBase app with one bucket, example.slow . GET /slow takes a second the first time and answers from the cache for the next minute. // Command example is a PocketBase app with cache/v1 and one bucket, "example.slow". GET /slow takes a second the first // time and answers from the cache for the next minute: // // go run ./example serve --http=127.0.0.1:8090 // curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/slow # slow // curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/slow # cached // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "net/http" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "pocketone.dev/ext/cache" cachev1 "pocketone.dev/ext/contracts/cache/v1" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{cache.New(cache.Config{})}, nil, nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { b, err := cachev1.Open(app, "example.slow", cachev1.Options{MaxItems: 100, TTL: time.Minute}) if err != nil { return err } se.Router.GET("/slow", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { ctx := e.Request.Context() if v, ok, _ := b.Get(ctx, "answer"); ok { return e.String(http.StatusOK, "cached: "+string(v)+"\n") } time.Sleep(time.Second) // the expensive part v := time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339) _ = b.Set(ctx, "answer", []byte(v), 0) return e.String(http.StatusOK, "computed: "+v+"\n") }) return se.Next() }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Cache
heading: How it works
text: One store per process. Each app's buckets are namespaces in it, / (just / when the app has the process to itself), so no app can read another's keys. Memory and disk follow different rules. In memory every key holds its own value, bytes or a Go value, and nothing is shared between keys. On disk values are files named by the SHA-256 of their bytes (an item's MarshalCache bytes): the same bytes under any number of keys, from any number of instances, are one file with a reference count, removed when the last key pointing at it goes. A key points at its file with the value's version beside it: (bucket, key, version) - SHA. Each bucket has its own budget: entries, memory (its keys and the values it holds there) and disk (the files its keys point at, each in full). When a bucket is over its memory, its values move to disk (by its own strategy); over its entries or its disk, its keys go. A busy bucket never evicts another bucket's values. The store's ceilings (memory, disk) hold over every bucket together, so the total stays bounded however many instances there are; reaching one evicts across buckets by the store's strategy. Memory is the hot tier and the disk tier the cold one: a value reaches disk only when memory evicts it (an item is marshaled then, never before), goes back to memory and leaves disk when it's read, and the folder is emptied when the process starts. Nothing on disk outlives the process, so nothing on disk can be stale after a restart or a crash. One lock guards the in-memory index, and it's never held across disk IO, marshaling or decoding. One IO goroutine, running only while it has work, marshals, writes and removes files in the order the lock decided them. A write waits in a slot of its key's, at most one per key, and writes whatever the key holds when its turn comes, so a key evicted again and again before the disk catches up is marshaled and written once, with its latest value. A value waiting to be written stays readable from memory (at most a quarter of max_memory waits; past that, evicted values are dropped). A file is read once however many readers want it, and a key's bytes are decoded once however many readers want its item; both are checked against the index again before they're used, so a key changed meanwhile never gets its old value back. The store is tested against a model under fuzzing (bytes and items: no value deleted, replaced, expired or belonging to another key ever comes back; no value is shared between keys in memory; every count and list stays consistent; the disk tier holds exactly the files it should) and under concurrent load with the race detector.

title: Config
text: Version 0.1.0 · Owners: @benallfree PocketOne's config file: pocketone.yaml , with secrets in a .env beside it. Put your app's settings in one file instead of a long line of flags. Each extension has its own section in the file. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Config
heading: Install
text: Config is built into pocketone and always on. Without a pocketone.yaml , nothing changes: every setting keeps its default and the flags work as usual. In your own Go build, load the file before the app is created, so its values can be the flags' defaults: cfg, err := config.Load(config.FromArgs(os.Args[1:])) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } a, err := standard.AppFromConfig(cfg) // the whole app section, ext/standard if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } app := standard.New().NewApp(a.PocketBase, a.JS) app.RootCmd.AddCommand(config.NewCommand(func() config.Options { return config.FromArgs(os.Args[1:]) })) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/config . examples/pocketone/main.go shows the full wiring: every app key as a flag default, and the server keys as the serve command's defaults.

title: Config
heading: Where the files are
text: pocketone.yaml is looked for in the working directory, then next to the executable. --config picks another file. The .env is looked for beside the config file (or in the working directory when there is no config file). --env-file picks another one. Relative paths in the file are relative to the file's folder, so it works from any working directory.

title: Config
heading: What goes in it
text: Each top-level key is one section, owned by the extension that uses it. This package owns three: app : your app, as every command that opens it reads it ( serve , migrate , superuser , pitr , token , oauth , template ): dir , dev , encryption_env , query_timeout , jsvm , hooks_dir , hooks_pool , migrations_dir , the defaults of those commands' flags of the same name, plus env_allow . server : what serve reads. http , https and origins are the defaults for serve --http , --https and --origins ; for a single app, public_dir , index_fallback , pages_dir , hooks_watch and automigrate are the defaults for --publicDir , --indexFallback , --pagesDir , --hooksWatch and --automigrate . multisite : add it only to run many instances from one binary (see Integrations); it runs pocker, or docker when there's a docker section. server: http: 127.0.0.1:8090 origins: [" "] public_dir: ./pb_public app: dir: ./pb_data hooks_dir: ./pb_hooks env_allow: [STRIPE_KEY] js_limits: # the JS engine's limits for the app memory: 128MiB task_time: 10s pitr: retention: 168h Other extensions' sections (such as pitr above) are described on their own pages. pocketone config lists every section your binary knows.

title: Config
heading: Flags win
text: A flag on the command line always wins over the file. The file only changes the defaults.

title: Config
heading: Secrets in the .env
text: Write $VAR or ${VAR} in any value, and keep the secret in the .env : autotls: dns: api_token: $CF_API_TOKEN # .env CF_API_TOKEN=abc123 A name is looked up in the .env first, then in the process environment. $$ is a literal $ . A name that is set nowhere stops the app at startup, with the missing names listed. The .env takes KEY=VALUE lines. Blank lines, # comments and an export prefix are fine. Quote a value to keep its spaces; double quotes also understand \n , \t , \" and \\ . The .env is used only for these references. It is never put in the process environment, so your JS hooks ( $os.getenv ) don't see it, unless you list a name in app.env_allow .

title: Config
heading: app:
text: The single app, for every command that opens it: data dir, dev mode, encryption, JS engine, hooks, migrations, and the .env names it may read (env_allow). Not used on a multisite host. dir string The data folder (pb_data). Default: pb_data next to the executable. The --dir flag wins. dev bool Dev mode: logs and SQL statements printed to the console. The --dev flag wins. encryption_env string Name of the environment variable holding a 32-character key that encrypts the app settings. The --encryptionEnv flag wins. query_timeout duration Default timeout for SELECT queries, such as 30s. The --queryTimeout flag wins. hooks_dir string The JS hooks folder. Default: pb_hooks next to pb_data. The --hooksDir flag wins. jsvm string The JS engine for pb_hooks and pb_migrations: quickjs (PocketOne's, the default) or goja (PocketBase's own, for pure PocketBase compatibility: pages, $mcp, $apiTokens and JS contracts are off). The --jsvm flag wins. hooks_pool int Only with jsvm: goja: how many JS runtimes are kept ready for hooks. Default 15. The --hooksPool flag wins. migrations_dir string The migrations folder. Default: pb_migrations next to pb_data. The --migrationsDir flag wins. env_allow list of string Names from the .env the app and its JS hooks may read. Default none. js_limits.memory int The app's JS memory: the JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds, such as 128MiB. Default 64MiB. js_limits.task_time duration JS time one task (a request, a hook, a cron job) may use, Go calls and waits not counted, such as 10s. Default 5s. js_limits.task_wall duration Wall time one task may take, Go calls included, such as 60s. Default 30s.

title: Config
heading: server:
text: The serve command: http, https and CORS origins, and for a single app its static files, pages, hooks watching and automigrate. http string Plain HTTP address, such as 127.0.0.1:8090. Single app: the --http default (the flag wins). Many instances: redirects to https when https is set. https string HTTPS address. Single app: the --https default (the flag wins). Many instances: the main address. origins list of string Allowed CORS origins. Single app: the --origins default (the flag wins). plain list of string Many instances only: extra plain HTTP addresses with no redirect. tls.cert string Many instances only: the certificate file, reloaded when it changes. tls.key string Many instances only: the private key file, reloaded when it changes. shutdown_timeout duration Many instances only: how long in-flight requests get to finish at stop. public_dir string Single app only: the static files folder. Default: pb_public next to the executable. The --publicDir flag wins. index_fallback bool Single app only: serve index.html for a missing static path, for single-page apps. On unless false. The --indexFallback flag wins. pages_dir string Single app only: the PocketPages folder, served when it exists. Default: pb_pages next to pb_data. The --pagesDir flag wins. hooks_watch bool Single app only: restart the app when a pb_hooks file changes. On unless false. The --hooksWatch flag wins. automigrate bool Single app only: write a migration file when you change collections in the dashboard. On unless false. The --automigrate flag wins.

title: Config
heading: See every section
text: pocketone config It prints each section with its description and defaults, as YAML you can copy into your file. For the same list as JSON (each section's name, description, owning extension, and each key with its type and default): pocketone config --json

title: Config
heading: Check your file
text: pocketone config check It reads the file and the .env and reports problems, or a line like: /srv/app/pocketone.yaml: ok (3 sections), secrets from /srv/app/.env With no file it says no config file: defaults only .

title: Config
heading: What stops startup
text: The app won't start, and says why, when the file has: a top-level key no extension in the binary owns (usually a typo); the error lists the sections it knows; the same section twice; a value that doesn't fit its key (for example text where a number goes); a $VAR that is set in neither the .env nor the environment. An empty section ( pitr: with nothing after it) is allowed and means all defaults.

title: Config
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Config
heading: Commands
text: What it adds to the pocketone binary (CLI reference): pocketone config Lists the pocketone.yaml sections this binary understands, with their defaults pocketone config check Checks the config file: every section known and valid, every $VAR set

title: Config
heading: Works with
text: Every extension with a section Each extension declares its own section; its values become that extension's defaults or flag defaults. PITR, S3 Redirect and Auto TLS are examples. Multisite Add a multisite section and pocketone serve runs many instances instead of one app, on one runtime: Docker with a docker section, else Pocker. The app section and env_allow don't apply then; each instance has its own folder under its runtime's root.

title: Config
heading: The server section with many instances
text: On a multisite host, server has a few more keys: https is the main address, http then redirects plain HTTP to it ( http alone serves plain HTTP), plain lists extra plain-HTTP addresses with no redirect, tls names a certificate and key file (reloaded when they change), and shutdown_timeout limits how long in-flight requests get at stop. multisite: {} server: https: ":443" http: ":80" plain: [":8080"] tls: { cert: /etc/certs/cert.pem, key: /etc/certs/key.pem }

title: Config
heading: Give your extension a section
text: Declare it in your own package with a typed key and defaults: type Config struct { Limit int yaml:"limit" doc:"Requests per minute. The --limit flag wins." } var Section = extkit.NewSection("firewall", Config{Limit: 60}, "Request limits for the app.") cfg, found := firewall.Section.Get() // the defaults with the file's values applied cfg, err := firewall.Section.Require() // fails when the file doesn't have the section An extension reads a section only through its owner's key, so it can read only sections from packages it imports. There is no lookup by name and no access to the raw file. The doc:"…" tag on each field describes the key in pocketone config --json and in the key table on pocketone.dev. config.Load checks every section when the app starts, so a bad value fails early.

title: Config
heading: Example
text: Config is built into pocketone : examples/pocketone/main.go loads pocketone.yaml with it before the app starts and adds the config command.

title: Config
heading: Go API
text: config.FromArgs(args) reads --config and --env-file before the full flag parse. config.Load(opts) finds, reads and checks the files, and makes them the source for every section. config.Read(opts) does the same without checking or installing them. ( Config).ResolvePath(p) makes a relative path from the file absolute, relative to the file's folder. ( Config).AllowEnv(names) copies those .env values into the process environment (what app.env_allow does). config.Describe() returns every section with its keys, types, defaults and docs (the data behind --json ). config.NewCommand(opts) is the config command.

title: Deploy
text: Version 0.1.0 · Owners: @benallfree Walkthrough for app owners: Deploy and live sync. This page is the technical reference. Send your project's code to a running app from your own machine: pb_hooks , pb_migrations , pb_pages , pb_public , packages and the production node_modules tree. Only changed files are uploaded and the app swaps them in; restart applies new migrations and packages. pocketone dev keeps your folder and the app in step both ways and streams the app's logs; pull and logs work the other way. clone starts a local project from a running app. pocketone link https://myapp.example.com # add the remote and sign in (Remotes) pocketone deploy # upload what changed pocketone logs Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Deploy
heading: Install
text: Deploy is built into pocketone and on in both directions: every app it serves accepts deploys from its superusers, and the deploy , dev , pull , logs and restart commands are there to deploy to other apps. There's nothing to install. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts. Remotes gives the commands their remotes and logins, and Tokens lets you deploy with API tokens: app := pocketbase.New() extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{ apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{}), // optional: API tokens with the deploy scope remotes.New(remotes.Config{}), // remote/v1 (whoami, restart, logs), login deploy.NewExtension(deploy.Config{}), // deploy/v1 + deploy/dev/pull/logs/restart commands }, nil, nil) app.Start() The standard set does this for you. The module is pocketone.dev/ext/deploy . deploy.Config{DisableServer: true} keeps only the commands, for a binary that deploys elsewhere but must not accept deploys.

title: Deploy
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or settings screen. Defaults on the receiving app: Who may deploy: superusers. You sign in with pocketone login (see Remotes) or use an API token. A token needs the deploy scope (or no scopes); deploy:read allows reading files and logs only. Where files land: next to pb_data , PocketBase's usual layout ( pb_hooks/ , pb_migrations/ , pb_public/ , node_modules/ beside it). Upload store: uploaded files and the last deploys' file lists are kept in pb_cache/deploy/ next to pb_data . It's only a cache: it's never backed up, deployed or reachable through the file API, and deleting it is safe (files already in the app's folder count as uploaded, so deploys still send only what changed). On your machine, the commands use the project's remotes and saved logins from Remotes. In CI, set P1_TOKEN (or P1_TOKEN_ ) instead of signing in.

title: Deploy
heading: Use
text: All commands take an optional remote name or URL; without one they use the project's default remote. Run them from your project folder (or any folder below it).

title: Deploy
heading: deploy
text: pocketone deploy # to the default remote pocketone deploy prod # to the remote "prod" pocketone deploy --restart # and restart if migrations or packages changed (CI) pocketone deploy --dry-run # list what would be sent, send nothing pocketone deploy --out /tmp/set # write the files to a folder instead You'll see how many files are deployed and how many are uploaded, then a line like Deployed: 3 changed, 0 deleted, 41 unchanged. With nothing changed it says Up to date: no changes. --restart Restart the app after the files are in, when migrations or packages changed. --dry-run List what would be deployed; deploy nothing. --force Deploy even when files changed on the remote since your last deploy, pull or dev, overwriting them. --out Write the deploy set to a local folder instead of deploying. -i , --include Add include patterns to the default set. -e , --exclude Exclude patterns ( pb_data is always excluded). --node-modules Ship the production node_modules tree (the default when there's a package.json ). --no-node-modules Don't ship node_modules ; leave the remote's alone. -v , --verbose List every file. What's sent: files matching pb_ and pb_ / / except pb_data , plus package.json , bun.lock(b) and patches/ . Dotfiles are included ( pb_public/.well-known ); .git files and symlinks are skipped. Packages: with a package.json , the production node_modules tree is collected the way Node resolves it (hoisted npm and bun, pnpm's store, workspace links; never devDependencies) and shipped as plain files, so plain JS hooks can require npm packages. The remote then owns its root node_modules : packages you no longer ship are removed there. Restarts: files are swapped in while the app runs, each rename atomic, and deploy never restarts the app on its own. pb_pages and pb_public are read from disk on each request, and hooks reload by themselves (PocketBase's --hooksWatch , or the runtime's watcher on a multisite host). Migrations and packages apply only when the app starts, so a deploy that changes them says Migrations or packages changed and leaves the restart to you: pass --restart (the app restarts once, after the whole batch is in, and you hear if it fails to start), run pocketone restart , or type r in dev . So does the first deploy that creates pb_hooks , since a watcher only sees folders that existed when the app started. Changes made on the remote: deploy , pull and dev record each file's hash as of the last time the project and the remote agreed on it, in .pocketone/sync.json . Before it sends anything, deploy compares the remote's files with that record. If a file changed there since (an edit made on the server, a migration the dashboard wrote, someone else's deploy) and the deploy would overwrite or delete it, it lists those files and deploys nothing: bring them down with pull or dev , or pass --force to overwrite them. A change the local copy already has doesn't count. A project with no record of the remote (a fresh checkout, CI) deploys without the check.

title: Deploy
heading: restart
text: pocketone restart prod Restarts the app so it applies new migrations and packages, and tells you if it fails to start. An app that isn't running (a sleeping instance on a multisite host) is left alone; it applies them when it starts.

title: Deploy
heading: dev
text: pocketone dev pocketone dev prod --prefer local # first sync: upload yours where both sides differ Keeps the project folder and the remote in step, both ways, and streams the remote's logs. Stop it with Ctrl+C. pb_hooks , pb_migrations , pb_pages , pb_public and other pb_ folders both ways package.json , bun.lock(b) , patches/ both ways node_modules uploaded only, when package.json or the lockfile changes pb_data never (it's the app's live data) Your edits go up half a second after you save. Changes on the remote , such as the migrations the dashboard writes when you edit a collection, come down within a few seconds ( --poll , default 5s). dev asks the remote for one hash and only looks further when it changed, so a large pb_public costs nothing while it's quiet. Restarts: dev never restarts the app by itself. Hooks reload by themselves, pages and public files are live on the next request. After you upload a migration or new packages, dev says so: type r and Enter to restart the app and apply them. Migrations that come down are already applied on the remote. Deletes go both ways too. Changed on both sides: your copy wins and is uploaded; the remote's is saved in .pocketone/conflicts/ and dev says so. First run: files that exist on only one side are copied to the other. If a file differs on both sides, dev lists them and asks whether to keep yours or take the remote's; --prefer local remote answers in advance. dev keeps what it last synced in .pocketone/sync.json (add .pocketone/ to .gitignore ). List files to leave out, such as ones your hooks generate, in .pocketoneignore , one gitignore-style pattern per line. --prefer local\ remote First sync: who wins where both sides differ (default: ask). --poll How often to check the remote (default 5s). --push-only Only upload, the way dev used to work. Also used by itself for remotes without two-way sync. --no-logs Don't stream the remote's logs. It takes the same file flags as deploy .

title: Deploy
heading: clone
text: pocketone clone https://myapp.example.com # into ./myapp pocketone clone https://myapp.pockethost.io site --token ph_pat_... Starts a local project from a running app, with nothing local to begin with: makes the folder (refusing one that isn't empty; default: the host's first label, or app for localhost), adds the app as the project's default remote, signs in like link (the same --token , --token-stdin , --device and --no-browser flags), and pulls the app's code as pull does. A folder clone made is removed again if it fails before any file came down. Then cd in, run bun install (or npm) if there's a package.json , and pocketone dev .

title: Deploy
heading: pull
text: pocketone pull prod # pb_hooks, pb_migrations, pb_pages, pb_public, pb_templates, package.json, the lockfile, patches/ pocketone pull prod pb_hooks pb_public/index.html pocketone pull prod --dry-run Downloads files from a remote into the project: its code, never pb_data (the deploy API doesn't reach it; data goes through the PocketBase API and backups).

title: Deploy
heading: logs
text: pocketone logs prod pocketone logs prod -n 20 Replays the last 100 lines ( -n , --lines , 0 to 1000), then follows. Requests show as GET /url → 200 (1.2 ms) and errors are marked ERR . PocketBase writes its logs in batches, so lines show up a few seconds late. The stream reconnects by itself if it drops.

title: Deploy
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Deploy
heading: Commands
text: What it adds to the pocketone binary (CLI reference): [ pocketone clone [dir] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-clone) Starts a local project from a running app: makes the folder, links and signs in, and pulls its code [ pocketone deploy [remote] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-deploy) Deploys pb\_hooks, pb\_migrations, pb\_pages, pb\_public and packages to a remote [ pocketone dev [remote] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-dev) Keeps the project's code and a remote in step both ways (and streams the remote's logs) [ pocketone logs [remote] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-logs) Streams a remote's app logs [ pocketone pull [remote] [paths...] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-pull) Downloads files from a remote into the project (default: pb\_hooks, pb\_migrations, pb\_pages, pb\_public, pb\_templates, package.json, the lockfile, patches/) [ pocketone restart [remote] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-restart) Restarts a remote's app so it applies new migrations and packages

title: Deploy
heading: deploy/v1
text: Its HTTP API under /api/_c/deploy/v1/ , as the contract describes.

title: Deploy
heading: Works with
text: Remotes Gives the commands their remotes, saved logins and CI tokens. The commands find deploy/v1 in the remote's whoami, and restart and logs use its remote/v1 (deploy requires it). OAuth (in Tokens) pocketone login signs in through the browser when the remote runs it. Tokens Deploy registers the deploy and deploy:read scopes, so you can make API tokens for CI that can only deploy or only read. Add remote for --restart and remote:read for dev 's logs. Multisite A multisite host can serve the same API for all its instances with its own backend: build it with deploy.New (below). PocketHost does this.

title: Deploy
heading: Building on Deploy
text: Go client. deploy.NewClient(ctx, rc) takes a remote/v1 client ( remoteclient.Open , from ext/contracts/remote/v1/remoteclient) and finds its deploy API. Deploy , Pull , Collect , Watch and NewSyncer (two-way sync: Sync , RemoteChanged ) are the commands' building blocks. Your own host. deploy.New(deploy.Options{Prefix, Backend, Files, PlatformPaths}) builds the API. Backend decides which instance a request is for ( Lookup(r) ) and who it acts as ( Authenticate(r, inst) → Auth{UserID, Scopes, Via, TokenLabel} , an AuthError , or ErrNoAccess for a 404). Files returns the host's instance.fs/v1 (Pocker and Docker provide it on the host scope: fsv1.Contract.In(h.Scope) ), which gives each instance's folder, its pb_cache/deploy and its restarts. Serve it as deploy/v1 for the host's instances ( deployv1.Contract.ProvideForInstances , extkit.HostRoutes in multisite.Host.InstanceRoutes ); restart and logs are the host's remote/v1. Restarts. Your runtime should reload an instance by itself when its pb_hooks change (pocker's Manager does); deploy only restarts it (instance.fs/v1's Restart ) when a client asks ( Client.Restart , or DeployOptions.Restart ). Discovery. Deploy provides the deploy/v1 contract, which whoami lists, so clients find it at /api/_c/deploy/v1 . A multisite host can provide it for its instances instead.

title: Deploy
heading: Example
text: example/main.go is an app that both accepts deploys and makes them: the deploy API, API tokens, remotes and the deploy commands. Its comment walks through a first deploy against itself. // Command example is a PocketOne app that accepts deploys and can deploy: deploy/v1 (/api/_c/deploy/v1), remote/v1 // (restart, logs), API tokens, and the deploy/dev/pull/logs/restart commands. // // go run ./example serve --http=127.0.0.1:8090 # the remote // cd myproject && mkdir pb_hooks && echo 'routerAdd("GET", "/hi", (e) = e.string(200, "hi"))' pb_hooks/main.pb.js // go run ./example link http://127.0.0.1:8090 # sign in in the browser as admin@example.com / password // go run ./example deploy // curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hi // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/api-tokens" "pocketone.dev/ext/deploy" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" "pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm" "pocketone.dev/ext/remotes" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" // registered through their contracts (the standard set does this for you); deploys land next to pb_data exts := []extkit.Extension{apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{}), remotes.New(remotes.Config{}), deploy.NewExtension(deploy.Config{})} if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, exts, nil, nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{}) // deployed pb_hooks and pb_migrations if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Deploy
heading: Deploy API
text: deploy/v1, at /api/_c/deploy/v1 (superusers, see Configure): the files only, on an app or a host. Whoami, restart and logs are remote/v1's ( /api/_c/remote/v1 ), which deploy requires. POST /check Takes a manifest, returns the hashes the server is missing. POST /blobs Gzipped PHB1 bundles: [sha256][uint32 length][bytes] …, every hash verified, 64 MB per request. POST /commit Stage, swap in, record. "restartNeeded": true in the answer when migrations or packages wait for a restart; "restart": true in the request restarts after the swap. With "partial": true only the listed files (and "delete" ) change. GET / DELETE /files List or delete files (the code set, node_modules , patches/ ; never pb_data or .git ). GET / PUT /files/raw Download or upload one file (same reach). GET /tree One folder of the code set ( ?path= , default the root) with a hash over everything below it; hashOnly=1 for just the hash. The protocol is the pockethost npm CLI's, so the same client deploys to PocketOne apps and PocketHost. The instance's folder, the lock that keeps commits and file writes apart, and its restart come from instance.fs/v1, which deploy requires. On a single app deploy provides it as the default (the app's own folder); a host that provides it for its instances replaces that.

title: Deploy
heading: How it works
text: Go module pocketone.dev/ext/deploy . example/main.go is an app that accepts deploys and can deploy (logins from devusers: admin@example.com / password). A deploy is a hash diff: the client sends a manifest, uploads only the missing files in bundles, then commits. On a single app the files are swapped in while it runs; a restart (when a client asks) is app.Restart() , which re-executes the process ( Config.Restart overrides it; not on Windows). Config.Dir and Config.StoreDir move the deploy folder and the upload store; Config.Prefix moves the API. Logs on a single app come from its own _logs table; entries at error level and above are marked as stderr. The node_modules collector is nodemodules , a port of the npm CLI's.

text: MIT

title: Building
text: Run pocketone desktop build in your app's folder, the one with pb_hooks , pb_migrations or pb_public . It embeds those folders in a desktop app for each platform you ask for. pocketone desktop build # this machine's platform pocketone desktop build --all # all six below pocketone desktop build --target windows/amd64,linux/amd64 # some of them pocketone desktop build --out builds # somewhere other than dist/ pocketone desktop build --no-sign # skip the sign section macOS, Apple Silicon darwin/arm64 dist/darwin-arm64/ .app and .dmg macOS, Intel darwin/amd64 dist/darwin-amd64/ .app and .dmg Windows, x64 windows/amd64 dist/windows-amd64/ .exe Windows, Arm windows/arm64 dist/windows-arm64/ .exe Linux, x64 linux/amd64 dist/linux-amd64/ Linux, Arm linux/arm64 dist/linux-arm64/ Each is one file (or one .app bundle) of about 40 MB, with your app and PocketOne inside. Windows builds open no console window. On a Mac, each macOS build also comes as a .dmg : the app and a link to Applications to drag it onto. With a sign section in pocketone.yaml , every build is signed for you; see Signing and sharing.

title: Building
heading: Name and size
text: pocketone.yaml 's desktop section names the app and sizes its window: desktop: name: Notes # window title and file name; default: the folder's name id: dev.example.notes # where each user's data lives; default: app.pocketone. width: 900 # starting window size; default 1024 × 768 height: 640 Choose the id once and keep it. It names the folder each user's data lives in, so a new id is a new, empty app for everyone who installed the old one.

title: Building
heading: The build image
text: Builds run in Docker, in the build image for your pocketone 's version: ghcr.io/pocketonehq/pocketone-build:v , pulled the first time. It holds Go, PocketOne's source and every dependency, vendored, so once it's here builds work offline, and the same pocketone version always builds the same app. pocketone desktop build mounts your app folder and the output folder into it, builds every platform there, and keeps Go's build cache in a Docker volume ( pocketone-build-cache ), so rebuilds take seconds. On a Mac it then signs the macOS bundles ad hoc, so they run on that Mac. A development pocketone , built from a PocketOne checkout, has no published image. It builds its own, pocketone-build:dev , from that checkout the first time (a minute or two). pocketone desktop image rebuilds it after you change the source.

title: Building
heading: Without Docker
text: With Go 1.27 or newer and a PocketOne checkout, --local builds with your own Go instead: pocketone desktop build --local --all # inside the checkout pocketone desktop build --local --source ~/src/pocketone # anywhere else (or set P1_SOURCE) It needs no C compiler either: every platform cross-compiles with plain Go.

title: Desktop
text: Version 0.0.2 · Owners: @benallfree The same app folder you run with pocketone serve becomes a desktop app: pocketone desktop build compiles your pb_hooks , pb_migrations and pb_public into one executable that runs the app's server on a private 127.0.0.1 port and shows it in a native window (the system webview, through Wails). Your users install nothing else, and each one's data stays on their machine. All you need is pocketone and Docker: the build runs in a build image with Go and PocketOne's source, and every platform builds from any machine, with no C compiler or Xcode. The desktop runtime uses Wails' cgo-free backends, which Wails marks experimental on macOS and Linux. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Desktop
heading: Install
text: Desktop is built into pocketone . Builds run in Docker, in the build image for your pocketone 's version ( ghcr.io/pocketonehq/pocketone-build:v ), pulled on first use. It holds Go and PocketOne's source with every dependency vendored, so once it's here builds work offline. A named volume ( pocketone-build-cache ) keeps Go's build cache, so rebuilds take seconds. A development pocketone (built from a checkout) builds its own image, pocketone-build:dev , from that checkout on first use ( pocketone desktop image rebuilds it). With Go 1.27 or newer and a checkout, --local skips Docker and builds with your own Go ( --source or P1_SOURCE names the checkout when you aren't in it).

title: Desktop
heading: Configure
text: pocketone.yaml 's desktop section names and sizes the app: desktop: name: Notes # window title and executable name; default: the folder's name id: dev.example.notes # names each user's data folder and the single-instance lock; default: app.pocketone. width: 900 # starting window size; default 1024 × 768 height: 640 Pick the id once and keep it: it's where your users' data lives, so a new id is a new, empty app for them. A sign section signs every build for the platforms it names ( --no-sign skips it): macOS with your Developer ID, notarized and packaged as a DMG; Windows with your signing command; Linux with a checksum and a GPG signature. See Signing and sharing. desktop: sign: macos: identity: "Developer ID Application: Your Name (ABCDE12345)" notary_profile: pocketone-notary windows: command: signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td SHA256 /a {file} linux: gpg_key: you@example.com

title: Desktop
heading: desktop:
text: How pocketone desktop build names and sizes the desktop app built from this folder. name string The app's name: the window title and the executable's name. Default: the folder's name. id string Reverse-DNS app id (dev.example.notes): names the app's data folder on each user's machine and its single-instance lock. Default: app.pocketone. . width int The window's starting width. Default: 1024. height int The window's starting height. Default: 768. sign.macos.identity string The signing identity in your keychain, as security find-identity -v -p codesigning shows it: Developer ID Application: Your Name (TEAMID). sign.macos.notary_profile string The notarytool keychain profile (xcrun notarytool store-credentials ). Set: each DMG is notarized and stapled. Empty: signed, not notarized. sign.windows.command string The command that signs one executable in place; {file} is its path. signtool on Windows, osslsigncode anywhere, or your signing service's tool. sign.linux.gpg_key string The GPG key to sign with (its email or id). Each build gets .sha256 and a detached .asc signature.

title: Desktop
heading: Use
text: In your app's folder: pocketone serve # the app as a normal server, as always pocketone desktop build # a desktop app for this machine, in dist/ pocketone desktop build --all # macOS, Windows and Linux, arm64 and amd64 pocketone desktop build --target windows/amd64,linux/amd64 # some of them dist/ - / gets .app on macOS (signed ad hoc when you build on a Mac, so it runs there), .exe on Windows (no console window), and on Linux. What the desktop app does when it starts: Its data goes in the user's own app-data folder, by id : ~/Library/Application Support/ /pb_data on macOS, %AppData%\ \pb_data on Windows, ~/.config/ /pb_data on Linux. Your migrations run on every start, so a new version of your app upgrades each user's data. Your hooks and public files are read from the executable, never from disk. It serves on a free 127.0.0.1 port and opens the window on it. Only one copy runs at a time (Wails' single-instance lock, by id ). There is no superuser and the installer page never opens; the app's users aren't its admins. What each platform needs: macOS: 11 or newer. Apps you send to others need signing and notarization with your own Apple Developer ID; unsigned, macOS asks them to approve the app in System Settings first. Windows: the WebView2 runtime, which Windows 10 and 11 already have. Linux: the GTK 4 and WebKitGTK 6.0 libraries; without them the app says which package to install.

title: Desktop
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Desktop
heading: Commands
text: What it adds to the pocketone binary (CLI reference): pocketone desktop build Build this folder's app as a native desktop app (this platform; --all for every platform) pocketone desktop image Build the desktop build image from a PocketOne checkout pocketone desktop prepare Write the build image's vendored module into <dir> (the build image's Dockerfile runs this)

title: Desktop
heading: Integrations
text: Bundle The desktop app serves your hooks, migrations and public files from the executable through Bundle. Standard The desktop app runs the standard set, as pocketone serve does. JSVM Your hooks run in PocketOne's QuickJS engine.

title: Desktop
heading: Building on Desktop
text: The runtime is its own module, ext/desktop/runtime , so the pocketone binary never links Wails. Your own Go program can use it directly: desktop.Run(desktop.App{Name: "Notes", ID: "dev.example.notes", Hooks: hooks, Migrations: migrations, Public: public}) Build it with CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags purego for macOS and Linux (Wails' cgo-free backends); Windows needs no tag. The build image is image/Dockerfile: a pocketone and the vendored module pocketone desktop prepare writes.

title: Desktop
heading: Example
text: example/hello is a hello-world app: a hook ( GET /api/hello ), a migration (a greetings collection with one row) and a page that lists and adds greetings. cd ext/desktop/example/hello pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com password pocketone serve # http://127.0.0.1:8090 pocketone desktop build # dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app on an Apple Silicon Mac example/main.go is a PocketBase app with only this extension, to show the command. // Command example is a PocketBase app with only the desktop extension: go run . desktop build in an app folder // (one with pb_hooks, pb_migrations or pb_public, like ./hello) builds it as a desktop app. The pocketone binary // has the same command. package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" clicmdv1 "pocketone.dev/ext/contracts/cli/commands/v1" "pocketone.dev/ext/desktop" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{desktop.New()}, nil, nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } clicmdv1.Mount(app, app.RootCmd) // the commands extensions provide; the standard set does this for pocketone if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Desktop apps
text: Your app is a folder: pb_hooks , pb_migrations and pb_public . pocketone serve runs it as a server, as always. pocketone desktop build turns the same folder into an app your users double-click: pocketone serve # the app as a server pocketone desktop build # a desktop app for this machine, in dist/ pocketone desktop build --all # macOS, Windows and Linux, arm64 and amd64 All you need is pocketone and Docker. The build runs in a build image that holds Go and PocketOne's source, so there's no Go, C compiler or Xcode to install, and every platform builds from any machine. Preview. Desktop builds work today, but how a desktop app handles trust and settings is still settling (see What's next). The desktop runtime uses Wails' cgo-free backends, which Wails marks experimental on macOS and Linux.

title: Desktop apps
heading: How it works
text: The desktop app is your PocketOne app plus a window: Your pb_hooks , pb_migrations and pb_public are embedded in the executable. Nothing is read from disk, so nobody can change a shipped app's hooks. When it starts, it runs your app's server on a private 127.0.0.1 port, applying your migrations to the user's data. It opens a native window on that server, using the system's own webview: WebKit on macOS, WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux. Your pages call the API with fetch , exactly as they do in a browser. The PocketBase JS SDK, realtime and file uploads work the same, because it's the same server.

title: Desktop apps
heading: Try it: hello world
text: PocketOne's source has a hello-world app in ext/desktop/example/hello : a hook, a migration and one page that lists and adds greetings. // pb_hooks/main.pb.js routerAdd("GET", "/api/hello", (e) = { const rows = $app.findRecordsByFilter("greetings", "", "-created", 50, 0) return e.json(200, { message: "Hello from PocketOne hooks", greetings: rows.map((r) = r.get("text")) }) }) Its pocketone.yaml keeps the server's data in the folder and names the desktop app: app: dir: pb_data server: public_dir: pb_public desktop: name: Hello id: dev.pocketone.hello width: 900 height: 640 Run it both ways: cd ext/desktop/example/hello pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com password pocketone serve # http://127.0.0.1:8090 pocketone desktop build # dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app on an Apple Silicon Mac open dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app The server and the desktop app keep separate data: the server's in pb_data/ , the desktop app's in your app-data folder.
