Signing and sharing: signing and notarizing for macOS, signing for Windows, and checksums for Linux. Extension reference: the desktop section of pocketone.yaml and building on the runtime from Go.

title: Desktop apps
heading: What's next
text: A desktop app has one person at the keyboard and data on their machine, so PocketBase's users and superusers don't quite fit. Being worked out: Trust: requests from the app's own window run as its owner, and nothing else on the machine can reach the server. Settings: a native Preferences window for the settings your app and its extensions declare, since the superuser dashboard isn't part of a shipped app.

title: How the app runs
text: A desktop app is your PocketOne app, with the standard extensions, its server on a private port, and a native window in front.

title: How the app runs
heading: Each user's data
text: Every user has their own data, in their own app-data folder, named by your app's id : macOS ~/Library/Application Support/ /pb_data Windows %AppData%\ \pb_data Linux ~/.config/ /pb_data It's an ordinary pb_data , so everything that works on one, from backups to point-in-time restore, works here too.

title: How the app runs
heading: Upgrades
text: Your migrations run every time the app starts. Ship a new version with new migrations, and each user's data is upgraded the first time they open it, the same way pocketone serve upgrades a server's.

title: How the app runs
heading: The server and the window
text: The server listens on a free 127.0.0.1 port, chosen each time, so it never collides with anything else. The window opens once the server answers. Only one copy runs at a time. Your hooks, migrations and public files come from the executable, never from disk. There is no superuser, and the superuser installer page never opens: the people using a desktop app aren't its admins.

title: How the app runs
heading: What each platform needs
text: macOS macOS 11 or newer Windows The WebView2 runtime, which Windows 10 and 11 already have Linux The GTK 4 and WebKitGTK 6.0 libraries; without them the app says which package to install

title: How the app runs
heading: Sharing your app
text: A build runs on the machine that built it. Before you give it to other people, sign it (and on macOS, notarize it), so it opens without warnings: Signing and sharing has the steps for each platform.

title: Signing and sharing
text: pocketone desktop build gives you apps that run on the machine that built them. Before you send them to other people, sign them, so each operating system knows the app comes from you and hasn't been changed since: macOS "can't be opened", until they approve it in System Settings An Apple Developer account and a Mac Windows A SmartScreen "Windows protected your PC" warning A code-signing certificate Linux Nothing; Linux doesn't check Optional: a GPG key, to publish a signature

title: Signing and sharing
heading: Let desktop build sign
text: Add a sign section to pocketone.yaml , and every pocketone desktop build signs what it built, on your machine, with your certificates. Name only the platforms you sign for: desktop: name: Hello id: dev.pocketone.hello sign: macos: identity: "Developer ID Application: Your Name (ABCDE12345)" notary_profile: pocketone-notary # omit to sign without notarizing windows: # any command that signs {file} in place command: signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td SHA256 /a {file} linux: gpg_key: you@example.com macOS: it signs each .app with your Developer ID and the hardened runtime, puts it in a .dmg , signs the DMG, sends it to Apple to notarize, and staples the result to both. You get the raw .app and the .dmg . Windows: it runs your command on each .exe , with {file} replaced by its path. Use signtool , osslsigncode or your signing service's tool, whichever fits your certificate. Linux: it writes .sha256 and a detached .asc GPG signature beside each binary. Before it builds anything, it checks that the tools are installed, that the identity is in your keychain and that the GPG key exists, so a missing piece fails in a second, not after the build. pocketone desktop build --no-sign skips the section, for a quick build to try out. Signing happens on your machine, not in the build image, because that's where your keychain and certificates are. So macOS builds are signed, notarized and put in a DMG only when you build on a Mac; built elsewhere, they're unsigned .app bundles. Windows and Linux builds sign anywhere their tools run ( signtool only runs on Windows; osslsigncode runs everywhere). The sections below are the one-time setup for each platform, and the commands desktop build runs, if you'd rather sign by hand.

title: Signing and sharing
heading: macOS
text: macOS wants two things for an app downloaded from the internet: a Developer ID signature , and notarization , where Apple scans the app and records that it did. You do both on a Mac, with the tools that come with Xcode.

title: Signing and sharing
heading: Once: get a Developer ID certificate
text: Join the Apple Developer Program (paid, yearly). In Xcode, open Settings → Accounts , add your Apple ID, select your team and choose Manage Certificates . Click + and pick Developer ID Application . Xcode creates the certificate and puts it in your keychain. Check that it's there and copy its name: security find-identity -v -p codesigning # 1) 3F2A… "Developer ID Application: Your Name (ABCDE12345)" ABCDE12345 is your team ID. Create an app-specific password for your Apple ID ( Sign-In and Security → App-Specific Passwords ), and save it for the notary tool under a profile name: xcrun notarytool store-credentials pocketone-notary \ --apple-id you@example.com --team-id ABCDE12345 --password

title: Signing and sharing
heading: By hand: sign, notarize, staple
text: desktop build does this for you with a sign.macos section. By hand, for each macOS build ( dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app , dist/darwin-amd64/Hello.app ): Sign with your Developer ID, the hardened runtime ( --options runtime , which notarization requires) and a secure timestamp. --force replaces the ad hoc signature the build added: codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \ --sign "Developer ID Application: Your Name (ABCDE12345)" dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app codesign --verify --strict --verbose=2 dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app Notarize: zip the app and send it to Apple. It usually takes a few minutes: ditto -c -k --keepParent dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app Hello.zip xcrun notarytool submit Hello.zip --keychain-profile pocketone-notary --wait If it says Invalid , xcrun notarytool log --keychain-profile pocketone-notary shows why. Staple the result to the app, so it opens even when the user is offline, and check it: xcrun stapler staple dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app spctl --assess --type execute --verbose dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app # dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app: accepted # source=Notarized Developer ID Package the stapled app to share it. A zip: ditto -c -k --keepParent dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app Hello-macos-arm64.zip or a disk image, which you sign too: hdiutil create -volname Hello -srcfolder dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app -ov -format UDZO Hello.dmg codesign --timestamp --sign "Developer ID Application: Your Name (ABCDE12345)" Hello.dmg One download for both kinds of Mac: join the two executables with lipo before you sign, and ship one app. cp -R dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app Hello.app lipo -create dist/darwin-arm64/Hello.app/Contents/MacOS/Hello dist/darwin-amd64/Hello.app/Contents/MacOS/Hello \ -output Hello.app/Contents/MacOS/Hello

title: Signing and sharing
heading: Without an Apple Developer account
text: Without a Developer ID, macOS still runs your app, but anyone who downloads it is warned first. What they see depends on how it's signed: Signed ad hoc (what desktop build does with no sign.macos ) "Apple could not verify it is free of malware", and the app doesn't open Signed with a self-signed certificate The same warning Signed with a Developer ID, not notarized A similar warning Signed with a Developer ID and notarized Only "downloaded from the internet, open it?" The warning only appears for downloaded apps, which macOS marks as quarantined. An app you build and run on your own Mac opens without it. Opening it anyway. For yourself, testers and people you know, that's fine. They: Open the app and dismiss the warning. Go to System Settings → Privacy & Security , scroll to Security and click Open Anyway next to the app. Confirm, and the app opens from then on. Or, if they're comfortable with Terminal, they remove the quarantine mark, and the app opens normally: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Hello.app Self-signing. You can make your own code-signing certificate: in Keychain Access, choose Keychain Access → Certificate Assistant → Create a Certificate , set Certificate Type to Code Signing , and then mark it Always Trust for code signing (double-click it, open Trust ). Its name then goes in sign.macos.identity , without notary_profile , since Apple only notarizes Developer ID apps. It doesn't remove the warning: macOS can't trust a certificate it doesn't know, so a self-signed app gets the same warning as an ad hoc one. What it gives you is the same identity from one version to the next, so macOS remembers what your users allowed the app to do (files, camera, keychain items) when they update. For an app you give to the public, only a Developer ID and notarization open it without warnings.

title: Signing and sharing
heading: Windows
text: Windows checks an Authenticode signature. You need a code-signing certificate from a certificate authority, such as DigiCert, Sectigo or SSL.com. Certificates issued today keep their key on a hardware token or in the CA's cloud signing service rather than in a file, so how you sign depends on which you get.

title: Signing and sharing
heading: Once: get a certificate
text: Organization validation (OV): the CA checks that your business exists. For an individual, pick a certificate issued to you by name. Extended validation (EV): a stricter check, for businesses. A cloud signing service , such as Azure Trusted Signing, signs without a token, for organizations it can verify. Either way, a new certificate starts with no reputation: SmartScreen may still warn for a while, until enough people have installed your signed app.

title: Signing and sharing
heading: By hand: sign with signtool
text: On Windows, with the Windows SDK installed (it includes signtool ) and your certificate on its token or in the certificate store: signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td SHA256 /a dist\windows-amd64\Hello.exe signtool verify /pa /v dist\windows-amd64\Hello.exe /a picks the best certificate it finds; /sha1 picks one exactly. A cloud signing service gives you its own signtool plugin or tool; follow its instructions for the same step. Sign windows-arm64 the same way.

title: Signing and sharing
heading: From a Mac or Linux
text: osslsigncode signs Windows executables on macOS and Linux, if your certificate's key is in a file or on a token it can reach: osslsigncode sign -pkcs12 certificate.pfx -pass "$PFX_PASSWORD" -n "Hello" \ -t http://timestamp.digicert.com -in dist/windows-amd64/Hello.exe -out Hello.exe

title: Signing and sharing
heading: Linux
text: Linux runs the binary you give it; there's no signature check to pass. What you can do is let people check the download is yours and intact: cd dist/linux-amd64 sha256sum Hello Hello.sha256 # a checksum to publish next to the download gpg --armor --detach-sign Hello # Hello.asc: a signature anyone with your public key can check Users check with sha256sum -c Hello.sha256 and gpg --verify Hello.asc Hello . Packaging the app as a .deb , Flatpak or AppImage, where the package or repository is signed, also works.

title: Docker
text: Version 0.0.3 · Owners: @benallfree Run every instance on a host in its own container, with the official PocketBase or PocketOne binary of the version the instance asks for. One host can serve PocketBase 0.23 and 0.36 and PocketOne side by side. Docker is one of the two runtime providers of the multi-instance multisite. The other is Pocker, which runs every instance inside one process. A host runs one of them. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Docker
heading: Install
text: Docker is built into pocketone . It needs a Docker daemon on the same machine; nothing else to install. It's off until pocketone.yaml has a multisite and a docker section (below). Then pocketone serve runs the host instead of a single app. In your own Go build, add it to the host's extensions; it provides the runtime/v1 contract when pocketone.yaml has a docker section: h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath, Extensions: []multisite.Extension{&docker.Provider{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath}}}) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/docker . Add docker.NewCommand(...) to your root command for the docker seed and docker update commands.

title: Docker
heading: Configure
text: Add a multisite section (host mode) and a docker section to pocketone.yaml . Listeners ( server ), instances ( instances ) and the firewall are the host's sections. The docker section makes docker the host's runtime instead of pocker; every instance runs in a container. multisite: {} docker: image: alpine:3.20 # base image the binaries run in binaries: /var/lib/pocketbase # release binary cache root: /var/lib/instances # one folder per instance: / versions: ["pb:0.23", "pb:0.36", "p1:0.0"] default_version: "pb:0.36. " idle_ttl: 10m max_concurrent_starts: 4 instances: file: ./instances.yaml image , binaries and root are required. Versions. An instance picks its binary with the prefix of its version : pb: is upstream PocketBase, p1: is PocketOne, no prefix means pb: . versions lists the minors the host serves; the newest cached patch that matches wins. A version that isn't listed gets a clear 503. Upstream PocketBase 0.22 and older are refused unless you lower min_upstream and keep those releases in the cache yourself. Per instance ( instances.yaml or a mothership): version , secrets (passed as environment), encryption_key , dev , and dir to put its folder somewhere other than / . An instance with runtime set to anything but docker isn't served here. Limits and hardening are optional: nano_cpus , pids_limit , nofile , cap_drop and no_new_privileges .

title: Docker
heading: docker:
text: Runtime provider docker: each instance in its own container with the PocketBase (pb:) or PocketOne (p1:) binary of its version (image, binary cache and manifest, instance root, default version, idle stop, limits). socket string The Docker socket. Default $DOCKER_HOST when it is unix://, else /var/run/docker.sock. image string Base image the binaries run in, such as alpine:3.20. Required; pulled when missing. binaries string Folder of the release binary cache and its releases.json. Required. versions list of string The minors this host serves, such as pb:0.36 or p1:0.0 (latest patch of each, from docker update). root string Folder with one folder per instance ( / ). Required. home string The instance folder inside the container. Default /home/pockethost. default_version string Version for instances that name none, such as p1:0.0. . Empty: such instances fail. min_upstream string Oldest upstream PocketBase release served. Default 0.23.0; lower it only for releases you cache yourself. idle_ttl duration Stop a container after this long without requests. Default 10m. max_concurrent_starts int Containers starting at once. Default 4. start_timeout duration How long a container gets to answer its health check. Default 60s. nano_cpus int CPU limit per container in billionths of a CPU (1000000000 = one CPU). 0: no limit. pids_limit int Process limit per container. 0: Docker's default. nofile list of int Open-file limit per container: [soft, hard]. Empty: Docker's default. cap_drop list of string Linux capabilities to drop, such as [ALL]. no_new_privileges bool Set no-new-privileges on every container. network string Docker network for the containers. Default the bridge. adopt_image string Also adopt running unlabeled containers of this image named after an instance id (taking over from another manager).

title: Docker
heading: Fetch the binaries
text: pocketone docker update # find the latest patch of each docker.versions minor, record and download it pocketone docker seed # download whatever is recorded but not in the cache yet update checks upstream PocketBase releases (ganigeorgiev.com, then the archived GitHub) and PocketOne releases on GitHub, verifies each download against the release's checksums.txt, and records the list in the cache's releases.json . Run it when you want new patches. Nothing is downloaded at request time: when the host starts, any listed release missing from the cache is downloaded in the background. The cache layout is / / /pocketbase for PocketBase (PocketHost's existing layout) and /p1/ / /pocketone for PocketOne.

title: Docker
heading: Run the host
text: pocketone serve A container starts on an instance's first request and is ready when /api/health answers. At most max_concurrent_starts start at once. It stops after idle_ttl without requests. It restarts on its next request when what it runs changed (secrets, version, mounts). A change to routing only doesn't restart it. It stops when the instance is deleted or moves to another edge. Containers keep running when the host restarts; the next process adopts them by their labels.

title: Docker
heading: Hooks and migrations
text: A change in an instance's pb_hooks restarts its container. PocketBase's own hooks watcher stays on too, so a hook file that fails to load is logged and skipped instead of stopping the instance. A request that arrives while the instance restarts waits for it instead of failing; one that lost its connection mid-restart is sent once more if it's safe to repeat (GET, HEAD or OPTIONS without a body). Migrations run when a container boots.

title: Docker
heading: Maintenance
text: Instance folders are ordinary folders under root . To work on one while nothing has it open, a host's Go code calls WithInstanceStopped (below); requests for that instance wait up to 30 s, then get a 503 with Retry-After . The host provides instance.fs/v1 on its scope from the same methods ( Runtime.Files(dir) ), so host-side code (a host's deploy or file drive) gets an instance's folder, writers' lock and restart from the contract.

title: Docker
heading: Remote control
text: Containers run stock images, and a PocketBase image has no PocketOne extensions, so the host answers remote/v1 for them at /api/_c/remote/v1/ on each instance's hostname: the pocketone remote commands work the same as against a Pocker instance or a single app. It answers after the host's gates (firewall, rate limits) and blocked check, so a blocked instance's remote/v1 gets the blocked answer and the container stays stopped. GET /api/_c/remote/v1 (whoami) is public and lists remote/v1 . status , restart and logs need a superuser token of that instance ( pocketone remote login with a superuser email and password). The host asks the instance itself to check it. A host with its own accounts sets docker.Provider.RemoteAuth to decide who may call them instead (PocketHost: the instance owner's tokens). remote/v1 is provided on the host's scope, so whoami also lists the other contracts the host provides for its instances (a host's deploy/v1 ). restart replaces the container; logs replays and follows the container's output, the last 1000 lines per instance kept by this host since it started following the container.

title: Docker
heading: Switching provider
text: Docker and Pocker both use / , so switching is a config change. Stop the containers first when leaving docker, since they keep running across a host restart on purpose. Data only moves forward: an instance started on a newer PocketBase than wrote its data is upgraded.

title: Docker
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Docker
heading: Commands
text: What it adds to the pocketone binary (CLI reference): pocketone docker seed Downloads the releases docker.versions lists that the cache doesn't have yet pocketone docker update Finds the latest patch of each docker.versions minor, records and downloads it

title: Docker
heading: remote/v1
text: whoami pocketone remote whoami GET /api/_c/remote/v1 remote_whoami status pocketone remote status GET /api/_c/remote/v1/status remote_status restart pocketone remote restart POST /api/_c/remote/v1/restart remote_restart logs pocketone remote logs --n GET /api/_c/remote/v1/logs remote_logs

title: Docker
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Docker is a runtime provider of the host: the host routes by hostname, runs the listeners and gates, and hands each request to docker. Pocker The other provider. A host runs one of them, over the same instance folders. Edge For a fleet: requests for instances on another edge are forwarded there. Mothership Instances (and their versions) come from a mothership instead of a file. Firewall Rate limits and allow lists in front of every instance. Remotes The host provides remote/v1 for every container, so the CLI's whoami, status, restart and logs work.

title: Docker
heading: Building on Docker
text: docker.Provider fields extend the provider from Go: Container adds mounts, environment and labels to each container; Version rewrites an instance's version before the binary is picked; OnLog receives container output (default: the debug log); Versions replaces the versions list (for example a fleet's list from a mothership); MinUpstream replaces min_upstream . Spec (what Container fills in): Binds , Env , Labels , plus Cmd to adjust the command (for example drop a flag an old release lacks) and HealthPath / HealthAnyStatus for the readiness check. VersionsSource : any type with Releases(ctx) decides which releases the host serves, each pinned to its download and sha256. YAMLVersions (the versions key) is the built-in one. Runtime API : docker.New(docker.Config{...}) builds the runtime without the config file. WithInstanceStopped(ctx, id, fn) stops an instance, holds its requests and runs fn on its folder (for deploys and restores); StartInstance starts one now; InstanceDir returns its folder. Remote(host, dir) and SuperuserAuth() are the remote/v1 provider and the host-side auth that Provider wires in, for a host built by hand ( remotev1.W.HostHandler(host, multisite.InstanceID, rt.SuperuserAuth(), next) in Host.InstanceRoutes ). Release helpers : ParseVersion , Pick / PickMin , LatestPatches , Update and Seed are what the commands use.

title: Docker
heading: Example
text: A minimal docker host: instances from a YAML file, each in its own container, routed by hostname on one listener. With a Docker daemon running, start it from this folder with go run ./example --instances instances.yaml --data ./instances --binaries ./bin --versions pb:0.23,p1:0.0 . // A minimal docker host: instances from a YAML file, each in its own container with the PocketBase or PocketOne // version it asks for, routed by hostname on one listener. // // go run ./example --instances instances.yaml --data ./instances --binaries ./bin --versions pb:0.23,p1:0.0 // // instances.yaml: // // instances: // - { id: blog, hosts: [blog.localhost], version: "pb:0.23. " } // - { id: shop, hosts: [shop.localhost], version: "p1:0.0. " } package main import ( "context" "flag" "log/slog" "os" "os/signal" "strings" "syscall" "pocketone.dev/ext/docker" "pocketone.dev/ext/multisite" ) func main() { instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file") data := flag.String("data", "./instances", "folder with one folder per instance") binaries := flag.String("binaries", "./bin", "PocketBase and PocketOne binary cache") versions := flag.String("versions", "pb:0.23,p1:0.0", "minors to serve (latest patch each; fetched at start)") image := flag.String("image", "alpine:3.20", "base image") listen := flag.String("listen", "127.0.0.1:8090", "listen address") flag.Parse() b := &docker.Binaries{Root: binaries} tracked := strings.Split( versions, ",") if err := docker.RunUpdate(context.Background(), os.Stdout, docker.DefaultDiscovery(), b, tracked); err != nil { slog.Error("versions", "error", err) os.Exit(1) } rt, err := docker.New(docker.Config{Image: image, DataRoot: data, Binaries: b, Versions: docker.YAMLVersions{Tracked: tracked, Root: b.Root}}) if err != nil { slog.Error("docker", "error", err) os.Exit(1) } ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) defer stop() h := &multisite.Host{Source: &multisite.YAMLSource{Path: instances}, Runtime: rt, Listeners: multisite.Listeners{Listen: listen}} if err := h.Run(ctx); err != nil { slog.Error("host", "error", err) os.Exit(1) } }

title: Docker
heading: How it works
text: Each instance folder is mounted at /home/pockethost and the binary read-only at /home/pockethost/pocketbase . The container runs ./pocketbase serve --http 0.0.0.0:8090 , plus --dev for dev instances and --encryptionEnv=PB_ENCRYPTION_KEY when the instance has an encryption key. Its secrets are its environment. The port is published on 127.0.0.1 and the host proxies to it. This is the layout PocketHost's Node edge uses, so its instance folders and binary cache move as they are. Every container carries labels: p1.runtime , p1.instance , p1.version (the resolved release, such as pb:0.36.9 ) and p1.spec (a hash of its configuration, used to tell when it must restart). adopt_image also adopts unlabeled containers of an image, for taking over from another manager. Docker is reached over its socket API directly; there's no Docker SDK dependency.

title: Docker
heading: Status
text: Tested against a real Docker daemon, with upstream PocketBase 0.23 and PocketOne 0.0.1 side by side, alone and as a host's runtime. Not yet in production. go test ./... runs the Docker tests when a daemon is reachable (they're skipped with -short ). The first run downloads an upstream release and a PocketOne release into the user cache.

title: Edge
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree The fleet layer for a Multisite: several servers (edges) share one set of instances, any edge accepts any request, and a request for an instance another edge runs is forwarded there over the private network. Works with either runtime provider, pocker or docker. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Edge
heading: Install
text: Edge is built into pocketone . It turns on in host mode (a multisite section in pocketone.yaml ) when the file has an edges section, or a mothership section (Mothership), which lists the edges too. In your own Go build, give the host a router as its forward hook: edges, err := edge.FromSection(log) // the edges section; nil when there is none if edges != nil { opts.Forward = edge.NewRouter(edge.RouterConfig{Edges: edges, Logger: log}).Forward } h, err := multisite.FromConfig(opts) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/edge .

title: Edge
heading: Configure
text: The edges section names this edge and lists the others (keys below): edges: self: lax-1 list: { id: sgp-1, internal_url: "http://10.88.0.4:8080", region: sgp } server: plain: [":8080"] # where the other edges reach this one (their internal_url for it) Each entry needs id and internal_url . An instance another edge runs names its owner in remote : instances: id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] remote: edge:@sgp-1 # also accepted: edge:sgp-1, or sgp-1 Without a mothership, instances come from the instances file. With one, instances and edges both come from it; a fixed edges.list entry wins over the mothership's for the same edge.

title: Edge
heading: edges:
text: The fleet: this edge's id and a fixed list of the other edges (id, internal_url, region). self string This edge's id, such as lax-1. list list of object The other edges: id, internal_url (where this edge reaches it) and optional region.

title: Edge
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to run by hand. A load balancer sends visitors to any edge, and each request ends up on the edge that runs its instance: Owner healthy: the request is forwarded to its internal_url , with the original hostname. An edge is healthy when its source heard from it in the last 30 seconds, or else when it answers /.well-known/health (an edge the source marks offline never is). Owner briefly unreachable but healthy: requests are held and retried every 250 ms until it answers. Only requests without a body (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) are replayed after a failed connection. Owner down or unknown: a 503 with Retry-After: 10 , at once. Never bounced: a request another edge already forwarded is never forwarded again; it gets a 421. CORS: for an instance with access.cors_origins , the entry edge answers preflights and sets the only Access-Control-Allow-Origin the browser sees. Headers: where both edges set the same header (such as the firewall's rate-limit headers), the owner's wins.

title: Edge
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Edge fills the host's forward hook for instances with remote set. Pocker, Docker Either runs the instances this edge owns; an app already running here stops when its instance moves to another edge. Firewall The entry edge checks the peer and the instance's rate limits before forwarding. Mothership Its mirror is an edge source: it follows the mothership's list of edges and their heartbeats.

title: Edge
heading: Building on Edge
text: Edge sources. Implement edge.EdgeSource ( Self , Resolve , Edges ) to say where the other edges are; add Run ( edge.Runner ) for background work. YAMLProvider is the edges.list one; MultiProvider combines several, the first to resolve an instance's remote winning. Router. edge.NewRouter(edge.RouterConfig{...}) takes the health path, healthy window, retry interval and the 503 and 421 messages. Plug Router.Forward into multisite.Host.Forward . Timing. edge.WithMark(ctx) records which edge a request was forwarded to and when, e.g. for Server-Timing.

title: Edge
heading: Example
text: Edge has no example program of its own. The stock binary wires it up in examples/pocketone/multi.go , together with the mothership's edge list.

title: Firewall
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Peer allow-lists, trusted proxies and client IPs, and per-IP and per-instance rate limits for a Multisite, with or without Edge. Every request is checked before an instance serves it or it's forwarded to another edge. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Firewall
heading: Install
text: The firewall is built into pocketone . It turns on in host mode (a multisite section in pocketone.yaml ), as the host's gate/v1, when the file has a firewall or rate_limits section; there's nothing else to install. In your own Go build, importing the package registers it with the host, with the same rule: import _ "pocketone.dev/ext/firewall" Or build one in Go and add it to the host's gates, as the example does. A single app doesn't need it: stock PocketBase has its own per-IP rate limits and trusted proxies.

title: Firewall
heading: Configure
text: Two sections, both optional; either one turns the firewall on (keys below). firewall: allow_cidrs: [] # peers allowed to connect (empty = everyone) trusted_proxies: [] # peers whose client-IP headers are believed client_ip_headers: [CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP] trusted_clients: [] # client IPs that get the trusted rate limits on every instance trusted_client_headers: [X-Client-IP] # a trusted client names its end user: each user gets their own limits rate_limit_header_prefix: X-RateLimit rate_limits: # defaults for every instance ip_hourly: 1000 instance_hourly: 10000 ip_concurrent: 15 instance_concurrent: 250 file_weight: 0.1 # a /api/files request costs a tenth trusted: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_hourly: 20000, ip_concurrent: 50, instance_concurrent: 250 } # off: true # no rate limiting The values shown are the defaults. In dev mode ( instances: { dev: true } ) rate limiting is off unless the file has a rate_limits section. A trusted limit is never lower than the normal one. Each instance can set its own limits and trusted IPs in its extensions.firewall settings; missing fields keep the defaults: instances: id: api hosts: [api.example.com] extensions: firewall: { rate_limits: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_concurrent: 500 }, trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] }

title: Firewall
heading: firewall:
text: Peers allowed to connect, trusted proxies and client-IP headers, trusted clients, the rate-limit header prefix. Turns the firewall on. allow_cidrs list of string Peers (IPs or CIDRs) allowed to connect; others get 403. Empty: everyone. trusted_proxies list of string Peers whose client-IP headers are believed. client_ip_headers list of string Headers read, in order, for the client IP from a trusted proxy. Default CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP. trusted_clients list of string Client IPs or CIDRs that get the trusted rate limits on every instance. trusted_client_headers list of string Headers a trusted client uses to name its end user's IP, so each user gets their own limits. Default X-Client-IP. rate_limit_header_prefix string Prefix of the rate-limit response headers. Default X-RateLimit.

title: Firewall
heading: rate_limits:
text: Default rate limits for every instance (per instance: extensions.firewall.rate_limits). Turns the firewall on. ip_hourly int Requests per hour from one client IP to one instance. Default 1000. instance_hourly int Requests per hour to one instance from everyone. Default 10000. ip_concurrent int Requests one client IP may have open on one instance at once. Default 15. instance_concurrent int Requests one instance may have open at once. Default 250. file_weight number What a /api/files request costs, as a share of a request. Default 0.1. trusted.ip_hourly int Requests per hour from one trusted client IP to one instance. trusted.instance_hourly int Requests per hour to one instance. trusted.ip_concurrent int Requests one trusted client IP may have open on one instance at once. trusted.instance_concurrent int Requests one instance may have open at once. off bool No rate limiting. The default in dev mode unless rate_limits is set.

title: Firewall
heading: Use
text: What callers see: Peers outside allow_cidrs get 403. Client IP: taken from client_ip_headers only when the peer is a trusted proxy; otherwise it's the peer. The app then sees that client as the request's IP, so PocketBase's logs and its own rate limits see the visitor. Over a limit: 429 with Retry-After and a message naming the limit and the IP. Every routed response carries X-RateLimit-{Ip,Instance}-{Hourly,Concurrent}-{Limit,Remaining} and X-RateLimit-{Ip,Instance}-Hourly-Reset (with your prefix), listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers so browser code can read them. Long-lived responses (realtime) count toward the concurrency limits until they end.

title: Firewall
heading: Trusted clients that serve many users
text: A trusted client (process-wide trusted_clients , or an instance's own trusted_ips ) that serves many users, such as a server-side proxy or SSR app, sends each request's end-user IP in a trusted_client_headers header. Per-IP limits then apply to that user, still with the trusted limits; without the header all its users share one bucket. The header is ignored from anyone else, so it can't be spoofed to escape a limit.

title: Firewall
heading: Works with
text: Multisite The firewall is a host gate: it checks the peer, then admits each request before the runtime or the forward hook. Pocker, Docker Either runtime; the firewall runs in front of it. Edge The entry edge applies the limits before forwarding. The owner edge's rate-limit headers replace the entry edge's, since the owner counted every request for the instance. Multitenant (planned) Will write each instance's extensions.firewall settings, such as its owner's trusted IPs.

title: Firewall
heading: Building on the firewall
text: Per instance. Write extensions.firewall.rate_limits and extensions.firewall.trusted_ips into an instance's settings (from the instances file or your own instance source). Go API. firewall.Firewall{Config, RateLimits} is a multisite.Gate you can add to Host.Gates yourself; NewFirewall(cfg) builds one ready to use. ClientIP(r) gives a request's client. firewall.SectionAdjust changes the settings read from pocketone.yaml before the firewall is built.

title: Firewall
heading: Example
text: The firewall in front of a toy host: only 127.0.0.1 may connect, at 100 requests an hour per IP. Run it from this folder with go run ./example --instances instances.yaml . // The firewall in front of a host: every request is checked (allowed peers, rate limits) before a toy runtime // answers. In a PocketOne binary the firewall turns on from pocketone.yaml's firewall / rate_limits sections; here // it is built in Go. // // go run ./example --instances instances.yaml package main import ( "context" "flag" "fmt" "net/http" "os" "os/signal" "syscall" "pocketone.dev/ext/firewall" "pocketone.dev/ext/multisite" ) type okRuntime struct{} func (okRuntime) Name() string { return "ok" } func (okRuntime) Serves(inst multisite.Instance) bool { return true } func (okRuntime) Ready() bool { return true } func (okRuntime) ServeInstance(w http.ResponseWriter, _ http.Request, inst multisite.Instance) { fmt.Fprintf(w, "hello from %s\n", inst.ID) } func main() { instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file") listen := flag.String("listen", "127.0.0.1:8090", "listen address") flag.Parse() fw := &firewall.Firewall{ Config: firewall.Config{AllowCIDRs: []string{"127.0.0.1"}}, RateLimits: &firewall.RateLimits{IPHourly: 100}, } ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) defer stop() h := &multisite.Host{Source: &multisite.YAMLSource{Path: instances}, Runtime: okRuntime{}, Gates: []multisite.Gate{fw}, Listeners: multisite.Listeners{Listen: listen}} if err := h.Run(ctx); err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err) os.Exit(1) } }

title: Extensions
text: Each extension is a Go module in ext/ with its own README; the pages here are those READMEs. Want to add one? Read Writing an extension.

title: Extensions
heading: Standard extensions
text: These ship with pocketone and add no work to an app that doesn't use them. Agent A language model for your app: your own API, or a small model PocketOne runs itself in the same binary. Agent Chat Stored conversations with your app's language model: $agent.chat(id).send(text), with history and summaries. API Tokens Long-lived API tokens with scopes. Auto TLS Certificates on demand and wildcards through ACME. Backups Restore an app to a moment from its own backups: the latest one before it. On by default. Bulk Mail Campaigns to your app's own users, with audiences from a collection, a view or SQL. Cache Cache buckets for every app in the process from one shared store: bytes or Go values, a budget per bucket, LRU/MRU/FIFO/LIFO eviction, TTLs, a cold disk tier that keeps identical values once. Config The pocketone.yaml config file, with secrets in a .env beside it. Deploy pocketone deploy, dev, pull and logs, and the deploy API. Desktop Build your PocketOne app into a native desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux, one executable each, from any machine. JSVM PocketOne's JS engine: one QuickJS VM per app, real globals, async handlers, hard limits. MCP An MCP endpoint at /mcp so agents can manage your app and call its tools. Pages Server-rendered pages from a pb_pages folder (formerly PocketPages). PITR Point-in-time restore of your database with Litestream. On by default. Remotes Named remotes and saved logins for the pocketone command. S3 Fallback A default bucket for uploads and backups when an instance has no S3 of its own. S3 Redirect File downloads as short-lived signed S3 redirects. Settings One API for the settings an app's admins change for its extensions. On by default. Templates Theme an extension's own pages (the OAuth sign-in screens): eject its templates to pb_templates and edit them. UI Cache Dashboard cache headers that let updates through browsers and CDNs. On by default. Upgrade pocketone upgrade to the latest release, keeping the old executable. Vacuum Compact your app's SQLite databases on a schedule, so space freed by deleted records goes back to the disk. WASM Bring your own WASM: Go, Rust or Zig modules called from page code, each a closed box.

title: Extensions
heading: Run many instances
text: Host hundreds of PocketBase instances in one process, across regions. Docker A host provider that runs each instance in its own container. Edge Forwards each request to the edge that owns the instance. Firewall Peer allow-lists, trusted proxies and rate limits for a host. Mothership A control plane and its edges, across regions. Multisite Many instances behind one listener, routed by hostname, run by one provider. Pocker Hundreds of PocketBase instances in one Go process, routed by hostname. Sandbox Confines untrusted JS hooks, SQL and outbound network. Schedules Planned. Scheduled webhooks that wake sleeping instances. Stats Measures disk use and last request for each instance a host serves.

title: Extensions
heading: Services for your instances
text: Shared services a host gives every instance it runs. Mail Relay Outgoing mail for instances without SMTP, through your relay, with limits. Server Timing Server-Timing headers for each step of a request.

title: Extensions
heading: Sell it as a service
text: Accounts, quotas and billing, for running PocketBase as a service. Lemon Squeezy Adapter Planned. Lemon Squeezy as the billing provider. Multitenant Planned. Accounts that own instances: quotas, owner logins, tokens and an API. Multitenant Billing Planned. Plans, quotas and the billing provider hook for Multitenant.

title: Extensions
heading: For extension authors
text: The extension contract and tools for building and testing extensions. Bundle An app's hooks, migrations and public files embedded in the binary. Contracts The versioned interfaces extensions use to work together, and the generator that writes their plumbing. Dev Users Local testing only: a superuser and a user with password "password". Extension Kit The extension contract: one extension works on every app, standalone or hosted. Mail Trap Dev mode: mail from an app without SMTP lands in a built-in inbox. Standard Set The extensions every PocketOne app has, as one set a host configures.

title: JSVM
text: Version 0.1.1 · Owners: @benallfree PocketOne's JS engine for pb_hooks and pb_migrations . It runs the same JS API as PocketBase ( $app , onX , routerAdd , cronAdd , $http , $security , ...) on QuickJS, with one VM per app: Real globals. Every hook file runs in the app's one global scope, so top-level helpers, constants and state are visible to every handler. No more require() inside each handler. ES modules. .pb.mjs (and TypeScript .pb.ts / .pb.mts ) hook files and modules use import / export , including top-level await ; .pb.js and .pb.cjs stay scripts with require() . Both share the same module instances. TypeScript. .ts , .mts and .cts hooks, migrations and modules run directly (types stripped by esbuild, linked into the binary), with error positions in your .ts source. Async. Handlers can be async . Every Go function has an .async(...) twin that runs off the VM and returns a promise, so one app serves other requests while it waits: await $app.findRecordById.async("posts", id) . Hard limits per app. A memory cap (JS heap plus Go objects JS holds), a CPU and a wall-clock budget per task, and caps on queued tasks and async calls. A runaway script stops with an error; other apps in the process keep running. Real error positions. Stack traces name pb_hooks/ : . Every PocketOne app runs on it: a standalone app or an instance on a multisite host, whatever the runtime. PocketBase's own plugins/jsvm (goja) is for pure PocketBase compatibility only: jsvm: goja under app: in pocketone.yaml (or --jsvm goja ) runs a standalone app on it, with pages, $mcp , $apiTokens , $bulkmail and JS contracts off. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: JSVM
heading: Install
text: The engine is pure Go (QuickJS translated to Go by modernc.org/libquickjs, the way PocketBase uses modernc.org/sqlite), so it needs no cgo: CGO_ENABLED=0 builds and cross-compiles work as with stock PocketBase. In your own Go build, register it where you'd register plugins/jsvm : jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", MigrationsDir: "pb_migrations"}) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm .

title: JSVM
heading: Configure
text: Config takes PocketBase's jsvm fields ( HooksDir , HooksWatch , HooksFilesPattern , MigrationsDir , MigrationsFilesPattern , TypesDir ; HooksPoolSize is accepted and ignored) plus: OnInit func(rt js.Runtime) : add globals after everything else is set up. VM : the limits. MemoryLimit (default 64 MiB), TaskBudget (JS time per task, default 5 s), TaskWall (wall time per task, Go calls included, default 30 s), QueueSize , MaxAsync , MaxPumpDepth . Array methods that walk every index ( join , indexOf , slice , forEach , concat , flat , ...) and arrays passed to Go throw a RangeError past MemoryLimit / 16 elements: QuickJS doesn't check TaskBudget inside those loops, and a sparse array ( new Array(1e9) ) or array-like costs no memory, so the cap is what stops them. No dense array that long fits in MemoryLimit . Extensions : values that extend it (below).

title: JSVM
heading: Use
text: Write hooks and migrations as in PocketBase's JS docs; they run unchanged. What's new: // pb_hooks/main.pb.js const cache = new Map() routerAdd("GET", "/post/{slug}", async (e) = { const slug = e.request.pathValue("slug") if (!cache.has(slug)) { cache.set(slug, await e.app.findFirstRecordByData.async("posts", "slug", slug)) } return e.json(200, cache.get(slug)) }) Hook files run before the app opens its database, as in PocketBase, so a $app query at a file's top level fails. Read data in onBootstrap after e.next() , or in a handler: let users = null onBootstrap((e) = { e.next() users = e.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("users") }) Globals live as long as the app's VM. A restart, a hooks reload or running out of memory starts a fresh one, so keep durable data in the database. After an await , other requests may have run: use e.app , not the global $app , and keep transactions short across await s (they hold SQLite's write lock). Use .async for anything slow ( $http.send , sleep , slow queries). Without it, other requests still run while a call waits, but they nest on one stack and wait on each other: under load, a plain sleep(100) served 19 requests a second where await sleep.async(100) served 481 (benchmark). process.env and a small Buffer ( from , toString with utf8, base64, hex) are there.

title: JSVM
heading: Modules: import and require
text: Name a file for what it is: .mjs is an ES module, .cjs is CommonJS. A plain .js file is CommonJS, so existing PocketBase hooks run unchanged (inside node_modules , Node's rule applies: "type": "module" in the package's package.json makes its .js files ES modules). TypeScript is written as ES modules, so .ts and .mts are ES modules and .cts is the CommonJS exception. pb_hooks/ .pb.mjs , .pb.ts , .pb.mts ES module: import , export , top-level await , import.meta export / import ; its top-level names are private pb_hooks/ .pb.js , .pb.cjs , .pb.cts script in the app's one global scope, with require() globals pb_migrations/ .mjs , .ts , .mts ES module each migration has its own scope either way pb_migrations/ .js , .cjs , .cts script in its own function scope All of them run in the app's one VM: scripts and modules share the global object (a module can read a script's globals) and one instance of every module. // pb_hooks/lib/store.mjs export const state = { hits: 0 } export const bump = () = ++state.hits // pb_hooks/main.pb.mjs import { bump } from "./lib/store.mjs" import legacy from "./lib/legacy.cjs" // CommonJS: module.exports is the default export import { hello } from "some-package" // node_modules, CommonJS or ES const { greeting } = await import("./lib/greeting.mjs") // top-level await: done before the app serves routerAdd("GET", "/hit", (e) = e.json(200, { hits: bump() })) import and require() resolve the same way: relative paths ( .js , .mjs , .cjs , .json and index. tried in turn), then node_modules packages by package.json exports (the import or require condition) or main . A module loads once per app, however many files import or require it, so its state is shared by every request. Importing a CommonJS module gives its module.exports as the default export, its keys as named exports, and the same instance require() returns. require() of an ES module returns its namespace (the same instance import gives), as in Node 22, as long as the module has no top-level await ; for one that does, use await import("./lib/x.mjs") .

title: JSVM
heading: TypeScript
text: .ts , .mts and .cts files run as they are: esbuild strips the types when the file loads, and each file's source map is kept, so an error names pb_hooks/main.pb.mts:12:5 in your source, not in the stripped code. There's no type checking at runtime. Check with tsc --noEmit or your editor; types.d.ts and tsconfig.json in the project root type the whole JS API. Imports may name the compiled file, as TypeScript's NodeNext style does: import { add } from "./math.js" loads math.ts when there's no math.js . import type and other type-only imports disappear, so a .pb.cts script can use them and stay a script. A .cts module may still be written with import / export ; it's turned into CommonJS.

title: JSVM
heading: Types
text: When the app starts, types.d.ts in the project root (the folder holding pb_hooks , next to pb_data and pocketone.yaml ) gets the declarations of the whole JS API, for your editor and tsc : PocketBase's API generated from PocketOne's core (its extra hooks included), by PocketBase's own generator. What this engine adds ( pocketone.d.ts ): .async on every Go function, fully typed ( await $app.findRecordById.async(...) is a Promise ), require , process , Buffer , console , import.meta . Each extension's own API, for the extensions on in that app ( $mcp , $apiTokens , $bulkmail , onContracts and the contracts' action hooks). Beside it, the app writes a tsconfig.json when the folder has none, so your editor and tsc --noEmit work right away. It's yours from then on: the app never overwrites it. { "compilerOptions": { "target": "ES2022", "module": "ESNext", "moduleResolution": "Bundler", "lib": ["ES2022"], "strict": true, "noEmit": true, "allowImportingTsExtensions": true, "skipLibCheck": true }, "include": ["types.d.ts", "pb_hooks/ / ", "pb_migrations/ / ", "pb_pages/ / "] } skipLibCheck skips two type errors inside PocketBase's own generated declarations. Commit both files: a fresh checkout is then typed before the app first runs, and a diff in types.d.ts shows what an upgrade or a new extension changed in the JS API. Empty hook files get a /// line. Config.TypesDir puts both somewhere else. With hooks embedded in the binary (Bundle) and no TypesDir , neither is written. In a PocketOne checkout, go generate in ext/jsvm regenerates the declarations after a core change (the TestTypes tests fail until you do).

title: JSVM
heading: Integrations
text: Extensions plug in through Config.Extensions with the engine-neutral types in ext/extkit/js . A value implements any of: OnInit(rt) : set up the VM. BindJS(app, rt) : expose a Go API. TypeScript() : declare it for editors and tsc (appended to types.d.ts ). FilterTypes(decl) : change the finished declarations (the sandbox declares what it hides never ). OnCall(rt) : wrap every handler call; an error refuses it. HTTPClient(rt) : the client $http.send uses. HookFiles , MigrationFiles , Modules : hooks, migrations and require() modules from somewhere other than disk. OnLoad(rt, root, file, content) : wrap loading each hook file. js.Run(app, fn) runs Go code on the app's VM; a js.Func kept from JS can be called from any goroutine. Bundle uses these to serve hooks and migrations embedded in the binary.

title: JSVM
heading: Example
text: // Command example serves example/pb_hooks with the jsvm extension: one QuickJS VM for the app, so the hook file's // top-level helpers and state are visible to every handler. // // cd example && go run . serve // curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hello/world package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", MigrationsDir: "pb_migrations"}) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: JSVM
heading: How it works
text: Each app's VM is owned by one goroutine, its loop; everything that touches the VM runs there. Go code elsewhere posts tasks and waits. A Go call made from JS that fires a hook runs it inline, so Go → JS → Go → JS works. Go values cross live through two QuickJS classes: GoObject (property get/set/has/keys go to Go by reflection, with PocketBase's JS names) and GoFunc (calls go to Go). Each holds a handle into the VM's table; QuickJS's refcounting frees it as soon as JS drops it. Memory: QuickJS caps its own heap. Go objects JS holds are charged to the same budget: a per-type estimate, and a reachability walk for fresh results of Go calls. QuickJS is modernc.org/libquickjs, Bellard's QuickJS translated to Go, so there is no cgo. It runs about as fast as goja; deep recursion stops at VM.StackSize (QuickJS stack slots, about one per call; default 5000) with "InternalError: stack overflow". Benchmarks and the red team (27 attacks against 50 VMs in one process) are in the package's tests ( ASYNCVM_BENCH=1 , ASYNCVM_REDTEAM=1 ).

title: JSVM

text: MIT

title: Mail Relay
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Outgoing mail for instances on a multisite host that haven't set up SMTP, when they share one process: isolates (an isolate runtime such as Pocker). Stock PocketBase falls back to the host's sendmail when SMTP is off. With apps sharing a process, that would run sendmail on the shared host for every tenant. With this extension: SMTP on in an instance's Settings → Mail: the app sends the mail itself. Bring your own SMTP always wins. SMTP off: the mail goes through your relay as @ , within per-instance limits. sendmail never runs. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Mail Relay
heading: Install
text: Mail Relay is not in the pocketone binary. In your own host build, add it to the standard set your runtime gets ( Standard on a Pocker server), with your sending domain and relay: set.Add(mailrelay.New(mailrelay.Config{ Domain: "mail.example.com", Upstream: mailrelay.SMTPUpstream{Addr: "smtp.provider.com:587", Username: "…", Password: "…"}, })) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/mailrelay . It also registers on a standalone app, but a standalone app can set up its own SMTP and doesn't need a relay.

title: Mail Relay
heading: The relay (Go)
text: Domain and Upstream are required; the host doesn't start without them. Domain : every relayed message is From @Domain . Upstream : what delivers the mail. SMTPUpstream ships here: Addr (host:port), optional Username and Password (PLAIN auth, only over TLS or to localhost), ImplicitTLS for port 465 (otherwise STARTTLS when the server offers it), and Timeout (default 30 s). It dials with its own dialer, so Pocker's egress rules for tenants (public addresses only) don't block a relay on a private address. Anything with Send(ctx, from, to, raw) works, for example an Amazon SES SendRawEmail sender. LocalPart : picks an instance's address from its id. The default is the first label of the id, lowercased: blog.localhost → blog . Limits: PerMinute (default 20) and Daily (default 200) per instance, MaxRecipients (To + Cc + Bcc, default 5) and MaxSize (encoded message, default 1 MiB) per message.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Defaults for every instance (pocketone.yaml)
text: mailrelay: { per_minute: 20, daily: 200 } Limits set in Go win over this section. Each instance can override it (see Per-instance settings).

title: Mail Relay
heading: Use
text: Once it's in, there's nothing to run. Each instance's mail is relayed whenever its SMTP is off. Settings → Mail in an instance's dashboard shows its superusers the relay: the address it sends as, its limits and how many messages it sent today. When sending is off for the instance, it says so and points to the SMTP settings. The app's log (Admin Logs, which Pocker copies to the instance's own log) gets one line per message, with masked addresses: mailrelay: sent from=blog@… to=a @x.org . Refusals and upstream failures are warnings. A refused message returns an error to whoever triggered the mail, such as a password-reset request: sending off, too many recipients, too large, or the limit reached.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Works with
text: Contracts Provides mail.fallback/v1 : with SMTP off, an app's mail goes to the contract's providers in order ( providers: { mail.fallback/v1: [mailtrap, mailrelay] } ); Mail Relay sends it within the instance's limits. Multisite What it's built for: isolates, instances that share the host's process (an isolate runtime such as Pocker). Every instance gets the relay, its own address and its own limits. Mail Trap In development, point SMTPUpstream at the trap's SMTP port and every relayed message lands in one inbox, tagged with the instance. The example below does this. Bulk Mail Campaigns go through PocketBase's mailer by default, so with SMTP off they are relayed and count against the instance's limits.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Per-instance settings (pocker)
text: Each instance can override the defaults in its extensions.mailrelay settings, from instances.yaml or your instance source (for example, per plan): instances: id: free-plan-app extensions: { mailrelay: { send: false } } # refuse its mail unless it uses its own SMTP id: big-app extensions: { mailrelay: { per_minute: 60, daily: 2000 } } A change to these settings restarts the instance's app on its next request. Use send: false , not enabled: false , to stop an instance sending. enabled: false turns the extension off for that instance, and with SMTP off PocketBase then falls back to the host's sendmail . Don't set it when apps share a process.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Building on Mail Relay
text: Your own upstream. Implement mailrelay.Upstream ( Send(ctx, from, to, raw) ) to deliver through an API. Your own hooks first. The relay runs after the app's own onMailerSend hooks, so they can still change or drop a message. Go API. ( mailrelay.Extension).Address(id) returns the From address an instance sends as. settings/v1 (superusers): GET /api/_c/settings/v1/get?extension=mailrelay returns the instance's relay status, a read-only section: active , send , address , perMinute , daily , sentToday .

title: Mail Relay
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs a Pocker host whose relay sends to the dev mail trap, so every instance's mail lands in one inbox at http://127.0.0.1:8025. Run go run ./example --dev from this folder, then trigger a password reset on any instance: curl -X POST http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/collections/users/request-password-reset -d email=user@example.com Log in to an instance's dashboard as admin@example.com / password to see the relay on Settings → Mail. --listen changes the instances' port; P1_MAILTRAP_HTTP and P1_MAILTRAP_SMTP change the trap's. // Command example is a Pocker build with mailrelay, relaying into PocketOne's dev mail trap: every instance // without its own SMTP sends as @mail.localhost, and all of it lands in one inbox. // // go run ./example --dev // // Then trigger mail on any instance, for example a password reset (each instance has the test user below): // // curl -X POST http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/collections/users/request-password-reset -d email=user@example.com // curl -X POST http://beta.localhost:8090/api/collections/users/request-password-reset -d email=user@example.com // // and read it in PocketOne's dev mail trap at http://127.0.0.1:8025 (filter by instance; P1_MAILTRAP_HTTP and // P1_MAILTRAP_SMTP change its ports). Settings → Mail in each dashboard shows the relay. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "context" "flag" "log" "os" "os/signal" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/mailrelay" "pocketone.dev/ext/mailtrap" "pocketone.dev/ext/pocker" "pocketone.dev/ext/standard" ) func main() { dev := flag.Bool("dev", false, "serve any hostname (alpha.localhost, beta.localhost, ...); otherwise instances.yaml is required") listen := flag.String("listen", "", "HTTP address for the instances (default :8090)") flag.Parse() cfg := pocker.DefaultConfig() cfg.Dev = cfg.Dev dev if listen != "" { cfg.Listen = listen } ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt) defer stop() // The dev mail trap (ext/mailtrap) stands in for the operator's real relay (SES, a provider's SMTP, ...) inbox, err := mailtrap.Default("mailrelay example: the relay sends to the trap") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } srv := &pocker.Server{ Config: cfg, Standard: standard.New(), // every instance gets the standard extensions Extensions: []pocker.Extension{ mailrelay.New(mailrelay.Config{ Domain: "mail.localhost", Upstream: mailrelay.SMTPUpstream{Addr: inbox.SMTPAddr}, }), }, // local testing: every instance gets superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" SetupApp: func(_ pocker.Instance, app core.App) error { return devusers.Ensure(app) }, } if err := srv.Run(ctx); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Mail Relay
heading: How it works
text: The extension binds PocketBase's OnMailerSend on every instance, last, after the app's own hooks. No core change. When SMTP is off it doesn't call e.Next() , so PocketBase's sendmail fallback never runs. It relays the message in-process instead. Nothing is written to the instance's settings. A backup restored somewhere else has no relay credentials in it, and falls back to stock PocketBase behavior. For each message: Check it's allowed. May this instance send ( send )? Are there no more than 5 recipients (To + Cc + Bcc)? Is the encoded size no more than 1 MiB? Count it. Each message counts once against the instance's limits, however many recipients it has. The day resets at midnight UTC. Counts are kept in memory. Set the sender. The From address becomes @ . The display name is kept, minus anything that looks like an address or a link. The app's own sender address becomes Reply-To , unless it's PocketBase's @example.com placeholder. Build and send. Bcc stays out of the headers. An X-Pocker-Instance header is added, then the message goes to the Upstream . Log it to the app's log.

title: Mail Relay
heading: License
text: MIT

title: Mail Trap
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree A development mail catcher (like MailDev or Mailpit) for testing an extension or app that sends mail. In dev mode, an app whose SMTP is off sends its mail here instead of the host's sendmail , and you read it at http://127.0.0.1:8025. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Mail Trap
heading: Install
text: Mail Trap is built into pocketone , for every app it runs: a standalone app, or an instance on a multisite host. There's nothing to install: run pocketone serve --dev with SMTP off and it's active. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: app := pocketbase.New() mailtrap.MustRegister(app) app.Start() With ext/standard's set, add it as an extra, as the stock binary does: set.Add(mailtrap.New()) . The module is pocketone.dev/ext/mailtrap .

title: Mail Trap
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section or settings screen. It turns itself on only when both are true: the app is in dev mode ( serve --dev , or a dev instance on a multisite host), and the app's SMTP is off (Settings → Mail). Turn SMTP on, or run without --dev , and it does nothing. Two environment variables move its ports: P1_MAILTRAP_HTTP 127.0.0.1:8025 (the web inbox) P1_MAILTRAP_SMTP 127.0.0.1:1025 (SMTP) Never expose these ports: anyone who can reach them can read the mail.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Use
text: Start the app with --dev . It prints the inbox address once it's active. Make your extension or app send mail: a verification, a password reset, $app.newMailClient() , a bulk mail campaign. Each caught message is also printed as one line in the terminal. Open http://127.0.0.1:8025. The list refreshes every 2 seconds. Click a message to see it as HTML , Text or Raw source. Clear empties the inbox. It keeps the last 500 messages, in memory only; they're gone when the process exits. If its ports are taken, it still catches mail and prints each message in the terminal.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Works with
text: Contracts Provides mail.fallback/v1 : with SMTP off, an app's mail goes to the contract's providers in order ( providers: { mail.fallback/v1: [mailtrap, mailrelay] } ); in dev mode Mail Trap takes it, otherwise it passes it on. Multisite With an isolate runtime (Pocker), one inbox for every dev instance. Each message is labeled with the instance that sent it (its X-Pocker-Instance header), and the inbox filters by instance. Mail Relay Mail Relay's example uses the trap's SMTP port as its relay, so relayed mail goes through the real SMTP path and lands here. Bulk Mail In dev mode with SMTP off, campaign mail lands in the inbox instead of being sent.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Building on Mail Trap
text: Its hook runs last. It binds OnMailerSend after the app's own hooks, so your onMailerSend hooks still run and can change the message first. When it takes a message it never calls the next handler, so sendmail never runs. SMTP for other tools. The SMTP listener accepts any message (and any AUTH), so anything that speaks SMTP can send to it. Go API. mailtrap.Default(reason) returns the process-wide trap, starting it on first use. A Trap has Messages() , Clear() , Add(from, to, raw, label) and AddMessage(msg, label) , and Handler() serves the inbox. Trap{SMTPAddr, HTTPAddr}.Start(ctx) runs a separate trap, for example in a test. Inbox API. GET /api/messages (newest first, without bodies), GET /api/messages/{id} , GET /api/messages/{id}/raw (.eml) and DELETE /api/messages , on the inbox address.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app in dev mode with the trap. Run go run ./example serve --dev from this folder, request a password reset for user@example.com (password password ) from the dashboard (log in as admin@example.com / password ), and read the mail at http://127.0.0.1:8025. // Command example runs one app in dev mode with the dev mail trap: request a password reset for user@example.com // in the dashboard and read the mail at http://127.0.0.1:8025. // // go run ./example serve --dev package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/mailtrap" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) mailtrap.MustRegister(app) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Mail Trap
heading: How it works
text: It's built on PocketBase's own OnMailerSend hook (the same way Mail Relay takes over an instance's mail), so PocketBase is unchanged. It used to live in core ( tools/mailer/trap.go ); it moved here on 2026-11-13.
