text: // pb_pages/auth/oauth/+page.ts module.exports = { post(ctx) { ctx.session.requestOAuth2(ctx.req.body().provider) }, } requestOAuth2 stores its state in a cookie and redirects the user to Google's consent screen.

title: Speedrun: Google OAuth2
heading: 4. Callback
text: // pb_pages/auth/oauth/confirm/+page.ts module.exports = { load(ctx) { try { ctx.session.signInWithOAuth2(ctx.req.query('state'), ctx.req.query('code')) } catch (e) { return { error: e.message } } return ctx.res.redirect('/') }, }

title: Speedrun: Google OAuth2
heading: 5. Migration
text: Set up Google OAuth2 in a PocketBase migration: migrate( (app) = { const users = app.findCollectionByNameOrId('users') users.oauth2.enabled = true users.oauth2.providers = [ { name: 'google', clientId: 'YOUR_CLIENT_ID', clientSecret: 'YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET', }, ] app.save(users) }, (app) = { const users = app.findCollectionByNameOrId('users') users.oauth2.enabled = false users.oauth2.providers = [] app.save(users) } )

title: Speedrun: Google OAuth2
heading: 6. Protected routes
text: // pb_pages/account/+middleware.ts module.exports = (ctx, next) = { if (!ctx.auth) return ctx.res.redirect('/login') return next() }

title: Speedrun: Google OAuth2
heading: 7. Auth state in the UI
text: Welcome, Log out Log in

title: Speedrun: Google OAuth2
heading: 8. Logout
text: // pb_pages/logout/+page.ts module.exports = { post(ctx) { ctx.session.signOut() return ctx.res.redirect('/') }, } See Authentication and the auth plugin.

title: Speedrun: Google OAuth2
heading: Troubleshooting
text: Common issues and solutions: Invalid redirect URI : Ensure your redirect URI exactly matches what's configured in Google Cloud Console Consent screen not showing : Make sure you've properly configured the OAuth consent screen Authentication failed : Verify your client ID and secret are correctly copied to the dashboard

title: Speedrun: Google OAuth2
heading: Security Considerations
text: Always use HTTPS in production Keep your client secret secure Regularly rotate credentials Review Google OAuth2 access regularly in your Google Cloud Console

title: Setting up a new email domain in Google Suite
text: The process of setting up a new email domain in Google Suite involves several steps. In this guide, we will walk you through the process, from adding the domain to activating Gmail and setting up a catch-all email. By following these steps, you'll be able to configure your email domain effectively and ensure smooth communication within your organization. Let's get started! Add the domain Domain Verification Activating Gmail Adding a Catch-All Email Test Your Email Setup Add a Sender Account to Gmail

title: Setting up a new email domain in Google Suite
heading: Add the domain
text: Go to the domains admin and add a new domain. Set up an "alias domain," which involves a verification step where you need to update your DNS records. Otherwise, you may have to do the following steps manually.

title: Setting up a new email domain in Google Suite
heading: Domain Verification
text: If you're using Cloudflare as your DNS manager, Google will automatically recognize it and add the necessary DNS records. Then, wait for domain verification to complete. It should be fast.

title: Setting up a new email domain in Google Suite
heading: Activating Gmail
text: Once again, Cloudflare makes it easy and automatic. Otherwise, this may involve manual steps if Google is not integrated with your DNS provider.

title: Setting up a new email domain in Google Suite
heading: Adding a Catch-All Email
text: I set up a catch-all email so that any email sent to @pocodex.dev is routed to ben@pocodex.dev if the specific email address doesn’t exist. This is optional, but you might want to consider what happens to unrecognized email addresses in your setup. This Google help article covers it, but here it is below too: I like to go to Default Routing and add a rule: Use a regex to match the entire domain like @pocodex\.dev$ . I also like to prepend [CATCHALL] - to the subject so I know that it wasn't sent to my "real" address. Redirect the emails to your "real" email address: Finally, make sure you only perform this on unrecognized email addresses.

title: Setting up a new email domain in Google Suite
heading: Test Your Email Setup
text: Send an email to yourself using the new domain to ensure that everything is working correctly. You may need to wait a bit for the MX records to propagate. Just because Google says everything is verified doesn't mean the Internet at large has received the memo. If you want to be extra sure, try sending from a completely different email provider like Proton or AOL. Once you receive messages, you're all set!

title: Setting up a new email domain in Google Suite
heading: Add a Sender Account to Gmail
text: Sometimes you might want to send email FROM your domain, such as replies or customer messages. To do that, go to your user settings in Gmail and add an account:

text: Prerequisite: Make sure you can receive emails first Create an SES Identity Add DNS Records Add a custom FROM domain Add DMARC settings Verifying the Setup Submit for Approval Creating SMTP Credentials Configure SMTP in the dashboard

title: Setting Up Email with Google Suite and AWS SES
heading: Prerequisite: Make sure you can receive emails first
text: To receive emails, you'll need an email provider. I use Google Suite, but you can choose any provider you prefer. Setting up a new email domain in Google Suite. (Someone should write about how to do it using Proton.me)

title: Setting Up Email with Google Suite and AWS SES
heading: Create an SES Identity
text: Log in to your Amazon SES account and follow their getting started guide to create a FROM address and sending domain. Make sure you're in the region you prefer. This is important if you have existing domains because AWS frowns upon approving multiple sending regions. Start by creating an Identity:

title: Setting Up Email with Google Suite and AWS SES
heading: Add DNS Records
text: You'll need to add DNS records provided by SES to your DNS provider. Unlike Google Suite, you'll need to enter these values manually. They do not provide integrations with any DNS providers. AWS SES DNS Setup Note for Cloudflare users: If you’re using Cloudflare, make sure these records are not proxied.

title: Setting Up Email with Google Suite and AWS SES
heading: Add a custom FROM domain
text: Deliverability is better if you add a custom FROM domain: It requires a few additional DNS entries. Note that the MX priority goes into a separate field, not the MX server field:

title: Setting Up Email with Google Suite and AWS SES
heading: Add DMARC settings

title: Setting Up Email with Google Suite and AWS SES
heading: Verifying the Setup
text: After adding the DNS records, go back to AWS SES and wait for the domain to show as verified. Then, send a verification email. You should receive it if everything is set up correctly. If verification takes too long, go to Identities DKIM , click Edit , then Save to trigger an immediate re-verification.

title: Setting Up Email with Google Suite and AWS SES
heading: Submit for Approval
text: Before you can send emails to anyone, you must submit everything for approval in AWS SES. This step is crucial to avoid issues when sending emails outside your verified domain. If you have previously had a domain approved, you may be able to skip this step. To find out, simply try sending a test message to anything with a different domain.

title: Setting Up Email with Google Suite and AWS SES
heading: Creating SMTP Credentials
text: Create SMTP credentials in the AWS SES console. These credentials will be used in your app's dashboard for sending emails.

title: Setting Up Email with Google Suite and AWS SES
heading: Configure SMTP in the dashboard
text: Once you have your SMTP credentials, head over to the dashboard (Settings → Mail). Enter the SMTP credentials in the dashboard, and ensure the SENDER address is correctly set. If SES hasn't verified your email yet, you can test it by sending an email to test@ , which should go through if the domain is the same.

title: Starter Kits
text: To start a new app from a starter kit, run: pocketone pages create myapp --starter Without --starter , pocketone pages create myapp creates a plain app (the minimal kit). pocketone pages starters lists the kits. The folder must not exist yet. Then run it: cd myapp pocketone serve --dir ./pb_data pocketone keeps pb_data next to its executable unless you pass --dir ; pb_pages and pb_migrations are found next to pb_data . Each starter kit is an ordinary pb_pages folder written against the v1 API, in TypeScript with ETS templates, so everything in these docs applies to it. The tsx kit starts an app in the component style instead. minimal A minimal PocketPages starter with just the basics pocketpages-minimal.pockethost.io mvp MVP.css, a minimalist classless CSS framework pocketpages-mvp.pockethost.io auth Password, anonymous, OTP and OAuth2 sign-in, plus verification, password reset and email change pocketpages-auth.pockethost.io daisyui Tailwind CSS with DaisyUI components pocketpages-daisyui.pockethost.io daisyui-docs Documentation site template with DaisyUI and navigation pocketpages-daisyui-docs.pockethost.io htmx HTMX integration for dynamic interactions pocketpages-htmx.pockethost.io datastar Realtime chat and counter using Datastar pocketpages-datastar.pockethost.io tsx The minimal app written as TSX components (layout, page and a partial)

title: Serving Static Content in PocketPages
text: Any file in pb_pages that isn't a page ( .ets , .md or .tsx , or the JavaScript versions .ejs and .jsx ), a framework file ( +... ), private ( _... ) or ignored (names starting with - or . ) is a static file. It's served as-is at its path, with groups removed: pb_pages/ assets/ app.css - /assets/app.css logo.png - /assets/logo.png documents/ terms.pdf - /documents/terms.pdf (marketing)/ brochure.pdf - /brochure.pdf favicon.ico - /favicon.ico index.ets - / (a page, not static) The content type comes from the extension. The ETag comes from the content hash; a matching If-None-Match gets 304 . A static file and a page can't claim the same URL (startup error). For cache-friendly URLs, reference files through asset() .

title: Serving Static Content in PocketPages
heading: pb_pages and pb_public
text: A URL nothing in pb_pages matches goes on to pb_public , so you can keep using pb_public for files you don't want next to your pages.

title: TypeScript
text: PocketOne strips the types from .ts and .tsx files and runs them; it never checks them. To check them, use tsc or your editor with the types PocketOne writes for your app. When the app starts, it writes types.d.ts next to pb_pages (in the project folder, beside pb_data and pocketone.yaml ) with the declarations of the whole JS API, PocketPages included. PocketPages adds no globals: its types live in the pages namespace and you use them by name.

title: TypeScript
heading: Set up
text: The app also writes a tsconfig.json there when you don't have one. It includes types.d.ts , pb_hooks , pb_migrations and pb_pages , with JSX checking on ( "jsx": "preserve" , so no React runtime is needed). Start the app once, then run npx tsc -p . or open the folder in your editor. Commit both files, so a fresh checkout is typed before the app first runs. If you keep your own tsconfig.json , include types.d.ts and pb_pages/ / , and set "jsx": "preserve" and "skipLibCheck": true (PocketBase's generated declarations have two type errors of their own).

title: TypeScript
heading: The types
text: pages.Context ctx : req , res , data , params , route , auth , app and the helpers pages.Handlers A +page.ts or +api.ts : load , get , post , put , patch , delete pages.Middleware A +middleware.ts : (ctx, next) = ... pages.Config +config.ts pages.PluginFactory , pages.Plugin A custom plugin pages.Props A .tsx page, layout or partial; L types an include 's locals satisfies keeps your own return types and checks the shape: // pb_pages/products/[id]/+page.ts export default { async load(ctx) { ctx.data.product = await ctx.app.findRecordById.async('products', ctx.params.id) }, post(ctx) { const { qty } = ctx.req.body () return ctx.res.redirect( /products/${ctx.params.id} , { flash: Added ${qty} }) }, } satisfies pages.Handlers // pb_pages/admin/+middleware.ts const admin: pages.Middleware = (ctx, next) = { if (!ctx.auth) return ctx.res.redirect('/login') return next() } export default admin // pb_pages/_private/badge.tsx, rendered with ctx.include('badge', { label: 'new' }) export default function Badge({ label, asset }: pages.Props ) { return {label} } A component you import and use as gets only the props you pass it, not ctx or asset , so give it a props type of its own.

title: TypeScript
heading: Your own data, plugins and helpers
text: ctx.data accepts any key. To type yours, or what a custom plugin adds to ctx , add to the interfaces in a .d.ts file of your own, say pb_pages/_private/types.d.ts (in _private/ , so it isn't served like other files in pb_pages ): declare namespace pages { interface Data { product?: core.Record section?: string } interface Context { hello(): string // added by your plugin's extendContext } } ctx.session and ctx.realtime are typed as always there; at runtime they exist only when the auth and realtime plugins are on in +config.ts .

title: PITR
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Walkthrough for app owners: Point-in-time restore. This page is the technical reference. Point-in-time restore: your database as it was at any moment in the last few days, restored from the dashboard. History is recorded with Litestream, next to your data or in an S3-compatible bucket. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: PITR
heading: Install
text: PITR is built into pocketone and on by default . Every app it serves starts recording history the first time it serves; there's nothing to install. To run without it: pocketone serve --pitr=false In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: app := pocketbase.New() pitr.MustRegister(app, pitr.Config{}) app.Start()

title: PITR
heading: On, off and how far back
text: Set it in pocketone.yaml : pitr: enabled: true # false turns it off retention: 72h # how far back a restore can go snapshot_interval: 24h # how often a full copy is taken Or with flags, which win over the file: --pitr true Record history while serving. --pitr=false turns it off. --pitrRetention 72h How far back a restore can go. A shorter snapshot_interval makes restores faster and uses more storage.

title: PITR
heading: Where the history is stored
text: By default the history is kept next to your database, in pb_data/litestream/ . That protects you from mistakes in your data, but not from losing the disk. To keep it somewhere else, use your own S3-compatible bucket: Open Settings → Backups in the dashboard and find Point-in-time restore . Tick Store the history in my own S3 bucket and fill in the endpoint, bucket, region, access key and secret. Tick Force path-style addressing for MinIO and similar servers. The prefix defaults to litestream . Click Test connection to check that the bucket accepts a write, then Save . From then on the history is recorded in the bucket, starting with a fresh copy, so restores go back to the moment you saved. The secret is never shown again after saving. If the app runs with an encryption key ( --encryptionEnv ), the secret is stored encrypted.

title: PITR
heading: pitr:
text: Point-in-time restore: on by default, retention, snapshot interval. The --pitr and --pitrRetention flags win. enabled bool On unless false. The --pitr flag wins. retention duration How far back a restore can go. Default 72h. The --pitrRetention flag wins. snapshot_interval duration How often a full copy is taken. Default 24h. Shorter: faster restores, more storage.

title: PITR
heading: What's covered
text: Your database: records, collections, settings and superusers. Not uploaded files, pb_hooks , pb_public or the logs database. Use PocketBase's backups for those. History starts with the first change after PITR is turned on, and goes back as far as the retention allows (72 hours by default).

title: PITR
heading: Restore from the dashboard
text: Open Settings → Backups . Restore to a moment (the restore/v1 contract's section) shows how far back you can go; Point-in-time restore shows how big the history is and where it's stored. Under Restore to , pick a date and time, then click Restore . The app keeps serving while the old database is rebuilt, then restarts with it. Only superusers see this section.

title: PITR
heading: Undo a restore
text: The database you replaced is kept in pb_data/litestream/before-restore.db , and history keeps recording, so a restore can be undone. After a restore, the section shows when you restored and to what time, with an Undo this restore button.

title: PITR
heading: From the command line
text: pocketone pitr status pocketone pitr restore --at 2026-11-11T14:05:00Z --to /tmp/then.db # a copy, any time pocketone pitr restore --at 2026-11-11T14:05:00Z # in place --at takes an RFC 3339 time. With --to , you get a copy of the database as it was, to inspect or pull records from; the app keeps running. Without --to , run it while the server is stopped: the restore is swapped in when it next starts.

title: PITR
heading: What it costs
text: About 176 KiB of memory per serving app, and the storage for your history. Replication runs only while the app is serving, never during CLI commands.

title: PITR
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: PITR
heading: Commands
text: What it adds to the pocketone binary (CLI reference): pocketone pitr restore Restore the database as it was at --at, into --to, or in place on the next start pocketone pitr status Show the restorable window and history size

title: PITR
heading: restore/v1
text: points pocketone remote restore points GET /api/_c/restore/v1 restore_points restore_to pocketone remote restore to --at POST /api/_c/restore/v1/restore restore_restore_to

title: PITR
heading: Works with
text: Multisite PITR is in the standard set, so every instance that runs PocketOne has it, and a restore restarts only that instance. With an isolate runtime (Pocker), the pitr section sets the defaults for all of them, each instance can override enabled and retention (below), and sleeping instances cost nothing. S3 Fallback Mount litestream on a backend and every app without its own bucket keeps its history there, under its own prefix. An app's own bucket (Settings → Backups) still wins. Multitenant (planned) Sets each instance's enabled and retention from its plan, for example a plan without PITR. PocketBase backups pb_data/litestream/ is left out of backup zips, and restoring a zip doesn't wipe it.

title: PITR
heading: Per-instance settings (pocker)
text: Each instance can override enabled and retention in its extensions.pitr settings, from instances.yaml or a provider: instances: id: abc extensions: { pitr: { retention: 168h } } id: free-plan-app extensions: { pitr: { enabled: false } } Each instance's history goes to instances/ /litestream/ in the shared bucket, or its own pb_data/litestream/ . A bucket in an instance's settings is refused, so credentials never sit in instance data.

title: PITR
heading: Building on PITR
text: Store history somewhere else. PITR asks PocketBase for a filesystem of kind litestream ( pitr.Kind ) through OnFilesystemCreate . Answer it and the history goes to your filesystem; S3 Fallback works this way. Set it per instance. Write extensions.pitr.enabled and extensions.pitr.retention into an instance's settings; PITR reads them when the instance starts. Multitenant will work this way. Go API. ( pitr.Extension).Status(ctx, app) returns the restorable window, size, destination and last restore; Restore(ctx, app, at) restores an app to a time. restore/v1. PITR provides the restore/v1 contract (superusers): GET /api/_c/restore/v1 for the window, size, destination and last restore, POST /api/_c/restore/v1/restore with {"at": " "} to restore. Without PITR the same calls restore the latest backup before the moment (Backups), so clients and agents don't care which is on.

title: PITR
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app with point-in-time restore on, keeping three days. Run it with go run ./example serve from this folder. // Command example runs one PocketOne app with point-in-time restore: Litestream copies data.db continuously into // pb_data/litestream/, and Settings → Backups gets a "Point-in-time restore" section. // // go run ./example serve // go run ./example pitr status // go run ./example pitr restore --at 2026-11-11T14:05:00Z --to /tmp/then.db // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/pitr" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" pitr.MustRegister(app, pitr.Config{ Retention: 72 time.Hour, // on by default; Enabled: false turns it off // Bucket: &pitr.Bucket{Endpoint: "...", Bucket: "...", Region: "auto", AccessKey: "...", Secret: "...", Label: "EU"}, }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: PITR
heading: How it works
text: Go module pocketone.dev/ext/pitr , Litestream v0.5.18 (pinned). example/main.go runs one app with local history. Litestream continuously copies data.db to its destination: the app's own bucket (its PITR settings), else a filesystem of kind litestream (an OnFilesystemCreate handler, such as S3 Fallback), else pb_data/litestream/ . Buckets go through PocketBase's own S3 client, not the AWS SDK. Each LTX file's timestamp is kept in object metadata, so restoring to a time doesn't depend on upload times. Replication runs only while the app serves ( OnServe ), never for CLI commands. On terminate it's flushed and detached, so under pocker a sleeping instance costs nothing. A restore is built into a side file while the app keeps serving, then swapped in by app.Restart() . The replaced database is kept as pb_data/litestream/before-restore.db . Apps with different retention get separate Litestream stores, since Litestream applies retention per store. Cost per serving app: about 176 KiB of memory, 4 goroutines, 5 file descriptors. Binary: about +4 MiB.

title: Pocker
text: Version 0.1.1 · Owners: @benallfree Walkthrough: PocketBase isolates. This page is the technical reference. Many PocketOne instances in one process (like Docker, but for PocketOne), routed by hostname. Each instance is a normal app folder and starts on its first request, in tens of milliseconds. Pocker provides runtime/v1 for Multisite; its peer Docker runs each instance in a container instead. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Pocker
heading: Install
text: Pocker is built into pocketone . Add a multisite section to pocketone.yaml and pocketone serve hosts many instances instead of one app, with pocker as the runtime (docker too, when it has its docker section): multisite: {} In your own Go build, add it to the host's extensions ( examples/pocketone/multi.go is the stock binary's version), or run a pocker.Server on its own as the example does: h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath, Extensions: []multisite.Extension{ &pocker.Provider{ Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath, Standard: standard.New(), // every instance gets the standard set (tokens, mcp, pitr, ...) Extensions: []pocker.Extension{ myextension.New(), // your own PocketOne extensions, on every instance too }, }, }}) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/pocker .

title: Pocker
heading: Configure
text: The pocker section sets where instances live, the JS pool, outbound network and the default limits for every instance (keys below). Listeners, instances and the firewall are the Multisite sections ( server , instances , firewall ). multisite: {} instances: { file: ./instances.yaml } pocker: root: ./pb_root # one folder per instance: / hooks_pool_size: 2 egress_allow: [] # private networks instances may still reach max_js_execution: 30s # default limits; each instance can override them max_js_allocation: 64MiB isolate_config: # every instance's config, in pocketone.yaml's shape api-tokens: { enabled: false } isolate_config holds one section per extension the instances run (the standard set's members and your own extensions), each taking what an instance's extensions. takes. It is every instance's base: an instance's own extensions. overrides it key by key, so one instance can turn back on what isolate_config turns off. A section for an extension the instances don't run stops startup. The top-level sections of pocketone.yaml configure a single app; on a multisite host they don't reach the instances. An instance overrides any limit in its own limits (missing fields keep the default): instances: id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] limits: { max_js_execution: 60s, max_concurrent_js: 32 } Every instance runs the PocketOne code in the binary; an instance's version is ignored.

title: Pocker
heading: pocker:
text: Runtime provider pocker: instances run as isolates in this process (root folder, hooks pool, egress allow list, instance limit defaults). root string ./pb_root The folder holding one folder per instance: / . hooks_pool_size int 2 Ignored: each instance has one JS VM (ext/jsvm). Kept so existing configs load. max_js_execution duration 30s Longest any single JS call (hook, route, cron job, migration) may run. max_js_allocation int 67108864 Largest result a JS built-in may allocate in one step, such as 64MiB. max_call_stack_size int 2000 Deepest JS recursion allowed. max_sleep duration 10s Longest a JS sleep() call may wait. max_query_duration duration 30s Longest an SQL statement without its own deadline may run. http_send_max_timeout duration 1m0s Longest timeout a JS $http.send call may use. http_send_max_body int 10485760 Largest response body a JS $http.send call may read, such as 10MiB. max_concurrent_js int 16 JS calls an instance runs at once; more wait up to max_js_execution, then fail. egress_allow list of string Private networks (CIDRs) instances may still connect to. Default none: public addresses only. isolate_config map of map of interface Every instance's config, in pocketone.yaml's shape: one section per extension the instances run, such as api-tokens: {enabled: false}. Each takes what an instance's extensions. takes, and an instance's own extensions. overrides it.

title: Pocker
heading: Try it with any hostname
text: # pocketone.yaml server: { http: "127.0.0.1:8090" } multisite: {} instances: { dev: true } pocker: { root: ./pb_root } pocketone serve curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/health # creates and serves ./pb_root/blog.localhost In dev mode a hostname no instance maps becomes an instance named after it, its folder is made on first use, and it runs in dev mode. In production only the hostnames in the instances file are served (see Multisite).

title: Pocker
heading: Each instance
text: A normal app folder, / : pb_data , pb_hooks , pb_migrations , pb_public . Its dashboard is at https:// /_/ . Its JS hooks see only its own secrets , through $os.getenv and process.env . A change to its secrets , encryption_key , access , limits , dev , dir , superusers , private , extensions or remote restarts it if it's running (the app stops, then a fresh one starts, as in a process restart). A hostname change doesn't restart it. A change in pb_hooks restarts just that instance. A broken hooks file affects only that instance (below).

title: Pocker
heading: Broken hook files
text: In dev mode, a pb_hooks file that fails to load is logged and skipped, and the rest of the instance runs, so you can fix it live. Otherwise an instance doesn't start with a broken file. When a running instance's pb_hooks change, Pocker restarts it as PocketBase's watcher restarts a process: the running app stops (requests in flight are cut off), then a fresh app starts with the new files. Only one app has an instance's folder open at a time, so migrations and bootstrap code never run beside a live app. A broken file in production leaves the instance down: requests get 502 with the error, which also goes to the instance log, and the first request after a fix starts it.

title: Pocker
heading: Logs
text: The app's own logs (the dashboard's Logs) are per instance, in its pb_data . console. from JS hooks goes to /logs/exec.log as JSON lines ( message , stream , time ), rotated to exec.log.1 at 10 MiB. A start failure is written there too.

title: Pocker
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Routing, listeners, instances file and gates. Pocker is one of its runtimes (runtime/v1). Sandbox Every instance's JS hooks, SQL and outbound network run in it, so one instance can't reach another or the host. Firewall Peer allow-list and rate limits in front of every instance; per-instance limits in extensions.firewall . Auto TLS In the stock binary: certificates for the hostnames instances map ( autotls section). Server Timing In the stock binary: Server-Timing headers on every response. Mailtrap In the stock binary: dev instances with SMTP off send mail to a local inbox. Edge Instances another edge runs are forwarded there instead of started here. Stats Measures disk use and last request for each instance under root . PocketOne extensions In your own build, any extension such as PITR, S3 Fallback or Mail Relay runs on every instance, and an instance's extensions. settings override the extension's defaults. enabled: false turns it off for that instance.

title: Pocker
heading: Building on Pocker
text: Standard set (required). pocker.Provider.Standard (or pocker.Server.Standard , ManagerOptions.Standard ) is ext/standard's set, and Pocker won't start an instance without it: a server without one refuses to run, so no host can make an instance that lacks the standard extensions. Every instance gets its members, each turned off per instance with extensions. .enabled: false , and its startup lines ( standard: on: ... ) are in the instance's own log. Listing a member in Extensions too is an error. Instance files. The host provides instance.fs/v1 on its scope ( Manager.Files() ): host-side code asks it for an instance's folder, takes its writers' lock, and restarts it around a change ( WithInstanceStopped , then StartInstance ). It isn't host-provided to the instances: inside an instance, its own app's provider answers. Instance tokens. The host provides instance.tokens/v1 on its scope ( Manager.Tokens() ): host-side code checks an API token one of its instances issued, with that instance's own api-tokens/v1 (starting the instance if it isn't running). A host uses it to accept an instance's own tokens on the routes it answers for that instance, so pocketone login and clone , which sign in to the instance, work there. Contracts the host provides. Server.Host (or Provider.Host ) is the host's contract scope. A contract the host provides for its instances steps aside inside each instance's app, and the host answers it on the instance's hostname in Server.InstanceRoutes (or Provider.InstanceRoutes , ManagerOptions.InstanceRoutes ): after the gates and the blocked answer, before the app. pocker.Remote(m, host) is remote/v1 for Pocker instances (restart through the Manager, logs from logs/exec.log ); add your own auth: host := extkit.NewScope("multisite") srv.Host = host srv.OnStart = func(m pocker.Manager) { remotev1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(host, pocker.Remote(m, host)) } srv.InstanceRoutes = append(srv.InstanceRoutes, func(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return remotev1.W.HostHandler(host, multisite.InstanceID, myAuth, next) }) deploy/v1 works the same way with deploy.New(...) as the handler: deployv1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(host, ...) and extkit.HostRoutes(host, deployv1.Contract, multisite.InstanceID, next) as an instance route. Extensions. pocker.Provider.Extensions (or pocker.Server.Extensions ) takes any extkit.Extension , registered on each instance's app before it starts with that instance's extensions. settings. Host-level code can implement AppIniter , JSIniter , Starter , or be a host extension ( multisite.Extension , registered on the host like any other: servertiming, autotls). See POCKER.md. Setup per instance. SetupApp(inst, app) runs after migrations and before the app serves, e.g. to add a route checked against inst.Private . Manager. OnStart hands host code the Manager : WithInstanceStopped(ctx, id, fn) changes an instance's files while it's stopped (deploys, restores), StartInstance , Running , InstanceDir , LogInstance . Restarts. app.Restart() (a backup restore, PITR) restarts only that instance.

title: Pocker
heading: Example
text: A Pocker build with one extension: a Go route and an admin dashboard page on every instance, in dev mode. Run it from this folder with go run ./example , then open http://blog.localhost:8090/_/ (login admin@example.com / password ). // Command pocker-extension is a Pocker build with one extension: a Go route and an admin dashboard page, // added to every instance. See docs/extensions.md. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "context" "embed" "io/fs" "log" "net/http" "os" "os/signal" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/apis" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/pocker" "pocketone.dev/ext/standard" ) //go:embed ui var uiFiles embed.FS func main() { cfg := pocker.DefaultConfig() cfg.Dev = true // any hostname; drop this for production (instances.yaml required) ui, _ := fs.Sub(uiFiles, "ui") srv := &pocker.Server{ Config: cfg, Standard: standard.New(), // every instance gets the standard extensions (tokens, mcp, pages, pitr, ...) // Runs for every instance's app after its migrations, before it serves. SetupApp: func(inst pocker.Instance, app core.App) error { // local testing: every instance gets superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" if err := devusers.Ensure(app); err != nil { return err } app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { // a Go route, superuser only se.Router.GET("/api/hello", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { return e.JSON(http.StatusOK, map[string]string{"instance": inst.ID}) }).Bind(apis.RequireSuperuserAuth()) // an admin dashboard extension: ui/main.js is loaded by the dashboard before its router starts se.UIExtensions = append(se.UIExtensions, core.UIExtension{Name: "hello", FS: ui}) return se.Next() }) return nil }, } ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt) defer stop() if err := srv.Run(ctx); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Pocker
heading: Untrusted instances
text: Pocker runs every instance's JS hooks in the sandbox. For why that's safe enough to host code from people you don't know, and where it isn't, see How is this safe?. Memory is the main limit: only one-shot allocations are capped, so a hook that grows memory slowly affects the whole process. POCKER.md lists what the sandbox covers.

title: Pocker
heading: Reference
text: POCKER.md is the full guide: production pocketone.yaml , every instance field, extension interfaces, the sandbox, PocketBase changes and versions.

title: Pocker
text: Pocker hosts many PocketOne instances in one process. It is PocketOne itself (this repo tracks upstream PocketBase and shares its history) plus a small engine in this folder, run by the stock pocketone binary as a runtime/v1 provider (a multisite section in pocketone.yaml). One port, many instances. Each request's hostname maps to a canonical instance id. Each instance is a normal app folder, / ( pb_data , pb_hooks , pb_migrations , pb_public ), with its own environment for JS hooks ( $os.getenv , process.env ), its own JS migrations and its own settings encryption key. An instance's app starts on its first request (tens of milliseconds) and keeps running.

title: Pocker
heading: Dev mode: any hostname
text: # pocketone.yaml server: { http: "127.0.0.1:8090" } multisite: {} instances: { dev: true } pocker: { root: ./pb_root } pocketone serve curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/health # creates and serves ./pb_root/blog.localhost A hostname the instance source doesn't map uses the hostname itself as its id (lowercase, no port, no trailing dot; anything that isn't a safe folder name gets 400), its folder is created on first use, and apps run in dev mode. The instances file (or another source) is optional in dev mode; hosts it maps keep their own ids.

title: Pocker
heading: Production: mapped hostnames only
text: Without dev mode, Pocker serves only what an instance source maps. The built-in source is the instances section's YAML file (reloaded when it changes; the host refuses to start without it): # instances.yaml instances: id: blog # folder /blog hosts: [blog.example.com, www.blog.example.com] id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: sk_live_... } # the app's environment encryption_key: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef # encrypts the app's stored settings; not visible to JS access: { cors_origins: [https://shop.example.com] } extensions: { firewall: { trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] } } # settings for extensions, by name id: old hosts: [old.example.com] blocked: { status: 402, message: "Payment required" } Unknown hosts get 404 and no folder is ever created from a request. Ids are lowercase letters, digits, dots and dashes. Pocker runs whatever instances the host's instance.source/v1 provider supplies, and nothing else: the file by default. Hosting platforms provide that contract themselves instead (for example a control plane streaming the hostname - id map over SSE); a community mothership is one (the mothership section, ext/mothership). Tests provide it with sourcetest. pocketone.yaml for a production host (each extension owns its section; every field has a default): server: https: ":443" http: ":80" # redirects to HTTPS (and answers ACME HTTP-01 challenges) plain: [] # extra plain-HTTP listeners (no TLS, no redirect), e.g. a private network other servers forward on tls: { cert: /path/fullchain.pem, key: /path/privkey.pem } # re-read when they change; or the autotls section multisite: {} instances: { file: ./instances.yaml } pocker: root: ./pb_root hooks_pool_size: 2 egress_allow: [] # private networks apps may still reach (default none) # default limits for every instance (each instance can override them, see below) max_js_execution: 30s # any single JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) max_js_allocation: 64MiB # one-shot JS allocations max_call_stack_size: 2000 max_sleep: 10s max_query_duration: 30s # any SQL statement without its own deadline http_send_max_timeout: 60s http_send_max_body: 10MiB max_concurrent_js: 16 # JS calls an instance runs at once; more wait up to max_js_execution, then fail rate_limits: # per client IP and per instance; trusted clients get the trusted set ip_hourly: 1000 instance_hourly: 10000 ip_concurrent: 15 instance_concurrent: 250 file_weight: 0.1 # a /api/files request costs a tenth trusted: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_hourly: 20000, ip_concurrent: 50, instance_concurrent: 250 } # off: true # no rate limiting (the default in dev mode unless rate_limits is set) firewall: allow_cidrs: [] # peers allowed to connect (empty = everyone); others get 403 trusted_proxies: [] # peers whose client-IP headers are believed client_ip_headers: [CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP] trusted_clients: [] # client IPs with the trusted limits on every instance trusted_client_headers: [X-Client-IP] # a trusted client names its end user (own buckets) rate_limit_header_prefix: X-RateLimit # autotls: # automatic certificates (ACME, via CertMagic, Caddy's certificate engine) # auto: true # email: ops@example.com # ca: letsencrypt # letsencrypt (default), letsencrypt-staging, zerossl, or an ACME directory URL # storage: ./pb_root/.pocker-certs # domains: [" .example.com", "example.com"] # obtained up front; wildcards need dns # dns: { provider: cloudflare, api_token_env: CF_API_TOKEN } # only needed for wildcards Firewall (ext/firewall; on whenever the config has firewall or rate_limits ). Peers outside allow_cidrs get 403. The client IP comes from client_ip_headers only when the peer is a trusted proxy, otherwise it is the peer. Rate-limited requests get 429 with Retry-After and a message naming the limit; every routed response carries -{Ip,Instance}-{Hourly,Concurrent}-{Limit,Remaining} and -{Ip,Instance}-Hourly-Reset , listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers . Long-lived responses (realtime) hold their concurrency slot until they end. TLS. Certificate files are core ( server.tls ). Automatic certificates are ext/autotls (its autotls section): with auto: true and no dns , every hostname the instance source maps gets its own certificate on its first TLS handshake (HTTP-01 / TLS-ALPN-01), with any DNS host and no API token; hostnames no instance serves never trigger issuance. A DNS provider (Cloudflare for now) is only needed for wildcard domains , proved through DNS-01; a wildcard without one is a config error. Each instance can override any of those limits (zero or missing fields keep the default): instances: id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] limits: max_js_execution: 60s max_js_allocation: 128MiB id: api hosts: [api.example.com] access: { cors_origins: [https://app.example.com] } limits: { max_concurrent_js: 32 } extensions: firewall: { rate_limits: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_concurrent: 500 }, trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] }

title: Pocker
heading: Extensions
text: pocker.Provider.Extensions (or pocker.Server.Extensions in Go) takes extensions (see extension.go ). Each implements Name() and any of: extkit.Extension a PocketOne extension, registered on every instance's app before it bootstraps ( Register(app, cfg) ) with the instance's extensions. settings, its id in extkit.AppID(app) ; e.g. mailtrap, mailrelay, storage. Members of the standard set (pitr, tokens, s3redirect, bulkmail, ...) come from Standard ; listing one here is an error. enabled: false skips it for that instance. A change to an instance's extensions: settings restarts its app on its next request. The same value works on a standalone app. multisite.Extension a host extension ( RegisterHost ): it provides host contracts (gate/v1, tls/v1, http.wrap/v1, ...) as on any runtime (docs/extensions.md) Starter background work that needs pocker's Manager AppIniter host code that needs the whole Instance when setting up its app ( InitApp(inst, app) ); runs on every start, including restarts. Extensions use extkit.Extension instead, so they run on a standalone app too and pass the conformance test. Per-instance settings for an extension go under the instance's extensions. (read them with pocker.DecodeExtensionConfig ). app.Restart() (a backup restore, pitr) restarts only that instance, not the process. Timings for the Server-Timing header are registered with multisite.Timing(ctx, fn) . The stock pocketone binary runs pocker with mailtrap, and its host with servertiming and autotls ( multisite.Options.Extensions , the same under docker); the firewall turns on from its sections.

title: Pocker
heading: Platform values and logs
text: Superusers ( superusers: [{email, password_hash, id?, token_key?}] ) are upserted into the app's _superusers in Go when it starts, e.g. so a hosting platform's login works in the dashboard. Nothing goes through env. Private values ( private: {...} ) are for the host application's Go code and never visible to JS. A host registers that code with Server.SetupApp(inst, app) , which runs after migrations and before the app serves (for example a backup route checked against inst.Private["backup_token"] ). Secrets ( secrets: {...} ) are the instance's environment: what its JS sees through $os.getenv / process.env , and nothing else. No names are reserved; platform settings are explicit fields. Encryption key ( encryption_key ) encrypts the app's stored settings (like --encryptionEnv ). JS never sees it. Access ( access: {cors_origins} ) is the owner's say over which browser origins may call the instance (PocketBase matching: exact, , wildcards; empty = any). Client IPs that get the trusted rate limits are the firewall's extensions.firewall.trusted_ips (on top of the process-wide firewall.trusted_clients ). Extensions ( extensions: { : ...} ) are per-instance settings for extensions; extensions read them once, so changing them restarts the app on its next request. Logs: the app's own logs (the dashboard's Logs) are per instance in its pb_data . console. from JS hooks goes to /logs/exec.log as JSON lines {message, stream, time} ( stdout for log/info/debug, stderr for warn/error), rotated to exec.log.1 at 10 MiB. A start failure (e.g. a broken hooks file) is written there too, and only that instance fails. When an instance's secrets , encryption_key , access , limits , dev , dir , superusers , private or remote changes, a running app restarts (it stops, then a fresh one starts, as in a process restart), so a rotated secret takes effect immediately and two apps never have the instance's folder open. Host changes apply without a restart. GET /.well-known/health on any host reports {status, instances, running} . Changing an instance's files from host code (deploys, restores): Manager.WithInstanceStopped(ctx, id, fn) stops the app, holds new requests for that instance, runs fn(dir) , then lets them through to a fresh app. Manager.StartInstance(ctx, id) starts it right away and returns the start error (for example to tell a deploy that a hook is broken), Manager.Running(id) says whether it is started, and Manager.InstanceDir(id) gives its folder. Manager.Ready() says whether the instance list has loaded. Manager.LogInstance(id, stream, message) appends to the instance's logs/exec.log (e.g. a scheduled job's result). Host code that runs in its own goroutines gets the Manager from Server.OnStart , before any request is served. Several servers, one set of instances. An instance with remote: runs on another server: Pocker checks the peer and the instance's rate limits here, then forwards the request (a reverse proxy to the URL by default; Server.Forward replaces it, e.g. to hold requests while the other server restarts). Its app never starts here, and an app already running here stops when remote is set. plain_listen gives the other servers a plain-HTTP port on a private network, and Manager.Firewall() lets host routes in front of the Manager use the same peer check.

title: Pocker
heading: Sandbox
text: Every instance's JS hooks and migrations run in a sandbox (the sandbox extension), and its SQL runs behind SQLite's authorizer ( sandbox/sqlguard.go ). The sandbox extension also owns the egress policy ( sandbox/egress.go ); pocker turns it on for its instances. sandbox_test.go runs one attack per route from one instance against another instance and the host; all of these are refused: Files: $os. , $filepath.glob/walk , $filesystem.fileFromPath , $template.loadFiles , $apis.static , require() Confined to the instance folder with an os.Root : the kernel resolves every path beneath it, refusing .. and symlinks that leave it. Relative paths and absolute paths inside the folder ( __hooks + "/x" ) work as before. Host primitives: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit , $os.args , $filesystem.local Disabled ( $os.args is empty). Environment: $os.getenv , process.env Only the instance's own secrets . Go internals: $app.restart/bootstrap/runAllMigrations/onServe/onTerminate/onBootstrap/cron/unsafeWithoutHooks , hook.bindFunc/bind/trigger/unbind , sql.DB/Conn/Tx/Stmt (e.g. dbx.DB.DB() ), database/sql/driver , os/exec , net , syscall , http.Server controls Hidden from JS (the sandbox's member filter: they read as undefined , including when promoted from an embedded app type). Top-level onRecord , routerAdd , cronAdd and the rest of $app work as usual. Raw SQL ( $app.db().newQuery ) Allowed. SQLite's authorizer refuses ATTACH (and VACUUM INTO ) outside the instance's pb_data , PRAGMA temp_store_directory/data_store_directory and load_extension ; the CLI-only readfile / writefile / fsdir don't exist in the library. Statements without a deadline get max_query_duration . CPU Every JS call is interrupted after max_js_execution , Go calls included; sleep() is capped at 10 s. At most max_concurrent_js calls are in flight per instance. Memory Each instance has one QuickJS VM (ext/jsvm) with a hard cap (64 MiB by default): its JS heap plus the Go objects its JS holds. Growth past it, gradual or at once, is an out-of-memory error for that instance only. The JS stack is capped by size, so deep recursion is an error, never a crash. $os.readFile , fileFromPath and readerToString / toBytes are capped at max_js_allocation . Outbound network: $http.send , $filesystem.fileFromURL , S3 storage and backups, OAuth2/JWK fetches, SMTP Public addresses only, checked on the address actually connected to (after DNS, so rebinding doesn't help): loopback, private ranges, link-local and cloud metadata, CGNAT, multicast, reserved and documentation ranges, and IPv6 equivalents/IPv4-in-IPv6 are refused unless listed in egress_allow . Installed process-wide on Go's default HTTP transport and PocketBase's SMTP client ( pocker/egress.go ). Host code that must reach private addresses (e.g. a control plane over a private network) uses its own http.Client with its own transport. $http.send timeouts and response bodies are capped. Limits of the memory controls: Go objects JS holds are charged by estimate, and Go's garbage collector can let the process use up to about twice the charge; set GOMEMLIMIT for the process as the backstop. Not covered yet: per-instance concurrency limits, and OS-level defence in depth: run Pocker as a non-root user with an OS firewall that only lets that user reach public addresses (a second, independent egress layer), plus seccomp and Landlock.

title: Pocker
heading: Changes to PocketBase
text: These live in the repo root (PocketBase's own files), not in this extension. Kept small and marked // PocketOne: so upstream merges stay easy: core.BaseAppConfig.AppMigrations : a per-app migrations list (JS migrations from jsvm register there instead of the global core.AppMigrations ). core.BaseAppConfig.EncryptionKey : the settings encryption key passed in directly instead of read from the process environment. The JS engine isn't a core change: Pocker runs jsvm (QuickJS), an extension, and the sandbox plugs into it. PocketBase's own plugins/jsvm is exactly upstream's. Mail needs no core change: the sandbox sends an app's own SMTP through the egress policy on OnMailerSend ( sandbox.BindMail ).

title: Pocker
heading: Versions
text: PocketOne has its own version line, starting at v0.0.1 , independent of PocketBase's numbers. When PocketBase releases, we merge it and decide then how to bump ours. Each release says which PocketBase version it's based on. The module path stays ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase , so a build pins a PocketOne version through the replace line: replace ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase = pocketone.dev v0.0.1

title: Remotes
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Walkthrough for app owners: Remote CLI. This page is the technical reference. Named remotes for the pocketone command: the apps a project deploys to, each signed in to once. Give an app a name like prod , log in, and commands such as pocketone deploy prod know where to go and who you are. pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com pocketone login prod pocketone deploy prod # Deploy Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Remotes
heading: Install
text: Remotes is built into pocketone and on : the remote , login , logout and link commands are always there, and every app provides remote/v1: whoami at GET /api/_c/remote/v1 (so other machines can sign in to it), status, restart and logs. There's nothing to install: it's in the standard set. In your own Go build, use the standard set, or register it through its contracts yourself: app := pocketbase.New() extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{remotes.New(remotes.Config{})}, nil, nil) // remote/v1; on pocketbase.PocketBase also the commands app.Start() The module is pocketone.dev/ext/remotes . Add Tokens for API tokens and the OAuth server for browser login.

title: Remotes
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or settings screen. Remotes keeps two files and reads a few environment variables.

title: Remotes
heading: The project's remotes
text: .pocketbase/remotes.json in the project holds names and URLs only, so commit it: {"default": "prod", "remotes": {"prod": {"url": "https://myapp.example.com"}}} Commands find it by walking up from the current folder. It isn't a pb_ name, since pb_ folders are deployed.

title: Remotes
heading: Saved logins
text: Logins are saved per user, keyed by URL, in ~/.config/pocketone/credentials.json (mode 0600). Set P1_CONFIG_DIR to use another folder; with XDG_CONFIG_HOME set, it's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pocketone/ .

title: Remotes
heading: Environment variables
text: P1_TOKEN_ A token for one remote, for CI. The name is upper case, other characters as _ ( P1_TOKEN_PROD ). P1_TOKEN A token for any remote. P1_CONFIG_DIR Where saved logins are kept. A token in the environment wins over a saved login. Every PocketOne variable starts with P1_ , in every build (the pockethost binary reads P1_TOKEN too). The pocketone folder comes from the command's name, so a build shipped under another name keeps its logins apart ( ~/.config/pockethost ).

title: Remotes
heading: Manage remotes
text: pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com --default pocketone remote list # names, URLs and who you're logged in as; marks the default pocketone remote default prod pocketone remote rm staging # the saved login stays; see logout pocketone remote whoami prod # who you are there, your token's scopes, and what the app offers A URL without a scheme gets https:// . The first remote you add becomes the default. A command that names no remote uses the default, else the only remote, else the one called default . Any command also takes a URL in place of a name: pocketone deploy https://other.example.com .

title: Remotes
heading: Log in
text: pocketone login prod link signs in the same way when it adds a remote. Either way you sign in as one of the app's superusers (or its users, on the browser pages). login tries, in order: The browser , when the remote runs the OAuth server. Your browser opens, you sign in and approve, and the command finishes. Over SSH or without a display it shows a code to enter on another device instead; --device asks for that, and --no-browser prints the URL without opening it. A superuser's email and password , when the remote has no OAuth server (stock PocketBase, such as an app a multisite host runs in Docker). The password isn't shown as you type. The login lasts 30 days; changing that superuser's password ends it. A superuser with multi-factor authentication on signs in with a token instead. A pasted token ( pbt_... , a PocketHost token, or a PocketBase auth token): paste it at the email prompt, or pass --token or --token-stdin . A browser login keeps a refresh token and renews itself when it's within a day of expiring. You'll see Logged in to https://myapp.example.com as admin@example.com (oauth).

title: Remotes
heading: Link in one step
text: pocketone link https://myapp.example.com pocketone link https://myapp.pockethost.io ph_pat_... link adds the remote (named default , or --name ), makes it the default if there's none yet, and logs in. It takes the same login flags.

title: Remotes
heading: Log out
text: pocketone logout prod Forgets the saved login. A browser login is also revoked on the remote (its refresh token); a pasted token stays valid until you revoke it in the dashboard. If the remote can't be reached, it tells you to revoke it in the dashboard.

title: Remotes
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Remotes
heading: Commands
text: What it adds to the pocketone binary (CLI reference): [ pocketone link [token] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-link) Adds a remote (default name "default") and signs in to it [ pocketone login [remote] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-login) Signs in to a remote and saves the login [ pocketone logout [remote] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-logout) Forgets the saved login (and revokes it, for a browser login) pocketone remote add Adds or replaces a remote pocketone remote default Sets the default remote pocketone remote list Lists remotes and whether you're logged in pocketone remote rm Removes a remote (its saved login stays; see logout) [ pocketone remote whoami [remote] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-remote-whoami) Shows who you are on a remote and what it offers

title: Remotes
heading: remote/v1
text: whoami pocketone remote whoami GET /api/_c/remote/v1 remote_whoami status pocketone remote status GET /api/_c/remote/v1/status remote_status restart pocketone remote restart POST /api/_c/remote/v1/restart remote_restart logs pocketone remote logs --n GET /api/_c/remote/v1/logs remote_logs

title: Remotes
heading: Works with
text: Deploy deploy , dev and pull resolve their remote and login through Remotes and find deploy/v1 in whoami's contracts; restart and logs use remote/v1. OAuth (in Tokens) Provides oauth/v1, so whoami lists it; login then signs in through the browser (loopback redirect on 127.0.0.1 with PKCE) or a device code. Tokens Provides the API tokens login takes when pasted. Whoami reports a token's id and scopes.

title: Remotes
heading: remote/v1
text: Remote control of an app, at /api/_c/remote/v1 : whoami GET /api/_c/remote/v1 none needed (any token may ask who it is) status GET /api/_c/remote/v1/status remote:read restart POST /api/_c/remote/v1/restart remote logs GET /api/_c/remote/v1/logs?n=100 (server-sent events) remote:read Whoami says who the request's credential is and what the app offers, so clients can discover it: {"auth": {"collection": "_superusers", "id": "…", "email": "admin@example.com"}, "via": "token", "tokenId": "…", "scopes": ["deploy", "remote"], "contracts": ["deploy/v1", "oauth/v1", "remote/v1", "api-tokens/v1"], "extensions": ["tokens", "remotes", "deploy"], "app": {"name": "Acme", "url": "https://myapp.example.com"}} via is token for an API token, jwt for a PocketBase auth token, and empty with no credential ( auth is then null , and extensions is left out). contracts are the contract APIs the app offers, each at /api/_c/ / : everything a client can use (oauth/v1's metadata is at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server ). Restart answers at once and restarts just after (on a multisite host, only that instance).

title: Remotes
heading: Building on Remotes
text: remote/v1 client. remotev1.NewClient(url, token, httpClient) (ext/contracts/remote/v1) calls whoami, status, restart and logs. Go client. The CLI client lives with the contract, in remoteclient (ext/contracts/remote/v1/remoteclient), so other extensions' commands use it without importing this one. remoteclient.Open(dir, name) resolves a remote and its credential (environment first, then the saved login, renewing a browser login when due) and returns a remoteclient.Client : base URL, bearer token, an HTTP client with short connect timeouts, and JSON , NewRequest , Do and Whoami . It also holds the linked project ( LoadProject ), saved logins ( LoadCredentials ) and the sign-ins ( LoginWithToken , OAuthLogin , PasswordLogin ). Deploy's commands build on it. Commands. remotes.Commands() returns the remote , login , logout and link commands, for a binary that isn't a pocketbase.PocketBase . The rest of remote is generated: every operation of every contract the binary links is a remote ... command (cli.commands/v1), such as remote status , remote restart , remote restore to --at -2h . Login. remotes.BrowserLogin is the sign-in login tries first ( remoteclient.OAuthLogin ; tests replace it).

title: Remotes
heading: Example
text: example/main.go is an app with remotes and API tokens. Run two copies and add one as a remote of the other; its comment has the commands. // Command example is a PocketOne app with remotes and API tokens: run two copies, add one as a remote of the other's // project and sign in. // // go run ./example serve --http=127.0.0.1:8090 # the "remote" // go run ./example remote add local http://127.0.0.1:8090 # in a project folder // go run ./example login local # browser sign-in: admin@example.com / password // go run ./example remote whoami // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/api-tokens" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" "pocketone.dev/ext/remotes" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" // registered through their contracts (the standard set does this for you): remotes provides remote/v1 (whoami at // /api/_c/remote/v1, status, restart, logs) and the remote/login/logout/link commands; tokens adds API tokens // and the OAuth server login signs in through if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{apitokens.New(apitokens.Config{}), remotes.New(remotes.Config{})}, nil, nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: S3 Fallback
text: Version 0.0.2 · Owners: @benallfree A default bucket for instances that have no S3 of their own. You name your S3-compatible backends once, then mount each kind of file on one: record uploads, backup zips, PITR history, or any extension's own kind. Every instance gets its own folder in the bucket and can't reach anything outside it. The credentials never reach the instance. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Install
text: S3 Fallback is in the standard set, so it's built into pocketone and every isolate on a multisite host has it (Docker containers run stock images). It does nothing until the storage section below mounts a backend. Its main use is a multisite host, where each instance gets its own folder in one bucket; a single app with mounts keeps its files at the backend's root. In your own Go build, reconfigure the member instead of adding it again: set := standard.New() set.S3Fallback = s3fallback.New(s3fallback.Config{Backends: backends, Mounts: mounts}) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/s3-fallback .

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Configure
text: The storage section of pocketone.yaml is read on first use. Fields set in Go win. storage: backends: # named S3-compatible destinations r2-eu: { endpoint: https:// .eu.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, bucket: pocketbase-eu, region: auto, access_key: $R2_KEY, secret: $R2_SECRET } b2-cold: { endpoint: ..., bucket: ph-backups, region: ..., access_key: ..., secret: ... } mounts: # filesystem kind - backend storage: r2-eu # record uploads backups: b2-cold # backup zips litestream: r2-eu # PITR history (ext/pitr) # enabled: false # off for every instance Each backend also takes prefix (prepended to every key, so several deployments can share a bucket) and force_path_style (for MinIO and similar servers). With no mounts the extension does nothing and files stay on local disk, as in PocketBase. Each instance can turn it off in its own settings, from instances.yaml or a mothership. Only enabled is read per instance; backends and mounts are the operator's: instances: id: blog extensions: { storage: { enabled: false } } The old shape ( bucket: with uploads: / backups: ) still works, with a warning: it becomes a backend named default , mounted for uploads and backups.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: storage:
text: A default S3 bucket for apps without their own (on a multisite host, one folder per instance): backends and mounts for uploads, backups, PITR history. enabled bool On for every instance unless false; an instance's extensions.storage.enabled overrides it. backends map of object Named S3-compatible destinations: endpoint, bucket, region, access_key, secret, prefix, force_path_style. mounts map of string Filesystem kind (storage, backups, litestream, ...) to backend name. bucket.endpoint string S3 endpoint URL. bucket.bucket string Bucket name. bucket.region string Bucket region (auto for R2). bucket.access_key string Access key id. bucket.secret string Secret key; use a $VAR from the .env. bucket.prefix string Prepended to every key, to share a bucket. bucket.force_path_style bool Path-style addressing, for MinIO and similar servers. uploads bool Deprecated: with bucket, false keeps uploads off it. backups bool Deprecated: with bucket, false keeps backups off it.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to do day to day. To an instance nothing is configured: Settings show S3 off, and uploads, thumbs, $app.newFilesystem() and the Backups screen work as before. Files land in the bucket under instances/ / / . Downloads stream through the server, or redirect to the bucket with S3 Redirect. When an instance turns on its own S3 (Settings → Files storage, or Settings → Backups), PocketBase's normal code takes over with the instance's credentials. Files already in the default bucket stay there, as PocketBase's own S3 switch doesn't move files either. It applies to instances created with the extension on. Files already on an instance's local disk are not read or moved.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Every instance the set reaches gets the extension. An isolate (Pocker) gets the root instances/ / . PITR Mount litestream and every instance without its own bucket keeps its history there. An instance's own PITR bucket still wins. S3 Redirect Downloads become signed redirects to the bucket. Nothing to wire: the fenced filesystem signs with its prefix, so S3 Redirect treats it like any S3 mount.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Building on S3 Fallback
text: Your own kind. Any kind an extension asks for through PocketBase's OnFilesystemCreate is served when it's mounted. PITR's litestream works this way. Uploads and backups step aside when the app turned on its own S3; for other kinds, the extension asking checks its own app setting first. Go API. Bind(app, root) serves an app's filesystems from the mounts under root ( "" for an app that has the process to itself, instances/ / for an isolate, as under Pocker). FS(root, kind) returns the same fenced filesystem outside a hook; close it when done. Config() returns the effective configuration.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go yet. modes_test.go shows it on the pocketone binary, as a single app and on a multisite host; storage_test.go and mounts_test.go show it in Go.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: How it works
text: PocketBase asks OnFilesystemCreate before it creates a filesystem. For a mounted kind, the extension answers with the backend, fenced to / . An instance can't list, read, write or delete anything outside it. The fence is a driver that adds the prefix to every key and strips it from listings. Signed download URLs are made with the backend's own credentials.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Status
text: Works and is tested, in-process and on the pocketone binary as a single app and on a multisite host, against an in-memory bucket that checks signed downloads ( modes_test.go ); not yet deployed.

title: S3 Redirect
text: Version 0.0.2 · Owners: @benallfree File downloads as short-lived signed redirects to your bucket, after PocketBase's own access check. When an app keeps its files in S3 (Settings → Files storage), PocketBase normally downloads each file from the bucket and streams it to the browser. With S3 Redirect, /api/files/... answers 302 with a presigned GET URL instead, and the browser fetches the file straight from the bucket. The app's bandwidth, memory and connections stay free. With Cloudflare R2 the downloads cost no egress either. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Install
text: S3 Redirect is built into pocketone and on by default . It only acts when S3 file storage is on: turn on S3 in Settings → Files storage and downloads redirect. With files on local disk, nothing changes. To stream files through the app as before: pocketone serve --s3Redirect=false In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: import "pocketone.dev/ext/s3redirect" app := pocketbase.New() s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 time.Minute}) app.Start() Then turn on S3 in Settings → Files storage.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Configure
text: Set it in pocketone.yaml : s3redirect: enabled: true # false streams files through the app ttl: 5m # how long each signed URL is valid Or with flags, which win over the file: --s3Redirect true Redirect downloads when S3 file storage is on. --s3Redirect=false streams them. --s3RedirectTTL 5m How long each signed URL stays valid (at most 7 days). Keep the TTL short: anyone holding a URL can fetch the file until it expires, protected files included. The bucket itself is PocketBase's own S3 setting, in Settings → Files storage . There are no other settings screens. Bucket CORS. A redirect followed by fetch() or from your site needs a CORS rule on the bucket allowing GET from your origin. Plain , and links need nothing.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: s3redirect:
text: Signed S3 redirects for file downloads: enabled, URL lifetime. The --s3Redirect and --s3RedirectTTL flags win. enabled bool On unless false (it only acts when S3 file storage is on). Flag: --s3Redirect. ttl duration How long each signed URL stays valid. Default 5m, max 7 days. Flag: --s3RedirectTTL.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Use
text: Once S3 is on, there's nothing to click. File URLs stay the same; they answer with a redirect: Access checks don't change. PocketBase still finds the record, checks protected-file tokens and the view rule, and creates thumbnails on first request. The redirect happens only after all of that. The file token stays private. It never goes into the bucket URL, and the redirect sends Referrer-Policy: no-referrer . Same headers as PocketBase: inline or attachment ( ?download=1 ), the filename, and forced content types (SVG, CSS, JS) are signed into the URL as S3 response- overrides. Range requests work, because S3 serves them. Caching: the browser may reuse the redirect for 80% of the TTL ( Cache-Control: private , never shared caches); the file itself gets PocketBase's usual 30-day Cache-Control . Falls back to streaming when S3 is off, the extension is turned off, or signing fails. A failed signature logs a warning, s3redirect: signing failed, streaming instead . Only GET and HEAD requests are redirected. Inline vs attachment: PocketBase decides this from the stored content type; S3 Redirect goes by the file extension (it doesn't ask the bucket, so a redirect costs no extra round trip). They agree for every file PocketBase names.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Try it
text: cd example && go run . serve The example runs one app with its own in-process bucket, nothing to set up. It: starts an S3-compatible bucket on 127.0.0.1:9199 (gofakes3, objects kept in pb_data/demo-s3.bolt ), and points the app's Files storage at it; seeds a demo_files record with an image (thumbs 100x100 ) and a protected text file, uploaded through PocketBase; prints the URLs to open. Each answers 302 to the bucket. The bucket only serves presigned GETs whose signature, re-computed with the AWS SDK's own SigV4 signer , matches and hasn't expired, and logs each one ( demo bucket: presigned GET ..., signature valid ). Unsigned or edited URLs get 403 . So a working download proves the signatures are AWS-compatible, not just accepted by a lenient fake. S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0 skips the demo bucket (use your own Files storage settings); S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR moves it. The example is its own Go module, so its demo dependencies (gofakes3, the AWS SDK signer) never reach the extension's go.mod .

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Works with
text: Multisite It's a standard member, so every instance that runs PocketOne has it. With Pocker, the s3redirect section sets the defaults and each instance can override enabled and ttl (below). S3 Fallback Apps without their own S3 settings keep files in its bucket (for isolates, as under Pocker, fenced to instances/ /storage/ ). Its driver signs, so those downloads redirect too.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Per-instance settings (Pocker)
text: set.S3Redirect = s3redirect.New(s3redirect.Config{}) // a standard member: reconfigure it on the host's set s3redirect: # server defaults enabled: true # on unless false ttl: 5m instances: id: abc extensions: s3redirect: { enabled: false } # per instance: enabled, ttl It's an extkit extension, so the same value works on a standalone app and on every instance of a multisite host; it doesn't link a runtime.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Building on S3 Redirect
text: Supply your own bucket. S3 Redirect signs for whatever filesystem PocketBase serves the download from: the app's own S3 settings, or one an extension supplies through OnFilesystemCreate . Implement s3redirect.Signer ( SignedURL(key, ttl, now, overrides) ) on your filesystem driver and its downloads redirect. Nothing else needs wiring; a filesystem that can't sign (local disk) streams as usual. Your own download handlers run first. The extension binds OnFileDownloadRequest last (priority 1000, id s3redirect.HookID , __ext_s3redirect__ ), so your Go or JS handlers can still change the served file or answer themselves without calling e.Next() . Unbind the id to turn it off for one app.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Example
text: example/main.go starts its own in-process S3 bucket, points the app's file storage at it and seeds a record, so every download redirect works with nothing to set up. Run go run . serve in example/ and open the URLs it prints. // Command example runs one PocketOne app whose file downloads redirect to an S3 bucket, with nothing to set up: // it starts its own S3-compatible bucket in-process (gofakes3, stored in pb_data/demo-s3.bolt), points the app's // Files storage at it, and seeds a "demo_files" record with an image and a protected document. // // go run . serve // // Open the URLs it prints. Each answers 302 with a signed URL; the bucket logs every fetch and only serves it if the // signature is valid and unexpired, checked independently with the AWS SDK's SigV4 signer. // // Set S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0 to skip the demo bucket and use whatever Files storage you configure in the dashboard. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "os" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/s3redirect" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 time.Minute}) if os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO") != "0" { addr := os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR") if addr == "" { addr = "127.0.0.1:9199" } registerDemo(app, addr) } if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: S3 Redirect
heading: How it works
text: Go module pocketone.dev/ext/s3redirect , no dependencies beyond PocketOne. The redirect is an OnFileDownloadRequest handler; the hook already exists upstream, so there's no core change. Signing is SigV4 query-string auth in sigv4 , checked against AWS's documented example. It needs no change to PocketBase's S3 client. The TTL is clamped to between 1 second and 7 days.
