title: Sandbox
text: Version 0.0.3 · Owners: @benallfree Confines one PocketOne app's JS hooks and migrations, so apps from people you don't know can share one process. File access stays inside the app's folder, host primitives are gone, every JS call has a time limit, raw SQL can't leave the app's own database files, and outbound connections reach public addresses only. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Sandbox
heading: Install
text: Sandbox isn't a switch in pocketone : Pocker applies it to every instance it runs. With a multisite section in pocketone.yaml (pocker as the runtime), every instance is sandboxed and there's nothing to install. A standalone app served by pocketone without a multisite section is not sandboxed. In your own Go build, give it to the JSVM engine as an extension: sb := &sandbox.Sandbox{Dir: dir, Env: map[string]string{"GREETING": "hi"}} execution, sleep := sb.Limits() jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: filepath.Join(dir, "pb_hooks"), Extensions: []any{sb}, VM: jsvm.VMConfig{TaskWall: execution, MaxSleep: sleep}, }) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/sandbox . The SQL guard and the outbound network rules are separate calls (see Integrations).

title: Sandbox
heading: Configure
text: Sandbox has no pocketone.yaml section of its own. Under Pocker its limits are set in the pocker section, as defaults for every instance, and each instance can override them in its own limits : pocker: max_js_execution: 30s # each JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) is interrupted after this max_js_allocation: 64MiB # biggest single file read or reader JS can ask for max_call_stack_size: 2000 # unused: the JS engine caps its stack by size max_sleep: 10s # cap on sleep() max_query_duration: 30s # deadline for SQL statements that have none http_send_max_timeout: 60s # cap on $http.send timeouts http_send_max_body: 10MiB # cap on $http.send response size max_concurrent_js: 16 # JS calls one instance runs at once egress_allow: [] # private networks apps may still reach, such as an internal SMTP relay The values shown are Pocker's defaults. An instance gets only its own secrets as environment. In a Go build, the same settings are Sandbox fields: Dir (required), Env , MaxExecution (default 30 s, negative turns it off), MaxSleep , MaxAllocation , HTTPSendMaxTimeout , HTTPSendMaxBody , and Console to send console. output somewhere other than the process's stdout and stderr. Limits() gives the execution and sleep limits for jsvm.Config.VM ; the memory cap and MaxConcurrent are set there too.

title: Sandbox
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to operate day to day. Hooks that stick to normal app code ( routerAdd , onRecord , cronAdd , $app.findRecordById and the rest) run unchanged. What changes for a hook author: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit and $filesystem.local fail with "not available on this host (sandboxed)"; $os.args is empty; process-wide Go methods such as $app.restart read as undefined . The app's types.d.ts declares each of them never , so tsc and your editor refuse a call to one before you deploy it. Files outside the app's folder can't be read or written, by any API, including through .. or symlinks. $os.getenv and process.env see only the app's own environment. A JS call that runs past its time limit is interrupted with an error; so is one that asks for a huge allocation. $http.send to a private or loopback address is refused. Under Pocker, console. output and hook errors go to the instance's own logs/exec.log .

title: Sandbox
heading: Works with
text: Pocker Runs every instance through the sandbox, the SQL guard and the outbound network rules, with limits from the pocker section and each instance's limits . Its attack tests are in sandbox_test.go . Multisite Carries the per-instance limits from instances.yaml or a mothership. Firewall Rate and concurrency limits in front of every request. Docker The alternative for untrusted apps: a container per instance instead of checks inside one process. Docker doesn't use the sandbox.

title: Sandbox
heading: Building on Sandbox
text: Sandbox is a jsvm extension ( OnInit , Modules , HTTPClient , HideField / HideMethod to hide process-reaching Go members, and FilterTypes to declare those members never in the app's types.d.ts ); add it to jsvm.Config.Extensions . GuardedDBConnect(maxQuery) is a core.DBConnectFunc : set it as the app's DBConnect to open the databases through SQLite's authorizer, with a deadline for statements that have none. InstallEgressPolicy(sandbox.EgressPolicy{Allow: ...}) routes Go's default HTTP transport through the public-only dialer, for the whole process. EgressPolicy.Dialer() gives the same check for your own connections. BindMail(app) sends the app's own SMTP through that dialer. ErrSandboxed is the error disabled bindings return.

title: Sandbox
heading: Example
text: One app whose JS hooks are sandboxed: file access confined to the app folder, host primitives disabled, and a 5 s limit per JS call. Run it from this folder with go run ./example serve . // Command example runs one PocketOne app whose JS hooks are sandboxed: file access is confined to the app folder, // host primitives ($os.exec, $os.exit, ...) are disabled, and every JS call has a time limit. // // go run ./example serve // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "os" "path/filepath" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm" "pocketone.dev/ext/sandbox" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" dir, _ := os.Getwd() sb := &sandbox.Sandbox{ Dir: dir, // JS may only touch this folder Env: map[string]string{"GREETING": "hi"}, // the only environment JS sees MaxExecution: 5 time.Second, } jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: filepath.Join(dir, "pb_hooks"), Extensions: []any{sb}, // OnInit, Modules, HTTPClient and the member filter }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Sandbox
heading: How is this safe?
text: With pocker, PocketOne can serve hundreds of instances from one Go process, each with its own owner, hooks and data. This section explains why that's safe enough to run code from people you don't know, and where it isn't. Configuration and the engine API are in POCKER.md. The attack tests are in sandbox_test.go .

title: Sandbox
heading: Why one process
text: Most hosted PocketBase instances are idle most of the time. A container per instance means paying idle memory and a cold start of a second or more for each one. In one process an instance's app starts on its first request in tens of milliseconds, costs a few MB while it runs, and shares the Go runtime with everyone else. What you give up is the kernel boundary between tenants. Everything below replaces it with checks inside the process.

title: Sandbox
heading: The threat
text: Assume every instance's owner is hostile. They control: their pb_hooks (JavaScript, run by the instance's own QuickJS VM, ext/jsvm); their pb_migrations ; their collections, rules and settings; any SQL their hooks run; requests to their own instance. They must not be able to: read or change another instance's files, database, environment or settings; read the host's files, environment, credentials or private network; take the process down, or starve everyone else of CPU and memory.

title: Sandbox
heading: 1. Each instance is its own app
text: Every instance has its own core.App , database, settings, JS VMs, migrations list, settings encryption key and log. Requests are routed by hostname to exactly one app. Nothing in one app holds a reference to another. In production only hostnames the instance source maps are served; unknown hosts get 404 and never create a folder.

title: Sandbox
heading: 2. Files: confined by the kernel, not by string checks
text: Every file API reachable from JS goes through an os.Root opened on the instance's folder. That covers: $os. $filepath.glob / walk $filesystem.fileFromPath $template.loadFiles $apis.static require() The kernel resolves each path beneath that root and refuses .. and symlinks that lead out. There is no path string for an attacker to get clever with.

title: Sandbox
heading: 3. Host primitives: removed
text: The following are gone from JS: process control: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit , $os.args ; $filesystem.local ; PocketBase internals that reach the whole process: $app.restart , bootstrap , onServe , onTerminate , raw hook triggers, sql.DB handles; Go's os/exec , net , syscall and database/sql/driver . A field-name mapper hides them, so they read as undefined . Everything a normal app uses still works: routerAdd , onRecord , cronAdd , $app.findRecordById and the rest.

title: Sandbox
heading: 4. Environment: only the instance's own
text: $os.getenv and process.env return the instance's own secrets and nothing else. Platform values never go through the environment: the settings encryption key; superusers the host keeps in sync; private tokens for the host's Go code.

title: Sandbox
heading: 5. SQL: SQLite's own authorizer
text: Raw SQL is allowed ( $app.db().newQuery(...) ), because PocketBase apps depend on it. Instead of parsing statements, PocketOne installs SQLite's authorizer callback on every connection, so SQLite itself refuses: ATTACH and VACUUM INTO outside the instance's pb_data ; load_extension ; the pragmas that move SQLite's files elsewhere. Statements without a deadline get one ( max_query_duration ).

title: Sandbox
heading: 6. Outbound network: public addresses only
text: PocketOne installs one dialer process-wide, on Go's default HTTP transport and PocketBase's SMTP client. It covers: $http.send $filesystem.fileFromURL S3 storage and backups OAuth2/JWKS fetches SMTP The dialer refuses: loopback, private ranges, link-local and cloud metadata; CGNAT, multicast, reserved and documentation ranges; the IPv6 forms of all of these, including IPv4-in-IPv6. It checks the address actually connected to, after DNS, so DNS rebinding doesn't help. $http.send timeouts and response sizes are capped.

title: Sandbox
heading: 7. CPU, memory and concurrency
text: CPU Every JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) is interrupted after max_js_execution , Go calls included. sleep() is capped. Concurrency At most max_concurrent_js JS calls per instance in flight at once; more wait, then fail. Per-IP and per-instance rate and concurrency limits sit in front of every request. Memory Each instance's VM has a hard cap (default 64 MiB): the JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds. A script that grows past it, slowly or at once, gets an out-of-memory error; other instances are unaffected. The JS stack is capped by size, so deep recursion is an error, never a crash. File reads are capped at max_js_allocation . Every limit has a process default and a per-instance override.

title: Sandbox
heading: 8. Failures stay with their instance
text: A broken hooks file, a panic during start or a failed migration fails that instance alone: it answers 502 and logs to its own logs/exec.log . Every other instance keeps serving. console. output goes to the instance's own log, never to the host's.

title: Sandbox
heading: What it doesn't cover
text: Be clear about these before you host strangers: Go memory is estimated. Go objects JS holds are charged to the instance by estimate, and Go's garbage collector can let the process use up to about twice that; set GOMEMLIMIT for the process. It's one address space. A bug in Go, QuickJS, SQLite or PocketOne's own checks would cross tenants in a way a container boundary wouldn't. The sandbox tests cover the known paths, but they don't prove nothing else exists. No OS-level layer yet. Seccomp, Landlock and a second, OS-level egress filter aren't built in.

title: Sandbox
heading: How to run it
text: For untrusted tenants, add the OS layers yourself: run PocketOne as a non-root user that owns only the instances folder; run it under a cgroup memory limit (with swap), so the worst case is a restart, not a host OOM; add an OS firewall rule that lets that user reach public addresses only, an egress layer independent of the process; keep secrets for host code out of the process environment; use private: values instead; put a proxy or the built-in firewall in front, with rate limits on. If you only run your own apps, the defaults are already more than stock PocketBase gives you.

text: MIT

title: Server Timing
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree A Server-Timing response header on every request to an instance of a multisite host: how long the instance's own handler took, and how long it took to wake the instance for the request (under Pocker). Your browser's dev tools show it in the request's Timing tab. Server-Timing: origin;dur=12.4, wake;dur=0.0 Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Server Timing
heading: Install
text: Server Timing is built into pocketone and on whenever it serves many instances, whatever the provider. There's nothing to install. It isn't used for a single app. In your own host build, list it first among the host extensions, so its header covers every other hop: h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Extensions: []multisite.Extension{servertiming.New() / , other host extensions /}}) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/servertiming .

title: Server Timing
heading: Configure
text: There's nothing to configure: no pocketone.yaml section, flag or settings screen.

title: Server Timing
heading: Use
text: Open your browser's dev tools, pick a request to an instance and look at its timing, or read the header with curl: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/health grep -i server-timing origin The instance's own handler: from handing it the request until it sent its response headers. wake Starting the instance for this request. 0 when it was already running. Each value is in milliseconds, one decimal, up to the response headers (time to first byte). The innermost hop comes first; values a server in front already sent are kept, and this host's entries are added after them.

title: Server Timing
heading: Integrations
text: Pocker registers origin and wake for every request it hands to an instance. Add your own entries. Host code and other extensions call multisite.Timing(ctx, fn) during a request; fn returns []multisite.TimingEntry{{Name, Dur, Desc}} and runs when the headers go out. Only extensions listed after Server Timing are covered. Put names in Desc , never addresses. Go API. FormatTiming , AppendServerTiming and WithServerTiming render entries, append them to a header and wrap a response writer, for a server that isn't a multisite host.

title: Server Timing
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go . See it used in examples/pocketone/multi.go , which lists it first in the pocketone binary's host extensions.

title: Server Timing
heading: How it works
text: It's a host wrapper ( multisite.Wrapper ). For each request it starts collecting timing entries in the request's context, then stamps them into the Server-Timing header just before the response headers go out (not on interim 1xx responses). Flush, Hijack and http.ResponseController keep working through its writer.

title: Standard Set
text: Version 0.1.0 · Owners: @benallfree The extensions every PocketOne app has: settings, page templates, a cache, API tokens (with the OAuth server), remotes (remote/v1), MCP, PocketPages, an S3 fallback bucket and S3 redirects, point-in-time restore, backups, bulk mail, deploy, WASM modules called from pb_hooks, and dashboard cache headers (UI Cache). Every app uses it, standalone or an instance on a multisite host, so an app never misses one because its host forgot to list it. Members can be reconfigured or turned off per app, never removed. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Standard Set
heading: Install
text: The standard set is built into pocketone . In your own Go build, make the app with it instead of pocketbase.New() : set := standard.New() app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks"}) app.Start() NewApp registers the members, loads pb_hooks with their JS APIs ( $mcp , $apiTokens , $bulkmail , $wasm , $agent ) and resolves their contracts. On an app you built yourself, call set.Register(app, jsvmConfig) instead. To build the app from pocketone.yaml 's app section (data folder, dev mode, hooks and migrations folders, JS engine and its limits), load the file and pass what AppFromConfig returns: cfg, err := config.Load(config.FromArgs(os.Args[1:])) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } a, err := standard.AppFromConfig(cfg) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } app := standard.New().NewApp(a.PocketBase, a.JS) Every app key reaches your build this way, including ones added in later releases. Your own flags override the fields they cover.

title: Standard Set
heading: Configure
text: Reconfigure a member: replace it, e.g. set.PITR = pitr.New(pitr.Config{Retention: 7 24 time.Hour}) . A member set to nil is an error. Turn one off: on a single app, enabled: false in its pocketone.yaml section ( api-tokens: {enabled: false} ); for every instance under Pocker, in its pocker: isolate_config: section, and for one instance, in its extensions. . Extensions that require it turn off too, and say why. cache, storage (s3-fallback), s3redirect and pitr read enabled in their own sections: off, they stay registered and do nothing. Keep one off in code: a binary whose own code does what a member does sets set.Switches , which Register reads each member's enabled from (nil: standard.ConfiguredSwitches , the pocketone.yaml sections). Wrap it: if name == "bulkmail" { return extkit.Config{{"enabled": false}} }; return standard.ConfiguredSwitches(name) . Add your own: set.Add(myextension.New()) . Extras register after the members, under the same rules. Pick providers: set.Providers is pocketone.yaml 's providers: section, for a contract more than one extension provides.

title: Stats
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Looks after the data of the instances a host serves. Today it measures facts about each instance (disk used, last request served) and reports them. Later it will also carry out decisions about that data, such as archiving. Status. Working, first step: facts and the measure decision. Archiving, restoring, offloading backups and purging come next, as further decisions. The rules engine is ready as a Go library but isn't read from pocketone.yaml yet. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Stats
heading: Install
text: Lifecycle runs on a host that serves many instances (ext/multisite, with pocker or docker), not on a standalone app. The stock pocketone binary turns it on by itself in host mode: when pocketone.yaml has a multisite section, every instance under the first runtime's root folder is measured. There's no switch to flip. multisite: {} instances: { file: ./instances.yaml } In your own host build, add it as a gate (to see requests) and a background job: lc := &stats.Lifecycle{Directory: h.Directory, Folder: func(i multisite.Instance) string { return filepath.Join(root, i.ID) }} h.Gates = append(h.Gates, lc) // records each local instance's last request h.Background = append(h.Background, lc.Run) // measures and reports on the policy's schedule Folder says where an instance's data lives. The stock binary uses the instance's own dir when it has one, else / .

title: Stats
heading: Configure
text: The lifecycle section in pocketone.yaml sets the schedule. Everything is optional. lifecycle: measure_every: 24h # how old a disk measurement may get report_every: 1h # how often changed last-request times are reported concurrency: 2 # instances measured at once

title: Stats
heading: The policy
text: What to do comes from a policy. The built-in one ( YAMLPolicy ) reads this section and decides one thing: measure an instance when it was never measured, or when its measurement is older than measure_every . Zero or missing values fall back to the defaults. Rules with criteria, all / any / not , vetoes and budgets exist in the rules engine, but the lifecycle section doesn't take them yet.

title: Stats
heading: lifecycle:
text: Instance data on this host: how often disk use is measured and last-request times are reported. measure_every duration 24h0m0s How old an instance's disk measurement may get before it is measured again. Default 24h. report_every duration 1h0m0s How often changed last-request times are reported to the sink. Default 1h. concurrency int 2 How many instances are measured at once. Default 2.

title: Stats
heading: What it measures
text: For each instance this host serves itself (not the ones it forwards to another edge): disk_bytes : the size of the regular files in the instance's folder (symlinks aren't followed; 0 when there's no folder), and measured_at , when that was measured. last_active : the last request this host served for it, recorded at most once a minute per instance.

title: Stats
heading: When
text: As soon as the instance list loads, every instance is measured, because none has been measured yet. After that it checks once a minute and measures the instances whose measurement is older than measure_every . Changed last-request times are reported every report_every . Facts are kept in memory. With the default log sink, a restart measures everything again.

title: Stats
heading: What you'll see
text: Log lines from the default sink and the measuring pass: INFO lifecycle: facts instances=12 disk_bytes=48213504 INFO lifecycle: measured instances=12 disk_bytes=48213504 ms=37 lifecycle: facts is each report the sink receives (after a measuring pass, and for last-request times). lifecycle: measured follows a measuring pass, with how long it took. Problems show as warnings: lifecycle: measuring (a folder couldn't be read), lifecycle: report (the sink failed; last-request times are retried next time) and lifecycle: policy .

title: Stats
heading: Try it
text: example/main.go measures the instance folders under a root once and prints each instance's size: go run ./example --root ./pb_root --instances instances.yaml

title: Stats
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Lifecycle is a multisite.Gate (it sees each request to record last_active ) and a host background job ( Run ). It lists instances from multisite.Directory . Pocker Instances under pocker.root (default ./pb_root ), one folder per instance. Docker Instances under docker.root , the same / layout. It knows nothing about plans, payments or tenants: that belongs to whichever policy provider is configured.

title: Stats
heading: Your own policy
text: Set Lifecycle.Policy to anything that implements PolicyProvider : type PolicyProvider interface { Decide(ctx context.Context, facts []Facts) ([]Decision, error) // what to do now, and why ReportEvery() time.Duration // how often last-request times are reported Concurrency() int // instances worked on at once } A control plane can provide its own, for example one that delegates the decisions to a mothership, and providers can wrap each other. Only the measure action is carried out today; any other action is logged as lifecycle: action not supported yet .

title: Stats
heading: Your own sink
text: Set Lifecycle.Sink to anything that implements Sink ( Report(ctx, facts []Facts) error ) to send facts somewhere other than the log. A sink that also implements Loader ( Load(ctx) ([]Facts, error) ) gives the facts back at start, so a restart doesn't measure everything again or forget last-request times.

title: Stats
heading: Rules: criteria an app can replace
text: rules (package pocketone.dev/ext/stats/rules , standard library only) is the engine policies are built from, on an edge or a mothership. A subject is whatever the caller evaluates: an instance's facts on an edge, an account with its instances on a mothership. Criteria answer one question about a subject (stale? orphaned? over its plan?) and say why. They live in a Registry by name: an app registers its own or replaces a built-in one ( Register("stale", ...) ), and every rule that refers to the name ( Ref("stale") ) follows, so what "stale" means is the app's to decide. Where they come from is pluggable too: code, or definitions from config ( Load ) built from kinds the app registered ( RegisterKind("idle", ...) ) and combined with all , any and not . A YAML section and a mothership are both just sources of definitions. Load registers nothing when a definition is wrong. Rules lead from a criterion to an action, with named vetoes that always win and a budget per run. Reports list each decision with its reasons, what was vetoed and by what, what the budget held back and what failed. Summary gives one line per rule ( archive-stale: 3 decided, 1 vetoed ). Evaluating does nothing by itself: acting on the decisions, or only logging them in a dry run, is the caller's. A definition, as config would supply it: stale: { kind: idle, params: { after: 8760h } } archivable: { kind: all, of: [stale, free_plan] } keep: { kind: not, of: [archivable] } And in Go: r := rules.NewRegistryFacts r.RegisterKind("idle", idleFor) // params: { after: 8760h } _ = r.Load(map[string]rules.Def{ "stale": {Kind: "idle", Params: map[string]any{"after": "8760h"}}, "archivable": {Kind: "all", Of: []string{"stale", "free_plan"}}, }) e := rules.Engine[Facts]{Key: id, Rules: []rules.Rule[Facts]{{ Name: "archive-stale", Action: "archive", When: r.Ref("archivable"), Unless: []rules.Veto[Facts]{{Name: "pinned", If: r.Ref("pinned")}}, Budget: 200, }}} report := e.Evaluate(ctx, facts) Every rule sees every subject, so one subject can get several decisions. Make rules exclusive by building them from exclusive criteria.

title: Stats
heading: Example
text: example/main.go measures the instance folders under a root once and prints their facts, which is what a host's lifecycle does daily. // Measure the instance folders under a root once and print their facts (what a host's lifecycle does daily). // // go run ./example --root ./pb_root --instances instances.yaml package main import ( "context" "flag" "fmt" "log" "log/slog" "path/filepath" "pocketone.dev/ext/multisite" "pocketone.dev/ext/stats" ) func main() { root := flag.String("root", "./pb_root", "one folder per instance: / ") instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file") flag.Parse() src := &multisite.YAMLSource{Path: instances, Required: true} list, err := src.Snapshot(context.Background()) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } dir := multisite.NewDirectory(slog.Default()) dir.Load(list) lc := &stats.Lifecycle{ Directory: dir, Folder: func(i multisite.Instance) string { if i.Dir != "" { return i.Dir } return filepath.Join( root, i.ID) }, Sink: stats.LogSink{}, } lc.Step(context.Background()) // never measured: every instance is measured now for _, f := range lc.Local() { fmt.Printf("%-24s %12d bytes\n", f.Instance, f.DiskBytes) } }

title: Stats
heading: How it works
text: Go module pocketone.dev/ext/stats . The stock binary wires it in examples/pocketone/multi.go . Run loads recorded facts from a Loader sink, then waits for the host's instance list to load (checking every second). From then on, once a minute, it asks the policy for decisions on the current facts, measures the instances it was asked to ( concurrency at a time) and reports what it measured to the sink. Measuring walks the folder and adds up regular file sizes. An instance's pending last-request time goes out with its measurement, so it isn't reported twice. Admit records last_active only for instances this host serves itself ( Remote empty), and never refuses a request.

title: Templates
text: Version 0.0.2 · Owners: @benallfree Some extensions serve pages of their own, such as the OAuth sign-in, consent and MFA screens the CLI and MCP agents sign in through. Templates lets you restyle them: eject an extension's templates into your app's pb_templates folder and edit them. Any file you keep there replaces the built-in one; delete it to go back. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Templates
heading: Install
text: Templates is built into pocketone and on by default; there's nothing to install. In your own Go build: extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{templates.New(templates.Config{})}, nil, nil)

title: Templates
heading: Configure
text: Nothing to configure. Your copies live in pb_templates/ next to pb_data (in a Go build, templates.Config.Dir moves it). pocketone deploy and pocketone dev sync it like pb_hooks .

title: Templates
heading: Use
text: See the template sets your app's extensions offer, and what you've changed: pocketone template list Eject one to edit it (leave out the name to eject every set): pocketone template eject oauth That copies every file of the set into pb_templates/oauth/ . Edit any of them; the next request uses your copy, no restart. Keep only the files you change if you like: the rest come from the built-in set. Ejecting again is safe: files you haven't changed are left alone and missing ones are written back. Files you did change are listed and only overwritten if you answer yes; without a terminal to ask in it refuses, and --force overwrites them without asking. The files are Go templates ( html/template ): {{.AppName}} prints a value (HTML-escaped), {{if .Error}}…{{end}} and {{range .Providers}}…{{end}} branch and loop, and {{template "head" .}} includes another file of the set ( head.tpl ). A broken file shows its error instead of the page, so you see what to fix.

heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Templates

text: What it adds to the pocketone binary (CLI reference): [ pocketone template eject [set] ](/docs/reference/cli#pocketone-template-eject) Copies a template set (every set without a name) into pb\_templates/<set>/ for you to edit pocketone template list Lists the template sets extensions offer, and what you've changed in pb\_templates

text: Tokens Its OAuth pages are the oauth set: sign-in, MFA, one-time code, consent, device code, done and error, with a shared head and foot . Without Templates it serves them built in.

title: Templates
heading: Building on Templates
text: An extension adds its own set through the templates/v1 contract: embed a folder of .tpl files, add it under a name in Register ( templatesv1.Add(app, "mine", files) ), and render a page with templatesv1.Contract.Of(app) 's Render . Declare templates/v1 in WorksWith and render the embedded set yourself ( templatesv1.Parse , templatesv1.Write ) when nothing provides it.

title: Templates
heading: Example
text: A PocketBase app with one inline set, hello , served at /hello . Run go run . template eject hello , edit pb_templates/hello/page.tpl , and reload. // Command example is a PocketBase app with templates/v1 and one template set, "hello", served at /hello. Run // go run . template eject hello , edit pb_templates/hello/page.tpl, and reload /hello. package main import ( "log" "net/http" "testing/fstest" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" templatesv1 "pocketone.dev/ext/contracts/templates/v1" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" "pocketone.dev/ext/templates" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{templates.New(templates.Config{})}, nil, nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } // an extension would go:embed its set; this one is inline templatesv1.Add(app, "hello", fstest.MapFS{"page.tpl": {Data: []byte( Hello, {{.}}! )}}) app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { se.Router.GET("/hello", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { return templatesv1.Contract.Must(app).Render(e, "hello", "page", http.StatusOK, "world") }) return se.Next() }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: UI Cache
text: Version 0.0.2 · Owners: @benallfree PocketBase tells browsers and CDNs to keep every dashboard file for 14 days, including files whose name never changes. Behind a CDN such as Cloudflare, that means a new or updated dashboard screen from an extension, or the dashboard's own libraries after an upgrade, can take up to two weeks to show up. UI Cache sends headers that let those changes through within minutes, and keeps the long cache for the files that can safely have it. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: UI Cache
heading: Install
text: UI Cache is built into pocketone and on by default ; there's nothing to install. In your own Go build: extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{uicache.New()}, nil, nil) The module is pocketone.dev/ext/uicache .

title: UI Cache
heading: Configure
text: There's nothing to configure. An app turns it off with uicache: {enabled: false} in its pocketone.yaml, which brings back PocketBase's own headers.

title: UI Cache
heading: Use
text: Nothing to do day to day. Check the headers with curl: curl -sI https://app.example.com/_/extensions.js grep -i cache-control /_/extensions.js , /_/index.html no-cache Checked on every load: extensions.js is every extension's screen joined into one file, rebuilt when any of them changes. /_/assets/ - .js (and .css ) PocketBase's own (14 days) The name changes with the content, so a new build is a new URL. Everything else ( libs/ , fonts/ , images/ , /_/extensions/ /... ) public, max-age=300 Five minutes: fresh soon after an update, still cached while you browse. /_/ itself (the dashboard page) is sent without a cache lifetime by PocketBase and left alone. In dev mode ( --dev ) UI Cache does nothing, as PocketBase sends no cache headers there. After turning it on for an app that sits behind a CDN, purge /_/ there once: copies cached under the old 14-day header stay until they expire.

title: UI Cache
heading: Integrations
text: Multisite Every instance gets it with the standard set; turn it off for one with extensions.uicache.enabled: false . Extensions with dashboard screens (Tokens, PITR, Bulk Mail, ...) Their main.js reaches the browser through /_/extensions.js , so an updated screen shows on the next load. An extension that serves other files from /_/extensions/ / gets the five-minute policy. To cache one longer, put a content hash in its name and set its own Cache-Control in a middleware that runs before UI Cache's ( uicache.MiddlewareID ); a header that's already set is kept.

title: UI Cache
heading: Example
text: A PocketBase app with UI Cache, to see the headers locally. // Command example is a PocketBase app whose dashboard sends cache headers that let changes through: run // go run . serve , then curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8090/_/extensions.js grep -i cache-control shows no-cache . // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" "pocketone.dev/ext/uicache" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{uicache.New()}, nil, nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: UI Cache
heading: How it works
text: PocketBase's dashboard middleware (in apis/serve.go and apis/extensions.go ) sets its 14-day Cache-Control only when the response has none yet. UI Cache binds a router middleware in OnServe , which runs before route and group middleware, and sets the header first. No PocketBase code changes.

title: Upgrade
text: Version 0.0.2 · Owners: @benallfree pocketone upgrade replaces the pocketone executable with the latest PocketOne release and keeps the old one beside it as - (for example pocketone-0.0.3 ), so a project can keep running the engine it was built with. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Upgrade
heading: Install
text: Upgrade is built into pocketone : the upgrade command is always there. There's nothing to turn on. In your own Go build, register the command before the app starts: import "pocketone.dev/ext/upgrade" app := pocketbase.New() upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{}) app.Start()

title: Upgrade
heading: Configure
text: Nothing to configure: no pocketone.yaml section, no environment variables, no settings screens. The command has one flag: --backup true Back up pb_data after upgrading, if the current folder has one. --backup=false skips it. --yes , -y false Move from a stable release to a prerelease without asking.

title: Upgrade
heading: Use
text: Run it from your project folder: pocketone upgrade It: Picks the newest release on GitHub that fits what you're running, and stops if you already have it: The newest release is offered, prereleases included: 0.1.0-alpha.2 goes to 0.1.0-alpha.3 or 0.1.0 , whichever is newest. From one prerelease to the next (or to a stable release), it just upgrades. From a stable release to a prerelease ( 0.1.0 to 0.1.1-alpha.1 ), it asks first. No means the newest stable release instead, if there's a newer one. --yes answers yes for you; with no answer (no terminal), it's no. A local build upgrades to the newest release without asking. Downloads the archive for your platform and checks it against the release's checksums.txt before touching anything. Renames the current executable to - and puts the new one in its place. Old copies are never deleted , so pocketone-0.0.3 serve still runs a project on that version. A local build with no release version is kept as .old , which the next such upgrade replaces. Backs up pb_data , when the current folder has one, as @upgrade_ .zip in PocketBase's backups. Prints the new version, where the old one was kept, and the release notes. Two cases where it does something else: Installed with Homebrew: it prints brew upgrade pocketone instead. Homebrew keeps the previous version until brew cleanup . In a Docker container: it refuses; upgrade the image instead. It needs write access to the folder the executable is in. A kept executable doesn't undo migrations: once a newer version has served a pb_data , an older one may not open it. The backup is the way back for that.

title: Upgrade
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Upgrade
heading: Commands
text: What it adds to the pocketone binary (CLI reference): pocketone upgrade Upgrades this executable to the latest release, keeping the old one as <name>-<version>

title: Upgrade
heading: Integrations
text: Nothing integrates with it yet. Other tools can reuse its release code: Custom builds that publish their own releases set Owner , Repo , ArchivePrefix and ArchiveExecutable in upgrade.Config . Release archives are named _ _ _ .zip , with a goreleaser-style checksums.txt in the same release. Go API. Config.FetchReleases(ctx) lists the published releases, prereleases included, and upgrade.UpgradeFor(current, releases, stableOnly) picks the one to upgrade to and upgrade.NeedsConfirm(current, release) says whether to ask first. Config.FetchRelease(ctx, tag) fetches GitHub's latest stable release (tag "" ) or a given one; Config.DownloadArchive(ctx, release, goos, goarch, dir) downloads and checks a platform's archive. upgrade.KeptName(exe, version) is the name an old executable is kept under.

title: Upgrade
heading: Example
text: example/main.go is a PocketOne app with just the upgrade command. Try it with go run ./example upgrade . // Command example is a PocketOne app with just the upgrade command. A local build has no release version, so it is // kept as "example.old"; release builds are kept as " - ". // // go run ./example upgrade package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "pocketone.dev/ext/upgrade" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{}) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Vacuum
text: Version 0.0.2 · Owners: @benallfree SQLite doesn't give space back to the disk when records are deleted; the file stays as big as it ever was. Vacuum compacts your app's databases on a schedule (SQLite's VACUUM ), so the space comes back. It only compacts a database when enough of it is free space (10%, or 64 MB), so a busy, tidy app is left alone. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Vacuum
heading: Install
text: Vacuum is built into pocketone . In your own Go build: extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{vacuum.New()}, nil, nil)

title: Vacuum
heading: Configure
text: The app's admins turn it on and set how often in the dashboard, in the Vacuum section at the bottom of Settings → Backups (a settings/v1 section, so the CLI and agents can change it too). pocketone.yaml sets the defaults until they do: vacuum: enabled: true every: 168h # weekly; at least 1h Without either, it's off.

title: Vacuum
heading: vacuum:
text: Defaults for compacting the app's SQLite databases (VACUUM): on or off, and how often. The app's admins change them in Settings. enabled bool Compact the databases on a schedule, until the app's admins change it in Settings. every string 168h How often, e.g. 24h or 168h (weekly).

title: Vacuum
heading: Use
text: Once on, every every while the app serves, Vacuum checks data.db and auxiliary.db and compacts the ones with enough free space (PocketBase's own online VACUUM ; writes wait while it runs). VACUUM needs free disk space about the size of the database it compacts. The same section shows its status: whether it's on, how often, the next run, and the last run's bytes given back and databases skipped. It's vacuum/v1, also on the command line: pocketone remote vacuum status

title: Vacuum
heading: Commands and APIs
text: Generated from the pocketone binary and the contracts this extension provides.

title: Vacuum
heading: vacuum/v1
text: status pocketone remote vacuum status GET /api/_c/vacuum/v1 vacuum_status

title: Vacuum
heading: Integrations
text: Settings Its on/off and schedule are a settings/v1 section, in the dashboard, the CLI and for agents. Multisite A host may compact its instances itself: when it provides vacuum/v1 for them, Vacuum steps aside in each instance: the Vacuum section shows the host's status, read-only, with no setting. PITR A compacted database is a new file to Litestream, so the next replication starts a fresh generation.

title: Vacuum
heading: Building on Vacuum
text: vacuum.App(app) compacts a running app now and returns what it did. LoadSettings / SaveSettings read and change the app's settings.

title: Vacuum
heading: Example
text: A PocketBase app that compacts its databases once when it starts serving. // Command example is a PocketBase app that compacts its databases once when it starts serving (vacuum.App), the work // the extension does on its admins' schedule. Run go run . serve and watch the log for "vacuum: once". package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" "pocketone.dev/ext/vacuum" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{vacuum.New()}, nil, nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(e core.ServeEvent) error { go func() { run := vacuum.App(app) app.Logger().Info("vacuum: once", "saved_bytes", run.Saved, "skipped", run.Skipped, "error", run.Error) }() return e.Next() }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: WASM
text: Version 0.0.2 · Owners: @octavonu Bring your own WASM (BYOW). Call code written in Go, Rust, Zig or anything else that builds for WASI from your page code, when you need a library from another language or more speed than JS gives you. A module is a small program compiled to WebAssembly that your code calls like a function. Input in, output out, or an error. It can't reach the database, files, network, environment or other processes; your code gives it what it needs and decides what to do with the result. One call does it: const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", { title: "Hello", body: "one two three" }) // out is { text: "Hello", words: 3 } "summary" names the module, pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm . The object is its input, sent to it as JSON, and out is the JSON it writes back, parsed. If the module fails, the call rejects with a WasmError . Calls are only async : the module runs off the JS engine, so the app keeps serving other requests while it works. In an API route, the input comes from the request and the output goes into the record it saves: // pb_pages/posts/+api.ts export async function post(ctx: any) { const { title, body } = ctx.req.body() const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", { title, body }) const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts")) record.load({ title, body, summary: out.text }) ctx.app.save(record) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id, summary: out.text }) } Use it for what JS does badly or slowly: parsing (EDIFACT, XML, binary formats), crypto, validation, number crunching, or a library that only exists in Go, Rust or C. WASM is an extension; the .pb.wasm files it runs are modules. Beyond this page: a page for each language (C, Go, TinyGo, Rust, Zig, AssemblyScript), keeping state in JS between calls, and recipes built on real libraries (Markdown, HTML sanitizing, thumbnails, QR codes, diffs, CSV). Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: WASM
heading: Install
text: WASM is built into pocketone : it's a member of the standard set, which every app gets, standalone or an instance on a multisite host, and the set binds $wasm into the JS engine ( ext/jsvm ). Put a .pb.wasm file in pb_hooks and call it from your page code. In your own build, the set already has it. To change its settings, replace the member: set := standard.New() set.WASM = wasm.New(wasm.Config{MaxConcurrent: 4}) Without the set, register it and bind it yourself: w := wasm.New(wasm.Config{}) app := pocketbase.New() extkit.MustRegister(app, w) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, w) }}) app.Start() $wasm needs PocketOne's JS engine; with PocketBase's own ( --jsvm goja ) extensions bind nothing. The module is pocketone.dev/ext/wasm . Modules are pb_hooks/ .pb.wasm ; nothing else needs setting up.

title: WASM
heading: Configure
text: The defaults suit most apps. To change them, pass them to wasm.New ( set.WASM = wasm.New(...) in a standard set): Dir pb_hooks beside the data dir The module folder. MaxCallMemoryMB 32 Memory each call may allocate (its heap, stack and input). Every call has its own, not shared: 8 calls at once may take 8 × 32 MB. A call that needs more crashes alone. Timeout 5s Time limit for a call's run (compiling comes before it). MaxConcurrent 8 Calls running at once in the app. More wait, up to Timeout , then fail as busy . MaxModulesMB 10 MB of modules running at once: the .wasm sizes of the calls running, added up (file sizes, not memory). More wait, as above. It's also the largest module that runs. MaxPayload 4 MB Largest input or output of a call. CacheDir pocketone/wasm in the user's cache folder ( ~/.cache on Linux, ~/Library/Caches on macOS) Where compiled modules are kept between calls and restarts (see How it works). "off" compiles every call. Keep it where only the server's process writes: it holds machine code the process runs. Its pocketone.yaml section has only enabled : wasm: {enabled: false} turns $wasm off on a single app. With Pocker, each instance can override all of these but CacheDir , which is the host's (see Integrations).

title: WASM
heading: Modules are files
text: A module is one file in pb_hooks/ , pb_hooks/ .pb.wasm , called as : pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm pb_pages/posts/+api.ts It ships with the rest of your code: git, pocketone deploy , or SFTP. Like node script.js , every call reads the module's file as it is then. A change in pb_hooks/ also restarts the app, as for a .pb.js (under pocker the new app takes over once it has started). To turn a module off, remove or rename it. Hidden files and files that don't end in .pb.wasm are ignored, so upload a new version under a hidden name ( .summary.pb.wasm.part ) and rename it over the old one: no call reads it half written. A module that can't run (a broken module, a module over MaxModulesMB ) fails its calls with not_loaded and says why, and $wasm.modules() says it too; the other modules run as usual.

title: WASM
heading: The manifest: --describe
text: A module says what it is itself: run as --describe (the function asked for is --describe , with nothing on stdin), it prints its manifest. Answering is optional, and so is each field; a module that exits non-zero or prints nothing gets the defaults: { "description": "Summarizes a post: its title and first words, and a word count", "version": "1.2.0", "functions": ["run"], "language": "Rust", "repository": "https://github.com/you/summary", "examples": [ { "function": "run", "input": {"title": "Hello", "body": "one two three"}, "output": {"text": "Hello: one two three", "words": 3} } ] } description what it does version the author's version, as you write it ( 1.2.0 , 2026-11-15 ): up to 32 letters, digits and .+_- ; only shown functions the functions your code may call (default ["run"] ) language what it's written in, shown when the module doesn't say: a Go module always does, a Rust one unless it's stripped ( strip = true ), a Zig one never repository where its source is: an http(s) URL (no javascript: , no credentials), at most 256 characters examples up to 16 calls to try it with: function (default run ), input (a JSON string is the module's stdin as it is, anything else goes as JSON, as with $wasm.run.async ) and, optionally, the output it gives The manifest is only shown, by $wasm.modules() , for people and for tests (run each example and compare its output): calls don't read it, nothing runs the examples, and nothing fetches the repository. A function that isn't in functions still reaches the module, which answers it; by convention, with the code no_such_function . Function names can't start with - , so --describe is never one of them. Try it locally: wazero run summary.pb.wasm --describe , and an example: printf '%s' '{"title":"Hello","body":"one two three"}' wazero run summary.pb.wasm run . The examples keep the manifest as manifest.json beside the source and build it in (Go's //go:embed , Rust's include_str! , Zig's @embedFile ), so the module is still one file. Any other field is refused: a module can't ask for anything, so a manifest that expects more (dependencies, permissions) is shown as an error in $wasm.modules() , and the module runs with the defaults. A manifest is at most 64 KB. $wasm.modules() checks it with wazero's interpreter (below), within the module's limits.

title: WASM
heading: Calling from page code
text: await $wasm.run.async(name, input) // the module's "run" await $wasm.call.async(name, fn, input) // one of its functions (its first argument) await $wasm.inspect.async(name, fn, input) // {output, stderr, error, compileMs, runMs}, for trying a module out $wasm.modules() // [{name, running, description, version, functions, language, repository, examples, size, error}] $wasm.limits() // {maxCallMemoryMB, timeoutMs, maxConcurrent, maxModulesMB, maxPayload} Calls are async only, in an async handler. The JS engine runs one VM per app and can't interrupt a call into Go, so a module called synchronously would hold the VM, and with it every other hook and request of the app, while it compiles and runs (a Go module's first call compiles for over a second). A call runs off the VM instead, and the app serves other requests meanwhile. $wasm.run(...) without .async throws, saying so. The input is the module's stdin: a string or bytes (an ArrayBuffer , a Uint8Array or another typed array) as they are, nothing for undefined or null , anything else as JSON. So $wasm.run.async("edifact", raw) , with raw a string, hands over the raw text, byte for byte. The output is the module's stdout: parsed if it's JSON, a string if not, null if empty. A failed call rejects with an Error named WasmError , with code , message , retryable and module : try { record.set("summary", (await $wasm.run.async ("summary", post)).text) } catch (err) { const w = err as WasmError if (w.name !== "WasmError" w.code !== "empty_body") throw err } not_found no .pb.wasm in the folder not_loaded in the folder, but it can't run (the message says why: a broken module, too large), or the app isn't serving no_such_function the module has no such function (the code modules give, by convention) timeout over the time limit (retryable) crashed it trapped, panicked or ran out of memory too_large input or output over the limit busy the calls running left no room for this one (retryable); the message gives the numbers module_error it exited non-zero without a code of its own anything else the module's own code (below) $wasm.inspect.async makes the same call but never rejects for it: it returns the output (or null ), the error as {code, message, retryable} (or null ), what the module wrote to stderr (up to 64 KB), and how long compiling and running took. It's for pages that let a superuser try a module out; other code uses run and call . The time limit covers the run; compiling comes before it (below). $wasm is declared in each app's types.d.ts ( wasm.d.ts ), for code completion and tsc .

title: WASM
heading: Writing a module
text: A module is a plain WASI program ( wasip1 ), the way you'd write a command-line tool: read stdin, write stdout, exit. The function asked for is its first argument ( os.Args[1] , "run" for $wasm.run.async , --describe for its manifest, above). To fail, exit non-zero; if stderr is a JSON object {"code", "message", "retryable"} , your code gets it as is, any other text becomes the message of a module_error . Anything it writes to stderr on success goes to the app's log (Logs in the dashboard), so stderr is its log. Go ( example/summary/go ): //go:embed manifest.json var manifest string // what --describe prints func main() { if os.Args[1] == "--describe" { fmt.Print(manifest) return } var post struct{ Title, Body string } if err := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&post); err != nil { fmt.Fprint(os.Stderr, {"code":"bad_input","message":"not a post"} ) os.Exit(1) } json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(map[string]any{"text": post.Title, "words": len(strings.Fields(post.Body))}) } GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm . Rust ( example/summary/rust ): a binary crate, serde for JSON. rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 # once cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/summary.wasm pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm Zig ( example/summary/zig ): an executable for wasm32-wasi (Zig 0.17). Set stack_size = 1 << 20 in build.zig : Zig's default stack is 16 MB, and every call would start with it. Any language that builds a WASI program works the same way: Languages has a page for C and C++, Go, TinyGo, Rust, Zig and AssemblyScript, each with a module to build, and what else runs. Try a module without an app: echo '{"title":"Hi","body":"one two"}' wazero run summary.pb.wasm run . Two things are refused when the module loads, with a message that says so: a library instead of a program: Go's -buildmode=c-shared , or any module without _start ("not a WASI program"); a module that imports anything outside wasi_snapshot_preview1 , such as an Extism plugin built with its PDK, or host functions this host doesn't have.

title: WASM
heading: Which language
text: C 25 KB 17 ms 0.5 ms 86 KB Rust 98 KB 33 ms 1.3 ms 389 KB Zig 95 KB 30 ms 1.2 ms 357 KB TinyGo 284 KB 74 ms 3 ms 988 KB Go 4.3 MB 1.05 s 38 ms 18 MB A module's first call compiles it and writes its machine code to the cache ( CacheDir ); every later call, after a restart too, loads it from there. Running the summary itself takes under a millisecond in every language. A call holds its module's machine code in memory only while it runs, plus the program's own memory (its stack and heap, Go's runtime and garbage collector included), which stays under MaxCallMemoryMB ; between calls, nothing. Measured on a laptop (2026-11-18), one call at a time; a Go module's size varies with what it imports (one that imports net/http is ~11 MB). Choosing a language has the same numbers with how to pick. Go calls compiling at once also slow each other down: one took +19 MB, two +38 MB, four +245 MB (2026-11-16, before the cache; calls that load from the cache take far less). That's why the calls running at once are limited by their modules' size, MaxModulesMB , and not only by their number. An admin picks the trade-off with that one number: 5 1 8 ( MaxConcurrent ) ~25 MB 10 (default) 2 8 ~45 MB 20 4 8 ~250 MB Pick by what the module does. With the cache, every language is quick after its first call; what still differs is memory and how many calls run at once. A Go call holds 18 MB of machine code and takes 38 ms to load it, and two run at once with the defaults: fine for a cron job, an import or an admin action. A module on a hot path (every record save, every request) is better in C, Rust, Zig or TinyGo (the same Go source, a module 15 times smaller), whose calls take a few milliseconds and under 1 MB.

title: WASM
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Add it to the host's standard set and Pocker gives it to every instance it runs (Docker containers run stock images): one extension value serves them all. Each instance has its own modules, in its own pb_hooks/ , its own call slots and limits. Each call reads the instance's module file as it is then; nothing runs between calls (below). A module change reloads just that instance, like a .pb.js change. Sandbox $wasm is safe to give a hostile tenant: a module gets nothing but its input. A call can't be interrupted by the JS engine's time limits, so Timeout (and compiling) bound it instead. Deploy pocketone deploy sends the modules with the rest of pb_hooks/ . MCP The app's /mcp gets wasm_list_modules (superusers only): every module by name, with its manifest (functions, examples) and whether it runs. Agents connecting are told how to call a module with $wasm , so one working on the site knows its modules even without their sources.

title: WASM
heading: Per-instance settings (Pocker)
text: Each instance can override maxCallMemoryMB , maxConcurrent , maxModulesMB , timeout (a duration, like 5s ) and maxPayload in its extensions.wasm settings, over the Config given to New , key by key. enabled: false turns $wasm off for that instance ( typeof $wasm === "undefined" in its JS). A change restarts just that instance, on its next request: instances: id: abc extensions: { wasm: { timeout: 10s, maxCallMemoryMB: 64 } } id: no-wasm extensions: { wasm: { enabled: false } } Leave dir unset there: each instance then gets the pb_hooks/ in its own folder. MaxConcurrent and MaxModulesMB count per instance, so one instance's busy modules never make another's calls wait. A restart (new settings, a pb_hooks change, a restore) lets calls in progress finish, and the instance's modules run as before after it, from its folder: nothing to reload.

title: WASM
heading: Building on WASM
text: There's no Go API, endpoint or form for calling a module: the app's JS code ( $wasm ) is the only way in, so whatever reaches a module went through the app's own code.

title: WASM
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app with a posts collection and a hook that fills each new post's summary; its folder is laid out like an instance ( pb_data/ , pb_hooks/ ). Build the module into example/pb_hooks/ , then cd example && go run . serve --dev and create a post. // Command example runs one app with ext/wasm and the summary module wired in from pb_hooks: a new post gets its // summary before it's saved (pb_hooks/main.pb.js). The example folder is the app's folder, laid out like an // instance on PocketHost: pb_data/ and pb_hooks/ side by side, the module beside the JS hooks. // // cd example && go run . serve --dev // // Build the module into pb_hooks/ (before or after starting the app: each call reads it): // // (cd summary/go && GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o ../../pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm .) // // Then create a post (dashboard, or the API) and look at its summary field. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "pocketone.dev/ext/devusers" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit" "pocketone.dev/ext/extkit/js" "pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm" "pocketone.dev/ext/wasm" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" app.OnBootstrap().BindFunc(func(e core.BootstrapEvent) error { if err := e.Next(); err != nil { return err } return posts(e.App) }) // the same extension value the standard set gives every app, standalone or an instance (set.WASM) w := wasm.New(wasm.Config{}) extkit.MustRegister(app, w) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: "pb_hooks", OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, w) }, // $wasm in pb_hooks }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } func posts(app core.App) error { if _, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts"); err == nil { return nil } c := core.NewBaseCollection("posts") c.Fields.Add(&core.TextField{Name: "title"}, &core.TextField{Name: "body", Max: 100000}, &core.TextField{Name: "summary", Max: 1000}, &core.NumberField{Name: "words"}) return app.Save(c) }

title: WASM
heading: More example modules
text: Each is a plain program with a manifest.json built in, which it prints for --describe (its functions and examples, so /wasm -style pages and the wazero CLI can try it), built with the command in its header. They answer the usual questions about a feature like this: summary/go , summary/tinygo , summary/rust , summary/zig , summary/c , summary/assemblyscript Go, TinyGo, Rust, Zig, C, AssemblyScript The same module in six languages: the summary above, and how much the language matters (a Go module is ~4 MB and compiles for over a second; TinyGo ~280 KB and ~65 ms; Rust, Zig, C and AssemblyScript under 100 KB and 10–25 ms). summary/wat , summary/llvm WAT, LLVM IR The C summary written by hand in two assembly languages, for fun: WebAssembly text calling WASI directly (1.8 KB), and LLVM IR built by clang with wasi-libc (3.8 KB). See WAT and LLVM IR. stats-tinygo TinyGo State kept by the app: running statistics whose state the app stores in a record and passes in with each call (Keeping state in JS). markdown , sanitize-html , diff , thumbnail , qrcode , csv Rust Real libraries for real jobs (pulldown-cmark, ammonia, similar, image, qrcode, csv), each with page code in the recipes. crypto Go What an app used to run with $os.exec : AES-256-GCM. The key comes in with each call; the module can't keep it or send it anywhere. waflows Rust What JS can't do: a WhatsApp Flows endpoint needs RSA-OAEP and AES-GCM with WhatsApp's key and IV. Your code keeps the JSON and HTTP; the module does only those two. edifact-orders-rust Rust A real format with a real library (edifact-rs): an EDIFACT ORDERS message, as raw text, read into an order. order-xml Rust The same order from XML (roxmltree), so one route takes either format and stores one shape. devil Rust Is it safe? It tries, in plain sight, to read the app's database and /etc/passwd , list folders, write a file, read the environment, run sh -c id and send to attacker.example . Every try says refused . memhog Rust What does it cost? It asks for more memory than MaxCallMemoryMB : that call fails as crashed , saying which limit it hit, and the app goes on. probe shows the limit from inside. Every one of them is also kept built, beside its source ( example/ / .pb.wasm : the Go ones about 4.5 MB, the rest under 1 MB), so they double as the extension's tests: every run of go test loads each one, checks that its --describe is its manifest.json , and runs its examples, with no compiler and no Docker needed. A change to ext/wasm that breaks a real module shows there. They're built in Docker, never with the compilers on your machine: example/toolchains/Dockerfile is the build environment of every example language, one stage each: Go 1.27.4, TinyGo 0.41.1, Rust 1.100.0 and Zig 0.17.0 (Zig, and C through zig cc ), each image pinned by digest and Zig's download by checksum, so a rebuild on any machine gives the same bytes. After changing a module's source: go test -run 'TestPrebuiltExamples/ ' -update . To check every kept file is what its source builds, byte for byte: go test -run TestPrebuiltMatchSources -rebuild (a few minutes). To move to a newer compiler, change it in the Dockerfile and rebuild them all with -update . The Go builds use -trimpath and the Rust builds remap the crates' paths to /cargo , so a module holds no path of the container that built it.

title: WASM
heading: What a module can't do
text: Modules run in wazero (pure Go, no cgo), in the app's process, with only the standard WASI functions and nothing behind them: No files: nothing is mounted, not even pb_hooks/ . open fails. No network: WASI preview 1 has no way to connect. (Go's net on wasip1 is an in-memory stand-in: a module can "listen", but nothing outside the program reaches it.) No environment, no processes , no arguments beyond the function name. No state between calls: every call gets a fresh instance, so nothing from one call (or one caller) reaches the next. Bounded: memory, time, input and output size, and how many calls run at once (see Configure). It does get a real clock and real random numbers (crypto nonces need them). Data from the app, secrets and API responses reach a module only as input from your code, and the result goes nowhere but back to it: the network stays with $http.send in your JS.

title: WASM
heading: How it works
text: Modules run only while the app serves (other commands, such as migrate , never read them). Like node script.js : each call reads its module's file ( .pb.wasm , once the call has room), compiles the module in a wazero runtime of its own (or loads its machine code from the cache), runs it, and closes it after. Nothing stays in memory between calls, so a folder of 100 modules costs nothing while they aren't called. Compiling validates the module: a broken or half-written one doesn't run. A call in progress finishes with what it read, whatever happens to the file meanwhile. Compiling counts toward MaxConcurrent and MaxModulesMB , so the memory it takes stays bounded too. Compiled modules are kept on disk, in wazero's compilation cache ( CacheDir ), keyed by each module's bytes: a changed module compiles again on its next call, and identical modules share one entry, across every app and instance in the process and across restarts. Loading from it is 20 to 30 times faster than compiling. Calls of the same module compile one at a time (wazero can't load one module twice at once safely); calls of other modules never wait for it, and a call whose caller gives up stops waiting ( busy ). When the process first opens the cache, it deletes entries older than 30 days, since nothing else does: a module still in use compiles once more then. The process runs the cache's contents as machine code, so it belongs where only the process writes, never in pb_data or pb_hooks . WASM watches nothing itself: no watches of its own, no timer, no work between calls, however many instances there are. (The JS engine's, or pocker's, watch on pb_hooks/ restarts the app when a module changes, as for a hook.) $wasm.modules() lists the folder each time. It checks each module with wazero's interpreter, which validates it and runs --describe without making machine code (~0.25 s for a Go module), and keeps only what it found (manifest, language, error) until the module's file changes size or time; when the app starts serving, it checks them all once, so the log says which ones can't run. A call waits for room: fewer than MaxConcurrent calls running, and its module's size left in MaxModulesMB ( $wasm.modules() gives each one's size ). Compiling takes time and memory in step with a module's size, so with the defaults (8 calls, 10 MB) a Rust or Zig module (~0.1 MB) runs 8 calls at once and a Go one (~4.4 MB) 2, beside small ones. A call goes in as soon as there's room for it, so a small call doesn't queue behind a big one that's waiting; under a steady stream of small calls, a big one may wait until it gives up as busy . No collection and no database use: what's in the folder, and why a module can't run, comes from the files ( $wasm.modules() and the log).

text: MIT

title: Keeping state in JS
text: Every call gets a fresh module: nothing a call leaves in memory reaches the next one. That's what makes a module safe to share, and it means a module that works on a series (running totals, a rate, a game, a parser that resumes) can't keep its own state. The app keeps it instead: Your page code loads the state: from a record, or from memory. It passes the state in with the call. The module returns the new state, and your code saves it. The module stays a pure function, (state, input) → new state , which also makes it easy to test: each example in its manifest is one step.

title: Keeping state in JS
heading: The module
text: example/stats-tinygo keeps running statistics of a series of readings: count, mean, standard deviation, min and max. It uses Welford's method, so the state is five numbers however many readings it has seen. It has two functions: add : {"state": , "values": [...]} → the new state report : a state → {count, mean, stddev, min, max} // State is everything the module needs to go on where the last call stopped. The app stores it as JSON. type State struct { Count int json:"count" Mean float64 json:"mean" M2 float64 json:"m2" // the sum of squared distances from the mean Min float64 json:"min" Max float64 json:"max" } func main() { switch os.Args[1] { case "--describe": fmt.Print(manifest) case "add": var in struct { State State json:"state" Values []float64 json:"values" } decode(&in) s := State{} if in.State != nil { s = in.State } for _, v := range in.Values { // ... update count, mean, m2, min, max } encode(s) case "report": // ... stddev = sqrt(m2 / count) default: fail("no_such_function", os.Args[1]) } } Build it with TinyGo: tinygo build -target=wasip1 -opt=z -no-debug -scheduler=none -o pb_hooks/stats.pb.wasm . It's 283 KB. Its first call compiles it (about 80 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 3 ms.

title: Keeping state in JS
heading: State in a record
text: Give the collection a JSON field for the state: here, a sensors collection with name (text) and stats (JSON). An API route takes new readings, runs them through the module with the sensor's state, and saves the new state on the record: // pb_pages/sensors/[id]/readings/+api.ts // POST /sensors/{id}/readings {"values": [21.5, 22]}: adds readings to the sensor's running statistics type Stats = { count: number; mean: number; m2: number; min: number; max: number } // the module's state type Report = { count: number; mean: number; stddev: number; min: number; max: number } export async function post(ctx: any) { const sensor = ctx.app.findRecordById("sensors", ctx.params.id) const { values } = ctx.req.body() as { values: number[] } try { const state: Stats null = JSON.parse(sensor.getString("stats")) // null until the first readings const next = await $wasm.call.async ("stats", "add", { state, values }) sensor.set("stats", next) ctx.app.save(sensor) return ctx.res.json(await $wasm.call.async ("stats", "report", next)) } catch (err) { const w = err as WasmError if (w.name !== "WasmError" w.retryable) throw err return ctx.res.json(400, { code: w.code, message: w.message }) // bad_input, bad_value: the caller's mistake } } curl -X POST localhost:8090/sensors/ /readings -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"values":[21.5,22]}' # {"count":2,"max":22,"mean":21.75,"min":21.5,"stddev":0.25} The record now holds the state, {"count":2,"m2":0.125,"max":22,"mean":21.75,"min":21.5} , and the next readings start from it. An empty JSON field reads as "null" , so JSON.parse gives null the first time, and the module starts a new series. The module's errors come back as WasmError , with its own code . Answer the caller's mistakes ( bad_input ) yourself, and let the rest ( busy , timeout ) fail the request. Two requests at once for the same sensor can both read the same state, and the second save drops the first one's readings. If that matters, send a sensor's readings one at a time, or save them as records and fold them into the state from a cron job.

title: Keeping state in JS
heading: State in memory
text: State the app can lose on a restart (a cache, a count since start) can stay in memory instead, in $app.store() . It's the app's own key-value store, shared by all its code, and it holds the module's output as it is: const store = ctx.app.store() const next = await $wasm.call.async ("stats", "add", { state: store.get("load") null, values: [1] }) store.set("load", next) Each app (each instance, under a host that runs many) has its own store, and a restart empties it: a change in pb_hooks/ restarts the app.

title: Keeping state in JS
heading: Why not keep it in the module?
text: A module can't: each call starts from the module's file, with fresh memory, and nothing outlives the call. That's on purpose. One caller's data never reaches another's call, a module that crashes takes nothing with it, and a folder of modules costs nothing between calls. Keeping state in the app also puts it where the app's other tools reach it: the dashboard shows it, backups keep it, and the API rules decide who reads it.

title: WASM
text: Bring your own WASM. Your page code is TypeScript, and most of the time that's all you need. Sometimes it isn't: the library you need only exists in Rust or Go, or the work (parsing, image processing, crypto, number crunching) is too slow in JS. WASM lets your page code call code written in another language, compiled to WebAssembly, as if it were a JavaScript function: const out = await $wasm.run.async ("hello", { name: "pocket" }) // out is { greeting: "Hello, POCKET!" } It's built into pocketone . There's nothing to install and nothing to configure: put a module in pb_hooks/ and call it from your page code.

title: WASM
heading: How it works
text: A module is a small program compiled to WebAssembly: a .pb.wasm file in pb_hooks/ . A call works like running a command-line tool: Your code calls $wasm.run.async(name, input) . The module starts fresh, reads the input, and writes its answer. Your code gets the answer back, parsed from JSON, and carries on. The module runs in a sealed box. It can't touch your database, your files, the network or other programs; it sees only the input your code gives it, and its answer goes only back to your code. Your code stays in charge: it decides what goes in and what to do with what comes out. A module that crashes, loops or runs out of memory fails its own call, and the app goes on.

title: WASM
heading: Try it in two minutes
text: You don't need a compiler to try it. The Markdown module from the recipes is kept built in the repository. In your app's folder: curl -L -o pb_hooks/markdown.pb.wasm \ https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/raw/main/ext/wasm/example/markdown/markdown.pb.wasm Add an API route that saves a note with its Markdown rendered to HTML: // pb_pages/notes/+api.ts export async function post(ctx: any) { const { body } = ctx.req.body() const note = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("notes")) note.load({ body, html: await $wasm.run.async ("markdown", body) }) ctx.app.save(note) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: note.id, html: note.getString("html") }) } Make a notes collection with two text fields, body and html , then post a note with # Hello and some bold text in its body: curl -X POST localhost:8090/notes -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"body":"# Hello\n\nSome bold text"}' The saved note's html field is the rendered HTML. This module passes raw HTML through, so for text your users write, add Sanitize HTML after it.

title: WASM
heading: Write your first module
text: A module is an ordinary program: it reads its input from stdin and prints its answer to stdout. Here's one in Go: // main.go package main import ( "encoding/json" "os" "strings" ) func main() { var in struct { Name string json:"name" } json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&in) if in.Name == "" { os.Stderr.WriteString( {"code":"no_name","message":"say who to greet"} ) os.Exit(1) } json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(map[string]string{ "greeting": "Hello, " + strings.ToUpper(in.Name) + "!", }) } Build it into your pb_hooks/ . Go can build WebAssembly with nothing extra; TinyGo makes the same program 15 times smaller and much faster to call: GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o pb_hooks/hello.pb.wasm . # Go: 4.3 MB tinygo build -target=wasip1 -opt=z -no-debug -scheduler=none -o pb_hooks/hello.pb.wasm . # TinyGo: 284 KB Call it from an API route: // pb_pages/hello/[name]/+api.ts export async function get(ctx: any) { const out = await $wasm.run.async ("hello", { name: ctx.params.name }) return ctx.res.json(out) } curl localhost:8090/hello/pocket # {"greeting":"Hello, POCKET!"} That's the whole contract: Input: your code's value arrives on stdin, as JSON (a string or bytes arrive as they are). Output: what the module prints comes back to your code, parsed if it's JSON. Errors: to fail, the module exits non-zero. If it prints {"code", "message"} to stderr, your code's catch gets those as err.code and err.message .

title: WASM
heading: Good to know
text: Calls are async. Use await $wasm.run.async(...) in an async handler. The module runs off the JS engine, so the rest of your app keeps serving requests while it works. Every call starts fresh. Nothing carries over from one call to the next, so a module can't remember anything. When it needs to, your code keeps the state and passes it in: see Keeping state in JS. The first call compiles, later calls don't. A module's first call compiles it and keeps the result on disk; every later call, after a restart too, loads it from there. A C, Rust or Zig module takes 17 to 33 ms the first time and 1 to 2 ms after; a Go module about a second, then 38 ms. Choosing a language compares them. Modules deploy with your app. They live in pb_hooks/ , so git, pocketone deploy and anything else that ships pb_hooks/ ships them too. Replacing a module's file takes effect on the next call.

title: WASM
heading: Next
text: Choosing a language: C and C++, Go, TinyGo, Rust, Zig, AssemblyScript, and what else runs. Recipes: modules built on real libraries, each with page code that calls it: Markdown, HTML sanitizing, thumbnails, QR codes, diffs, CSV. Keeping state in JS: modules that work on a series, with the state held by your app. Extension reference: every call, error code, limit and setting, and how it works inside.

title: AssemblyScript
text: AssemblyScript looks like TypeScript and compiles straight to WebAssembly, so it's the closest you can get to writing a module in the language your page code is in. Its modules are tiny: the summary example is 10 KB, its first call compiles in about 13 ms, and later calls load it from the cache in half a millisecond.
