It looks like TypeScript, but it isn't: types are WebAssembly's ( i32 , f64 , u8 ), there's no any and no union types, and npm packages written for JavaScript don't work in it. Only packages written for AssemblyScript do.

title: AssemblyScript
heading: Set up
text: AssemblyScript builds for the browser by default. @assemblyscript/wasi-shim makes it build a WASI program instead, with process.argv , process.stdin , process.stdout and process.exit : npm install --save-dev --save-exact assemblyscript @assemblyscript/wasi-shim asconfig.json extends the shim's settings and sets the release build: { "extends": "./node_modules/@assemblyscript/wasi-shim/asconfig.json", "targets": { "release": { "outFile": "summary.pb.wasm", "optimizeLevel": 3, "shrinkLevel": 2, "noAssert": true, "runtime": "stub" } } } The shim is required. Without it, a module imports env.abort from the browser's world, and it's refused when it loads. "runtime": "stub" leaves out the garbage collector: a call reads, computes and exits, so nothing needs collecting, and the module is smaller. A module that builds large data in a loop can use "incremental" instead.

title: AssemblyScript
heading: The module
text: example/summary/assemblyscript counts the words of a text and returns the first twelve. AssemblyScript's standard library has no JSON, so, like the C example, it takes the text as it is (your code can pass a string) and prints JSON: // what summary --describe prints: AssemblyScript can't embed a file, so the manifest is a string here const manifest = { "description": "Summarizes a text: its first words, and a word count", ... } function fail(code: string, message: string): void { process.stderr.write( {"code":"${code}","message":"${message}"} ) process.exit(1) } const fn = process.argv.length 1 ? process.argv[1] : "" if (fn == "--describe") { process.stdout.write(manifest) } else if (fn != "run") { fail("no_such_function", "only run") } else { const text = readStdin() // process.stdin.read() into a growing buffer, then String.UTF8.decode // ... split into words, keep the first 12 process.stdout.write( {"text":${jsonString(short)},"words":${words.length}} ) } To take JSON in, add a JSON package written for AssemblyScript, such as json-as.

title: AssemblyScript
heading: Build
text: npx asc assembly/index.ts --target release cp summary.pb.wasm pb_hooks/ The manifest says "language": "AssemblyScript" , since the module doesn't say it itself.

title: AssemblyScript
heading: Call it
text: An API route that saves a post with its summary and word count: // pb_pages/posts/+api.ts export async function post(ctx: any) { const { body } = ctx.req.body() const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", String(body ?? "")) // a string goes in as it is const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts")) record.load({ body, summary: out.text, words: out.words }) ctx.app.save(record) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id, summary: out.text, words: out.words }) }

title: C and C++
text: C makes the smallest and fastest modules: the summary example is 25 KB, its first call compiles in about 17 ms, and later calls load it from the cache in half a millisecond. The easiest compiler is zig cc : Zig ships clang and wasi-libc together, so there's no SDK to install.

title: C and C++
heading: Set up
text: brew install zig # or download it from ziglang.org Clang with wasi-sdk works too: replace zig cc -target wasm32-wasi below with $WASI_SDK_PATH/bin/clang --target=wasm32-wasip1 .

title: C and C++
heading: The module
text: example/summary/c counts the words of a text and returns the first twelve. C has no JSON in its standard library, so it takes the text as it is (your code can pass a string) and prints JSON: // what summary --describe prints: manifest.json, built in (C23 #embed) static const char manifest[] = { #embed "manifest.json" , 0}; static void fail(const char code, const char message) { fprintf(stderr, "{\"code\":\"%s\",\"message\":\"%s\"}", code, message); exit(1); } int main(int argc, char argv) { const char function = argc 1 ? argv[1] : ""; if (strcmp(function, "--describe") == 0) { fputs(manifest, stdout); return 0; } if (strcmp(function, "run") != 0) fail("no_such_function", "only run"); // read stdin, count the words, keep the first 12 ... fputs("{\"text\":", stdout); put_json_string(short_text, m); printf(",\"words\":%zu}", words); return 0; } To take JSON in, add a parser such as cJSON (one .c file and a header) beside main.c and list it on the command line.

title: C and C++
heading: Build
text: zig cc -target wasm32-wasi -std=c23 -Os -s -Wl,-z,stack-size=1048576 \ -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm main.c -Os -s : smallest code, no symbols. -Wl,-z,stack-size=1048576 : a 1 MB stack. Without it, zig cc gives a WASI program a 16 MB stack, and every call would start with 16 MB of memory. -std=c23 : for #embed . Without it, keep the manifest in a string instead.

title: C and C++
heading: Call it
text: An API route that saves a post with its summary and word count: // pb_pages/posts/+api.ts export async function post(ctx: any) { const { body } = ctx.req.body() const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", String(body ?? "")) // a string goes in as it is const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts")) record.load({ body, summary: out.text, words: out.words }) ctx.app.save(record) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id, summary: out.text, words: out.words }) }

title: C and C++
heading: C++
text: zig c++ builds C++ the same way, with -fno-exceptions added: zig c++ -target wasm32-wasi -fno-exceptions -Os -s -Wl,-z,stack-size=1048576 \ -o pb_hooks/mymodule.pb.wasm main.cpp WebAssembly exception handling doesn't run here, so code that throws, the standard library's included, fails to link ( undefined symbol: __cxa_throw ) until exceptions are off. What you use of the standard library sets the size: a program that uses std::string and printf is 20 KB, one that reads stdin with iostreams 204 KB.

title: C and C++
heading: Libraries
text: C libraries that only compute (parsers, codecs, compression, math) usually build as they are: add their .c files to the command. What WASI preview 1 doesn't have fails to build or fails at run time: threads, sockets, fork , and files (no folder is mounted, so fopen fails).

title: Go
text: Go builds a module with nothing extra to install: GOOS=wasip1 is a target of the Go you already have, and the whole standard library comes along. The cost is size. The summary example is 4.3 MB: its first call compiles it for about a second, and later calls load 18 MB of machine code from the cache in about 38 ms. That's fine off the hot path: a cron job, an import, an admin action. For a module that runs on every save or every request, build the same code with TinyGo instead: 3 ms and under 1 MB a call.

title: Go
heading: The module
text: example/summary/go is a plain command-line program: //go:embed manifest.json var manifest string // what summary --describe prints func main() { switch os.Args[1] { // the function asked for case "--describe": fmt.Print(manifest) return case "run": default: fail("no_such_function", os.Args[1]) } var post struct { Title string json:"title" Body string json:"body" } if err := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&post); err != nil { fail("bad_input", "the input isn't a post: "+err.Error()) } // ... the summary json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(map[string]any{"text": text, "words": len(words)}) } // fail ends the program with an error your code can read (err.code / err.message). func fail(code, message string) { b, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]string{"code": code, "message": message}) fmt.Fprint(os.Stderr, string(b)) os.Exit(1) }

title: Go
heading: Build
text: GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm . -ldflags="-s -w" saves little here (about 80 KB of 4.4 MB). A Go module always says it's Go, so its manifest needs no language .

title: Go
heading: Call it
text: An API route that saves a post with its summary: // pb_pages/posts/+api.ts export async function post(ctx: any) { const { title, body } = ctx.req.body() const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", { title, body }) const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts")) record.load({ title, body, summary: out.text }) ctx.app.save(record) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id, summary: out.text }) }

title: Go
heading: Size
text: What you import sets the size. The summary ( encoding/json , strings , fmt ) is 4.3 MB; a module that imports net/http is about 11 MB, over the default MaxModulesMB of 10, so it can't run until that's raised. Two Go calls run at once with the defaults, and calls that compile at the same time slow each other down (Which language has the numbers).

title: Go
heading: What doesn't work
text: GOOS=wasip1 programs get no files, no network and no environment here. net builds but reaches nothing outside the program, and goroutines run, one at a time. A library ( -buildmode=c-shared ) isn't a program and is refused when it loads.

title: Choosing a language
text: A module is a plain WASI program, so any language that builds one works. The program reads its input on stdin, writes its output on stdout, and gets the function it was asked for as its first argument ( run unless your code says otherwise). It fails by exiting non-zero with a JSON error on stderr. Writing a module has the whole contract; each page here shows it in one language, with a module you can build and page code that calls it.

title: Choosing a language
heading: What each language costs
text: A module's first call compiles it, which takes time in step with its size, and keeps the machine code in a cache on disk; later calls, after a restart too, load it from there, 20 to 30 times faster. Measured on a laptop (2026-11-18) with the summary example in each language, one call at a time. C summary/c 25 KB 17 ms 0.5 ms AssemblyScript summary/assemblyscript 10 KB 13 ms 0.5 ms Rust summary/rust 98 KB 33 ms 1.3 ms Zig summary/zig 95 KB 30 ms 1.2 ms TinyGo summary/tinygo 284 KB 74 ms 3 ms Go summary/go 4.3 MB 1.05 s 38 ms WAT, by hand summary/wat 1.8 KB 9 ms 0.4 ms LLVM IR, by hand summary/llvm 3.8 KB 7.5 ms 0.5 ms The last two are written by hand in assembly languages, for fun: they show how small a module can get when nothing comes along that the program doesn't use. Running the summary itself takes under a millisecond in every language; the rest is compiling or loading. A bigger program (a library that parses XML, a crate that resizes images) takes longer in every language, about in step with its size. A call also holds its module's machine code in memory while it runs: under 1 MB for C, Rust, Zig or TinyGo, 18 MB for Go.

title: Choosing a language
heading: How to pick
text: On a hot path (every record save, every request): C, Rust, Zig or AssemblyScript. TinyGo if you'd rather write Go. Off the hot path (a cron job, an import, an admin action): any of them, Go included. Go's 38 ms and 18 MB per call are fine there, and its standard library is all there. For a library that only exists in one language: that language. Rust has the most libraries that build for WASI as they are; C libraries that only compute (parsers, codecs, compression) build with zig cc . Many calls at once: smaller modules run more at once. With the defaults, 8 calls of a Rust or Zig module run side by side, but only 2 of a Go one ( MaxModulesMB , in Configure).

title: Choosing a language
heading: What runs
text: Modules run in wazero, which runs WebAssembly 2.0 (SIMD, bulk memory, multi-value and reference types included) and WASI preview 1. Building for these targets works: C, C++ wasm32-wasi ( zig cc , or clang with wasi-libc) Rust wasm32-wasip1 AssemblyScript asc with @assemblyscript/wasi-shim Zig wasm32-wasi TinyGo wasip1 Go GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm WebAssembly text wat2wasm (WABT) LLVM IR wasm32-wasi ( zig cc , or clang) These don't run, and fail when the module loads, with a message that says why: WASI preview 2 and components (Rust's wasm32-wasip2 , cargo component , componentize-py ): a component isn't a preview 1 program. Languages that need WebAssembly GC or exception handling (Kotlin/Wasm, Dart, Java through WasmGC, C++ with exceptions on). Modules that import anything but WASI , such as an Extism plugin or a module built for the browser ( wasm32-unknown-unknown , wasm-bindgen). Other languages covers the rest.

title: LLVM IR
text: LLVM IR is the language Clang, Rust, Zig and Swift translate your code into before LLVM turns it into machine code, or here, WebAssembly. It reads like a portable assembly language: typed values, basic blocks, branches. Written by hand, it gets LLVM's optimizer and wasi-libc for free. The summary example is 3.8 KB; its first call compiles in about 7.5 ms, later calls load it from the cache in half a millisecond. Like WAT, it's here for fun and to show what compilers produce. Seeing your C or Rust as IR is the useful part: clang -S -emit-llvm or rustc --emit=llvm-ir .

title: LLVM IR
heading: Set up
text: Nothing new if you have Zig: zig cc is clang, and it reads .ll files as well as .c ones. brew install zig

title: LLVM IR
heading: The module
text: example/summary/llvm does what the C summary does, in IR, and calls wasi-libc's read , write , malloc and exit like C would: target datalayout = "e-m:e-p:32:32-p10:8:8-p20:8:8-i64:64-i128:128-n32:64-S128-ni:1:10:20" target triple = "wasm32-unknown-wasip1-unknown" @err_nsf = private constant [48 x i8] c"{\22code\22:\22no_such_function\22,\22message\22:\22only run\22}" declare i32 @write(i32, ptr, i32) declare void @exit(i32) noreturn ; space, tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return define internal i1 @space(i8 %c) { %is.sp = icmp eq i8 %c, 32 %d = sub i8 %c, 9 %is.ctl = icmp ult i8 %d, 5 %r = or i1 %is.sp, %is.ctl ret i1 %r } ; main(argc, argv): on WASI, C compilers name it __main_argc_argv define i32 @__main_argc_argv(i32 %argc, ptr %argv) { ; ... } Two things hand-written IR has to get right that a compiler would do for you: The datalayout and triple must be wasm32-WASI's. Get them from clang: zig cc -target wasm32-wasi -S -emit-llvm -o - x.c head . main is called __main_argc_argv . For WASI, clang renames a C main(argc, argv) , and wasi-libc's _start calls it by that name. Name it main and it isn't the function libc calls with the arguments. The example keeps its locals in alloca stack slots, which is easier to write than SSA with phi nodes; -Os turns them into registers.

title: LLVM IR
heading: Build
text: zig cc -target wasm32-wasi -Os -s -Wl,-z,stack-size=1048576 -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm summary.ll The flags are the C ones: smallest code, no symbols, a 1 MB stack instead of 16 MB.

title: LLVM IR
heading: Call it
text: const { body } = ctx.req.body() const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", String(body ?? "")) // a string goes in as it is

title: Other languages
text: Any language works when it builds a WASI preview 1 program : a module with a _start function that imports nothing but wasi_snapshot_preview1 , and uses only WebAssembly 2.0 (no GC, no exception handling, no threads). Load it and $wasm.modules() says at once whether it runs: a module that needs anything else shows an error that says what. The languages below weren't tried for these docs. What's said of each is what its own tools document. Swift Yes The Swift SDK for WASI ( swift build --swift-sdk wasm32-unknown-wasi ) builds WASI preview 1 programs. Foundation makes modules several MB, so a first call compiles for a long time and every call holds more memory. C# / .NET Likely too big .NET's WASI build carries its runtime: tens of MB, over the default MaxModulesMB . Nim, Odin, D Through C or LLVM Each can target wasm32-wasi , through C ( zig cc ) or its own LLVM backend. Grain, MoonBit Check the target Both build WebAssembly; a module runs here only if their WASI output is preview 1 with no other imports. Kotlin/Wasm, Dart, Java (WasmGC) No They need WebAssembly GC. Python, Ruby, JavaScript Not as interpreters An interpreter built for WASI (CPython, Ruby, QuickJS) needs its standard library as files, and no folder is mounted. A tool that bundles the script and interpreter into one preview 1 program (Javy's static mode for JavaScript) can work, at a few MB per module. For JS, your page code is already JavaScript. To check a module without an app, run it with the wazero CLI, which runs it with the same engine: wazero run mymodule.wasm --describe echo '{"text":"hi"}' wazero run mymodule.wasm run Then copy it to pb_hooks/ .pb.wasm and look at $wasm.modules() : a module that can't run says why there.

title: Rust
text: Rust makes small, fast modules (the summary is 98 KB: about 33 ms for its first call, which compiles it, and 1.3 ms for later ones), and most crates that only compute build for WASI as they are. It's the best choice when you need a library: a parser, a codec, a format. The recipes are all Rust for that reason.

title: Rust
heading: Set up
text: rustup target add wasm32-wasip1

title: Rust
heading: The module
text: example/summary/rust is a binary crate with serde for JSON: fn fail(code: &str, message: &str) - ! { eprint!("{}", serde_json::json!({ "code": code, "message": message })); std::process::exit(1) } fn main() { match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("--describe") = { print!("{}", include_str!("../manifest.json")); return; } Some("run") = {} other = fail("no_such_function", other.unwrap_or("")), } let post: Post = serde_json::from_reader(std::io::stdin()) .unwrap_or_else( e fail("bad_input", &format!("the input isn't a post: {e}"))); // ... the summary serde_json::to_writer(std::io::stdout(), &Summary { text, words: words.len() }).unwrap(); } Keep the release profile small: [profile.release] opt-level = "z" lto = true strip = true codegen-units = 1

title: Rust
heading: Build
text: cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/summary.wasm pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm strip = true also drops what tells $wasm.modules() the module is Rust, so the manifest says "language": "Rust" .

title: Rust
heading: Call it
text: const { title, body } = ctx.req.body() const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", { title, body })

title: Rust
heading: Crates
text: A crate works when it only computes. One that needs threads, sockets, files or a C library built for another target won't build or won't run: rayon , tokio 's runtime, reqwest , openssl . Turn off default features you don't need ( image = { version = "0.25", default-features = false, features = ["png"] } ); it keeps the module small and leaves out code that can't build for WASI. A panic ends the call as crashed ; return an error with fail instead when the input is wrong. Don't build for wasm32-wasip2 or with cargo component : those make a component, which doesn't run here.

title: TinyGo
text: TinyGo compiles Go for small targets. The same source as the Go summary builds to a 284 KB module instead of 4.3 MB. Its first call compiles in about 74 ms instead of a second, and later calls load it from the cache in 3 ms instead of 38, holding under 1 MB of machine code instead of 18 MB. It's the way to write Go for a module on a hot path.

title: TinyGo
heading: Set up
text: brew install tinygo TinyGo supports a range of Go versions (TinyGo 0.41: Go 1.19 to 1.26) and uses the go on your PATH . With a newer Go installed, TinyGo stops with requires go version 1.19 through 1.26 . The go command can fetch a supported one for it: export PATH="$(GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.0 go env GOROOT)/bin:$PATH" tinygo version

title: TinyGo
heading: The module
text: example/summary/tinygo is the Go summary, unchanged: encoding/json , os.Args , stdin and stdout work as they do in Go. Its manifest says "language": "TinyGo" , since a TinyGo module doesn't say it itself.

title: TinyGo
heading: Build
text: tinygo build -target=wasip1 -opt=z -no-debug -scheduler=none -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm . -opt=z : smallest code. -no-debug : no debug information. -scheduler=none : no goroutine scheduler. A module is one call that reads, computes and exits, so it rarely needs one, and leaving it out takes the summary from 481 KB to 284 KB. A program that starts a goroutine doesn't build with it; leave the flag off then.

title: TinyGo
heading: Call it
text: The page code is the same as for Go: const { title, body } = ctx.req.body() const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", { title, body })

title: TinyGo
heading: What's different from Go
text: Most of the standard library works , encoding/json , strings , math , sort , time , crypto/ and encoding/ included. Packages that lean hard on reflection or on the operating system may not build; TinyGo's package list says which. Memory starts small: a TinyGo module starts with 128 KB and grows as it needs, where a Go one starts with 3 MB. Third-party packages build when they stay inside what TinyGo supports. Try the build: TinyGo says which import it can't compile. Keeping state in JS builds a second TinyGo module, with two functions and the state held by the app.

title: WebAssembly text (WAT)
text: WAT is WebAssembly's assembly language: the instructions a module is made of, written as text. Writing a module in it means no compiler, no runtime and no libc, only the module and the WASI functions it imports. The summary example is 1.8 KB, the smallest module here: its first call compiles in about 9 ms, later calls load it from the cache in under half a millisecond. It's for fun and for learning what's under every other page here. For real work, any other language is less code: the summary takes about 200 lines of WAT.

title: WebAssembly text (WAT)
heading: Set up
text: brew install wabt # wat2wasm, wasm2wat, and friends

title: WebAssembly text (WAT)
heading: The module
text: example/summary/wat takes a text on stdin, like the C one, and prints {"text", "words"} . It does by hand what libc and a compiler do for the other languages: It imports WASI directly: args_sizes_get and args_get for the function asked for, fd_read for stdin, fd_write for stdout and stderr, proc_exit to fail. It lays out its own memory: fixed addresses for its strings, the arguments and the manifest, and the input from 64 KB up, growing memory with memory.grow as the input needs it. It exports _start , the function a WASI program runs. (module (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "fd_read" (func $fd_read (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32))) (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "fd_write" (func $fd_write (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32))) (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "proc_exit" (func $proc_exit (param i32))) ;; ... (memory (export "memory") 2) (data (i32.const 160) "{\22code\22:\22no_such_function\22,\22message\22:\22only run\22}") ;; end the program with an error your code can read (err.code / err.message) (func $fail (param $ptr i32) (param $len i32) (call $write (i32.const 2) (local.get $ptr) (local.get $len)) (call $proc_exit (i32.const 1))) ;; space, tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return (func $space (param $c i32) (result i32) (i32.or (i32.eq (local.get $c) (i32.const 32)) (i32.lt_u (i32.sub (local.get $c) (i32.const 9)) (i32.const 5)))) (func $main (export "_start") ;; read argv[1], print the manifest for --describe, read stdin, count the words, ;; write {"text": ..., "words": ...} )) The manifest is a data segment, the compacted manifest.json with its quotes written \22 . WAT can't include a file, so the tests check the two say the same thing.

title: WebAssembly text (WAT)
heading: Build
text: wat2wasm summary.wat -o pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm wasm2wat turns any module back into text, which is a good way to see what a compiler made: wasm2wat pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm less .

title: WebAssembly text (WAT)
heading: Call it
text: const { body } = ctx.req.body() const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", String(body ?? "")) // a string goes in as it is

title: WebAssembly text (WAT)
heading: What to know
text: A trap is a crash. An out-of-bounds load, a division by zero or unreachable ends the call as crashed . The example uses unreachable when memory can't grow. Only WebAssembly 2.0 runs , so instructions from later proposals (tail calls, GC, exceptions, threads) fail when the module loads. memory.copy (bulk memory) and SIMD are fine. The manifest's language is up to you; a WAT module says nothing about itself. The example says "WAT" .

title: Zig
text: Zig makes small, fast modules (the summary is 95 KB: about 30 ms for its first call, which compiles it, and 1.2 ms for later ones) and needs nothing but Zig: WASI is one of its targets. Its standard library has JSON, so a module reads and writes JSON with no packages.

title: Zig
heading: Set up
text: brew install zig # Zig 0.17 Zig's standard library changes between versions. The example is written for Zig 0.17, where I/O goes through std.Io and main takes std.process.Init .

title: Zig
heading: The module
text: example/summary/zig : pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void { const io = init.io; const allocator = init.arena.allocator(); var out_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined; var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf); const out = &stdout.interface; const args = try init.minimal.args.toSlice(allocator); const function: []const u8 = if (args.len 1) args[1] else ""; if (std.mem.eql(u8, function, "--describe")) { try out.writeAll(@embedFile("manifest.json")); return out.flush(); } if (!std.mem.eql(u8, function, "run")) fail(io, "no_such_function", function); var in_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined; var stdin = std.Io.File.stdin().readerStreaming(io, &in_buf); const input = try stdin.interface.allocRemaining(allocator, .unlimited); const post = std.json.parseFromSliceLeaky(Post, allocator, input, .{ .ignore_unknown_fields = true }) catch fail(io, "bad_input", "the input isn't a post"); // ... the summary try std.json.Stringify.value(.{ .text = text.items, .words = words.items.len }, .{}, out); try out.flush(); } Flush the writer before returning: output still in its buffer is lost when the program exits.

title: Zig
heading: Build
text: In build.zig , target WASI, make the manifest importable, and set the stack: const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{ .default_target = .{ .os_tag = .wasi, .cpu_arch = .wasm32 }, }); // ... mod.addAnonymousImport("manifest.json", .{ .root_source_file = b.path("manifest.json") }); const exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "summary", .root_module = mod }); exe.stack_size = 1 << 20; // Zig's default stack is 16 MB: every call would start with 16 MB of memory zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall cp zig-out/bin/summary.wasm pb_hooks/summary.pb.wasm A Zig module never says it's Zig, so the manifest says "language": "Zig" .

title: Zig
heading: Call it
text: const { title, body } = ctx.req.body() const out = await $wasm.run.async ("summary", { title, body })

title: Zig
heading: C libraries
text: Zig compiles C as well: add C files to the module with mod.addCSourceFiles(...) and link libc ( mod.link_libc = true ), and a Zig module can use a C library directly. For C alone, see C and C++.

title: CSV import
heading: What it's for
text: Customers, products, price lists: the data people already have is in a spreadsheet, and the easiest way out of one is CSV. Splitting lines on commas works until a field holds a comma, a quote or a line break, which real files do. The module reads CSV properly with the csv crate (quotes, "" inside quotes, CRLF line ends, Excel's UTF-8 BOM) and gives back one JSON object per row, keyed by the header line.

title: CSV import
heading: The route
text: An API route a superuser posts a file to, which imports it into contacts ( name text, required; email email): // pb_pages/import/contacts/+api.ts: superusers import contacts from a CSV file (the request body) interface CsvImport { rows: Array // one object per row, keyed by the header line errors: Array } export async function post(ctx: any) { if (!ctx.auth?.isSuperuser()) throw ctx.httpError(403, "Superusers only") const csv = new Uint8Array(toBytes(ctx.req.event.request.body)) const { rows, errors } = await $wasm.run.async ("csv", csv) const contacts = ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("contacts") ctx.app.runInTransaction((txApp: any) = { for (const row of rows) { const contact = new Record(contacts) contact.load({ name: row.name, email: row.email }) txApp.save(contact) // an invalid row throws: nothing is imported } }) return ctx.res.json({ imported: rows.length, skipped: errors }) } curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" --data-binary @contacts.csv http://127.0.0.1:8090/import/contacts The file is the request body, sent as it is; ctx.req.event is PocketBase's request event, and its request.body is the raw body. In a transaction, the import is all or nothing: a row the collection refuses (a blank name , a bad email) stops it with that row's error, and nothing is saved. A row with the wrong number of fields doesn't stop it; it's skipped and listed with its line number: {"imported": 2, "skipped": [{"line": 4, "message": "CSV error: record 3 (line: 4, byte: 64): found record with 1 fields, but the previous record has 2 fields"}]}

title: CSV import
heading: The module
text: src/main.rs : let mut reader = csv::ReaderBuilder::new().delimiter(delimiter).from_reader(data); for result in reader.records() { match result { Ok(record) = { / one object: column name - value / } Err(e) = { / {line, message} into errors / } } } run reads comma-separated files, tsv tab-separated and semicolon semicolon-separated, which is what spreadsheets save in many European locales: $wasm.call.async("csv", "semicolon", csv) . Every value comes back as a string, as it is in the file; convert numbers and dates in your page code, or let the collection's field types do it.

title: CSV import
heading: Build
text: cd ext/wasm/example/csv cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/csv.wasm pb_hooks/csv.pb.wasm

title: CSV import
heading: Cost
text: 108 KB. The first call compiles it (about 30 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 1.5 ms and read a small file in under 1 ms.

title: CSV import
heading: Limits
text: The file and the JSON that comes back are each at most 4 MB ( MaxPayload ). The JSON repeats the column names on every row, so it's bigger than the file: keep files to about 2 MB, or split them. Spreadsheet formulas come through as their saved values, if the file has them; CSV has no types or formatting.

title: Text diffs
heading: What it's for
text: A wiki page, a contract, a blog post: when people edit text, you want to see who changed what, and maybe roll back. Storing a diff of each edit shows exactly the lines that changed, the way git diff does. The module compares two texts line by line with similar and returns a unified diff and how many lines were added and removed.

title: Text diffs
heading: The route
text:
A pages collection with a body text field, and a revisions collection with page (text or a relation), diff (text), added and removed (numbers): An API route saves an edit of a page's body ( PUT with {"body": "..."} ) and keeps it as a diff: // pb_pages/wiki/[id]/+api.ts: every edit of a page's body is kept as a diff in revisions interface Diff { changed: boolean unified: string added: number removed: number } export async function put(ctx: any) { if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in to edit") const page = ctx.app.findRecordById("pages", ctx.params.id) const { body } = ctx.req.body() const d = await $wasm.run.async ("diff", { old: page.getString("body"), new: body }) page.set("body", body) ctx.app.save(page) if (d.changed) { const rev = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("revisions")) rev.load({ page: page.id, diff: d.unified, added: d.added, removed: d.removed }) ctx.app.save(rev) } return ctx.res.json({ changed: d.changed, added: d.added, removed: d.removed }) } The old body is read before the page changes. The revision is saved after the page, so only once the page itself is saved. What an edit gives: {"old": "Pocket
base
", "new": "Pocket
One
rocks
"} {"unified": " old
+++ new
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
 Pocket
-base
+One
+rocks
", "added": 2, "removed": 1, "changed": true}

title: Text diffs
heading: The module
text: src/main.rs : let diff = TextDiff::from_lines(&input.old, &input.new); // count the inserted and deleted lines... let unified = diff .unified_diff() .context_radius(input.context.unwrap_or(3)) .header("old", "new") .to_string(); context in the input sets how many unchanged lines show around each change (3 by default, as in git diff ).

title: Text diffs
heading: Build
text: cd ext/wasm/example/diff cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/diff.wasm pb_hooks/diff.pb.wasm

title: Text diffs
heading: Cost
text: 130 KB. The first call compiles it (about 35 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 1.6 ms and diff a page in under 1 ms.

title: Text diffs
heading: Limits
text: Both texts together are at most 4 MB ( MaxPayload ), as JSON. It's a line diff: a change inside a long line shows as the whole line removed and added.

title: Recipes
text: A module can't reach the database, files or network, so what it's good for is computing: turning one thing into another. Each recipe here is a module built on a library from another language, with page code that uses it. Every module is kept built in the repository and checked by the extension's tests. All of them are Rust: it has the most libraries that build for WASI as they are (see Rust). Copy a module's .pb.wasm from its folder into your pb_hooks/ , or build it from its source, and call it from your page code.

title: Recipes
heading: Content
text: Markdown to HTML pulldown-cmark 258 KB Renders a Markdown field to HTML when a record is saved. Sanitize HTML ammonia 803 KB Cleans HTML users wrote, so it's safe to show. Text diffs similar 130 KB Keeps a revision history of a text field as unified diffs.

title: Recipes
heading: Files and data
text: Image thumbnails image 448 KB Makes a PNG thumbnail of each uploaded photo. QR codes qrcode 109 KB Draws a QR code as SVG, for a ticket or a check-in link. CSV import csv 108 KB Reads a CSV file, quoted fields and all, into records.

title: Recipes
heading: From the extension's examples
text: These came with the extension, to answer real questions. Each is kept built beside its source, in example/ 's folders.

title: Recipes
heading: Orders from EDIFACT and XML
text: edifact-orders-rust reads an EDIFACT ORDERS message (raw text, as trading partners send it) into an order: parties, lines, prices and allowances, with the message's own counts checked. order-xml reads the same order from XML into the same JSON. So one route takes either format and stores one shape: // pb_pages/orders/+api.ts: the raw message is the request body, as text: a string goes in as it is export async function post(ctx: any) { const raw = toString(ctx.req.event.request.body) const module = raw.trimStart().startsWith(" (module, raw) const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("orders")) record.load({ raw, number: order.number, lines: order.lines }) ctx.app.save(record) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id }) }

title: Recipes
heading: Crypto JS doesn't have
text: waflows does what a WhatsApp Flows endpoint needs and the JS runtime can't: RSA-OAEP to unwrap the request's key, and AES-GCM with WhatsApp's key and IV. Your page code keeps the JSON, the base64 and the HTTP; the module does only those three steps, with bytes as base64: type Data = { data: string } // what each waflows function gives: bytes as base64 const body = ctx.req.body() // in the endpoint's +api.ts post handler const { data: key } = await $wasm.call.async ("waflows", "rsa-decrypt", { privateKey, data: body.encrypted_aes_key }) const { data: request } = await $wasm.call.async ("waflows", "gcm-open", { key, iv: body.initial_vector, data: body.encrypted_flow_data }) // ... answer the request, then seal the answer with the flipped IV const flipped = Buffer.from(body.initial_vector, "base64").map((b) = ~b).toString("base64") const { data } = await $wasm.call.async ("waflows", "gcm-seal", { key, iv: flipped, data: Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(answer)).toString("base64") }) crypto (Go) is AES-256-GCM with a key your code passes in: encrypt takes {key, text} , decrypt takes {key, data} . The module can't keep the key or send it anywhere. Built with Go it's 4 MB: its first call compiles for about a second, and later calls load it in about 40 ms. The same source built with TinyGo is 348 KB: about 75 ms the first time, a few ms after.

title: Recipes
heading: Write your own
text: A recipe is a module like any other: a program that reads stdin and writes stdout. Pick the library first, then the language it's in, and check it builds for WASI: one that needs threads, sockets or files won't run (password-strength checking with zxcvbn, for one, reads the browser's clock and fails here). Choosing a language has the costs, and Keeping state in JS covers modules that work on a series.

title: Markdown to HTML
heading: What it's for
text: Your users write posts, docs or product descriptions in Markdown, and your pages show HTML. Render it once, when the record is saved, and keep the HTML beside the Markdown: pages then show it with no work per view. The module is pulldown-cmark, the CommonMark parser behind rustdoc and mdBook, with tables, strikethrough and task lists on.

title: Markdown to HTML
heading: The route
text: A posts collection with a body text field (the Markdown) and an html text field: // pb_pages/posts/+api.ts: posts are written in Markdown; html is what your pages show async function renderPost(markdown: string): Promise { const html = (await $wasm.run.async ("markdown", markdown "")) ?? "" return (await $wasm.run.async ("sanitize-html", html)) ?? "" // users wrote it: keep only safe HTML } export async function post(ctx: any) { if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in to post") const { body } = ctx.req.body() const record = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("posts")) record.load({ body, html: await renderPost(body) }) ctx.app.save(record) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: record.id }) } A route that saves an edit sets html the same way, from the new body, before it saves. CommonMark passes raw HTML through, so in a post would reach your pages. The second call runs the result through sanitize-html, which keeps the formatting and drops scripts, event handlers and javascript: links. Leave it out only for Markdown you wrote yourself. ?? "" is there because an empty output comes back as null .

title: Markdown to HTML
heading: The module
text: The Markdown is the module's stdin, as text, and the HTML is its stdout ( src/main.rs ): let mut input = String::new(); if let Err(e) = std::io::stdin().read_to_string(&mut input) { fail("bad_input", &format!("the input isn't UTF-8 text: {e}")); } let opts = Options::ENABLE_TABLES Options::ENABLE_STRIKETHROUGH Options::ENABLE_TASKLISTS; let mut out = String::with_capacity(input.len() 3 / 2); html::push_html(&mut out, Parser::new_ext(&input, opts)); std::io::stdout().write_all(out.as_bytes()).unwrap(); Other options (footnotes, heading ids, smart punctuation) are one more flag each.

title: Markdown to HTML
heading: Build
text: cd ext/wasm/example/markdown cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/markdown.wasm pb_hooks/markdown.pb.wasm

title: Markdown to HTML
heading: Cost
text: 258 KB. The first call compiles it (about 60 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 2.5 ms and render a short post in under 1 ms. With sanitize-html after it, a save takes under 10 ms more than without, once both are in the cache.

title: Markdown to HTML
heading: Limits
text: Input and output are each at most 4 MB ( MaxPayload ). Each call still loads and starts the module (a few ms), so render on save, not on every page view.

title: QR codes
heading: What it's for
text: Event tickets, check-in links, a table's ordering page, a Wi-Fi login: a QR code your users scan from a screen or paper. The module draws one as an SVG image from any text, with the qrcode crate. SVG stays sharp at any size and prints well.

title: QR codes
heading: The route
text: An API route that gives a ticket's owner their ticket's QR code. tickets has a code text field and an owner relation to users : // pb_pages/tickets/[id]/qr/+api.ts: a ticket's QR code, for its owner, as SVG export async function get(ctx: any) { if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in first") const ticket = ctx.app.findRecordById("tickets", ctx.params.id) if (ticket.get("owner") !== ctx.auth.id) throw ctx.httpError(403, "Not your ticket") const svg = await $wasm.run.async ("qrcode", https://example.com/check-in/${ticket.get("code")} ) return ctx.res.json({ svg }) } A plain doesn't send the user's PocketBase token, so fetch the SVG with it (the JS SDK's pb.send ) and show it from a blob URL ( new Blob([svg], { type: "image/svg+xml" }) ). Or draw it once, when the ticket is created, and save it in a protected file field: then an with a file token shows it.

title: QR codes
heading: The module
text: The text is stdin; the SVG is stdout ( src/main.rs ): let code = QrCode::with_error_correction_level(&input, EcLevel::M) .unwrap_or_else( e fail("too_long", &format!("can't encode it: {e}"))); let image = code.render:: ().min_dimensions(200, 200).build(); std::io::stdout().write_all(image.as_bytes()).unwrap(); Error correction M survives about 15% of the code being damaged or covered. Change the colors with .dark_color(svg::Color("#1d4ed8")) .

title: QR codes
heading: Build
text: cd ext/wasm/example/qrcode cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/qrcode.wasm pb_hooks/qrcode.pb.wasm

title: QR codes
heading: Cost
text: 109 KB. The first call compiles it (about 30 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 1.3 ms and draw a code in about 2 ms.

title: QR codes
heading: Limits
text: A QR code holds at most 2,331 bytes at level M ; longer text fails with too_long . An empty input fails with empty_input .

title: Sanitize HTML
heading: What it's for
text: A comment box with a rich text editor, an import of HTML from somewhere else, the output of Markdown: any HTML a user controls can carry a , an onerror= or a javascript: link. Showing it as is lets one user run code in another's browser. ammonia parses the HTML the way a browser does (html5ever) and keeps only an allow list of tags and attributes. Links get rel="noopener noreferrer" .

title: Sanitize HTML
heading: The route
text: A comments collection with an html text field, cleaned before it's saved: // pb_pages/comments/+api.ts: comments arrive as HTML from a rich text editor export async function post(ctx: any) { if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in to comment") const { html } = ctx.req.body() const comment = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("comments")) comment.set("html", String((await $wasm.run.async ("sanitize-html", html "")) ?? "")) ctx.app.save(comment) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: comment.id }) } Clean edits too if comments can be edited: the route that saves an edit makes the same call. String(...) is there because a module's output comes back parsed when it's JSON: a comment that's just 42 comes back as the number 42. What it does to a hostile comment: Hi there alert(1) Hi there

title: Sanitize HTML
heading: The module
text: The whole program is one call to ammonia's defaults ( src/main.rs ): let mut input = String::new(); if let Err(e) = std::io::stdin().read_to_string(&mut input) { fail("bad_input", &format!("the input isn't UTF-8 text: {e}")); } let clean = ammonia::clean(&input); std::io::stdout().write_all(clean.as_bytes()).unwrap(); For your own rules (allow class on , drop images), build an ammonia::Builder in its place.

title: Sanitize HTML
heading: Build
text: cd ext/wasm/example/sanitize-html cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/sanitize-html.wasm pb_hooks/sanitize-html.pb.wasm

title: Sanitize HTML
heading: Cost
text: 803 KB, most of it a full HTML parser. The first call compiles it (about 120 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 5 ms and clean a comment in under 1 ms.

title: Sanitize HTML
heading: Limits
text: Input and output are each at most 4 MB ( MaxPayload ). style attributes are removed, not filtered; allow them only with your own CSS rules in the builder.

title: Image thumbnails
heading: What it's for
text: A gallery, a product list or a profile page shows many images small. Sending each one full size is slow on a phone. PocketBase can make thumbnails of a file field on request ( ?thumb=100x100 ); a module lets you make your own when the file is uploaded: a fixed size, a PNG whatever came in, kept in its own field you can query and send anywhere. The module uses the image crate, built with PNG and JPEG only.

title: Image thumbnails
heading: The route
text: A photos collection with two file fields, image (what the user uploads) and thumb . An API route takes the upload (a multipart form with an image field) and saves the photo with its thumbnail: // pb_pages/photos/+api.ts: an uploaded photo is saved with a 256 px PNG thumbnail in its thumb field export async function post(ctx: any) { if (!ctx.auth) throw ctx.httpError(401, "Sign in to upload") const [file] = ctx.req.files("image") if (!file) throw ctx.httpError(400, "No image") const reader = file.reader.open() let bytes: Uint8Array try { bytes = new Uint8Array(toBytes(reader)) } finally { reader.close() } const thumb = await $wasm.run.async ("thumbnail", bytes) const photo = new Record(ctx.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("photos")) photo.set("image", file) photo.set("thumb", $filesystem.fileFromBytes(Array.from(Buffer.from(thumb.png, "base64")), "thumb.png")) ctx.app.save(photo) return ctx.res.json(201, { id: photo.id }) } ctx.req.files gives the files uploaded with this request, ready for a record field. A Uint8Array goes to the module as raw bytes. The module answers with JSON, {width, height, png} , the PNG as base64; $filesystem.fileFromBytes takes the bytes as a plain array, hence Array.from .

title: Image thumbnails
heading: The module
text: src/main.rs reads the image, scales it to fit, and writes a PNG: let size = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("run") = 256, Some("small") = 64, // ... }; let img = image::load_from_memory(&input) .unwrap_or_else( e fail("bad_image", &format!("not a PNG or JPEG image: {e}"))); let thumb = if img.width() size img.height() size { img.thumbnail(size, size) } else { img }; run fits the image in 256×256 and small in 64×64, kept in proportion ( $wasm.call.async("thumbnail", "small", bytes) for the small one). It also takes the image as base64 text, which is how its manifest's examples pass one.

title: Image thumbnails
heading: Build
text: cd ext/wasm/example/thumbnail cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 # rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 first cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/thumbnail.wasm pb_hooks/thumbnail.pb.wasm

title: Image thumbnails
heading: Cost
text: 448 KB. The first call compiles it (about 110 ms); later calls load it from the cache in about 4.5 ms. Decoding is most of the run: a 1280×853 JPEG takes about 230 ms, a 1920×1280 one about 460 ms, a 2560×1706 one about 780 ms (2026-11-18, a laptop).

title: Image thumbnails
heading: Limits
text: The decoded image has to fit in the call's memory, 32 MB by default ( MaxCallMemoryMB ): 3 bytes a pixel, so up to about 2560×1706 with the defaults. A 4000×2666 photo fails with crashed and a message naming the limit; raise MaxCallMemoryMB (and the timeout) for big camera photos. The upload is at most 4 MB ( MaxPayload ). PNG and JPEG only. WebP, GIF and others are one Cargo feature each on the image crate, and make the module bigger.

title: Bulk mail
text: Got a newsletter, a launch or a change to announce? Write it once, pick which users get it, and your app sends it at a steady pace through its own mail settings. Every message gets an unsubscribe link, and people who unsubscribe, bounce or complain are never mailed again. This is on for every PocketOne app. Nothing is sent until a superuser starts a campaign.

title: Bulk mail
heading: Before your first campaign
text: Sign in to the dashboard as a superuser and open Settings → Mail . Set up your mail server and sender there, as you would for any PocketBase app. Campaigns send through them. Below that form, in the Bulk mail section, fill in Postal address . It's shown in every campaign footer, and anti-spam laws require one. Click Save bulk mail settings . Open Settings → Application and check that Application URL is the address people reach your app on. Unsubscribe links are built from it.

title: Bulk mail
heading: Send a campaign from the dashboard
text: Open Mail in the dashboard menu and click New campaign . It starts as a draft for the verified users of users . Fill in Name , Subject and Body . Use {{record.name}} (any field of the user's record), {{email}} and {{campaign.name}} to fill in each message. Under Audience , pick who gets it. With Filter , choose the Collection , an optional Filter in the same syntax as API rules (such as verified = true ), and the Email field . Click Count recipients to see how many match, how many are suppressed, and a few sample addresses. Click Save changes . Click Preview to see the message for one recipient, or fill in Test address and click Send test . Click Send and confirm. The campaign page shows its progress and a Recipients table. While it runs, you can Pause , Resume or Cancel it. To send later, set Schedule (UTC) before you save. The button then says Schedule . To send slower than your app's limit, set Max per second . For audiences a filter can't express, choose SQL and write a read-only SELECT that returns an email column. Every other column it returns can be used in the message as {{record.column}} . A view works too: pick it as the Collection .

title: Bulk mail
heading: Send it again to new users
text: Each address gets a campaign at most once. Click Send on a finished campaign and only users who match now but weren't mailed before get it.

title: Bulk mail
heading: From your terminal
text: Write the campaign in the dashboard first. Then sign in to your app once (Remote CLI) and run it from your terminal: pocketone remote bulkmail preview --campaign # see the message pocketone remote bulkmail test --campaign --to you@example.com pocketone remote bulkmail start --campaign pocketone remote bulkmail pause --campaign # also resume, cancel --limit 100 on start queues at most 100 new recipients, to send a campaign in batches. To see who an audience reaches before you send: pocketone remote bulkmail count --audience '{"collection": "users", "filter": "verified = true", "email_field": "email"}'

title: Bulk mail
heading: From pb_hooks
text: $bulkmail does the same from your JS hooks: const { count, suppressed } = $bulkmail.count({ collection: "users", filter: "verified = true", email_field: "email" }) $bulkmail.start("CAMPAIGN_ID") $bulkmail.suppress("someone@example.com")

title: Bulk mail
heading: From an agent
text: An agent connected to your app over MCP has a tool for each step: bulkmail_count , bulkmail_preview , bulkmail_test , bulkmail_start , bulkmail_pause , bulkmail_resume and bulkmail_cancel . Count and preview need a token with the bulkmail:read scope, the rest the bulkmail scope. Only superusers can run campaigns.

title: Bulk mail
heading: Unsubscribes, bounces and complaints
text: Unsubscribe: every message ends with a footer holding your postal address and an unsubscribe link. It also carries the one-click unsubscribe headers that Gmail and Yahoo require from bulk senders. Opening the link shows a confirm button, so link scanners can't unsubscribe anyone. Suppressions: Mail → Suppressions lists the addresses that never get campaign mail, whatever the audience says. Unsubscribes are added automatically. Click Add address to add one by hand, or Export CSV to download the list. Bounces and complaints: to add those to the list too, open Bounces and complaints in the Bulk mail section. For Amazon SES, subscribe your SNS topic to the Amazon SES (SNS) endpoint shown there. For other providers, set a Webhook secret and point the provider at the Generic webhook URL.

title: Bulk mail
heading: Limits
text: Your app sends at most 5 messages a second and 5,000 a day (UTC), across all campaigns. The Bulk mail section shows your app's limits and how many it sent today. A host may set other limits for your app. A message counts as sent only once the mail server accepts it, so a restart doesn't send twice or skip anyone. A permanent error from the mail server fails that recipient. Other errors are retried, up to three attempts. A campaign pauses itself when more than 5% of its sends fail after the first 100, or when spam complaints pass 0.3% of its sends (at least 3). The reason shows next to its status.

title: Bulk mail
heading: Try it locally
text: In dev mode with SMTP off, pocketone catches every mail, campaigns included, in an inbox at http://127.0.0.1:8025: pocketone serve --dev

title: Bulk mail
heading: Change it
text: There's no pocketone.yaml section for bulk mail; the pocketone.yaml reference lists none. Sending uses your Settings → Mail server and sender, and you lower the pace per campaign with Max per second .

title: Bulk mail
heading: How it works
text: Bulk Mail runs the campaigns, the pages in the dashboard and $bulkmail . bulkmail/v1 is the contract behind the command, the REST API and the MCP tools. mail.suppression/v1 keeps the suppression list and the unsubscribe link. mail.feedback/v1 takes bounce and complaint reports from your mail provider.

title: Deploy and live sync
text: Write your hooks, migrations and pages on your own machine, then send them to your running app with one command. Only the files that changed are uploaded, and the app swaps them in while it keeps serving. This is on for every PocketOne app. Its superusers can deploy to it, and the pocketone command can deploy to any PocketOne app. You don't need to set anything up.

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: Deploy from your terminal
text: Run these from your project folder, the one that holds pb_hooks , pb_pages and the rest: pocketone link https://myapp.example.com # add the app as a remote and sign in, once pocketone deploy # upload what changed link signs you in through your browser when the app offers it, or asks for an API token. When the deploy is done you see a line like Deployed : 3 changed, 0 deleted, 41 unchanged. With nothing to send, it says Up to date: no changes. A few more ways to run it: pocketone deploy prod # to the remote named prod pocketone deploy --dry-run # list what would be sent, send nothing pocketone deploy --restart # restart afterwards if migrations or packages changed pocketone deploy --force # overwrite files that changed on the server since your last deploy pocketone restart # restart later instead Every command takes a remote's name or a URL. Without one, it uses the project's default remote. Remote CLI covers adding more remotes and signing in.

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: When changes take effect
text: Right away: pb_hooks , pb_pages and pb_public . Hooks reload by themselves, and pages and public files are read fresh on the next request. After a restart: migrations and npm packages. The deploy tells you Migrations or packages changed and leaves the restart to you: pass --restart , or run pocketone restart . Your first deploy that creates pb_hooks needs a restart too. A deploy never restarts the app on its own.

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: When the server changed too
text: If a file changed on the server since your last deploy, pull or dev (someone edited it there, or the dashboard wrote a migration) and your deploy would overwrite it, the deploy stops, lists those files and sends nothing. Bring them down with pocketone pull or pocketone dev , then deploy again, or pass --force to overwrite them. The record of what you last deployed lives in .pocketone/ in your project, so a fresh checkout or a CI run deploys without the check.

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: Work live with dev
text: pocketone dev dev keeps your folder and the app in step both ways, and streams the app's logs. Your edits go up half a second after you save. Changes made on the app, such as the migrations the dashboard writes when you edit a collection, come down within a few seconds. After you upload a migration or new packages, type r and Enter to restart the app. Stop with Ctrl+C. If a file changed on both sides, your copy wins and the app's copy is saved in .pocketone/conflicts/ . dev keeps its state in .pocketone/ , so add that folder to .gitignore . To leave files out, list gitignore-style patterns in .pocketoneignore .

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: Start from a running app
text: With nothing local, clone gets you a project folder in one step: pocketone clone https://myapp.example.com # makes ./myapp, signs you in, downloads the app's code cd myapp bun install # if there's a package.json: dev and deploy upload packages from here pocketone dev It downloads the same files as pull , never pb_data , and remembers the app as the folder's remote. From there, dev keeps both sides in step: a save is live on the app's next request.

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: Pull files and read logs
text: pocketone pull # download pb_hooks, pb_migrations, pb_pages, pb_public, pb_templates, package.json, the lockfile, patches/ pocketone pull pb_hooks pb_public/index.html pocketone logs # the last 100 lines, then follow

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: Deploy from CI
text: Sign in to the dashboard as a superuser and open Settings → API tokens . Fill in a Name , such as ci . Under Scopes , tick deploy . Add remote if CI will pass --restart . Click Create token and copy it. It's shown only once. In CI, set P1_TOKEN (or P1_TOKEN_PROD for the remote named prod ) to that token, then run pocketone deploy --restart .

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: From an agent
text: An agent with a terminal runs the same pocketone deploy . Over MCP, it can restart the app with remote_restart and read its log with remote_logs . There's no MCP tool that uploads files.

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: What's sent
text: Sent: every pb_ folder except pb_data (so pb_hooks , pb_migrations , pb_pages , pb_public , pb_templates ), plus package.json , bun.lock or bun.lockb , and patches/ . Dotfiles are included, such as pb_public/.well-known . Packages: with a package.json , the production node_modules tree goes too, so your hooks can require npm packages. Dev dependencies stay behind. --no-node-modules leaves the app's node_modules alone. Never sent: pb_data (your live data), .git files and symlinks. Add your own patterns with -e . Only superusers, or an API token with the deploy scope, can deploy. A token with deploy:read can only pull files and read logs.

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: Change it
text: There's nothing to set in pocketone.yaml . Your project's remotes are kept in .pocketbase/remotes.json , which you can commit. Your logins are saved in your home folder, never in the project. Every pocketone.yaml key is in the pocketone.yaml reference.

title: Deploy and live sync
heading: How it works
text: Deploy gives the app its deploy API and adds the deploy , dev , pull , logs and restart commands. Remotes keeps your remotes and logins, and gives the app its restart and logs. Tokens makes the API tokens CI uses. The commands talk to the deploy/v1 and remote/v1 contracts, so they work against any app or host that offers them.

title: New in PocketOne
text: PocketOne does everything PocketBase does, and adds the features below. They're all built into the pocketone binary, and most are on by default. There's nothing to install. Three of them set PocketOne apart: hooks with async , import and TypeScript, async pages in TSX, and hundreds of apps running as isolates in one process.

title: New in PocketOne
heading: Modern JavaScript on the server
text: Hooks with async, import and TypeScript. Your pb_hooks run on QuickJS with the same JS API you already use, plus: async handlers and await . The app keeps serving other requests while a handler waits on the database or an HTTP call. ES modules: import and export between your files, and packages from node_modules . TypeScript: write .pb.ts files and they run as they are. Globals shared by every handler, and memory and time limits that stop a runaway script instead of the app. // pb_hooks/orders.pb.ts import { total } from "./lib/pricing.mjs" routerAdd("GET", "/api/orders/{id}/total", async (e) = { const order = await e.app.findRecordById.async("orders", e.request.pathValue("id")) return e.json(200, { total: total(order) }) }) Pages in TSX, TypeScript or EJS. Put a .tsx , .jsx , .ejs or .md file in pb_pages and it's a server-rendered page, with your records a function call away. Components import each other, and +page.ts and +api.ts route files are TypeScript. Every part of a page can await : loaders, handlers, middleware, EJS tags and async components, and sibling components render at the same time. esbuild is built into the binary: no Node, no npm install , no build step. // pb_pages/products/[id].tsx import Price from './_private/Price' export default async function Product({ ctx }: any) { const product = await ctx.app.findRecordById.async('products', ctx.params.id) return ( {product.getString('name')} ) }

title: New in PocketOne
heading: Hundreds of apps in one process
text: PocketBase isolates. One pocketone process runs hundreds of PocketBase apps as isolates, routed by hostname. Each is a complete app with its own data, hooks and dashboard. It starts on its first request in tens of milliseconds, costs about 3 MB while it runs, and is sandboxed from the others: its own memory cap, time limits, files, SQL and secrets. No container per app, no idle memory to pay for. # pocketone.yaml: every hostname you ask for becomes its own app (dev mode) multisite: {} instances: { dev: true } pocker: { root: ./pb_root }

title: New in PocketOne
heading: Everything new at a glance
text: QuickJS hooks async / await , ES module import , TypeScript, shared globals and hard limits, on the same JS API PocketPages sites Server-rendered pages in TSX, JSX, TypeScript, EJS or Markdown, with await everywhere and no build step PocketBase isolates Hundreds of apps in one process, each starting in tens of ms, about 3 MB each, sandboxed Point-in-time restore Every change recorded; restore to any second in the last 72 hours, and undo the restore Deploy and live sync pocketone deploy uploads only what changed; pocketone dev syncs a folder both ways and streams logs Remote CLI Admin commands against any app, from your terminal, a script or an agent API tokens and OAuth Named, scoped tokens you revoke one by one; your app is an OAuth server MCP for AI agents /mcp on every app, with OAuth sign-in and your own tools from pb_hooks Bulk mail Campaigns from the dashboard, with unsubscribes, suppression and pacing Desktop apps The same folder builds into native macOS, Windows and Linux apps with pocketone desktop build , each user's data on their machine (preview) pocketone.yaml One config file, with every extension's options and a .env for secrets Each page shows the feature in the dashboard, from your terminal and from an agent. For how a feature works or how to build on it, follow its How it works links to the extension pages.

title: New in PocketOne
heading: Also built in
text: Smaller additions you'll notice without a page of their own: Mail you can see in dev mode: with serve --dev and no SMTP settings, mail is caught and shown at http://127.0.0.1:8025 instead of being sent (Mail Trap). S3 redirects: files kept in S3 download straight from the bucket through short-lived signed links (S3 Redirect). Restylable sign-in pages: copy the OAuth sign-in screens into your app with pocketone template eject and edit them (Templates). Settings and cache: one settings screen and one shared memory budget for every feature (Settings, Cache). Coming from PocketBase? What stays the same, and how each feature compares.

title: PocketBase isolates: hundreds of apps in one process
text: An isolate is a complete PocketOne app: its own folder, pb_data , pb_hooks , pb_migrations , dashboard and superusers, at its own hostname. What's different is where it runs. Instead of a process or container of its own, it runs inside one shared pocketone process, with its own JavaScript VM, and the host routes each request to it by hostname. Most apps sit idle most of the time, so a process or container per app is mostly paying for nothing. Isolates make a server full of PocketBase apps cheap: SaaS with one app per customer, a site per client, a preview app per branch. It's built into pocketone . You don't need Docker, Kubernetes or a separate host program.

title: PocketBase isolates: hundreds of apps in one process
heading: Try it in a minute
text: Put this pocketone.yaml in an empty folder: server: { http: "127.0.0.1:8090" } multisite: {} instances: { dev: true } pocker: { root: ./pb_root } Start it, then ask for any hostname: pocketone serve curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/health curl -H 'Host: shop.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/health In dev mode, each new hostname becomes an app: its folder appears under pb_root/ and it starts on that first request. Open http://blog.localhost:8090/_/ for that app's own dashboard. On a laptop, each new app answered its first request in about 45 ms, and later requests in under a millisecond. A hundred running apps took the process from 53 MB to 365 MB: about 3 MB each.

title: PocketBase isolates: hundreds of apps in one process
heading: Run it for real
text: List your apps and their hostnames in an instances file: # instances.yaml instances: id: blog # also its folder: pb_root/blog hosts: [blog.example.com] id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: sk_live_... } # seen only by this app's hooks limits: { max_js_execution: 60s } # pocketone.yaml multisite: {} instances: { file: ./instances.yaml } pocker: { root: ./pb_root } The host checks the file every 2 seconds, so adding, changing or removing an app needs no restart. In production, only the hostnames listed there are served. Auto TLS gets certificates for them.

title: PocketBase isolates: hundreds of apps in one process
heading: What each app gets
text: Everything a PocketOne app has. Point-in-time restore, API tokens, MCP, PocketPages, bulk mail and the rest are on in every isolate. Each can be turned off per app. Its own deploys. pocketone deploy and the Remote CLI work against each app's hostname. Its own restarts. A change to its pb_hooks , a restore or its settings restarts that app alone. Nothing else notices.

title: PocketBase isolates: hundreds of apps in one process
heading: Sandboxed from each other
text: Isolates share a process, so PocketOne puts the walls inside it. Assume every app's owner is hostile: Memory: each app's JS has a hard cap (64 MiB by default). Going past it is an out-of-memory error for that app only. CPU: every JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) is stopped after max_js_execution . At most max_concurrent_js calls per app run at once. Files, SQL and network: an app's hooks and SQL reach only its own data. Outbound requests can't reach private networks unless you allow them. Failures stay put: a broken hooks file, a panic or a failed migration takes down that app alone. It answers 502 until it's fixed. Secrets: each app's hooks see only its own secrets . Every limit has a default for the whole host and an override per app. Sandbox lists every check.

title: PocketBase isolates: hundreds of apps in one process
heading: When to use containers instead
text: An isolate runs the PocketOne code in the pocketone binary. For an app that needs a specific PocketBase release, use the Docker runtime, which runs each app in its own container with the official binary of the version it asks for. One host can run both.

title: PocketBase isolates: hundreds of apps in one process
heading: How it works
text: Multisite takes over serve when pocketone.yaml has a multisite section. It routes each request by hostname, applies the gates, and hands it to a runtime. Pocker is the runtime that runs apps as isolates in the host's process. Sandbox confines each isolate's JS, SQL and outbound network. Docker is the container runtime, for apps that need it.

title: MCP for AI agents
text: Point Claude, or any other MCP client, at your app and sign in. The agent can then read and change your data, check on the app and run admin tasks, as you and with your rights, nothing more. Every PocketOne app serves MCP at /mcp . It's on by default. You don't need to set anything up.

title: MCP for AI agents
heading: Connect Claude
text: In your MCP client, add https:// /mcp as a remote MCP server. In Claude, that's a custom connector. A browser opens on your app's sign-in page. Sign in as an app user, or click Sign in as a superuser . The consent page names the client and the account it will act as. Choose Full access , or Only these and tick what the agent may do. Click Allow . The agent stays connected until you disconnect it. In Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http my-app https:// /mcp claude mcp login my-app # or /mcp in a session Claude and Claude Code connect without any setup on your side. Other MCP clients register themselves with your app first.

title: MCP for AI agents
heading: What the agent can do
text: Every tool call is one request to your app's own API, made as whoever signed in. Your API rules, hooks and rate limits apply as they would to any request. PocketBase's whole API , as pb_ tools: records ( pb_list_records , pb_create_record , …), files and auth for everyone; collections, settings, logs, crons, SQL and backups for superusers. SQL ( pb_run_sql ) goes straight to the database, past API rules and hooks. Admin tasks each feature adds, such as restore_points and restore_restore_to to undo a mistake, or remote_status and remote_logs to check on the app. The MCP reference lists them all. Your app's own tools , from pb_hooks (below). A superuser gets what the API gives superusers. An app user gets what your collection rules give them, and doesn't see the superuser-only tools.

title: MCP for AI agents
heading: Add your own tools
text: Write the endpoint as you would anyway, then declare its tool at the top level of a pb_hooks file: // pb_hooks/blog.pb.js routerAdd('POST', '/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish', (e) = { / … / }, $apis.requireSuperuserAuth()) $mcp.addEndpoint({ name: 'blog_publish_post', description: 'Publish a draft post and email subscribers.', method: 'POST', path: '/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish', // {id} comes from the tool's id argument inputSchema: { type: 'object', required: ['id'], properties: { id: { type: 'string' } } }, }) $mcp.instructions('blog_publish_post also emails subscribers.') The tool runs the request as the caller, so the route's own auth check is what protects it. When your app has its own tools, agents are told to prefer them over pb_ .

title: MCP for AI agents
heading: What's covered
text: Limited to scopes: with Only these , each call is checked like a request from an API token with those scopes. Calls they don't cover get 403 , and tools they can't reach are hidden. Only for MCP: the agent's token works on /mcp and nowhere else. Not tools: sign-in endpoints that hand out a new token, and realtime subscriptions. A file download through pb_download_file is capped at 10 MB. Browsers: a web page on another site can't call /mcp . Clients that send no Origin header, such as Claude's servers and Claude Code, can. Anyone who can sign in to your app can connect an agent, with their own rights. To give an agent less, choose Only these , or sign it in as an account with fewer rights.

title: MCP for AI agents
heading: Disconnect an agent
text: Each connection is an API token named (OAuth) . Open Settings → API tokens , find the one with the oauth: label, and click Revoke .

title: MCP for AI agents
heading: Paste a token instead
text: A client that can't sign in can send a PocketBase auth token, or an API token, as Authorization: Bearer … . An API token with scopes works only if one of them covers /mcp , so to limit an agent, use the consent page instead.

title: MCP for AI agents
heading: Change it or turn it off
text: There's no pocketone.yaml key for MCP: it always serves /mcp , and an agent can do nothing until someone signs it in. The name agents see is your app's Settings → Application → Application name . Every key is in the pocketone.yaml reference. $mcp isn't available in pb_hooks when the app runs PocketBase's own JS engine ( jsvm: goja ).

title: MCP for AI agents
heading: How it works
text: MCP serves /mcp and turns each tool call into a request to your app's API. The OAuth server in Tokens runs the sign-in and consent pages, and issues the agent's token. Admin tools come from the contracts your app answers. Another MCP server can stand in through the mcp/v1 contract and serve the same tools. Looking to teach a coding agent how to build with PocketOne? That's a different thing: see Teach your coding agent.

title: Remote CLI
text: Everything an extension lets you do to an app, you can do from afar, three ways: the pocketone command, against any app you've signed in to; the REST API, from a script or another service; MCP, from an agent such as Claude. Nobody writes these by hand. Each extension API is a contract: a Go interface with one method per operation. PocketOne generates the command, the endpoint and the tool from that interface. Install an extension, or use a host that provides a contract, and its commands show up in the pocketone you already have. There's no other tool to install.

title: Remote CLI
heading: From your terminal
text: Sign in to an app once, then run its commands: pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com --default pocketone login prod pocketone remote whoami # who you are there, your token's scopes, and the contracts the app offers pocketone remote restore points pocketone remote restore to --at -2h remote restore to calls restore/v1 on the app. On an app with PITR, you get the data as it was two hours ago, to the second. On an app with Backups only, you get the latest backup before that. The command is the same either way. How a command is named and read: Name: remote , the contract's name, then the operation. restore/v1's restore_to is remote restore to , mail.suppression/v1's check is remote mail suppression check , remote/v1's status is remote status . Flags: one per field of the operation's input: --at , --email , --campaign . Times take RFC 3339 ( 2026-11-10T15:00:00Z ), a local time ( 2026-11-10 15:00 ) or a duration from now ( -2h ). Lists take a,b or a repeated flag. Anything else takes JSON, or @file to read it from a file. Whole input: --json takes the whole input as JSON ( @file reads a file, - reads stdin). Flags you also give override its fields. Which app: --remote ( -r ) takes a remote's name or a URL. Without it you get the project's default remote. Output: JSON, so you can pipe it to jq . A stream ( remote logs ) prints one JSON line per entry until Ctrl-C. Errors: if the app doesn't offer the contract, the command says so ("this remote doesn't offer restore/v1"). In CI, set P1_TOKEN (or P1_TOKEN_PROD for one remote) to an API token instead of signing in. Remotes covers remotes and saved logins.

title: Remote CLI
heading: From a script: REST
text: Every operation is an endpoint under /api/_c/ / : curl -X POST https://myapp.example.com/api/_c/restore/v1/restore \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"at": "2026-11-10T15:00:00Z"}' GET /api/_c/remote/v1 is the one fixed path. It answers who you are and lists every contract the app offers.

title: Remote CLI
heading: From an agent: MCP
text: An app serves MCP at /mcp (MCP). Each operation is a tool named after its contract and operation ( restore_points , restore_restore_to , remote_status ). Add https://myapp.example.com/mcp to Claude and sign in.

title: Remote CLI
heading: The same checks every way
text: The command, the endpoint and the tool all call the contract, so each passes the same checks: Token scope: each operation needs a token scope ( restore , restore:read ). An API token carries only the scopes it was given. A superuser's own sign-in passes all of them. Superuser: only superusers may call an operation, unless it's public. Hooks: the same hooks run, in Go and in pb_hooks ( onRestoreRestoreTo ).

title: Remote CLI
heading: Every command, endpoint and tool
text: CLI reference: every command of pocketone , PocketBase's own included. REST reference: every contract endpoint. MCP reference: every contract tool. Each contract page lists its operations all three ways. Each extension page lists the commands it adds and the contracts it answers.

title: Remote CLI
heading: Your own commands
text: An extension can replace a generated command with its own, or add new ones under remote , by providing cli.commands/v1. Writing an extension explains how.

title: Point-in-time restore
text: Deleted the wrong records, ran a bad migration, or let a script loose on production? Pick a moment from before it happened, and your app's data goes back to how it was then. This is on for every PocketOne app. You don't need to set anything up.

title: Point-in-time restore
heading: How far back you can go
text: PocketOne records every change to your database as it happens and keeps the last 72 hours . You can restore to any second inside that window. If history recording is turned off, the app restores from your PocketBase backups instead: the latest backup made at or before the moment you pick. The steps below are the same either way. The app tells you which point it used.

title: Point-in-time restore
heading: Restore from the dashboard
text: Sign in to the dashboard as a superuser and open Settings → Backups . Find Restore to a moment . It shows how far back you can go. Under Restore to , pick the date and time to go back to, then click Restore . The app keeps serving while it rebuilds the old data, then restarts with it. That takes a few seconds for most apps.

title: Point-in-time restore
heading: Changed your mind? Undo the restore
text: The data you replaced is kept, and changes keep being recorded after a restore. So after a restore, the section shows when you restored and to what time, with an Undo this restore button. Click it to put things back as they were just before you restored.

title: Point-in-time restore
heading: What's covered
text: Restored: your database: records, collections, rules, settings and superusers. Not restored: uploaded files, pb_hooks , pb_public and the logs. Keep those in your PocketBase backups, or in your own source control. Only superusers can see or run a restore.

title: Point-in-time restore
heading: From your terminal
text: Sign in to your app once (Remote CLI), then: pocketone remote restore points # how far back you can go pocketone remote restore to --at -2h # back to two hours ago --at takes a duration from now ( -2h , -30m ), a local time ( 2026-11-10 15:00 ) or an RFC 3339 time ( 2026-11-10T15:00:00Z ). On the machine that runs the app, you can also work from its files directly.
