Pull a copy of the old database to look through without touching the live one, or restore in place while the server is stopped (it's swapped in at the next start): pocketone pitr restore --at 2026-11-10T15:00:00Z --to /tmp/then.db # a copy, safe any time pocketone pitr restore --at 2026-11-10T15:00:00Z # in place, server stopped

title: Point-in-time restore
heading: From an agent
text: An agent connected to your app over MCP has two tools: restore_points to see how far back it can go, and restore_restore_to to restore. It needs a token with the restore scope, and only a superuser can grant one.

title: Point-in-time restore
heading: Keep history somewhere safer
text: By default, history is kept on the same disk as your database. That protects you from mistakes, but not from losing the disk. To keep it in your own S3-compatible bucket, open Settings → Backups → Point-in-time restore , tick Store the history in my own S3 bucket , fill in the bucket details, click Test connection , then Save .

title: Point-in-time restore
heading: Change how far back it goes, or turn it off
text: In pocketone.yaml : pitr: retention: 168h # keep a week instead of 72 hours # enabled: false # stop recording; restores then use your backups A longer window uses more storage. Every key is in the pocketone.yaml reference.

title: Point-in-time restore
heading: How it works
text: PITR records the history with Litestream and restores to any second. Backups restores from PocketBase's own backups when PITR is off. Both answer the same restore/v1 contract, which is why the dashboard, the command and the MCP tools don't care which one is on.

title: PocketPages: sites in TSX, TypeScript or EJS
text: Put a .tsx , .jsx , .ejs or .md file in a pb_pages folder next to pb_data , and your app serves it as a web page. Each file is a route. Components import each other, route files can be TypeScript ( +page.ts , +api.ts ), and page code reads and writes your records directly. Every part of a page can await , and the app keeps serving other requests while it waits. This is PocketPages, built into PocketOne. esbuild is built into the pocketone binary, so TSX and TypeScript compile the first time a page is used: no Node, no npm install , no bundler, no build step. It's on for every PocketOne app whenever a pb_pages folder exists. No folder, no pages.

title: PocketPages: sites in TSX, TypeScript or EJS
heading: A product page in TSX
text: The page is an async component: it awaits its record, then renders it with another component. // pb_pages/products/[id].tsx import Price from './_private/Price' export default async function Product({ ctx }: any) { const product = await ctx.app.findRecordById.async('products', ctx.params.id) return ( {product.getString('name')} ) } // pb_pages/products/_private/Price.tsx export default ({ cents }: { cents: number }) = ${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)} /products/ now answers with Mug $12.50 . Edit any of the files and reload: the change shows up with no restart.

title: PocketPages: sites in TSX, TypeScript or EJS
heading: await anywhere
text: .async twins of Go functions ( findRecordById.async , countRecords.async , ...) do their work outside the JS VM, so the app serves other requests while a page waits. Components: any component can be async . Sibling components run at the same time, so these two counts load in parallel: async function Count({ collection }: { collection: string }) { const n = await $app.countRecords.async(collection) return {n} } export default () = orders, users Loaders and handlers: load , get , post and the rest in +page.ts , +api.ts handlers, and +middleware can be async . EJS: a tag can await : . Sync stays free: a page without await runs exactly as before. Loading data, EJS and JSX and TSX have the details. JSX renders to plain HTML on the server. There's no virtual DOM and no client-side React, so pair it with htmx, Datastar or plain tags for interactivity. TypeScript types are stripped, not checked; run tsc --noEmit or rely on your editor. JSX and TSX has the details.

title: PocketPages: sites in TSX, TypeScript or EJS
heading: Prefer EJS? Hello world
text: Make a folder for your app with a page in it: mkdir -p myapp/pb_pages && cd myapp echo ' ' pb_pages/index.ejs Create a superuser, then start the app: pocketone superuser upsert you@example.com --dir ./pb_data pocketone serve --dir ./pb_data Open http://127.0.0.1:8090. You see Hello, world! Edit the file and reload the browser. Changes show up right away, with no restart. To start from something bigger, pocketone pages starters lists the starter kits and pocketone pages create myapp --starter makes a new app from one.

title: PocketPages: sites in TSX, TypeScript or EJS
heading: What's covered
text: Files are routes: pb_pages/about.ejs serves /about , and pb_pages/blog/index.ejs serves /blog . Templates: TSX, JSX, EJS and Markdown, mixed freely (an EJS page can sit in a TSX layout), with layouts, partials, middleware and JSON routes. Route files ( +page , +api , +middleware ) can be .ts or .js . Leftovers go on: a URL no page matches goes on to pb_public , then to PocketBase. URLs under /api/ and /_/ always belong to PocketBase. Errors: in dev mode you get detailed error pages. Otherwise visitors see a plain error page and the details go to the log. Not with --jsvm goja : pages run in PocketOne's own JS engine, so they're off when you serve with PocketBase's. To send your pages to a running app, see Deploy and live sync.

title: PocketPages: sites in TSX, TypeScript or EJS
heading: Change it
text: To serve pages from another folder, pass --pagesDir to pocketone serve , or set server.pages_dir in pocketone.yaml (pocketone.yaml reference). Settings for the site itself, such as which PocketPages plugins to load, go in pb_pages/+config.js (+config.js).

title: PocketPages: sites in TSX, TypeScript or EJS
heading: Learn more
text: The full PocketPages docs: Installation and starter kits JSX and TSX Creating a page and routing Loading data Layouts and slots Authentication Going live

title: PocketPages: sites in TSX, TypeScript or EJS
heading: How it works
text: Pages serves the pb_pages folder and adds the pages create and pages starters commands. Page code runs in your app's JS engine. PocketPages is the home of its docs, guides and plugins.

title: API tokens and OAuth
text: A script, a CI job or another service can't type a password. Give it an API token instead: a long secret that starts with pbt_ , acts as the account that owns it, and can be limited to a few scopes and given an expiry. Revoke it, and it stops working at once. This is on for every PocketOne app. You don't need to set anything up. Ordinary PocketBase sign-ins keep working as before.

title: API tokens and OAuth
heading: Create a token in the dashboard
text: Sign in to the dashboard as a superuser and open Settings → API tokens (under Access ). Fill in a Name , so you can recognize the token later. Optionally set Expires in (days) . Leave it empty and the token never expires. Tick the Scopes the token needs. Tick none and it gets its owner's full rights. The token is yours by default. To make one for another account, fill in Owner collection and Owner (id or email) . Click Create token , then copy it. It's shown only once and never stored. Send it with each request: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_…" https://myapp.example.com/api/collections/notes/records

title: API tokens and OAuth
heading: See and revoke tokens
text: The same screen lists every token: its name, its first characters, owner, scopes, expiry and when it was last used (time and IP). Click Revoke and confirm to delete one. Anything using it stops working at once.

title: API tokens and OAuth
heading: Let apps and tools sign in
text: Some clients sign in for you instead of asking for a pasted token: pocketone login , Claude and other AI agents, or an app of your own. They send you to your app's own sign-in pages: Sign in with whatever the collection allows: a password, an emailed code, or (for app users) Google and other providers, plus a second step if the account has MFA. Click Sign in as a superuser to sign in as one. The consent page names the client and the account it will act as. Choose Full access , or Only these and tick the scopes it may use. Click Allow . On a machine with no browser (over SSH, say), the client shows a code instead. Open https:// /api/_c/oauth/v1/device/verify , enter it under Connect a device , sign in and allow. Codes last 10 minutes. Each sign-in becomes an API token named (OAuth) , bound to exactly what you approved. It shows up under Settings → API tokens with an oauth: label. Click Revoke to disconnect the client. pocketone logout revokes a browser login from your terminal.

title: API tokens and OAuth
heading: From your terminal
text: On the machine that runs the app, the token command works on the app's data folder, even before the first serve: pocketone token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci --scope deploy --ttl 720h # prints the secret pocketone token create --collection users --record user@example.com --name script pocketone token list pocketone token revoke pocketone token revoke --all --superuser admin@example.com --scope can be repeated. Without --ttl the token never expires. For CI that runs pocketone against your app, put the token in P1_TOKEN instead of signing in (Remote CLI). To let an app of your own sign people in, register it once: pocketone oauth clients add --name "My app" --redirect https://myapp.example.com/callback It prints the client id, and a secret once. Add --public for a desktop or mobile app with no secret. Claude, the pocketone CLI and other MCP clients don't need this.

title: API tokens and OAuth
heading: From pb_hooks
text: Add your own scopes, and they show up in the dashboard and on the consent page: // pb_hooks/scopes.pb.js $apiTokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes:read', description: 'Read notes', paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'], methods: ['GET'] }) routerAdd('GET', '/api/notes/summary', (e) = { / ... / }, $apis.requireAuth(), $apiTokens.requireScope('notes:read')) A collection rule can check a scope too: @request.headers.x_token_scope_notes_read = "1" . A scope can also limit a token to some records. Register it with values: { description: 'a note id' } , and a token can hold notes=abc123 instead of all of notes . Your route checks the record with $apiTokens.hasScope(e, 'notes', id) . In the dashboard, a ticked scope that takes values has a box for them; leave it empty for every value.

title: API tokens and OAuth
heading: What a token can do
text: No scopes: everything its owner can do. With scopes: only the requests its scopes cover. Anything else gets 403 . Which scopes: the ones features add ( deploy , and one for each admin feature, often with a :read version, such as restore and restore:read ), plus your own. Some, like deploy , only superusers can hold. The CLI reference and MCP reference name the scope each operation needs. Expiry: never, unless you set one. Tokens from a sign-in last 30 days, and the client renews them; AI agents' tokens never expire. Expired tokens are deleted once a day. Gone with the account: deleting an account deletes its tokens. No way around a revoke: a token can't be traded for a PocketBase auth token, so revoking it really ends its access. Only superusers see Settings → API tokens . Other signed-in users manage their own tokens through the token API. A token with scopes can only create tokens within those scopes.

title: API tokens and OAuth
heading: Change it or turn it off
text: There's no pocketone.yaml key for API tokens: they're always on, and a token does nothing until someone creates one. To limit what a token can do, give it scopes and an expiry, or revoke it. Every key is in the pocketone.yaml reference. To restyle the sign-in pages, copy them into your app with pocketone template eject oauth .

title: API tokens and OAuth
heading: How it works
text: API Tokens stores the tokens (only a hash of each secret), checks them on every request and adds the dashboard screen. OAuth server runs the sign-in and consent pages and issues tokens for what you approved. They answer the api-tokens/v1 and oauth/v1 contracts. Templates lets you restyle the sign-in pages.

title: Folders
text: A PocketOne app is a folder. PocketBase's own folders sit next to each other in it, and PocketOne adds pb_cache . pb_data the database, uploaded files, logs yes never no: it's your data pb_hooks your JS hooks (and .pb.wasm modules) as code, in git yes no pb_migrations your app's migrations as code, in git yes no pb_public static files the app serves as code, in git yes no pb_pages PocketPages pages as code, in git yes no pb_templates page templates you ejected ( pocketone template eject ) as code, in git yes no pb_cache files extensions can rebuild, one folder each never never yes, at any time Add pb_data/ and pb_cache/ to your .gitignore .

title: Folders
heading: pb_cache
text: Each extension that keeps disposable files has its own folder: pb_cache/ / (say, pb_cache/agent/ for the built-in model's saved conversation state). Everything in it can be rebuilt, so deleting it is always safe: the app carries on, perhaps a little slower until the cache fills again. pocketone cache # each extension's folder, its file count and size pocketone cache clear # empty every folder pocketone cache clear agent # empty one On a multisite host every instance has its own pb_cache , kept by the host outside the instance's folder, in the host's pb_cache/instances/ / . Copies, archives and moves of an instance's folder never carry it, and a Docker container never sees it.

title: Folders
heading: Extension tables
text: Extensions that store records keep them in collections named _ _ ( _bulkmail_campaigns , _tokens_oauth_clients ), so you can tell them from your own collections at a glance and see which extension owns each. They live in pb_data like the rest of your data, so they're backed up with it. Extensions create and update those collections themselves when the app starts, with their own migrations. Those are recorded apart from your pb_migrations , so pocketone migrate never touches them: pocketone extensions migrations # every extension's migrations and when each was applied pocketone extensions migrate down bulkmail # revert bulkmail's last migration (its data goes with it)

title: Contracts: how PocketOne fits together
text: PocketOne is PocketBase plus extensions. What keeps those extensions from turning into a pile of plugins that know too much about each other is how they meet: through contracts .

title: Contracts: how PocketOne fits together
heading: The idea
text: A contract is a promise with a name and a version. restore/v1 promises one thing: put this app's data back as it was at a moment . It says what you can ask and what you get back. It says nothing about how. An extension that keeps the promise provides the contract. Everything else talks to the contract, never to the extension behind it: the dashboard, the pocketone command, an AI agent over MCP, your pb_hooks , and other extensions. That's the whole rule: every API an extension offers is a contract. Extensions have no private routes and never import each other.

title: Contracts: how PocketOne fits together
heading: An example: restore/v1
text: Every PocketOne app can restore its data to a moment. Who does the work depends on the app: PITR Any second in the last three days, from continuous history. Backups, the default The latest backup made at or before the moment. It steps aside when PITR is on. A multisite host It could restore an instance from the host's own disk snapshots. Asking looks the same whoever answers: pocketone remote restore to --at -2h # the command line curl -X POST https://app.example.com/api/_c/restore/v1/restore \ -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -d '{"at": "2026-11-10T15:00:00Z"}' # HTTP An agent asked to "restore my app to yesterday at 3pm" calls the same operation as an MCP tool. Settings → Backups shows the contract's own "Restore to a moment" screen. The answer always says which point the data came from: exactly 3pm with PITR, or the 2:00 backup without it. If something better than PITR comes along tomorrow, it provides restore/v1 , and nothing that restores apps has to change.

title: Contracts: how PocketOne fits together
heading: Why it matters
text: Swap anything. Any extension that provides a contract can stand in for another. One line in pocketone.yaml chooses when several could. Build on anything. Extensions depend on contracts, not on each other: Deploy requires remote/v1 , not "the Remotes extension". Replace Remotes and Deploy keeps working. One surface, promised. If a client can call it, it's in a contract: named, versioned, documented and checked. Every extension route lives under /api/_c/ / ; only paths a standard fixes stay at the root ( /.well-known/ , /mcp ). Written once, reachable everywhere. A contract's interface is the source for everything around it. Each operation is at once an HTTP endpoint, a pocketone remote command, an MCP tool, a hook in Go and in pb_hooks , and a typed client call. Every one of those paths passes the same checks: superusers only unless the operation is public, the token's scopes, and the action hooks. Nothing hidden. Each app prints who provides what when it starts; pocketone remote whoami lists the contracts an app offers; the catalogue lists every contract with the extensions that provide it, require it and work with it.

title: Contracts: how PocketOne fits together
heading: What one interface gives you
text: Write the interface, run go generate , and a contract like restore/v1 gets all of this: HTTP API GET /api/_c/restore/v1 , POST /api/_c/restore/v1/restore Command line pocketone remote restore points , pocketone remote restore to --at -2h MCP tools restore_points , restore_restore_to Hooks restorev1.OnRestoreTo(app, ...) in Go, onRestoreRestoreTo(...) in pb_hooks Client restorev1.NewClient(url, token, nil).RestoreTo(...) Dashboard "Restore to a moment" on Settings → Backups, shown for any provider

title: Contracts: how PocketOne fits together
heading: Who provides what
text: When an app starts, PocketOne settles every contract and says what it decided: standard: restore/v1 ← pitr (default backups stepped aside) standard: mail.fallback/v1 ← mailtrap standard: deploy/v1 ← deploy (default) Defaults. A standard extension often provides a contract as the default: it steps aside as soon as anything else provides it. Choices. When two extensions provide a contract that takes one, the app won't start until pocketone.yaml picks one: providers: restore/v1: pitr Chains. Some contracts take several providers in order. Mail with SMTP off goes through mail.fallback/v1 's chain: the dev inbox in dev mode, then a host's relay. Your own JS. An app's pb_hooks can provide contracts too, in onContracts((e) = e.provide(...)) . The host. On a multisite host, some contracts are answered by the host for its instances. An instance running a stock PocketBase image in Docker has no PocketOne extensions inside it, but the host still answers remote/v1 for it, so pocketone remote logs works there too. The host's own parts are contracts as well: what runs instances ( runtime/v1 , Pocker or Docker), what admits requests ( gate/v1 ), its TLS ( tls/v1 ).

title: Contracts: how PocketOne fits together
heading: Versions
text: A contract's id carries its major version only: restore/v1 . Within v1 the promise doesn't change. Changing it means a restore/v2 beside v1 , so whatever relies on v1 keeps working. A new optional ability is usually a new, small contract rather than a change to an old one.

title: Contracts: how PocketOne fits together
heading: Where contracts live, and who owns them
text: Every contract, from the standard set or the community, lives in one place: ext/contracts/ /vN/ ( mail.fallback/v1 is ext/contracts/mail/fallback/v1/ ). Extensions live in ext/ / . Keeping contracts together means one namespace, so two authors can't publish different rehash/v1 s, and it means one place to look for what you can build on. Each contract has a README like an extension's, with its owners and a one-line promise at the top. Its list of the extensions that provide it, require it and work with it is generated from the code, so it's never out of date. Whoever first creates a contract owns it. An extension author who needs a contract that doesn't exist yet writes it first, and then owns both the contract and the extension that provides it. Changes to a contract are reviewed carefully, because every provider and every caller relies on the promise. Name a contract for what it does ( restore/v1 ), not for the extension that happens to provide it first.

title: Contracts: how PocketOne fits together
heading: Words
text: Contract A named, versioned promise: a Go interface plus the API, commands, tools and hooks generated from it. Provide An extension keeps the promise for an app. Require An extension can't work without the contract; without a provider it's turned off, and the startup lines say why. Works with An extension uses the contract when something provides it. Default A provider that steps aside when any other extension provides the contract. Host-provided A multisite host answers the contract for its instances.

text: Contracts: what each one promises, and who provides, requires and works with it. Writing an extension: declare, provide and use contracts in your extension. Add a contract: the folder, the README and the generated code.

title: Installation
text: PocketOne is one executable, pocketone . It is built on PocketBase v0.42 and takes the same commands and flags, plus its own.

title: Installation
heading: Homebrew (macOS and Linux)
text: brew install pockethost/tap/pocketone The formula lives in pockethost/homebrew-tap.

title: Installation
heading: Download a release
text: Download the zip for your platform from Releases, unzip it, and put pocketone somewhere on your PATH .

title: Installation
heading: Build from source
text: With Go installed: git clone https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone.git cd pocketone/examples/pocketone go build -o pocketone .

title: Installation
heading: Run it
text: Create your first superuser before the first serve: pocketone superuser upsert pocketone serve Opening http://127.0.0.1:8090/_/ to create it also works, as in PocketBase. To start a site with server-rendered pages: pocketone pages create myapp cd myapp pocketone serve --dev --dir ./pb_data In dev mode ( serve --dev ), an app with no SMTP settings doesn't send mail through the system's sendmail . PocketOne catches the mail and shows it at http://127.0.0.1:8025 .

title: Installation
heading: Upgrade
text: pocketone upgrade This replaces the executable with the latest release. The old one is kept beside it as pocketone- , never deleted, so you can go back.

title: Installation
heading: Moving from PocketBase
text: PocketOne reads the same pb_data , pb_hooks , pb_migrations and pb_public folders. Point it at your existing data directory with --dir , as you would with pocketbase . Back up pb_data first.

title: What is PocketOne?
text: PocketOne is a community fork of PocketBase. It tracks upstream PocketBase and keeps its own changes to the core small: only the hooks that let extensions extend and override PocketBase. Every feature lives in an extension. It's maintained by Ben Allfree and contributors. Ben also created PocketHost, which runs PocketOne in production, but PocketOne is its own project, open to anyone who wants to help. PocketOne is not affiliated with or endorsed by the PocketBase project.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Why a fork
text: PocketBase is a remarkable piece of software, and a lot of that comes from how it's made: one author, a deliberately narrow scope, and a careful, steady pace. That focus is a big part of why it's so good, and how PocketBase is run is Gani's call to make. It also means PocketBase isn't set up to take larger contributions from the community, so ideas people want to build have nowhere to land upstream: hooks that can do more, apps that run many instances, features anyone can write and share. PocketOne is a different path for that work. It stays close to upstream and passes PocketBase's own tests, keeps its changes to PocketBase small, and puts everything else in extensions that anyone can build on, improve and send back.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: What it adds
text: Run pocketone the way you run pocketbase . These are the differences you'll notice; New in PocketOne compares each one with PocketBase.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Hooks with async, import and TypeScript
text: Your pb_hooks run on QuickJS with PocketBase's JS API, so they work unchanged, and they also get: async handlers with await (the app keeps serving while one waits), ES module import and node_modules packages, .pb.ts TypeScript files, globals shared by every handler, and memory and time limits. QuickJS hooks walks through each one.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Pages in TSX, TypeScript or EJS
text: Put .tsx , .jsx , .ejs or Markdown files in a pb_pages folder and they're server-rendered pages, with your records a function call away. Components import each other, route files can be TypeScript, and every part of a page can await . esbuild is built into the binary, so there's no Node, no npm install and no build step. This site is one. pocketone pages create myapp starts a new site from a starter kit. PocketPages shows a page in TSX.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Hundreds of apps in one process
text: Add a multisite section to pocketone.yaml and one pocketone process runs hundreds of PocketBase apps as isolates, routed by hostname. Each is a complete app with its own data, hooks and dashboard. It starts on its first request in tens of milliseconds, costs about 3 MB while it runs, and is sandboxed from the others. No container per app. PocketBase isolates shows it running in a minute.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Point-in-time restore, on by default
text: Your database is replicated with Litestream, so you can restore it to any moment from Settings → Backups or with pocketone pitr restore . Turn it off with --pitr=false .

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Mail you can see in dev mode
text: In dev mode ( serve --dev ), an app with no SMTP settings doesn't send through the system's sendmail . The mail is caught and shown at http://127.0.0.1:8025 .

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: A config file
text: Settings can live in pocketone.yaml , with secrets in a .env file beside it that your JS hooks never see. Without the file, PocketOne behaves like stock PocketBase. pocketone config lists every section, and pocketone config check checks a file. The config reference lists every section.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Commands for working with remote apps
text: pocketone login , remote and link : save logins to your apps. pocketone deploy , dev , pull and logs : ship pb_hooks , pb_migrations and pb_public to an app and watch it. pocketone upgrade : move to the latest release, keeping the old executable. pocketone remote … : every operation of every contract an app offers is a command, such as pocketone remote restore to --at -2h . The same operations are REST endpoints and MCP tools. Remote CLI explains it, and the CLI reference lists every command.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Agents and API tokens
text: An MCP endpoint at /mcp lets agents such as Claude manage your app and call its tools. Long-lived API tokens ( pbt_… ) with scopes, for scripts and integrations. Your app can act as an OAuth provider; pocketone login and MCP sign-in use it.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Extensions that fit together
text: PocketOne's extensions meet through contracts: named, versioned promises like restore/v1 that any extension can keep. The dashboard, the pocketone command, agents and your pb_hooks call the contract, so you can swap the extension behind it without changing anything else. How PocketOne fits together explains it.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Everything else
text: Automatic TLS certificates, bulk mail to your own users, scheduled VACUUM, signed S3 download redirects, and more. See all extensions.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: What stays the same
text: The admin dashboard, collections, rules, the REST and realtime APIs, JS hooks and migrations all work as in PocketBase. For those, the PocketBase docs are the reference.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: How it's built
text: A small core. PocketBase's own code changes only to add hooks. Each change is marked in the source, reviewed by someone who didn't write it, and kept minimal so upstream releases merge cleanly. You can review the complete core changes here. Everything else is an extension. Extensions live in ext/ in the repo. Each is its own Go module, with a README and a small example. Off until you use it. The extensions in the pocketone binary add no work to an app that doesn't use them. One app or hundreds. An extension written against the extension contract works the same on a single app and on every instance under a multi-instance host.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Open to contributions
text: PocketOne is open to everyone. Ask questions and share ideas in GitHub Discussions, report bugs in Issues, and send extensions as pull requests. Start with Writing an extension.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Where to next
text: Install PocketOne Browse the extensions

title: Coming from PocketBase
text: PocketOne is PocketBase with more built in. Run pocketone the way you run pocketbase : the same commands and flags, the same API, the same dashboard and the same pb_data , pb_hooks and pb_migrations folders.

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: What stays the same
text: Your API and SDKs. Collections, records, auth, files and realtime work as in PocketBase. The JS and Dart SDKs work unchanged. Your hooks. The JS API ( $app , routerAdd , onRecordCreate , cronAdd , …) is PocketBase's, so existing pb_hooks run as they are. They run on QuickJS, which adds imports, TypeScript and async handlers on top. PocketBase's own tests. PocketBase's test suite runs unmodified against PocketOne's core on every change and every day. See the live results on PocketBase compatibility. PocketOne is built on PocketBase v0.42. When pocketbase.io describes a newer release, some of it may not be in PocketOne yet.

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: What's added
text: Everything below is on by default. For each one, here's how you'd handle it in PocketBase and what PocketOne brings.

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Hooks
text: PocketBase runs pb_hooks on goja: CommonJS require , synchronous handlers, and a pool of runtimes that each load your hook files. PocketOne runs the same JS API on QuickJS, so your hooks keep working, and adds async / await , ES module import with node_modules packages, .pb.ts TypeScript, globals shared by every handler, and memory and time limits. QuickJS hooks

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Sites
text: PocketBase serves static files and single-page apps from pb_public , and hooks can render HTML with $template . PocketOne adds server-rendered pages: a .tsx , .jsx , .ejs or .md file in pb_pages becomes a route, with await everywhere and no build step. PocketPages sites

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Many apps on one server
text: A PocketBase app is one process, and you host several by running a process, container or VM for each. PocketOne can run hundreds of apps as isolates inside one process; each starts on its first request in tens of milliseconds, uses about 3 MB and is sandboxed from the others. PocketBase isolates

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Backups and restore
text: PocketBase makes backups on a schedule, to local disk or S3, and restores a whole backup. PocketOne also records every change, so you can restore to any second in the last 72 hours, and undo the restore. Point-in-time restore

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Deploying
text: A PocketBase app is a folder you copy to the server; hooks reload when they change, and migrations run on the next start. PocketOne adds pocketone deploy , which uploads only what changed, and pocketone dev , which keeps a local folder and the running app in step both ways and streams the logs. Deploy and live sync

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Admin from anywhere
text: PocketBase's CLI runs on the machine that holds pb_data , and the dashboard and REST API work from anywhere. PocketOne adds a remote CLI: sign in once, then run admin commands against any app from your terminal, a script or an agent. Remote CLI

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Tokens
text: A PocketBase auth token acts as its account, and changing the account's token key signs out all of its tokens at once. PocketOne adds named, scoped API tokens that you revoke one by one, and makes your app an OAuth server that apps and agents sign in through. API tokens and OAuth

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: AI agents
text: PocketBase offers a REST API and realtime subscriptions, with official JavaScript and Dart SDKs. PocketOne also serves MCP at /mcp on every app, with OAuth sign-in, so Claude and other agents work with your app as you, using your own tools from pb_hooks too. MCP for AI agents

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Mail
text: PocketBase sends account mail (verification, password reset, email change, one-time codes), and your hooks can send any message through its mailer. PocketOne adds campaigns from the dashboard, with unsubscribes, suppression and pacing handled. Bulk mail

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Desktop apps
text: A PocketBase app is a server: you host it, and people reach it from a browser. PocketOne can also build the same app folder into a native desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux, with your hooks, migrations and public files inside one executable and each user's data on their own machine. It's a preview. Desktop apps

title: Coming from PocketBase
heading: Configuration
text: In PocketBase, app settings live in the dashboard and serve takes its options as command-line flags. PocketOne adds pocketone.yaml , one file next to your app for those options and every extension's, with a .env for secrets. pocketone.yaml Smaller additions are listed under Also built in.

title: pocketone.yaml
text: Every pocketone flag has a default. pocketone.yaml lets you change those defaults in one file, next to your app, instead of typing them on every start. The same file holds each extension's options, and your secrets go in a .env beside it. Without the file, nothing changes: PocketOne behaves like stock PocketBase. Every step below was run on pocketone .

title: pocketone.yaml
heading: 1. Write the file
text: In your app's folder, create pocketone.yaml : server: http: 127.0.0.1:8090 app: dir: ./pb_data dev: false Check it, create a superuser, and start the app: pocketone config check # pocketone.yaml: ok (2 sections) pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com password pocketone serve pocketone serve listens on the address under server , and the data folder is pb_data next to the file. Relative paths are relative to the file's folder, so the app starts the same from any working directory. PocketOne looks for pocketone.yaml in the working directory, then next to the executable. --config picks another file.

title: pocketone.yaml
heading: 2. Flags still win
text: A flag always beats the file. The file only changes the defaults: pocketone serve --http=127.0.0.1:8091 # listens on 8091, whatever the file says

title: pocketone.yaml
heading: 3. Keep secrets in a .env
text: Put secrets in a .env beside the file, and refer to them as $VAR or ${VAR} in any value: # .env LISTEN=127.0.0.1:8090 STRIPE_KEY=sk_test_123 OTHER_SECRET=hidden server: http: ${LISTEN} Your JS hooks don't see the .env unless you allow each name: app: env_allow: [STRIPE_KEY] // pb_hooks/env.pb.js routerAdd("GET", "/env", (e) = { return e.json(200, { stripe: process.env.STRIPE_KEY null, other: process.env.OTHER_SECRET null }) }) curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/env # {"stripe":"sk_test_123","other":null} pocketone config check says when it read secrets from a .env . Keep the .env out of git.

title: pocketone.yaml
heading: 4. Set an extension's options
text: Each top-level key is a section owned by one extension. For example, keep three days of point-in-time history, and give the app's JS more room: pitr: retention: 72h app: js_limits: memory: 128MiB task_time: 10s js_limits sets the limits of the JS engine your hooks run on; QuickJS hooks shows what they stop. To see every section your binary knows, with each key, run: pocketone config The pocketone.yaml reference lists the same, with each key's type, default and meaning.

title: pocketone.yaml
heading: 5. Choose which extension does a job
text: Extensions offer their abilities through contracts. When more than one extension can do the same job, providers picks one. Both PITR and Backups can restore your data. PITR is used when it's on, but you can choose Backups: providers: restore/v1: backups The startup lines show the choice: INFO standard: restore/v1 ← backups (providers:)

title: pocketone.yaml
heading: The whole file
text: server: http: ${LISTEN} app: dir: ./pb_data dev: false env_allow: [STRIPE_KEY] js_limits: memory: 128MiB task_time: 10s pitr: retention: 72h providers: restore/v1: backups

title: pocketone.yaml
heading: Next
text: pocketone.yaml reference: every section and key. Config: how the file is found, .env rules, and loading it in your own Go build.

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
text: PocketOne runs your pb_hooks and pb_migrations on QuickJS instead of goja, the engine stock PocketBase uses. It's the same JS API ( $app , routerAdd , onRecordCreate , cronAdd , $http , …), so your existing hooks run unchanged. On top of that you get: Shared globals. Top-level helpers and state are visible to every handler. Imports. ES modules with import / export , and node_modules packages. TypeScript. .ts hooks run directly. Async. Handlers can await , and the app keeps serving other requests while they wait. Limits. A runaway script stops with an error instead of taking the app down. Each app gets one QuickJS VM. The engine is pure Go, so builds need no cgo, as with stock PocketBase. This tutorial builds a small app that tries each of these. Every example below was run on pocketone , and the outputs are real.

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: Set up
text: Make a folder for the app, create a superuser, and start it: mkdir -p qjs/pb_hooks/lib && cd qjs pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com password --dir=pb_data pocketone serve --dir=pb_data Leave it running. PocketOne watches pb_hooks , so each file you add below is picked up without a restart.

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: 1. Your PocketBase hooks run unchanged
text: Here's a hook written for stock PocketBase, with require() inside the handler and the global $app : // pb_hooks/legacy.pb.js routerAdd("GET", "/legacy", (e) = { const util = require( ${__hooks}/lib/util.cjs ) return e.json(200, { shout: util.shout("hello"), users: $app.countRecords("users") }) }) // pb_hooks/lib/util.cjs module.exports = { shout: (s) = s.toUpperCase() + "!" } curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/legacy # {"shout":"HELLO!","users":0} A plain .pb.js file is still a CommonJS script, as in PocketBase. Nothing in it needs to change.

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: 2. Top-level code is shared by every handler
text: On goja, each handler runs in a separate runtime from a pool, so it can't see the variables at the top of its own file. That's why PocketBase hooks call require() inside every handler. On QuickJS, every hook file runs in the app's one global scope: // pb_hooks/counter.pb.js let hits = 0 function greet(name) { return hi ${name} } routerAdd("GET", "/hits", (e) = { hits++ return e.json(200, { hits, msg: greet("there") }) }) curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hits # {"hits":1,"msg":"hi there"} curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hits # {"hits":2,"msg":"hi there"} The same file on goja ( pocketone serve --jsvm goja ) answers every request with a 400, because the handler can't see hits or greet . Globals live as long as the app's VM. A restart or a change to pb_hooks starts a fresh one ( hits goes back to 0), so keep anything that must last in the database. Use globals for caches, helpers and constants. Hook files run before the app opens its database, as in PocketBase. A $app query at a file's top level fails, so to fill a global from the database, do it in onBootstrap : let users = null onBootstrap((e) = { e.next() // the database is open after this users = e.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("users") })

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: 3. Split your code into modules
text: Name a hook file .pb.mjs and it's an ES module, with import and export : // pb_hooks/lib/slug.mjs export const slugify = (s) = s.toLowerCase().trim().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-").replace(/^- -$/g, "") // pb_hooks/modules.pb.mjs import { slugify } from "./lib/slug.mjs" routerAdd("GET", "/slug/{text}", (e) = { return e.json(200, { slug: slugify(e.request.pathValue("text")) }) }) curl "http://127.0.0.1:8090/slug/Hello%20World%21" # {"slug":"hello-world"} .mjs files are ES modules; .js and .cjs files are CommonJS. Both kinds can load each other. import and require() find files the same way: relative paths first, then packages in node_modules . A module loads once per app, so every file that imports it shares the same instance and its state.

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: 4. Write hooks in TypeScript
text: Name the file .pb.ts and write TypeScript: // pb_hooks/typed.pb.ts interface Total { count: number label: string } function total(count: number): Total { return { count, label: ${count} users } } routerAdd("GET", "/typed", (e) = { return e.json(200, total(e.app.countRecords("users"))) }) curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/typed # {"count":0,"label":"0 users"} PocketOne removes the types when it loads the file, with no build step. An error names the line in your .ts file. Types aren't checked at run time: run tsc --noEmit or rely on your editor. The app writes the whole JS API's types to types.d.ts in your project folder, next to pb_hooks , and a tsconfig.json that uses it if you don't have one (JSVM page).

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: 5. Async handlers
text: A handler can be async . Every Go function has an .async twin that does its work outside the VM and returns a promise: // pb_hooks/async.pb.js routerAdd("GET", "/slow", async (e) = { await sleep.async(2000) // waits outside the VM const n = await e.app.countRecords.async("users") return e.json(200, { waited: "2s", users: n }) }) Call /slow , and call /hits while it waits: curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/slow & curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hits /hits answered after 0.35 s, and /slow after 2.06 s. The app went on serving requests while /slow waited. Without .async , a call that waits ( $http.send , sleep ) still lets other requests run, but those requests nest on one stack and wait on each other: under load, a plain sleep(100) served 19 requests a second where await sleep.async(100) served 481 (How it performs). Use .async for anything slow. Two things to watch: After an await , other requests may have run in between. Use e.app , not the global $app . A transaction holds SQLite's write lock, so keep it short across await s.

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: Why there's no VM pool
text: goja runs JS synchronously: while a handler waits on the database or an HTTP call, its runtime can't do anything else. To serve requests at the same time, PocketBase keeps a pool of runtimes (15 by default, --hooksPool ) and makes more when they're all busy. Each runtime loads every hook file separately. That's why a handler can't see the top of its own file, why state can't be shared between requests, and why memory grows with load. QuickJS here works like a Node.js process. Each app has one VM with an event loop. While a handler waits, the loop runs other requests, and the handler picks up again when its result arrives. There's one copy of your code and your globals, so nothing needs a pool ( --hooksPool is accepted and ignored). As in Node.js, the JS itself runs one piece at a time. A handler that computes for a long time holds the loop until it finishes or hits its time budget. Keep heavy work out of the request path, or move it into Go.

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: 6. Memory and time limits
text: Each app has a memory cap, and each task has a time budget: // pb_hooks/limits.pb.js routerAdd("GET", "/hog", (e) = { const junk = [] while (true) junk.push("x".repeat(1024 1024)) }) routerAdd("GET", "/spin", (e) = { while (true) {} }) Both requests fail and the app keeps running: /hog 0.08 s InternalError: out of memory at pb_hooks/limits.pb.js:3:36 /spin 5.0 s InternalError: interrupted at pb_hooks/limits.pb.js:5:27 Calls to /hits right after each one answered normally. These are the limits in the pocketone binary: Memory: the JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds 64 MiB per app JS time per task 5 s Wall time per task, Go calls included 30 s Change them in pocketone.yaml (pocketone.yaml): app: js_limits: memory: 128MiB # the JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds task_time: 10s # JS time per task task_wall: 60s # wall time per task, Go calls included With task_time: 1s , /spin stopped after 1.0 s instead of 5. A custom Go build sets the same limits in jsvm.Config.VM (JSVM). On a multisite host each app has its own VM and its own limits, so one app's runaway script doesn't stop the others.

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: How it performs
text: The same hook file, on the pocketone binary with each engine (QuickJS, and --jsvm goja with its default pool of 15): // pb_hooks/bench.pb.js routerAdd("GET", "/b/ping", (e) = e.json(200, { ok: true })) routerAdd("GET", "/b/db", (e) = e.json(200, { n: e.app.findRecordsByFilter("_superusers", "id != ''", "", 10, 0).length })) routerAdd("GET", "/b/cpu", (e) = { const items = [] for (let i = 0; i { sleep(100); return e.json(200, { ok: true }) }) routerAdd("GET", "/b/waitasync", async (e) = { await sleep.async(100); return e.json(200, { ok: true }) }) Each route got 50 concurrent clients for 10 seconds ( hey -c 50 -z 10s , after a 3-second warm-up), with --dev=false , on an Apple M1 Max (10 cores): A JSON reply 19,471 2.2 ms 9.4 ms 55,901 0.8 ms 3.3 ms A database query (10 rows) 18,116 1.9 ms 12.8 ms 40,447 0.8 ms 7.9 ms CPU-heavy JS (2,000-object JSON round trip) 84 591 ms 648 ms 409 91 ms 525 ms Waits 100 ms with sleep(100) 19 1.93 s 12.0 s 491 102 ms 113 ms Waits 100 ms with await sleep.async(100) 481 103 ms 110 ms – – – Idle, after start 46 MB 49 MB After all the routes above 313 MB 3.1 GB What it shows: goja does more requests a second. Its pool runs handlers on every core at once. QuickJS runs an app's JS on one thread, like Node.js: about 18,000 short requests a second for one app, on one core. QuickJS uses a tenth of the memory. goja's runtimes each hold a copy of every hook file, and it makes more of them as load grows. On a host running many apps, that's the difference that counts. Waiting costs nothing with .async . await sleep.async(100) kept pace with goja's pool. A plain sleep(100) didn't, so use .async for anything slow. CPU-heavy JS is slower. Move heavy work into Go, a cron job, or a background task.

title: QuickJS hooks: async, import and TypeScript
heading: Going back to goja
text: To run an app on PocketBase's own engine, set it in pocketone.yaml : app: jsvm: goja You can also pass --jsvm goja . The startup lines list what that turns off: pages, $mcp , $tokens , $bulkmail , JS contracts, shared globals and async handlers.

title: CLI reference
heading: pocketone deploy
text: Deploys pb\_hooks, pb\_migrations, pb\_pages, pb\_public and packages to a remote pocketone deploy [remote] Deploys the project's code set (pb\_\ folders except pb\_data and pb\_cache, package.json, bun.lock(b), patches/, and the production node\_modules tree) to a remote. Only changed files are uploaded and the remote swaps them in. Hooks, pages and public files take effect by themselves; migrations and packages apply when the app restarts: pass --restart, or run 'pocketone restart' later. A deploy stops when files changed on the remote since your last deploy, pull or dev (an edit through the file drive, a migration the dashboard wrote) and lists them; --force overwrites them. A project with no record of the remote yet (a fresh checkout, CI) deploys without that check. --dry-run bool – list what would be deployed, deploy nothing -e , --exclude stringSlice – exclude patterns (pb\_data and pb\_cache are always excluded) --force bool – deploy even when files changed on the remote since your last deploy, pull or dev, overwriting them -i , --include stringSlice – add include patterns (default set: pb\_\ ,pb\_\ /\ \ /\ ,package.json,bun.lockb,bun.lock,patches,patches/\ \ /\ ) --no-node-modules bool – don't ship node\_modules; leave the remote's alone --node-modules bool – ship the production node\_modules tree (default with a package.json) --out string – write the deploy set to a local folder instead of deploying --restart bool – restart the app after deploying when migrations or packages changed -v , --verbose bool – list every file From Deploy.

title: CLI reference
heading: pocketone desktop build
text: Build this folder's app as a native desktop app (this platform; --all for every platform) pocketone desktop build Compiles the PocketOne app in the current folder into a desktop app: pb\_hooks, pb\_migrations and pb\_public are embedded in the executable, which runs the app's server on a private 127.0.0.1 port and shows it in a native window. Each user's data lives in their own app-data folder, named by the app id. Without flags it builds for this machine. --all builds macOS (arm64, amd64), Windows (amd64, arm64) and Linux (amd64, arm64); --target picks some. The apps land in dist/, macOS's as an .app and a .dmg. With a sign section in pocketone.yaml it signs what it built afterwards, here on this machine: macOS with your Developer ID (and notarizes), Windows with your command, Linux with GPG. --no-sign skips it. It runs in Docker, in the build image matching this pocketone (Go and PocketOne's source, vendored, so it needs nothing else and works offline once the image is here). --local builds with your own Go and a PocketOne checkout. --all bool – build for every platform --image string – the build image (default pocketone-build:dev) --local bool – build with your own Go instead of the build image --no-sign bool – skip pocketone.yaml's desktop.sign section (builds stay signed ad hoc) --out string dist the folder the apps are written to -r , --remote string – the remote (a name or URL); default: the project's default remote --source string – a PocketOne checkout: --local builds against it; a development pocketone builds its image from it (default $P1\_SOURCE, else the checkout this folder is in) --target stringSlice – platforms to build, as os/arch (darwin/arm64,windows/amd64,...) text: Keeps the project's code and a remote in step both ways (and streams the remote's logs) pocketone dev [remote] Syncs pb\_hooks, pb\_migrations, pb\_pages, pb\_public and the other pb\_\ folders, package.json, bun.lock(b) and patches/ both ways: edits here are uploaded half a second after you save, and changes on the remote (such as migrations the dashboard writes) are downloaded within seconds. node\_modules is only uploaded, when package.json or the lockfile changes. pb\_data is never synced. text: Starts the web server (default to 127.0.0.1:8090 if no domain is specified) pocketone serve [domain(s)] --automigrate bool true enable/disable auto migrations --autotls bool – HTTPS certificates through CertMagic instead of the built-in autocert (with serve <domain> or --https ): other CAs, extra domains, wildcards through DNS-01 --autotlsCA string – certificate authority for --autotls : letsencrypt (default), letsencrypt-staging, zerossl, or an ACME directory URL --autotlsDNS string – DNS provider for DNS-01 challenges with --autotls (supported: cloudflare) --autotlsDNSTokenEnv string CF_API_TOKEN environment variable holding the DNS provider's API token for --autotlsDNS --autotlsDomains stringSlice – extra domains for --autotls , obtained at start (comma separated; wildcards like \ .example.com need --autotlsDNS ) --autotlsEmail string – ACME account email for --autotls (expiry notices from the CA) --dev bool – enable dev mode, aka. printing logs and sql statements to the console --dir string /pb_data the PocketBase data directory --encryptionEnv string – the env variable whose value of 32 characters will be used as encryption key for the app settings (default none) --hooksDir string – the directory with the JS app hooks --hooksPool int 15 only with --jsvm goja: the JS runtimes kept ready for hooks --hooksWatch bool true auto restart the app on pb\_hooks file change; it has no effect on Windows --http string – TCP address to listen for the HTTP server (if domain args are specified - default to 0.0.0.0:80, otherwise - default to 127.0.0.1:8090) --https string – TCP address to listen for the HTTPS server (if domain args are specified - default to 0.0.0.0:443, otherwise - default to empty string, aka. no TLS) The incoming HTTP traffic also will be auto redirected to the HTTPS version --indexFallback bool true fallback the request to index.html on missing static path, e.g. when pretty urls are used with SPA --jsvm string quickjs the JS engine: quickjs (PocketOne's) or goja (PocketBase's own, for pure PocketBase compatibility) --migrationsDir string – the directory with the user defined migrations --origins stringSlice [ ] CORS allowed domain origins list --pagesDir string – the directory with the PocketPages app (default pb\_pages next to pb\_data); title: MCP reference
text: A PocketOne app serves MCP at /mcp (MCP): PocketBase's whole API as pb_ tools, the tools your pb_hooks add, and one tool per operation of every contract the app provides, listed here for the standard set. Each contract tool calls the contract, so it passes the same token scope check and hooks as the REST API and the CLI (how). Uploads and downloads have no tool.

title: MCP reference
heading: agent.chat/v1
text: Contract page. Answered by Agent Chat in the standard set. agent_chat_new Starts a chat and returns it; its id is how the app finds it again. chat title (string), meta (json) agent_chat_send Asks the chat a question: the provider sends the system text, the chat's summary, its recent messages and the question (with Context after it) to agent/v1, saves both turns, and folds older messages into the summary when it's due. chat id (string), text (string), system (string), window (int), summarizeEvery (int), context (string), schema (json), maxTokens (int), temperature (json), wait (string) agent_chat_send_stream Is Send with the answer as it's written: agent/v1 chunks, the last one with done and the result. chat id (string), text (string), system (string), window (int), summarizeEvery (int), context (string), schema (json), maxTokens (int), temperature (json), wait (string) agent_chat_get Returns a chat. chat:read id (string) agent_chat_history Returns a chat's messages, oldest first: the last Limit before the message Before (all when 0 and ""). chat:read id (string), limit (int), before (string) agent_chat_update Sets a chat's title or meta (fields left out stay). chat id (string), title (json), meta (json) agent_chat_list Returns chats, most recently updated first; Meta keeps those whose meta has each of its top-level keys with that value. chat:read meta (json), limit (int), offset (int) agent_chat_forget Deletes a chat, its messages and the model's state for it. chat id (string) agent_chat_forget_where Deletes every chat whose meta matches (as in List), e.g. chat meta (json), limit (int), offset (int)

title: MCP reference
