title: Create your own extension
text: A PocketOne extension is Go code compiled into your build. There are two kinds, by where they run: App extensions add to an app: Go routes, PocketBase hooks, collections, admin dashboard screens, a JS API for pb_hooks , contracts other extensions use. They run on every app: a standalone app, or each instance of a multisite host. Almost every extension is one. Host extensions add to a multisite host, the process that serves many instances: request gates (firewall, rate limits), TLS, middleware around every instance, instance sources, background jobs. How a multisite host runs its instances (as isolates in its own process with pocker, in containers with docker, or both) is the host's runtime/v1 contract. App extensions don't depend on it.

title: Create your own extension
heading: App extensions: extkit
text: Write an extension once, against extkit (its own module, pocketone.dev/ext/extkit ; core has no part in it), and the same value runs on every app: type Extension struct{ cfg Config } func New(cfg Config) Extension { return &Extension{cfg: cfg} } func (p Extension) Name() string { return "hello" } // config key, _hello_ collections, pb_cache/hello, logs func (p Extension) Register(app core.App, cfg extkit.Config) error { c := p.cfg if err := cfg.Decode(&c); err != nil { // this app's settings over the defaults (json tags) return err } app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { / routes, UI extensions / return se.Next() }) return nil } // optional: a $hello global in the app's JS hooks func (p Extension) BindJS(app core.App, rt js.Runtime) { / rt.Set("$hello", ...) / } // optional: its TypeScript declarations, added to each app's types.d.ts func (p Extension) TypeScript() string { return declare var $hello: { greet(name: string): string }; } Every app has the standard set (tokens, mcp, pitr, deploy and the rest). Add yours to it: set.Add(myextension.New(...)) . On a standalone app, build the app with set.NewApp(...) , or build it yourself and call set.Register(app, jsvm.Config{...}) . The stock binary does the second: pocketbase.NewWithConfig , then set.Register ( examples/pocketone ). Without the set: extkit.MustRegister(app, extensions...) , and extkit.BindJS(app, vm, extensions...) in jsvm's OnInit . On a multisite host every instance gets the set, with that instance's extensions. settings over your constructor's defaults. enabled: false there means Register and BindJS are never called for that instance. What runs inside an instance depends on its runtime: pocker registers the set in each isolate; a docker instance runs the pocketone binary in its container, so it has the stock set (your own extras need your own image); an instance on a stock PocketBase image runs none, and gets only the contracts the host provides for it (Working together). Routes: an extension has none of its own. Its API is contracts, mounted for you under /api/_c/ / ; design the contract in ext/contracts first (Working together). Admin settings go through settings/v1 ( settingsv1.Add ). Only paths a standard fixes stay at the root ( /.well-known/ , /mcp ). The conformance test fails any other route unless conformance.Options.AllowRoutes lists it with a reason. Process-wide settings come from a pocketone.yaml section your extension owns ( extkit.NewSection ). State per app: keep it in app.Store() . Something shared across apps (a pool, a client) closes through extkit.Closer . Data that must survive a restart goes in your own collections (Your schema); files you can rebuild go in pb_cache (Disposable files). Never write into pb_data yourself, and never into the app's pb_migrations . Name the command with extkit.Command : when a message tells people what to run ("run 'pocketone login prod'"), build it from extkit.Command (default pocketone ), never a literal. A build shipped under another name (PocketHost's, say) sets it once in main , or with -ldflags "-X pocketone.dev/ext/extkit.Command=pockethost" . bulkmail is the reference implementation, and ext/standard/example a complete program.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Your schema: migrations and table names
text: An extension that stores records owns its collections and creates them with its own migrations, in Go, shipped in its module. Never copy its schema into an app's pb_migrations . func (p Extension) Migrations() []extkit.Migration { return []extkit.Migration{ {Name: "0001_chats", Up: createChats, Down: dropChats}, {Name: "0002_chats_title_index", Up: addTitleIndex, Down: dropTitleIndex}, } } func createChats(txApp core.App) error { c := core.NewBaseCollection("_hello_chats") c.Fields.Add(&core.TextField{Name: "title"}) return txApp.Save(c) } An extension with a Migrations() method is an extkit.Migrator . extkit applies its pending migrations on every app it runs on (each isolate has its own database): at bootstrap, right after PocketBase's own system migrations, so its collections exist for every command, before the app's pb_migrations run at serve, and an app migration may refer to them. Order: within an extension, by Name (zero-pad the numbers: 0001_chats ); across extensions, in the order they register, which puts a contract's provider before the extensions that require it. Each migration runs in a transaction , like PocketBase's: one that fails leaves nothing behind and stops the ones after it, and the app doesn't start. History is in _extension_migrations (extension, name, applied), apart from the app's _migrations , so the app's migrate down and migrate history-sync never touch your tables, and turning your extension off keeps its history. pocketone extensions migrations lists every extension's migrations; pocketone extensions migrate down [n] reverts the last n ( 0 : all). A migration with no Down can't be reverted. Never edit a migration that has shipped. Change the schema with a new one. To rename a collection, use extkit.RenameCollection(name, id, from, to) : it renames by id (keep the id, so code that finds it by id keeps working), works on system collections, and reverts. They build into the binary , so there are no files to copy into the app. A migration that needs a file (a SQL script, a JSON schema) embeds it with //go:embed and reads it in Up . Table names: every collection your extension creates is named _ _ : your extension's name with hyphens as underscores, then the table: _bulkmail_campaigns , _api_tokens_oauth_clients , _agent_chat_messages (for agent-chat). The leading underscore keeps them apart from the app's own collections, and the name says which extension owns a table. The conformance test fails any other name unless conformance.Options.AllowCollections lists it with a reason (a collection the app's users are meant to see and edit, say). When one extension's prefix starts with another's ( agent 's _agent_ and agent-chat 's _agent_chat_ ), the shorter one never names a table under the longer one's prefix; go run ./.github/extensions check refuses it. The conformance test checks a Migrator's migrations too: they apply at bootstrap, applying again does nothing, reverting all of them changes the schema, and applying them again brings back exactly what they made.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Disposable files: pb_cache
text: Files your extension can rebuild (a download, a computed index, a model's saved state) go in pb_cache/ / , next to pb_data . Get the folder from extkit, never build the path: dir, err := extkit.CacheDir(app, p.Name()) // this app's pb_cache/hello, created shared, err := extkit.HostCacheDir(app, p.Name()) // one folder for every app of the process (a shared store) Anything in it may be deleted at any time ( pocketone cache clear , an admin, a cleanup), and your extension carries on: it rebuilds, re-downloads or re-reads what it needs. If losing a file loses data, it doesn't belong here: put it in a collection. Never backed up, deployed or synced: it's outside pb_data , so backups skip it, and deploy and dev leave it out like pb_data . Apps add pb_cache/ to their .gitignore . Per app: each app has its own, and one instance never sees another's. On a multisite host an instance's pb_cache is outside its folder, in the host's pb_cache/instances/ / ( CacheDir returns it), so copies, archives and moves of the instance folder never carry it. HostCacheDir is for caches that serve every instance at once; it is the host's own pb_cache/ / (a single app is its own host). Never put one instance's data there. Keep it bounded. Give your cache a size budget (a setting with a sensible default) and evict past it; on a host, every instance's cache shares the host's disk. pocketone cache shows each folder and its size; say in your README what yours holds and whether it may grow large.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Working together: contracts
text: Start with How PocketOne fits together for the idea: every API an extension offers is a named, versioned contract, any extension can provide one, and everything else (the dashboard, the CLI, agents, pb_hooks , other extensions) calls the contract, never the extension. This section is how to do it in code. In short, when you design an extension: Find the contracts you need in the catalogue. Use them; don't reach into another extension. Decide what you offer. Anything a client calls is a contract. If one already promises it, provide that one (your extension then stands in for the current provider). If not, write the contract first, named for what it does, not for your extension. Declare it in Contracts() and provide it in Register . The startup lines, whoami and the catalogue show it from then on. Extensions never depend on each other by name. They depend on contracts : versioned Go interfaces in ext/contracts , such as deploy/v1 or mail.fallback/v1 . Every API an extension offers is a contract too, served at /api/_c/ / : extensions have no routes of their own. Every contract, standard or community, lives in ext/contracts/ /vN/ with a README like an extension's (owners and a one-line summary in its front matter; ## Use , ## Provide , ## Extensions , ## License ). Its Extensions section is generated from every extension's Contracts() : who provides it, requires it and works with it ( go run ./.github/extensions contracts ; CI fails when it's stale or when an extension names a contract that doesn't exist). Whoever first creates a contract owns it, so an extension author who adds one owns both. Design the contract first, then the extension that provides it. An extension declares what it implements, requires and works with: func (e Extension) Contracts() extkit.Contracts { return extkit.Contracts{ Implements: extkit.IDs("deploy/v1"), Defaults: extkit.IDs("deploy/v1"), // steps aside if another extension provides it WorksWith: extkit.IDs("api-tokens/v1"), // used when present } } func (e Extension) Register(app core.App, cfg extkit.Config) error { deployv1.Contract.ProvideDefault(app, myDeployer{}) return nil } At startup PocketOne resolves every contract and prints who provides it: standard: deploy/v1 ← fastdeploy (default deploy stepped aside) standard: bulkmail off: needs mail.fallback/v1, which nothing provides Look contracts up after registration (in hooks, at serve time): deployv1.Contract.Must(app) . A lookup inside Register panics. Defaults, conflicts, choices. A default steps aside for any other provider. Two other providers of a contract that allows one fail the start until pocketone.yaml picks one ( providers: { mail.fallback/v1: mailrelay } ). Wrappers decorate whatever provides a contract ( Contract.Wrap ), in registration order. Wire contracts have an HTTP API at /api/_c/ / , action hooks in Go ( deployv1.OnUpload ) and JS ( onDeployUpload ), an MCP tool per operation and a client. Every caller passes the same scope check and hooks. From pb_hooks: an app's JS declares and provides its contracts in onContracts , which runs once after pb_hooks load and before the seal (so before bootstrap): onContracts((e) = { e.provide("mail.fallback/v1", { send(m) { / ... / } }) // a contract open to JS e.require("restore/v1") // the start fails (dev mode: warns) when nothing provides it e.worksWith("api-tokens/v1") // shown in the startup lines e.next() }) The startup lines show it ( pb_hooks: provides mail.fallback/v1; requires restore/v1 ). Methods run on pooled runtimes like any hook handler, so they can't use the file's local variables. A Go extension that requires a contract only JS provides is resolved before the JS runs: name pb_hooks under providers: for it in pocketone.yaml . types.d.ts types both sides from the contract's Go interface: e.provide checks the object against the contract ( contracts.Providers ), and each action hook's e.input has its operation's input type. CLI: every operation of a wire contract is a pocketone remote ... command with no code ( remote restore to --at -2h ), flags from its input. Provide cli.commands/v1 to replace one with your own, or to add one ( remote rehash ). No imports between extensions. An extension imports extkit and contract packages, never another extension's module (tests and examples may). What it needs from another goes in the contract package: api-tokens/v1 has RegisterScope , FromRequest and WithScopes ; remote/v1 has its CLI client ( remoteclient ), which deploy's commands use.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Compiled in, not loaded at run time
text: Extensions are Go packages linked into the binary, the way Caddy modules work. Go's plugin package ( .so files) isn't used: it needs identical toolchain and dependency versions; it can't unload; it rules out static CGO_ENABLED=0 builds. A build is a small main.go : the standard set with your extensions added, as a standalone app or a multisite host.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Your module
text: PocketOne keeps PocketBase's module path, so upstream merges stay clean. Point it at PocketOne in your go.mod : require ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase v0.41.1 replace ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase = pocketone.dev Go only honors replace in the main module, so the final binary's go.mod needs this line, not only your extension's.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Admin screens: UIExtensions
text: The dashboard loads extensions before it starts its router: Each extension is a named file system served at /_/extensions/ / . Every extension's main.js is bundled into /_/extensions.js . Add yours in the same OnServe hook: //go:embed ui var uiFiles embed.FS ui, _ := fs.Sub(uiFiles, "ui") se.UIExtensions = append(se.UIExtensions, core.UIExtension{Name: "hello", FS: ui}) ui/main.js runs in the dashboard with its UI kit ( t. ) and globals ( app.routes , app.store , app.pb ): // a new page, with a link in the header app.routes.superuserOnly("#/hello", async () = { const res = await app.pb.send("/api/hello"); return t.div({ className: "page" }, t.div({ className: "page-content" }, t.h1({}, "Hello"), t.p({}, Instance ${res.instance} )), ); }); app.store.headerLinks.push({ href: "#/hello", icon: "ri-emotion-happy-line", label: "Hello" }); // add to an existing screen: screens marked with pbEvent fire mount: with their element document.addEventListener("mount:pageBackupsSettings", (e) = { e.detail.prepend(t.p({ className: "txt-hint" }, "Hello from an extension.")); }); More hooks: app.store.settingsNavGroups adds entries to the Settings sidebar. Search pbEvent: in ui/src for every screen you can add to (Backups exposes pageBackupsSettings , backupsList , backupsSettingsForm , backupCreateModal and backupRestoreModal ). No build step: plain JS works. Bundle with Vite if you prefer. Experimental upstream: this UI extension API is undocumented and can change between PocketBase releases ( ui/README.md ). Keep main.js small, and test it after each upstream update.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Host extensions
text: A multisite host is one process serving many instances. A host extension works on that process, for every instance. Like app extensions, host extensions work together through contracts, on the host's own scope: What runs the instances (one or several, in preference order) runtime/v1 pocker, docker Which instances exist (the instance record) instance.source/v1 instances.yaml (default), mothership Admit requests (firewall, rate limits) gate/v1 firewall TLS for the host's listener tls/v1 autotls Middleware around everything http.wrap/v1 servertiming A host extension is a multisite.Extension : Name() and RegisterHost(h) , which provides its contracts on h.Scope and provides nothing when it isn't configured (no section). Pass it in multisite.Options.Extensions (in preference order), or multisite.Link it from an init so linking its package is enough. The host seals its scope once, with providers: choices for host contracts, and logs who provides what: h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Choices: providers, Extensions: []multisite.Extension{ servertiming.New(), // http.wrap/v1, outermost autotls.New(), // tls/v1 from the autotls section &pocker.Provider{}, // runtime/v1 &docker.Provider{}, // runtime/v1 too, when there's a docker section }}) multisite: runtime/v1 ← pocker, docker multisite: tls/v1 ← autotls Background work goes on h.Background , and an extension with Close(ctx) error is closed once every app has stopped. Some contracts are provided by the host for its instances (host-provided contracts), because the instance can't answer them itself: docker runs stock PocketBase images, so the host answers remote/v1 for them. The host serves them in h.InstanceRoutes , which run after the peer check, the blocked answer and the gates (firewall, rate limits) and before the runtime, with the resolved instance in multisite.InstanceOf(r) : remotev1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(h.Scope, myRemote) h.InstanceRoutes = append(h.InstanceRoutes, func(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return remotev1.W.HostHandler(h.Scope, multisite.InstanceID, myAuth, next) }) runtime-only hooks are pocker's Starter , SetupApp , OnStart , OnEvent and Manager (POCKER.md). App extensions that only need settings shared by every instance (mailrelay, s3-fallback, pitr) read their own pocketone.yaml section on first use and stay app extensions: they work on any host and on a single app.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Rules on a multisite host
text: On a multisite host, instances can belong to people who don't trust each other, and your Go code runs with the host's full power, outside the JS sandbox: Act only for the app you were called for. Keep per-app state in app.Store() , and use extkit.AppID(app) for anything shared that must differ per instance (a bucket prefix, a rate-limit key); never build a path from request input. Instance data needs instance auth. Protect routes that read or change it with PocketBase's auth middlewares ( apis.RequireSuperuserAuth() , record auth). Exposing something to JS is a sandbox decision. Expose a function to an instance's JS only if it's safe for a hostile tenant to call. See How is this safe?. Outbound calls follow the egress policy. Go's default HTTP client already refuses private addresses. If your extension must reach a private service, give it its own http.Client and transport, and never let instance input pick the address.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Contributing an extension
text: Extensions are welcome, from us and from you. Open a pull request that adds ext/ / .

title: Create your own extension
heading: Change PocketBase's core as little as possible
text: PocketOne stays close to upstream so every PocketBase release merges cleanly. If your extension needs something the core doesn't offer yet: Add the smallest hook that makes it possible: an extension point or an override, not your extension's logic. A nil-checked function field, a list callers can append to, or an event, with upstream behavior unchanged when nothing is registered. Make it generic. Name it for what it allows ("storage backend for an app"), not for your extension. Assume someone else's extension will use it too, and that we'll offer it to upstream PocketBase. Mark every changed line in PocketBase's own files with // PocketOne: and a few words on why, so the next upstream merge knows what to keep. Keep it separate: the core change goes in its own commit, with a test, ahead of the extension. Prefer what exists: jsvm OnInit , OnServe , the record and request hooks, BaseAppConfig.DBConnect , UIExtensions . Many extensions need no core change at all.

title: Create your own extension
heading: What an extension folder contains
text: ext/ / go.mod module pocketone.dev/ext/ README.md the extension's docs, and its page on pocketone.dev (below) CHANGELOG.md its changes, newest first (see Changelogs) TODO.md optional: work that waits for something else to exist first (see Blocked work) .go the extension _test.go conformance_test.go the shared extension test (below) modes_test.go the feature on the real binary, in every mode it runs in (below) example/main.go a minimal program that builds cleanly and shows the feature ui/ optional: admin screens (embedded main.js) docs/ optional: end-user docs (tutorials, guides), as PocketPages pages (below) blog/ optional: posts for the pocketone.dev blog example/main.go is required. Keep it as small as possible: just enough to build a binary that shows the feature working, with no extra harness. go build ./example and go vet ./... must pass with no warnings. ext/standard/example and ext/sandbox/example are the size to aim for. Examples come with two logins: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com (verified, in users ), both with password password . Every example/main.go calls devusers.Register(app) right after the app is created (on a multisite host, devusers.Ensure(app) in the host's per-instance setup), from ext/devusers . A fresh data dir is then ready to log in to, with no installer page and no CLI step. Never register it in a production build. conformance_test.go is required. It runs the shared extension test from ext/extkit/conformance once: func TestConformance(t testing.T) { conformance.Run(t, func() extkit.Extension { return myextension.New(myextension.Config{}) }) } It checks that the extension registers, migrates, serves and shuts down on a fresh app with no goroutines left behind; that its only routes are contracts' ( /api/_c/ / ); that PocketBase's own collections are unchanged and every collection it adds is named _ or _ _… ; and that one extension value serves several apps at once (as on a multisite host) without registering on one app touching another's hooks. An extension that requires another ( Contracts().Requires ) lists it in conformance.Options{Deps: ...} . An extension that adds MCP tools ( ext/mcp ) also passes conformance.Options{Setup: ...} that registers MCP on the test apps; the test then checks each tool is named _ _ , is described, and has an object input schema ( pb_ is reserved). Run it with go test -race . It's the minimum every extension passes; your own tests cover the feature. modes_test.go tests the feature in every mode it runs in , on the real pocketone binary, with ext/extkit/modetest . Declare the instances the test needs, each configured in full (files, extension settings, secrets), and the harness lays them out once per mode: Single (each its own pocketone serve ), Host (one multisite host serving them all) and Fleet (several hosts that forward to each other). An app extension runs modetest.AllApp (Single and Host); a host extension picks Host and/or Fleet. func TestModes(t testing.T) { top := modetest.Topology{Instances: []modetest.Inst{{ID: "app", Extensions: map[string]any{"myextension": map[string]any{"limit": 5}}}}} modetest.Run(t, top, modetest.AllApp, func(t testing.T, w modetest.World) { s := w.Instance("app") s.MustJSON(http.MethodGet, "/api/_c/myextension/v1", s.Token(), nil, 200, nil) }) } The same test body runs in every mode: each instance has the URL http:// .localhost: in all of them, and World.Update , World.Add , World.Restart and Site.WaitRestarted do what each mode does (a host reloads its instances file; a single app restarts its process). Where a mode really behaves differently, check w.Mode and say why in a comment. -short skips mode tests. The README starts with front matter : who owns the extension and its version (see Ownership), and its entry in the catalogue on pocketone.dev: its title , its group (one of the ids in site/extensions.json : binary , many , services , saas , authors ) and a one-line summary . Nothing outside your folder lists your extension: the site finds it there. owners: ["@your-github-handle"] version: 0.1.0 title: "My Extension" group: services summary: "One line: what it does for someone running an app." The README has five required sections , in this order. It is also your extension's page on pocketone.dev. ## Install : how to get it (built into pocketone , or the lines to add to a Go build). ## Configure : the pocketone.yaml section, flags and settings screens. The site adds a table of your section's keys, generated from your extkit.NewSection defaults; describe each key with a doc:"…" struct tag. ## Use : day to day: the admin screens and what to click, the commands. ## Integrations : the extensions yours works with and how (multisite hosting goes here, not in the sections above), and how other extensions can build on yours (hooks, filesystem kinds, per-instance settings, Go and REST APIs). Hosting is a Multisite row: what an instance gets and its extensions. settings. Pocker and Docker are two runtime/v1 providers, not the host: name one only for what differs by runtime (isolates, which share the host's process; sleeping instances; and today per-instance settings and the host's extras, which only Pocker applies), never as the stand-in for "a multisite host". ## Example : the code that uses it. A sentence on what your example/main.go runs, then the whole file in a differ. Without an example (an extension built into pocketone ), say where to see it used. Write the first three for someone running one PocketOne app, not for a Go developer. Anything else (how it works, limits) goes in sections after these, and extra guides can sit next to the README as other .md files. Your README is your extension's reference; end-user docs go in docs/ . The README is your extension's page in the Extensions reference. Tutorials, guides and recipes, written for someone learning to use it, go in an optional docs/ folder of PocketPages pages beside it, which pocketone.dev serves under your extension's URL: docs/ctx/req.md is /docs/extensions/ /ctx/req . ext/pages/docs (PocketPages' docs) and ext/wasm/docs are the examples. docs/index.md is required: the docs' landing page, at /docs/extensions/ . Its front matter names the main nav section that links it, one of the # Section headings of the main docs nav ( Tutorials , Reference , ...), and the link's text is its title : title: WASM section: Reference description: Bring your own WASM ... Your README moves to /docs/extensions/ /extension , where the Extensions reference links it. docs/_private/toc.md is its nav: # Section headings and - Title links. Your docs pages show it as their sidebar, in place of the main docs nav, under a link back and a link to index.md . The README and the guides beside it aren't in it: they're in the Extensions reference. Pages are templates: EJS runs in .md files as in any PocketPages app, so a code sample writes , with the same front matter as the blog's own (title, description, date, author, tags) and links relative to the file. Examples are TypeScript page code and Go. Show server code as PocketPages page code in TypeScript ( +api.ts , +page.ts , modules in _private/ , and an .ets template when the example needs a page), and the same thing in Go when an app's Go code can do it. Not pb_hooks , and not JavaScript: pages give routes a file structure people can read, and TypeScript carries the types. In docs/ , put the versions of one example in consecutive fenced blocks ( ts , go , and a time. TS and ETS are the same choice, TypeScript, against Go: a group has one or the other, never both (a +page.ts next to the .ets template it feeds shows both blocks), and picking any tab switches every group on every page to that side and remembers it. On GitHub they're just consecutive blocks. In the README , keep samples inline: when you show the Go version too, put a line of text before it ("In Go:") so the two don't become tabs and the README reads as plain Markdown. Extensions here are MIT. The README ends with ## License and the single line MIT . An extension under another license lives in its author's own repository, not here. ext/pitr/README.md is the example to follow. Your pull request touches only your folder (and, for a new contract, its folder in ext/contracts ). Don't commit generated files: the site pages, nav, search index, llms.txt and contract indexes are rebuilt on main after your change merges ( .github/regenerate.sh ). To preview your page, run cd site/sync && go run . and don't commit what it writes outside your folder. CI enforces all of this. .github/workflows/extensions.yml fails when an extension README is missing its owners, version, title, group or summary, one of the five sections or its MIT ## License , or its Example doesn't match example/main.go , when it has no CHANGELOG.md , or when a module that implements extkit.Extension has no conformance test, then builds, vets and runs go test -race on every module the change affects: the modules it touches, every module that reaches one of them through a replace , or all of them for a core change. .github/workflows/site.yml checks that the site builds from your README. Run everything CI runs on your pull request, locally, from the repository root: go run ./.github/extensions test # what you changed since origin/main, committed or not go run ./.github/extensions test ext/ # or name the modules When it ends with ok , CI passes too. Tests that need an external tool (MinIO, Docker) skip themselves when it isn't installed, so they don't block CI. Dependencies stay in your module. Heavy libraries go in your extension's go.mod , never in core's. Standalone first. Where it makes sense, an extension works on one standalone app, and adds more on a multisite host. MIT , like PocketBase and the rest of this repo.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Changelogs
text: Each extension keeps its changelog in its own folder, ext/ /CHANGELOG.md , so a change to it touches nothing else. The root CHANGELOG.md is for the rest: core, the pocketone binary, the site. A user-visible change adds its line under ## Unreleased in the same commit, grouped under ### Upgrading (steps for anything breaking), ### Added , ### Changed or ### Fixed . One line per change, written for someone running an app, with the command, flag or config key. Don't raise version: yourself. Each PocketOne release raises the version of every extension with lines under its ## Unreleased : minor when it has ### Upgrading lines, otherwise patch. It renames that section to the new version and lists the extension in the release's notes, linked to its changes ( go run ./.github/extensions release vX.Y.Z ). # My Extension changelog ## Unreleased ### Added myext.retries in pocketone.yaml : how many times to retry a failed delivery (default 3).

title: Create your own extension
heading: Blocked work
text: An extension may keep a TODO.md in its folder: the work on it that waits for something else to exist first (a contract, another extension's change, a host feature). Each item says what it waits on, under a Waits on: line, and what to do once that lands; delete the item when it's done. Work that isn't blocked doesn't go here: do it, or leave it out. So a look across ext/ /TODO.md shows what each missing piece would unblock. The file isn't published: pocketone.dev skips it.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Ownership
text: Every extension and every contract has owners, listed in its README's front matter (GitHub handles); an extension also has a version there. Whoever submits an extension or first creates a contract owns it, so an author who adds a contract with their extension owns both. Who approves an outside pull request: PocketBase's own code, the standard extensions, the site, docs, examples, CI a maintainer A community extension one of its owners, or a maintainer A contract one of its owners, or a maintainer A new extension or a new contract a maintainer Owners are read from the base branch, never from the pull request, so a pull request can't make its author an owner and approve itself. Nothing merges unless the checks pass. An extension's version goes up when PocketOne releases with changes to it (Changelogs), and its Go module tag ( ext/ /vX.Y.Z ) follows that version. A planned extension (a README and no code yet) stays at 0.0.0 . go run ./.github/extensions approvers origin/main HEAD # who may approve each area a change touches

title: Create your own extension
heading: Planned extensions
text: Our own extensions live in this repo under ext/ , each as its own Go module ( pocketone.dev/ext/ ). See ext/README.md.
